title: correctness(ravel subclass): the build-mechanism heuristic is NOT sufficient - np.matrix OVERRIDES ravel, so the method and the function disagree and the cheap no-conversion fix would have introduced a new divergence
description: MEASURED, TanBridge, thinkstation1, numpy 2.4.3 live. Continues deadlock-audit-30d18's remaining 35. Details in the ledger row.
close_reason: SHIPPED ca584ab7 + 86fa51a0, ledger banked. ravel parity 8 -> 0; subclass audit 35 -> 34 of 198. TWO LESSONS: (1) the build-mechanism rule is NECESSARY BUT NOT SUFFICIENT - np.ravel(np.matrix(a)) is an ndarray (12,) while np.matrix(a).ravel() is a matrix (1,12), so the cheap no-conversion fix would have traded one divergence for another; the rule reasons about how OUR code builds the result, not about a subclass that REIMPLEMENTS the operation. Checked against numpy before writing it. (2) the first delegation gated on 'not an exact ndarray' and swept in lists/tuples, costing them 0.851x WIN -> 1.142x LOSS with DISJOINT CIs; its own A/B caught it before banking and 86fa51a0 narrowed the gate to ndarray_subclass_needs_numpy. PERF: the three array cells improve DECIDABLY 0.640x -> 0.517x (the exact-ndarray path no longer calls asarray on an array); from list ends at 0.902x WIN. All 24 nulls PASS. elf a8d128e11767... -> 6aa981502995... NEXT: np.matrix reimplements ravel/sum/mean/std/var/argmax/argmin/any/all/max/min/prod/ptp - for all of those the method and function can disagree, so the safe default is the FUNCTION gated on ndarray_subclass_needs_numpy.

title: [test][fnp-python] Add choose Python-container mode differential conformance
description: br ready is empty and all remaining in-progress beads are fresh claims. Add a no-mock fnp-python conformance test for numpy.choose non-ndarray public surfaces: Python list indices with list choices, tuple indices with tuple choices, nested-list choices, mode=wrap, mode=clip, and out-of-range raise error parity. Validate with local CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/data/projects/.rch-targets/franken_numpy-cod-b cargo check -p fnp-python --tests only.
close_reason: CLOSED by fixing FIVE real divergences in fnp.choose that this bead's own earlier test (conformance_compress_choose_diagonal.rs, commit e86f54c8 lineage) was RED on. Discovered by running the full fnp-python suite: 'cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_compress_choose_diagonal' = 25 passed / 1 FAILED. These were PRODUCT bugs, not test defects (unlike the qkt72 sibling). Captured actual=fnp expected=numpy: (1) SCALAR RETURN - np.choose(1,[10,20,30]) gave fnp ('ok','ndarray','int64',(),20) vs numpy ('ok','int64','int64',(),20); same dtype, same shape, different TYPE, visible to any caller reading type(). (2) BOOL INDICES - fnp raised TypeError 'choose(a): expected an integer index array, got dtype bool' where numpy accepts a bool array as a 0/1 selector and returns [1,9,1]; fnp was REJECTING input numpy accepts. (3) STRING CHOICES - fnp raised TypeError 'choose(choices)[0]: expected a bool/int/uint/float array, got dtype <U1' where numpy selects among them and returns dtype <U1. (4) INVALID MODE MESSAGE - fnp said \"choose: unsupported mode 'bad'; expected 'raise', 'wrap', or 'clip'\" vs numpy \"clipmode must be one of 'clip', 'raise', or 'wrap' (got 'bad')\". (5) OUT-OF-RANGE INDEX under mode=raise - fnp said 'choose: index 3 out of range for 2 choices' vs numpy's own text. Note 4 and 5 were MASKED behind 1-3 until those were fixed. FIX, following the pattern the file already documents for searchsorted's invalid side: broaden the up-front deferral so the native path claims only what it reproduces exactly (integer non-scalar index over b/i/u/f choices), and hand any case where the native reduction returns Err back to numpy so numpy raises its own error. That cannot mask a wrong ANSWER - it only runs when the native path produced no answer at all. Deferring a 0-d index costs nothing since the native path exists for bulk selection. ALSO UPDATED the stale unit test choose_rejects_unknown_mode, which pinned OUR house wording and so encoded the divergence; it is now choose_unknown_mode_raises_numpys_own_error and asserts exception TYPE and MESSAGE equality against whatever the installed numpy raises for the identical call - differential rather than a pinned literal, so it verifies parity without re-breaking on the next numpy rewording. EVIDENCE: shard 26 passed / 0 failed (was 25/1); 'cargo test -p fnp-python choose' = 5 + 5 passed / 0 failed; 'cargo clippy -p fnp-python --all-targets -- -D warnings' exit 0; rustfmt --check clean. NOT CLAIMING THE SUITE IS GREEN: running the full suite after this fix surfaced a further, UNRELATED pre-existing red (conformance_diagnostics divide_float_zero_warning - numpy emits RuntimeWarning on float divide-by-zero, fnp emits none) which was masked because cargo aborts at the first failing target. Filed separately.

title: [bench][fnp-python] AUDIT: every group timing a Rust replica against an ALLOCATING numpy call is measuring a 32MB buffer, not a kernel - bench_maximum_arms_vs_numpy is confirmed, hzl1w's REJECT rests on it
description:
CONFIRMED DEFECT, measured on thinkstation1 in ONE session on ONE ELF (ef5467cb2a43c00b, numpy 2.4.3), so host/worker/ISA variance are all excluded as explanations:

  bench_native_binary_family_vs_numpy  op=maximum n=2^22  numpy 6441077 ns  fnp 7075751 ns  ratio 0.907848  LOSS
  bench_maximum_arms_vs_numpy          op=maximum n=2^22  numpy 5046854 ns  fnp 2086990 ns  ratio 2.430654  WIN (parallel)
                                                          numpy 5046609 ns  fnp 3504376 ns  ratio 1.446484  WIN (serial)

2.7x disagreement in the ratio for the SAME op at the SAME n.

ROOT CAUSE - an allocation asymmetry between the two arms, NOT the operands. The operand sets do differ (the arms group injects NaN and signed-zero lanes) and that was my first hypothesis; it is wrong, because numpy is FASTER on the NaN operands (5.05 ms) than on the clean ones (6.44 ms). The 3.4x is on OUR side: 2.09 ms vs 7.08 ms for the same op at the same n.

bench_maximum_arms_vs_numpy does not measure the shipped route. Its candidates are the Rust replicas maximum_serial/maximum_parallel writing into Vec<f64> buffers allocated ONCE outside the timing loop. Its incumbent is np_maximum.call1(&args) - positional only, no out= - allocating a fresh 32 MB output every iteration and paying its first-touch page faults. The candidate is handed for free the most expensive thing the incumbent does. This is the same large-buffer allocation mechanism already proven in this ledger to dominate elementwise work (2.8x repo-wide, collapsing to 1.015x under MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_).

WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE: both groups carry CLEAN dual A/A nulls. A null proves each arm is internally reproducible; it can NEVER detect that the two arms are not comparable. Both nulls sit on unity while the effect between them measures a buffer rather than a kernel. This is a gap in what the null gate can see, and it is worth stating in the harness docs.

WHAT IT INVALIDATES: the 2026-08-16 REJECT of deadlock-audit-hzl1w declined delegating f64 maximum/minimum to numpy because 'the serial native arm BEATS NumPy 1.352401x'. That figure comes from this group and is the flattered comparison. The REJECT's evidence does not support its conclusion. Route-level numbers on this host: maximum 0.907848, minimum 0.913424 - we LOSE by ~1.10x, which is what hzl1w originally claimed about the parallel arm.

SCOPE OF THE AUDIT (this is why it is P0 and a bug, not a task): the defect is structural, not specific to maximum. Every group whose candidate is a Rust replica on a preallocated buffer, timed against an allocating numpy call, prices a 32 MB buffer. Enumerate them and classify each as (a) fix by giving the incumbent out=, (b) fix by making the candidate allocate per iteration, or (c) legitimately a kernel-only comparison whose row must SAY SO and must never be quoted as vs-incumbent.

REFERENCE FOR THE CORRECT SHAPE: bench_divide_accumulate_isolation_vs_numpy (landed b0107749) gives numpy a preallocated out= so neither side allocates, and says so in its row.

NEGATIVE CASE a naive fix would fail: 'fixing' this by giving the CANDIDATE a fresh allocation each iteration while leaving numpy allocating is also wrong unless both allocate the same way - numpy.empty and a Rust Vec do not have the same first-touch behaviour. The row must state which side allocates and prove it, not assume symmetry.

ACCEPTANCE: an enumerated list of affected groups with each classified, the maximum arms group corrected, and hzl1w re-decided on route-level numbers only. Bank the corrected maximum numbers either way.

comments.author: RedLynx
comments.text:
AUDIT COMPLETE + GROUP FIXED (e5d5a67d), both UNBUILT - build freeze at /data 42G, so rustfmt --check exit 0 is the only gate and the corrected numbers are NOT yet measured.

THE ENUMERATION NARROWS THIS BEAD'S PREMISE. The bead says the defect is structural, not specific to maximum, and asks for the affected groups to be enumerated. Scanned every bench file for the shape (preallocated candidate buffer + allocating numpy call). FOUR groups match the shape; exactly ONE is defective:

  bench_maximum_arms_vs_numpy                     DEFECTIVE, class (a). Fixed here.
  bench_divide_fast_accepts_without_fp_error      NOT AFFECTED. Its 'route' arm is OUR OWN fnp.divide - the code even asserts !divide.is(&numpy_divide) before quoting a share. No numpy incumbent exists, so the asymmetry cannot arise; it is a route-share self-comparison.
  bench_f64_exp_log_probe                         NOT AFFECTED.  is INSIDE run_candidate, so the candidate allocates AND zero-inits on every timed iteration - deliberately, per its own comment ('a deliberate vec![0.0; n] zero-init handicap the real zero-copy path would not pay'). Biased AGAINST us, so its numbers are floors.
  bench_realistic_clickstream_..._median_gate     NOT AFFECTED. The Vec::with_capacity is a results accumulator (scaling), not an output buffer; its call1 sites are RNG setup.

So: structural in principle, empirically confined to one group. Worth knowing before anyone sweeps the other three and 'fixes' code that is already correct or already conservative - two of them are biased against us, and 'fixing' those would inflate our own numbers.

THE FIX APPLIED, class (a): numpy now writes into a preallocated out= (numpy.empty_like), matching the replicas' preallocated Vecs, so NEITHER side allocates. Applied to both timed arms AND to the parity probe, so the probe validates the exact call shape that gets timed. I did NOT take the alternative the bead warns about - making the candidate allocate per iteration while numpy still allocates - because numpy.empty and a Rust Vec differ in first-touch behaviour and that just swaps one asymmetry for another.

BOTH ROWS NOW STATE WHICH SIDE ALLOCATES rather than assuming symmetry: allocation=neither_arm_allocates, incumbent_writes_into_preallocated_numpy_out=true, candidate_writes_into_preallocated_vec=true, and additionally arms_are_replicas_not_the_shipped_route=true so the row cannot be quoted as a route-level number even after the correction.

hzl1w RE-DECIDED, in the ledger rather than by flipping a bead: the REJECT's stated evidence is WITHDRAWN in an in-place correction appended to its ledger row. Its 1.352401x came from this flattered group, so neither replica figure may be read against NumPy. What survives is the INTERNAL serial-beats-parallel ordering, since both replicas were flattered identically. The route-level numbers (maximum 0.907848, minimum 0.913424) now point the other way - we lose ~1.10x, as hzl1w originally claimed - but that does not by itself license delegating, which needs both options measured against each other in one binary.

REMAINING FOR ACCEPTANCE, needs a build: re-run bench_maximum_arms_vs_numpy on the corrected group and bank the true numbers either way. Until then quote 0.907848 / 0.913424 (route level) and nothing from the arms group. AGENT_NAME=RedLynx.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
AUDIT ENUMERATED, BUILD-FREE - and the P0 scope claim in my own filing was WRONG. I wrote 'the defect is structural, not specific to maximum' without counting. Counted:

  total bench groups                                              273
  groups that time a numpy callable                               247
  groups whose CANDIDATE is a Rust replica handed a &mut buffer     2

  bench_maximum_arms_vs_numpy                 WAS the defect, FIXED in e5d5a67d (numpy.empty_like + out=, neither side allocates)
  bench_divide_accumulate_isolation_vs_numpy  correct by construction (b0107749), incumbent given a preallocated out= deliberately
  bench_f64_exp_log_probe                     flagged then CLEARED - its vec![0.0; n] zero-init is a DELIBERATE handicap, stated in-source, and it biases AGAINST us, so any win it reports is understated

The other 245 vs-numpy groups call the real fnp route, which allocates via numpy.empty exactly as numpy does. Both arms pay the buffer, so the asymmetry cannot arise there by construction. The mechanism reasoning in this bead was right and your fix was right - the SCOPE was asserted, not measured, and scope was what set the priority. One confirmed instance is a bug, not an epidemic.

METHOD LIMITS, stated because this audit is only as good as its detector: (1) my FIRST detector missed the known case entirely - because you had already fixed it - and a detector that cannot find the confirmed instance is worthless, so the pass was redone; (2) it matched bench_divide_fast_accepts_without_fp_error as a false positive from body-bleed, which is a scalar predicate helper and not a registered group (registration count 0); (3) it keys on the (&a, &b, &mut out) call shape, so it would MISS a replica whose loop is written inline in the closure. Treat 2-of-247 as a floor on the clean groups, not a proof of zero.

CHEAP STANDING CHECK for the future, instead of re-running this enumeration: require set_item("out" to be present in any group where a bench-local replica appears.

WHAT REMAINS AND IS BLOCKED: this bead's third acceptance item, re-deciding hzl1w on corrected numbers. The available ELF predates e5d5a67d, so the fixed maximum arms have never run. That needs a build and the freeze is on. I have left the warning on hzl1w not to quote 1.352401x in either direction until then. Banked in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
PLANTED NEGATIVE BUILT, RUN AND MEASURED (2026-08-24, AmberFalcon swarm). Commits f1cc5457 (group) and 4606a0a6 (corrected + measured), both pushed to main and master. Headline: THE HARNESS IS ALLOCATION-NEUTRAL, and the asymmetry is 1.65% in this regime - so the scope of this bead is narrower than "poisons every number in the repo".

GROUP: bench_allocation_symmetry_planted_negative, two rows in ONE invocation, no kernel anywhere in it.
  ROW 1 symmetry  - both arms allocate numpy.empty_like AND FILL IT. Identical work in both slots, so it MUST read ~1.0. Any decidable verdict here is a defect in the MEASUREMENT, not a finding.
  ROW 2 asymmetry - arm A allocates fresh + fills; arm B does the SAME fill into a buffer allocated once outside the loop. The fill cancels, so the ratio isolates allocation plus its first-touch faults.

EXACT COMMAND (env vars: CARGO_TARGET_DIR unset, RCH_CARGO_WRAPPER_BYPASS=1, FNP_BENCH_GROUPS=bench_allocation_symmetry_planted_negative):
  cargo test --release -p fnp-python --bench criterion_python_elementwise

RESULTS. host=thinkstation1 (Threadripper PRO 5975WX 32P/64L, governor=powersave), numpy 2.4.3, n=2^20, harness=common::run_dual_null_median_ci_contract, profile=stock release (ratios fair within the one binary; absolute ns are TRIAGE-GRADE, not release-perf). loadavg 18.24 -> 16.13 across the run, disclosed because this host is shared and I did NOT have exclusivity.

  row=symmetry   ratio 1.000485  ci95=[0.999062,1.001134]  arm_a 133138 ns  arm_b 133107 ns
                 incumbent_null 1.000470  candidate_null 1.000346
  row=asymmetry  ratio 1.016536  ci95=[1.014951,1.017857]  arm_a 133112 ns  arm_b 130613 ns
                 incumbent_null 0.999800  candidate_null 1.000390
                 MEDIAN_CI_GATE both_nulls=true, both nulls straddle unity

WHAT ROW 1 SETTLES - and it is the thing this bead actually needed. The contract is ALLOCATION-NEUTRAL: identical allocate-and-fill work in both slots reads 1.000485 with a CI half-width of about 0.001. So an asymmetric reading in any real group comes from THAT GROUP'S ARMS, not from arm position in the harness. The dual A/A nulls could never establish this - a null proves each arm is internally reproducible, never that two arms are comparable, which is precisely the blind spot this bead identified. Row 1 is the missing guard and it now runs on every invocation of the group.

WHAT ROW 2 SETTLES, AND ITS LIMIT. In THIS regime the allocation asymmetry is worth 1.65% (about 2499 ns on top of a 130.6 us fill), NOT a blanket poison. That number is REGIME-BOUND and must not be generalised. This ledger already records large-buffer mmap churn at 2.8x collapsing to 1.015x under MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_, and 26.1x at 8 MiB when the buffer is a RETAINED output - the floor is object LIFETIME, not byte count. In row 2 each fresh buffer is dropped at the end of its own iteration, so the allocator recycles the same mapping and the faults are cheap. 1.0165 landing on the documented "collapsed" 1.015 figure is consistent, not coincidence.

THE TRAP'S SIZE, MEASURED BY MY OWN FIRST MISTAKE. My first version allocated and touched ONE element rather than filling. numpy.empty is close to a bare mmap, so its pages are not resident until written - that form paid the allocation CALL and almost none of the first-touch faults, and arm B did essentially nothing (60 ns). It read ratio=26.466667 ci95=[26.3,26.47] DECIDABLE_WIN with both nulls on unity. That is a clean demonstration of how a preallocated arm can be handed a 26x head start while every null looks perfect - but it is NOT the defect's value, and I record it as the trap rather than as a result.

SO THE HONEST SCOPE OF THIS BEAD, stated against its own framing: the instrument is clean; the asymmetry is real but its cost is regime-dependent, governed chiefly by buffer lifetime; and the enumeration in this bead's own comments (2 of 247 vs-numpy groups carried the defective shape) stands. Groups must still be built allocation-symmetric - that is what e5d5a67d and my 909d91b5 did - but "every number in the repo is poisoned" is not supported by measurement.

SCOPE NOTE ON WHERE THE FIX CAN LIVE, since I was asked to put it in the contract: allocation symmetry CANNOT be enforced inside common::run_dual_null_median_ci_contract. That function takes two opaque FnMut() -> ContractObservation closures and sees only elapsed times - there is no buffer for it to preallocate and no way for it to know one exists. Symmetry is a property of how a GROUP builds its arms, which is why every fix so far lives in a group. Forcing preallocation harness-side would also BREAK the roughly 245 route-level groups that are correct precisely BECAUSE both arms allocate: fnp.divide against numpy.divide should both allocate, since that is what the real call does. This planted negative is the closest thing to a harness-level guard that is actually possible.

NOT DONE: the RETAINED-buffer regime (where the ledger's 26.1x lives) is not reproduced here and is the obvious next row if anyone wants the upper bound. Neither row is a perf claim - both arms are numpy allocation calls, there is no incumbent algorithm in the group, and it says so in its own output (is_instrument_row_not_a_perf_claim=true).

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
THE RETAINED ROW BOUNDS IT: 2.16x, and LIFETIME is what sets the size (2026-08-24, AmberFalcon swarm). Commit e920264d, pushed to main and master.

Row 2 drops each fresh buffer at the end of the iteration that made it, so the allocator hands the same mapping straight back and the first-touch faults are already paid. Row 3 holds a bounded ring of 16 live buffers, which the allocator cannot recycle, so every call takes fresh pages. Arm B is IDENTICAL in both rows, so the fill still cancels and the ratio is still allocation-plus-faults - only the allocator's freedom to reuse differs.

EXACT COMMAND (env: CARGO_TARGET_DIR unset, RCH_CARGO_WRAPPER_BYPASS=1, FNP_BENCH_GROUPS=bench_allocation_symmetry_planted_negative):
  cargo test --release -p fnp-python --bench criterion_python_elementwise

ALL THREE ROWS IN ONE INVOCATION. host=thinkstation1 (5975WX 32P/64L, governor=powersave), numpy 2.4.3, n=2^20, harness=common::run_dual_null_median_ci_contract, profile=stock release (ratios fair within the binary; absolute ns TRIAGE-GRADE). loadavg 28.75 -> 32.74 across the run - HIGH, disclosed, no host exclusivity.

  row=symmetry  ratio 0.998160 ci95=[0.995783,1.004465] arms 151026 / 152885 ns  nulls 1.000584 / 1.001096
  row=asymmetry ratio 1.081328 ci95=[1.051095,1.174524] arms 261165 / 220257 ns  nulls 1.000516 / 1.000210
  row=retained  ratio 2.164564 ci95=[1.949821,2.549030] arms 623151 / 287926 ns  nulls 0.982981 / 0.999925

THE RESULT: 1.08x when the output is DROPPED, 2.16x when it is RETAINED. A 2.0x amplification from LIFETIME alone - same n, same host, same invocation, same fill on both arms, only reuse differs. That is the mechanism this ledger already asserted (mmap churn 2.8x; 26.1x for a retained 8 MiB output) now isolated in a group that contains nothing else, and it is why "how big is the allocation asymmetry" has no single answer. It is also why the honest form of this bead's claim is regime-scoped rather than "poisons every number in the repo".

THE GUARD HOLDS UNDER LOAD: row 1 reads 0.998160 at loadavg 32, so the contract stays ALLOCATION-NEUTRAL even on a busy host. That is the property the whole group exists to establish, and it is the one thing the dual A/A nulls structurally could never supply.

COMPARISON WITH THE EARLIER, QUIETER RUN of rows 1-2 (loadavg 18): symmetry 1.000485, asymmetry 1.016536. Same direction, tighter CIs, and the asymmetry row moved 1.017 -> 1.081 with load. A further reason the MAGNITUDE is regime-bound and every row must name its regime; the guard row is stable across both.

TWO HONEST LIMITS ON ROW 3.
1. The retained arm keeps 16 x 8 MiB = 128 MiB live, so it enlarges the resident working set as well as forcing fresh pages. The row therefore bounds the cost of "the output outlives the call" - which IS the real route's situation, since numpy returns its output to the caller - but it does NOT separate fault cost from working-set cost.
2. Absolute ns drifted inside the run: arm B does identical work in rows 2 and 3 yet read 220257 and 287926 ns, 31% apart, at loadavg 30+. Only WITHIN-row ratios are fair here; do not compare ns across rows.

NO PERF CLAIM ANYWHERE IN THIS GROUP: every arm is a numpy allocation call, there is no incumbent algorithm, and each row says so in its own output (is_instrument_row_not_a_perf_claim=true).

STATE OF THE BEAD AS I LEAVE IT: the instrument is proven clean (row 1, twice, at two load levels); the defect's cost is measured and bounded at 1.08x-2.16x for n=2^20 depending on lifetime; the two groups that carried the defective shape are fixed (e5d5a67d, and 909d91b5 which also removed the provenance tax and the residency race); and the enumeration in this bead's own comments - 2 of 247 vs-numpy groups - stands.

title: [parity][fnp-ufunc] legmul/hermmul/hermemul/lagmul lose accuracy exponentially with degree - power-basis round-trip where numpy uses a direct recurrence
close_reason: FIXED for all four families. legmul landed in d522605c; hermmul, hermemul and lagmul convert in this commit. Each now runs numpy's own in-basis recurrence with a new *mulx helper, replacing the X2poly -> convolve -> poly2X round trip that lost accuracy exponentially with degree. numpy's operation ORDER is preserved throughout - it computes (c1 * k) / nd, so the Rust multiplies then divides rather than folding into one multiply by k/nd, which would land on different bits; lagmul's inner term divides the whole lagsub difference by nd, not either operand; and lagmulx's writes overlap (prd[i+1] assigned while prd[i] accumulates in the same iteration) so its statement order is load-bearing. ACCEPTANCE TEST MET: the randomised differential's mul bound is now 1e-14 for ALL FIVE families, down from the 1e-9 this bead was opened with, and it passes. Locked additionally by legmul_stays_accurate_at_high_degree_after_the_in_basis_rewrite, extended here from Legendre to all four, which pins degree 16 against the live numpy oracle at 1e-13 relative - the differential only runs lengths 1..=5 and structurally cannot see a degree-dependent defect, which is why a second test exists. EVIDENCE for the Legendre case, measured on IDENTICAL inputs via a temporary probe routing legmul back through the old path: old 7.12e-08 relative, new <1e-13, about six orders of magnitude; probe removed before commit. chebmul was correct throughout and is untouched - it already used the direct T_m*T_n identity, and the measurements on this bead show why it must never be 'simplified' to match its siblings (2.1e-07 at degree 16 via the round trip). VERIFIED: timeout cargo test -p fnp-ufunc --lib = 2281 passed / 0 failed; cargo test -p fnp-conformance --lib polynomial = 2 passed; cargo clippy -p fnp-ufunc --all-targets -- -D warnings = clean; cargo fmt --check exit 0 run UNPIPED.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FOUND by a seeded randomised differential added under hjg9x (CreamGlen, 2026-08-09), not by the goldens beside it - the goldens only cover shapes I thought of. First failing case, at ordinary small sizes:

  lagmul([0.0, 1.0, 2.5, -1.0, 7.0], [-3.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.5])[0]
    fnp   0.4999999999956799
    numpy 0.4999999999999985      relative 8.6e-12

MECHANISM: legmul, hermmul, hermemul and lagmul all compute X2poly(c1) -> convolve -> poly2X. That round trip through the power basis is ill-conditioned for these bases, and numpy instead multiplies with a direct recurrence in-basis. chebmul is NOT affected - it uses the T_m*T_n = (T_{m+n} + T_{|m-n|})/2 identity directly.

SEVERITY, measured by reproducing the round trip in numpy and comparing against numpy's own *mul, random normal coefficients, max relative error:
        n=3       n=5       n=8       n=12      n=16
  leg   5.0e-17   4.7e-16   1.9e-14   1.2e-11   1.2e-08
  lag   2.4e-16   9.9e-16   3.8e-14   1.7e-12   2.0e-10
  herm  3.9e-17   6.1e-16   3.0e-15   2.1e-12   1.9e-11
  herme 1.1e-16   5.8e-16   2.4e-15   7.3e-13   1.4e-11
  (cheb via the same round trip reaches 2.1e-07 at n=16, which is why it is worth keeping chebmul's direct identity and never 'simplifying' it to match its siblings.)

So by degree 16 a Legendre product has lost roughly eight significant digits relative to numpy. The failing case above shows the smooth-random table UNDERSTATES it: with cancellation (a result of 0.5 formed from operands of magnitude 7) degree 5 already reaches 8.6e-12.

FIX: implement each *mul with the in-basis recurrence numpy uses (multiply by x via the family's *mulx three-term recurrence, accumulating), rather than converting to the power basis and back. That also removes the X2poly/poly2X dependency from the multiply path entirely.

INTERIM: the randomised differential bounds mul at 1e-9 relative with a comment pointing here, so it still catches shape and logic errors - which is what it exists for - without asserting an accuracy property the current algorithm does not have. Tightening that bound to the add/sub standard (bit-exact) is the acceptance test for this bead.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
LEGENDRE FIXED (CreamGlen, 2026-08-09). legmul now runs numpy's in-basis recurrence, with a new legmulx helper implementing x*P_n = (n+1)/(2n+1)*P_{n+1} + n/(2n+1)*P_{n-1}. numpy's operation ORDER is preserved deliberately - it computes (c1 * k) / nd, so the Rust does the multiply and the divide separately rather than folding them into one multiply by k/nd, which would land on different bits.

MEASURED ON IDENTICAL INPUTS, degree 16, via a temporary probe that routed legmul back through the old power-basis round trip:
  old (leg2poly -> convolve -> poly2leg)   7.12e-08 relative
  new (in-basis recurrence)                < 1e-13  relative
about six orders of magnitude, on the same coefficients rather than inferred from a separate simulation. The probe was removed before commit.

LOCKED BY TWO TESTS: legmul_stays_accurate_at_high_degree_after_the_in_basis_rewrite pins degree 16 against the live numpy oracle at 1e-13 relative (the randomised differential only runs lengths 1..=5 and cannot see a degree-dependent defect), and the differential's leg bound is tightened from 1e-9 to 1e-14, i.e. this bead's acceptance test is now met for Legendre.

STILL OPEN for herm, herme and lag, which remain on the power-basis round trip and keep the 1e-9 bound. Their recurrences, from numpy:
  hermmul   c0 = hermsub(c[-i]*xs, c1*(2*(nd-1)));            c1 = hermadd(tmp, hermmulx(c1)*2);        return hermadd(c0, hermmulx(c1)*2)
  hermemul  c0 = hermesub(c[-i]*xs, c1*(nd-1));               c1 = hermeadd(tmp, hermemulx(c1));        return hermeadd(c0, hermemulx(c1))
  lagmul    c0 = lagsub(c[-i]*xs, (c1*(nd-1))/nd);            c1 = lagadd(tmp, lagsub((2*nd-1)*c1, lagmulx(c1))/nd); return lagadd(c0, lagsub(c1, lagmulx(c1)))
with mulx bodies: herm prd[1]=c[0]/2, prd[i+1]=c[i]/2, prd[i-1]+=c[i]*i; herme prd[1]=c[0], prd[i+1]=c[i], prd[i-1]+=c[i]*i; lag prd[0]=c[0], prd[1]=-c[0], prd[i+1]=-c[i]*(i+1), prd[i]+=c[i]*(2i+1), prd[i-1]-=c[i]*i. Each needs the same zero-series special case legmulx has. Converting each family and tightening its bound in the differential is that family's acceptance test.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FOLLOW-UP: *div CHECKED, HYPOTHESIS REFUTED (CreamGlen, 2026-08-09). Every *div in fnp-ufunc still does the same round trip this bead condemned for *mul - X2poly -> poly_div -> poly2X - while numpy's *div works in basis via repeated *mul/*sub. Same mechanism, adjacent function, so it was worth testing rather than assuming either way.

polynomial_div_randomised_differential_matches_numpy (25 random dividend/divisor pairs x 5 families, quotient AND remainder, lengths asserted exactly) passes with worst relative deviation 6.19e-15 against a 1e-11 bound. Pushed further in numpy directly, comparing its in-basis *div against a poly-round-trip *div at degrees 6/10/14/18: worst was 1.12e-13 (cheb, n=14) and it does NOT grow monotonically with degree - unlike *mul, which went 1.9e-14 -> 1.2e-11 -> 1.2e-08 over the same span.

WHY the same round trip is harmless here: the ill-conditioned step is poly2X at HIGH DEGREE. A product's degree is the SUM of its operands', so mul converted a doubled-degree polynomial back; a quotient and remainder are LOWER degree than the dividend, so div converts back something smaller and better conditioned. That distinction is worth recording because the naive reading - 'div uses the same round trip, so div is broken too' - is wrong, and someone will otherwise 'fix' four working functions.

No code changed. The differential is kept as a regression guard and prints its worst observed deviation under --nocapture, so drift shows up as a number rather than as a silent pass.

title: [perf][fnp-python] the wrapper residual is now 64% of the delegating route's excess (~1169.6 insns/call) and ~800 of it is diffuse - attack ENTRY COUNT, not any one symbol
description:
SUCCESSOR to deadlock-audit-ei9jz (closed) and deadlock-audit-rz8g0 (closed). Filed because the sniff lever shipped in d29b508e and NO open bead now carries the largest remaining component of this route.

WHERE THE ROUTE STANDS, all figures counted on one ELF unless noted:

  whole-route excess over NumPy, f64 multiply n=256      1830.5 insns/call  (pre-lever)
    dtype sniff          593.5 -> 204.8   SHIPPED d29b508e, 388.7 saved (21% of the excess)
    branch logic / binop match / out= predicate    67.4
    WRAPPER RESIDUAL                             ~1169.6  <- 64%, and now the only large item left

The wrapper residual is what our delegating call costs over NumPy's own with every native route
skipped, measured directly as one difference (probes-off arm minus numpy_plain), NOT derived. It is
corroborated: probe 660.9 + wrapper 1249.6 = 1910.5 against an independently measured whole of
1913.5 on the same ELF - a 0.16% closure.

WHAT IS INSIDE IT, from per-symbol attribution at fixed sampling period:
  ~251 insns/call   <fnp_python::PyUFunc>::__pymethod___call____   (4 recordings, 17% spread)
   ~73              pyo3 FunctionDescription::extract_arguments
   ~35              pyo3 extract_pyclass_ref::<PyUFunc>
   ~23              PyMember_GetOne
  ~800              DIFFUSE - no shared symbol clears twice the ~60 insns/call noise floor

WHY THE OBVIOUS LEVERS ARE ALREADY DEAD, so nobody re-proposes them:
 - The nine-parameter signature is NOT the cost: 7ocfa measured 3->9 parameters at 0.0 ns, and a
   later replica put the whole binding at ~73 insns/call.
 - Caching the bound callable instead of the module is FORBIDDEN: a live test pins that a
   post-warmup monkeypatch of numpy.multiply must still be honoured.
 - The ufunc-name getattr is already interned (interned_ufunc_name, all 8 sites).
 - Removing the delegation entirely is MEASURED as a 5.63x regression at n=256
   (deadlock-audit-sjpmo): a native route replaces NumPy's dispatch with our own zero-copy entry,
   which costs ~10,300 insns/call more at that size.
 - Extracting the delegation tail into a helper costs +57 to +76 insns/call (1c77e966, reverted in
   9450a237 for failing its neutrality gate) - so refactors here are not free either.

THE SHAPE OF WHAT REMAINS: ~800 of the ~1170 is diffuse across CPython machinery with no symbol
above the noise floor. That is the signature of ENTRY COUNT rather than any one expensive step -
our route makes roughly 7 CPython entries where the incumbent makes 1 (source-derived; the class is
supported by three measured results, the integer is not). So the tractable direction is removing an
ENTRY, not making one cheaper.

METHOD REQUIREMENTS, every one learned the hard way in ei9jz/rz8g0:
 - Run experiments in a GIT WORKTREE. rch syncs the WORKING DIRECTORY, so an experiment on the
   shared tree is compiled by every peer's remote build.
 - Do NOT gate an experiment on neutrality - that gates a MERGE. A flag-on/flag-off A/B on ONE ELF
   cancels any refactor cost in both arms.
 - Prefer ONE DIFFERENCE over an identity. A five-term replica identity gave 1189.4 where a direct
   A/B measured 660.9; one replica being 22% off inverted its conclusion.
 - Pin OPENBLAS/OMP/MKL_NUM_THREADS=1: perf stat counts the OpenBLAS spinners at 15.5x, and the
   inflation is time-proportional so it does NOT cancel in a matched difference.
 - Any comparison crossing a BUILD boundary inherits ~1.74% / ~32 insns/call. Never gate it with a
   within-ELF floor.
 - Quote the WORST cell and state the ceiling, not the headline.

Filed by SlateFinch on shipping the sniff lever; not started.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FIRST FINDING ON THIS BEAD, source-derived and quantified from profile data already in hand. No build.

THE ASYMMETRY: NumPy's ufunc implements the VECTORCALL protocol; our PyUFunc does not, so every call into us pays the tp_call bridge NumPy skips.

  from the high-density perf profile (the reliable one, fixed -c period):
    _PyObject_MakeTpCall    fnp  83.4   numpy   3.2   delta +80.2 insns/call
    PyTuple_New             fnp  89.3   numpy  37.5   delta +51.8
    combined                                          +132.0  = 11.3% of the wrapper residual

  per-symbol noise floor on that profile is ~60 insns/call, so:
    _PyObject_MakeTpCall's +80.2 is ABOVE the floor - a real signal
    PyTuple_New's +51.8 is BELOW it individually - suggestive, not established
  Quote the finding as "the tp_call bridge costs us on the order of 100 insns/call", with only the
  MakeTpCall half individually solid.

MECHANISM, confirmed by reading pyo3 0.28.3 rather than inferred:
 - pyo3's `call1` with a Rust tuple already uses `PyObject_Vectorcall` and materialises NO tuple
   (types/tuple.rs: PyObject_CallOneArg for arity 1, PyObject_Vectorcall with
   PY_VECTORCALL_ARGUMENTS_OFFSET otherwise). So the DELEGATION side is already optimal - that lever
   is dead, do not re-propose it.
 - The cost is on the ENTRY side. A vectorcall-capable caller invoking a type that lacks
   Py_TPFLAGS_HAVE_VECTORCALL falls back through _PyObject_MakeTpCall, which materialises an args
   tuple. NumPy's ufunc avoids this: `ufunc_generic_fastcall` is 4.35-5.91% of both profiles.
 - pyo3-ffi HAS the primitives (Py_TPFLAGS_HAVE_VECTORCALL at object.rs:555, `vectorcallfunc`,
   tp_vectorcall_offset). pyo3 ITSELF references vectorcall only in internal/get_slot.rs and wires
   NONE of it into #[pyclass]. There is no supported way to opt a pyclass into vectorcall in 0.28.3.

FEASIBILITY, assessed rather than assumed:
 - NOT policy-blocked: fnp-python already contains ~934 `unsafe` uses (it is the FFI binding layer),
   so the "#![forbid(unsafe_code)]" directive that governs the kernel crates does not bar this here.
 - BUT it means hand-setting a type flag and a vectorcall slot on a type object pyo3 constructs and
   owns, without pyo3 support, and keeping it correct across pyo3 upgrades. That is a high-risk
   change to the hottest entry point in the crate for ~11% of one component.
 - The honest ordering: this is the WRONG first lever for this bead. Cheaper entries exist in the
   remaining ~1037 insns/call, and this one carries upgrade-fragility that a measured 132 does not
   justify yet.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THAT: if the diffuse remainder turns out to be dominated by CPython call
machinery generally, then the tp_call bridge is not one lever among many but a symptom of the entry
shape, and worth the risk. Deciding that needs the remaining ~1037 attributed first, which is this
bead's actual job.

RECORDED SO IT IS NOT RE-DERIVED: the delegation-side tuple lever is dead (already vectorcall); the
entry-side bridge is real, ~100 insns/call, and blocked on pyo3 support rather than on our code.

AGENT_NAME=SlateFinch.

comments.text:
WRAPPER RESIDUAL ATTRIBUTED BY SYMBOL, and it is mostly UNATTRIBUTABLE - which is itself the answer this bead needs. No build: re-used the rz8g0 ELF, which still carries FNP_DISABLE_NATIVE_ROUTES, to profile the wrapper in isolation (probes-off arm vs numpy_plain) rather than through the whole-route profile that mixes in the decision section. Fixed sampling period -c 50000. Host: loadavg 8.61/8.70/9.70, CPU idle 83%, 3176 MHz, /data 102G.

NOISE FLOOR, from symbols inside NumPy's own call that BOTH arms must execute identically:
  DOUBLE_multiply_X86_V3        241.0 vs 203.6   +37.4
  ufunc_generic_fastcall        445.1 vs 384.8   +60.2
  fetestexcept                  162.5 vs 165.3    -2.8
  PyUFunc_DefaultLegacyInnerLoop 134.8 vs 98.2   +36.6
  PyArray_NewFromDescr_int      110.8 vs 99.0    +11.8
  -> per-symbol precision bound 60.2 insns/call

ONLY THREE SYMBOLS CLEAR IT:
  168.0  OURS  <fnp_python::PyUFunc>::__pymethod___call____
   72.9  OURS  pyo3 FunctionDescription::extract_arguments
   68.7  ld    __tls_get_addr
  309.7  TOTAL above floor  =  25% of the 1249.6 wrapper residual

RECONSTRUCTION ERROR 18.9% (net 1012.9 against a measured 1249.6), noticeably worse than the 8.5% the whole-route profile achieved. Treat the three figures as indicative magnitudes, not as certified numbers; what is solid is which symbols clear the floor and that 75% of the residual does not.

SO THE ANSWER TO THIS BEAD'S CENTRAL QUESTION IS CONFIRMED, NOT OVERTURNED: the wrapper residual is diffuse. Three quarters of it sits below a 60 insns/call per-symbol floor. It will not yield to a symbol-level lever, and anyone proposing one should be asked which symbol, with a number above 60.

NEW AND UNEXPECTED: __tls_get_addr at +68.7 insns/call. That is the dynamic linker's GENERAL-DYNAMIC TLS access path - the slowest of the four TLS models - and it is 2.24% of our arm against 1.73% of NumPy's. fnp-python is built `crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]` and NO tls-model is set anywhere in .cargo/config.toml or Cargo.toml, so it defaults to global-dynamic.

WHY THIS IS WORTH A LOOK BEFORE THE HARDER LEVERS: it is a BUILD FLAG, not a code change - `-C tls-model=local-dynamic` or `initial-exec` - so it is cheap to test and carries no correctness risk to the route. CAVEAT THAT MUST BE CHECKED FIRST: a Python extension module is dlopened, and `initial-exec` can fail to load in a dlopened object once the static TLS surplus is exhausted; `local-dynamic` is the safer candidate. Verify the module still imports before believing any number.

WHAT I AM NOT CLAIMING: that 68.7 is recoverable. It is the cost of ACCESSING TLS, and a cheaper model reduces the per-access cost rather than removing the accesses. A plausible outcome is a fraction of 68.7, i.e. under 5% of the wrapper residual - which is why it is recorded as the cheap next probe rather than as a lever with a number attached.

DEAD, from the previous comment, so it is not re-tried: the delegation-side tuple lever (pyo3 already vectorcalls) and, for now, the entry-side tp_call bridge (~100 insns/call, blocked on pyo3 pyclass vectorcall support).

AGENT_NAME=SlateFinch.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
PRE-REGISTERED before the TLS probe ELF finishes building.

THE CHANGE IS A BUILD FLAG, NOT A CODE CHANGE: `-Z tls-model=local-dynamic` added to RUSTFLAGS, everything else identical, built from unmodified main. No worktree needed and no source risk - which is why this is worth probing before the harder levers on this bead.

WHY: the wrapper attribution put `__tls_get_addr` at +68.7 insns/call, one of only three symbols clearing the 60.2 floor. That symbol IS the dynamic linker's general-dynamic TLS path, and fnp-python is a cdylib with no tls-model set anywhere, so it defaults to global-dynamic.

PREDICTIONS:
 1. PRIMARY, and deliberately modest: the route excess falls by SOMETHING between 0 and 68.7
    insns/call. A cheaper TLS model reduces the per-access COST; it does not remove the accesses.
    Anything at or above 68.7 would mean the accesses vanished entirely, which the model change
    does not do - if I see that, something else changed and the row is suspect.
 2. I expect the realistic outcome to be a FRACTION, plausibly 20-50 insns/call, i.e. under 5% of
    the wrapper residual. Recorded so a small number reads as SUCCESS-AS-EXPECTED rather than as
    disappointment, and so a large number reads as suspicious rather than as a win.
 3. NULL IS A PERFECTLY GOOD OUTCOME and closes the lead for one build. `local-dynamic` may not
    change the access sequence at all for a dlopened cdylib whose TLS is reached through the
    module's own dtv.

MUST-CHECK BEFORE ANY NUMBER IS BELIEVED, because this flag can break loading rather than slow it:
 - the bench ELF must RUN (it links the extension statically, so this is necessary but not
   sufficient)
 - the resulting libfnp_python.so must still IMPORT into CPython. A dlopened object using a static
   TLS model can fail at load once the surplus is exhausted. `initial-exec` is the dangerous one and
   I deliberately did NOT pick it; `local-dynamic` should be safe, but "should be" is why the import
   check is mandatory rather than optional.
 - parity must still hold on the counter probe's oracle assertion.

MEASUREMENT: same cell, same arms, cross-build comparison against the shipped 1478.0 insns/call. Per
the correction banked earlier today, the band for a cross-build comparison here must come from the
ARMS' drift (44-48 insns/call), not from the spread of the difference - so a change smaller than
~50 insns/call CANNOT be resolved by comparing against 1478.0. If the effect is in the 20-50 range I
predict, this comparison is UNDERPOWERED BY CONSTRUCTION and I will say so rather than quote a
number the method cannot support.

THAT IS THE TRAP IN THIS PROBE and it is registered before the build lands: the honest way to
measure a sub-50 insns/call effect here is a per-symbol look at __tls_get_addr in the two profiles,
not a route-level cross-build difference.

comments.text:
CONVERGENCE. Three independent lines now agree on the same account, and every lever this bead was filed to consider is either shipped, measured dead, or blocked outside our code. Recording where the floor is rather than opening a fourth probe.

THE ACCOUNT:
  wrapper residual                    1249.6 insns/call
    attributed above the 60.2 floor    309.7  (25%)  our __call__ 168.0, pyo3 extract 72.9, tls 68.7
    diffuse below the floor            939.9  (75%)
  our route makes ~7 CPython entries where the incumbent makes 1, so 6 EXTRA entries.
  939.9 / 6 = 157 insns per extra entry - an ordinary figure for a CPython call or attribute entry.
  The entry-count account is therefore QUANTITATIVELY CONSISTENT with the diffuse remainder, not
  merely compatible with it.

THREE LINES, ARRIVED AT SEPARATELY, SAYING THE SAME THING:
 1. Per-symbol attribution: 75% sits below the per-symbol floor. There is no hot symbol because
    there are many small entries, not one expensive step.
 2. The TLS probe: `__tls_get_addr` is real but our .so has ZERO direct call sites - the resolver
    calls are libpython's, touched more often because we make more entries. TLS cost is a SYMPTOM of
    entry count. Build-flag tuning cannot reach it.
 3. deadlock-audit-sjpmo: removing the delegation entirely made things 5.63x WORSE, because a native
    route substitutes a LARGER set of entries (buffer acquisition, validation, output construction)
    for a smaller one. Entry count governs this route at n=256 from the other direction too.

EVERY REMAINING ENTRY, AND WHY IT STAYS:
  1  tp_call into PyUFunc::__call__   ~100 insns/call of bridge vs NumPy's vectorcall. BLOCKED:
                                      pyo3 0.28.3 wires no vectorcall into #[pyclass]; pyo3-ffi has
                                      the primitives but pyo3 does not use them. Not our code.
  2  pyo3 argument extraction          72.9. Not reducible by signature shape - 7ocfa measured
                                      3->9 parameters at 0.0 ns and (*args, **kwargs) at parity.
  3  dtype getattr                     ALREADY MINIMISED - shipped d29b508e cut this from three
                                      entries to one, worth 352.5 insns/call.
  4  numpy.getattr(interned name)      REQUIRED. A live test pins that a post-warmup monkeypatch of
                                      numpy.multiply must still be honoured, which forbids caching
                                      the bound callable. Already interned.
  5  the delegation call itself        REQUIRED unless a native kernel beats NumPy's, which sjpmo
                                      measured as a 5.63x regression at this size.

SO THE DELEGATING f64 BINARY ROUTE IS AT ITS FLOOR given (a) pyo3's pyclass call protocol and
(b) the monkeypatch contract. The next real move is not a lever on this route; it is either pyo3
gaining pyclass vectorcall support, or a native kernel that wins at LARGE n where per-element work
amortises the entry cost - which is a different bead and a different size regime.

WHAT I AM NOT CLAIMING: that 157 insns per entry is measured. It is a quotient, offered as a
consistency check on an account built from measurements, and the ~7 entry count is source-derived.
The measured facts are the 1249.6, the 309.7 above the floor, the zero direct TLS call sites, and
sjpmo's 5.63x.

comments.text:
CORRECTION 2026-08-18 (SlateFinch, ledger row 453f75a1): this bead was closed saying the ~800-insn diffuse remainder was accounted for by ENTRY COUNT. That rested on a QUOTIENT - the remainder divided by an entry count - and I got its denominator wrong once (6 vs 3) before publishing 313 insns/entry.

The retry predicate registered here ("price ONE CPython entry directly rather than inferring one by division") is now DISCHARGED. Three arms, identical loops, 0/1/2 getattr("dtype") per iteration, 400k iterations, 3 reps, threading pinned, all arms selected_groups=1 / probe-printed / 0 panics:

    getattrs=0   863,752,136      spread 0.0167%
    getattrs=1   945,826,381      spread 0.0500%
    getattrs=2 1,025,118,306      spread 0.0391%

    (1-0) = 205.2 insns      (2-1) = 198.2 insns      3.4% apart
    -> the linear model HOLDS; MEASURED cost per CPython attribute entry = 201.7 insns

CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS BEAD'S CLAIM: 3 extra entries x 201.7 = 605.1 against a 939.9 diffuse remainder. Entry cost explains 64%, NOT the whole. ~335 insns/call remain UNEXPLAINED. My inferred 313/entry was 1.6x the measured value - it was tuned to the gap it had to close.

The bead stays CLOSED: its inventory of WHY each entry is still there does not depend on this arithmetic, and no lever here was justified by the 313. But anyone citing this bead must quote "64% explained, ~335 unexplained", not "explained".

NEXT PROBE ON THIS LINE: price the tp_call bridge the same DIRECT way - one arm calling through tp_call, one not - instead of carrying the ~100 insns/call figure over from a per-symbol profile. If it lands near 100 the account reaches ~75% and the rest is plausibly refcount traffic; if it does not, the remainder is something I have not identified.

title: [perf][fnp-linalg] cholesky/det 3-3.6x slower at moderate n (packed_gemm thin-band over-dispatch)

title: [test][infra] 4 fnp-python lib goldens fail ONLY on rch worker hz2 (numpy/libm host drift)
description:
Measured 2026-08-04 by SilentBadger while verifying deadlock-audit-i546h. 'cargo test -p fnp-python --lib' returns 551 passed / 4 FAILED when rch lands the job on worker hz2, and 555/0 on ovh-a, vmi1264463 and vmi1227854. The four are: every_probed_f64_transcendental_is_byte_exact_with_numpy, float_setops_delegate_to_numpy_golden_sha256, geomspace_matches_numpy_across_scalar_negative_complex_dtype_and_axis, ufunc_special_value_parity_matches_numpy.

NOT caused by the lstsq/TSQR change that surfaced it: the identical 4-test filter passes WITH that change on vmi1264463 (exit 0) and passes at clean baseline dd7735d9 on ovh-a (exit 0). Only the hz2 draw fails.

Two of the four prove the mechanism is environmental by construction. float_setops_delegate_to_numpy_golden_sha256 hashes the output of a path that DELEGATES to numpy, so its sha can only move when numpy moves: got 3f892e7ad93a703edd23fba5a0241af88204ef94a70a49a6b0e5e472fcee3981, golden ec0d35d19fdfc33accacb0c9a96cfd020ccd007989c970f193948b449a5a1e4b. geomspace differs from numpy in the LAST ULP at 4 of 50 elements (3.5564803062231287 vs ...283, 4.714866363457394 vs ...93, 9.54095476349994 vs ...938, 244.205309454865 vs 244.20530945486496) - the version-dependent-reduction-tree signature.

hz2 is the odd host: it runs python 3.14 while ovh-a and every contabo vmi* run 3.13, and the fleet carries at least four numpy builds (2.2.4 on ovh-a and vmi1149989, 2.3.5, 2.4.2 on trj, 2.4.6 on most vmi*). These goldens were captured against one of them and are being asserted against all.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND NOISE: rch picks the worker and cannot be pinned here (RCH_WORKER fails alias_wrong_target fleet-wide), so any agent's test run has a chance of drawing hz2 and reading 4 spurious failures - which is exactly the kind of red that gets 'fixed' by regenerating a golden (the golden-regeneration reflex). ACCEPTANCE: either (a) gate these 4 tests on the numpy version they were captured against and skip otherwise, printing the captured-vs-live versions so a skip is visible rather than silent, or (b) widen the assertions to the tolerance the version spread actually justifies, with the spread measured and quoted. Do NOT simply re-capture the goldens on whichever host runs next; record which numpy each golden pins.

THE REPO ALREADY KNOWS THIS MECHANISM, which is what makes it actionable rather than mysterious. crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs:7616-7638 documents it for exp/log/log2/log10 (bead deadlock-audit-gkznn): numpy ships AVX-512-SKX SIMD kernels for those f64 ops and dispatches them ONLY on avx512f hosts, where numpy's output is NOT byte-equal to the system libm (0.3-26.8% of elements, 1-2 ULP). The gate numpy_explog_matches_libm() is literally '!is_x86_feature_detected!(avx512f)', and that comment records the correct ISA-vs-version control: hz1 (numpy 2.3.5, avx512f=false) byte_equal 4/4, hz2 (numpy 2.3.5, avx512f=true) byte_equal false 4/4. Same numpy, opposite result. My finding is the same variable showing up again.

SO THE FOUR FAILURES ARE NOT NOISE - they are surfaces where fnp computes via scalar libm and is NOT behind that deferral, so on an AVX-512 host they diverge from numpy by ~1 ULP. Note geomspace_matches_numpy_across_scalar_negative_complex_dtype_and_axis is a LIVE differential (assert_array_matches_numpy(fnp_out, numpy_out), both computed on the same host in the same process) - not a golden pin - and it still failed, with 4 of 50 elements off in the last ULP. That is a real user-visible parity break for anyone on an AVX-512 machine, not a test artifact. float_setops_delegate_to_numpy_golden_sha256 is the only one of the four that is a stored golden.

THE REMEDY PATTERN ALSO ALREADY EXISTS, one line below the gate: the runtime per-op byte-equality probe at lib.rs:7645+, added 2026-08-04 precisely because 'that finding does not generalize op-by-op - NumPy's dispatch table is per-op, per-ISA AND per-version, and for tanh it is already different' (measured: np.tanh differs from libm tanh on up to 47.2% of elements by up to 3 ULP on an AVX2 host). Its comment says adding an op is one call site. So the fix direction is to route the still-uncovered ops through that probe and let them fail closed to the numpy passthrough, NOT to widen tolerances and NOT to re-capture the setops golden.

SUPERSEDES the acceptance criteria in this bead's description: (a) 'gate on the numpy version' is REFUTED as the wrong key, and (b) 'widen the assertions to the tolerance the version spread justifies' would encode a parity break as acceptable. title: [bug][test][fnp-python] cargo test -p fnp-python --lib aborts mid-suite: stack overflow in a non-test thread (RUST_MIN_STACK does not help)
description:
## Symptom

`cargo test -p fnp-python --lib` never reaches a `test result:` line. Partway through the
550-test suite the whole process dies:

    thread '<unknown>' (3725699) has overflowed its stack
    fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting
    error: test failed, to rerun pass `-p fnp-python --lib`
    ... (signal: 6, SIGABRT)

G2 has not caught it because G1 (clippy) has been red on main, so G2 never runs.

## Confirmed pre-existing, non-deterministic, and NOT owned by any one test

Found 2026-08-04 while regression-testing the tanh deferral
(deadlock-audit-d4mc2); it is not caused by that change.

- The abort point MOVES between runs: after 212 completed tests in one run, 194 in
  another, with different last-completed tests (`linspace_...` vs `ix_rejects_non_1d_inputs`).
- It still aborts with the tanh change's new test skipped
  (`--skip tanh_f64_is_byte_exact_with_numpy_on_every_input_route`), so no new test owns it.
- The tests nearest the abort pass fine in isolation:
  `cargo test -p fnp-python --lib -- logspace geomspace linspace` => 3 passed.
- `RUST_MIN_STACK=33554432` does NOT fix it. That is the tell: RUST_MIN_STACK only sizes
  libtest's own test threads. The overflowing thread is named `<unknown>`, i.e. NOT a
  libtest thread — almost certainly a Rayon worker, which takes rayon's default stack and
  ignores RUST_MIN_STACK entirely.

## Likely cause to check first

A deep recursion or large stack frame on a Rayon worker in a debug build (no inlining, no
tail-call folding, every frame full-size). Candidates: the recursive divide-and-conquer
kernels — the pairwise reduction tree, FFT/Bluestein, par_sort recursion, or a recursive
einsum/broadcast walk — reached from whichever test happens to be co-scheduled.

## Suggested approach

1. Reproduce under `--test-threads=1` to get a deterministic culprit, or run with
   `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` and a core dump to name the frame.
2. If it is a Rayon worker, set the pool's stack explicitly
   (`ThreadPoolBuilder::stack_size`) rather than raising RUST_MIN_STACK, and make the
   choice load-bearing with a comment.
3. Do NOT 'fix' it by splitting or skipping the suite: a suite that cannot run to
   completion is a real defect and G2 depends on it.
close_reason: Fixed non-progressing masked pairwise Rayon split: remote hz2 regression passed and full serial suite ran 551 tests without stack overflow; workspace check passed.

title: fmod: the pre-scan-removal design is a MEASURED REJECT (3 variants, all worse), and inf % finite still misses numpy's invalid event
description:
TWO findings on `fmod`: a PERFORMANCE DESIGN THAT IS A MEASURED REJECT, and a CORRECTNESS
divergence that is real and still open.

TanBridge, thinkstation1, numpy 2.4.3 live, 2026-08-26. Work reverted; tree is at abdf2d33.

## THE CELL

`fmod[f64_f64]` is the worst remaining sweep cell by absolute headroom: 64001 ns delta, 1.45x
(numpy 142610, fnp 206611). Decomposed serially, the loss is a constant ~350-400 ns entry plus
~0.67 ns/element (fnp 2.86 ns/elem against numpy 2.20 - a 30% kernel deficit):

```
       n   numpy_ns     fnp_ns   delta_ns   ratio   delta/elem
      16      403.8      763.7      359.9   1.89x     22.4964
    2048     4904.6     6462.6     1558.0   1.32x      0.7607
   16384    36030.1    46896.9    10866.8   1.30x      0.6633
```

fnp WINS at n=2^20 with threads (0.32-0.49x); the loss is the small-to-medium serial regime.

## THE HYPOTHESIS, AND WHY IT LOOKED RIGHT

`fn fmod` runs `b_raw.contains(&0.0)` - a full cold read pass over the DIVISOR - on every call,
purely to decide whether to defer so NumPy emits the `invalid` event. NumPy reads `a` and `b` once
each; that makes us read `b`, then `a` and `b` again: THREE array reads against two. On a
memory-bound op that predicts ~1.5x, and 1.30-1.67x was measured. A 512 KB scan at n=2^16 is ~26 us
against a ~27-95 us delta. Everything lined up.

## IT IS A MEASURED REJECT - THREE VARIANTS, ALL WORSE

Replaced the pre-scan with a post-hoc gate: compute natively (the native output is bit-identical to
NumPy for every case once the NaN sign is canonicalised, see below), then detect the event from the
OUTPUT - one pass over freshly-written memory instead of one cold pass over the divisor - and raise
a single witness. Same pass count, warmer data. Same-session A/B, interleaved, alternating builds:

```
  variant                                   1thr/2^12   1thr/2^16   64thr/2^20
  PRE-SCAN (current, committed)               1.31x       1.36x       0.35-0.49x
  v1 output gate via ReadOnlyCell closure     1.41x       1.40x       0.61x
  v2 gate through a raw &[f64] (vectorises)   1.40x       1.41x       0.60x
  v3 + operand buffers acquired behind gate   1.43x       1.39x       0.59x
```

Every variant is WORSE, and the n=2^12 point - the quietest, least noisy row - is a stable 7-9%
regression across all three rounds. v3 was aimed at the ~800 ns cost of three `PyBuffer::get`
acquisitions and did remove that, and it still lost.

**The hypothesis is refuted: the pre-scan is not the dominant cost.** Whatever the ~0.67 ns/element
deficit is, it is not the extra read pass. DO NOT RE-ATTEMPT A POST-HOC GATE. The remaining
candidate is fusing event detection into `zerocopy_f64_binary_flat_with_out` so detection rides the
loads the kernel already performs - a shared 200-line helper serving many binary ops, so it needs
its own bead and its own care.

## THE CORRECTNESS DIVERGENCE, STILL OPEN

The zero-divisor scan is INCOMPLETE. NumPy's invalid set for fmod is

    !a.is_nan() && !b.is_nan() && (a.is_infinite() || b == 0.0)

verified across inf%nan, nan%0.0, -inf%2, inf%0.0, nan%nan, inf%inf, 2%-0.0, -0.0%2. **`inf % 2.0`
raises invalid and has no zero divisor at all**, so the scan cannot see it: NumPy warns and fnp is
silent. Reproduced on the shipped build.

A SECOND divergence appears the moment the deferral is removed, and it is worth recording because
any future fix will meet it: Rust's `%` returns POSITIVE quiet NaN (0x7ff8000000000000) for a zero
divisor where NumPy returns NEGATIVE (0xfff8000000000000). 1%0, 1%-0, -1%0 and 0%0 all differ; the
infinite-dividend cases already agree at 0xfff8. NumPy writes 0xfff8 for EVERY invalid element, so
canonicalising the whole predicate is uniform. The reverted branch did this and passed an exhaustive
10x10 operand grid (100 cases) on values, BITS and events, plus errstate raise/ignore/warn - so the
correctness fix itself is known-good and only its cost is unacceptable.

## ACCEPTANCE

A fix that closes the `inf % finite` divergence WITHOUT the 7-9% regression - which almost certainly
means fusing detection into the shared binary kernel rather than adding a pass at either end. Verify
with the same exhaustive operand grid (values + uint64 bits + events x errstate modes) and a
same-session interleaved A/B against the current build.

title: perf: the RESIDUAL small-n entry tax - argsort +1901, sort +1614, concat +778, sqrt +752, isnan +687, sum +495 ns per call, all flat in n
description:

is LEFT, measured on the SHIPPED tree (commit 9a105810), worker hz4, numpy 2.5.2 live in the same
invocation, harness crates/fnp-python/examples/h2h_decompose.rs seed 555, all nulls clean:

  argsort n=64    +1901.0 ns   1.615x     sort n=64      +1614.4 ns   1.813x
  sort n=1024     +1671.4 ns   1.209x     concat n=64     +778.0 ns   1.611x
  concat n=16384   +796.8 ns   1.087x     sqrt n=64       +751.8 ns   1.916x
  isnan n=64       +687.1 ns   1.858x     sum n=64        +495.4 ns   1.161x
  divide n=64      +373.9 ns   1.434x     multiply n=64   +297.8 ns   1.337x

THE DIAGNOSTIC IS ALREADY DONE: the excess is FLAT IN n, which is what identifies the chain rather
than the kernel. add is +270 / +276 / +294 ns at n = 8 / 64 / 1024; sum is +465 / +495 / +488 /
+538 at n = 8 / 64 / 1024 / 16384; sort is +1614 at n=64 and +1671 at n=1024; concat is +778 at
n=64 and +797 at n=16384. So the ~275 ns floor on the binary ufunc route and the ~1600 ns floor on
the ordering routes are per-CALL costs, not per-element ones.

WHERE TO LOOK, in priority order:
  1. argsort (+1901) is now the worst and was barely touched - it classifies once already, so its
     cost is downstream of the classifier: twenty-two dtype gates and whatever the f64 flat gate
     does before it commits.
  2. sort (+1614) after the double-classification was removed. Same question.
  3. isnan (+687) and sum (+495) were NOT TOUCHED AT ALL by deadlock-audit-2nudi and are the
     cheapest unexplored routes. isnan's chain is zerocopy_f64_isnan -> PyBuffer -> np.empty(u8)
     -> a view to bool; sum's has not been read.

     this board - it is paid by every small elementwise call - but PyUFunc::__call__ has already
     been through two rounds of this, so expect it to be hard.

METHOD IS FIXED: h2h_decompose.rs, same seed, same worker, and CARRY THE CONTROLS. The cross-run
comparison in deadlock-audit-2nudi was licensed by numpy's own arm being stable to +/-1.5% and by
six untouched routes moving less than 40 ns; any claim here needs the same two anchors or it is
not a measurement.

ACCEPTANCE: either a route's excess drops by more than the +/-40 ns control floor with tests green,
or an honest null recorded per route attacked.
notes:
ROUND 3 SHIPPED (commit 21a849ae): np.concatenate had a CROSSOVER and nothing marked it.

This is the largest single lever of the lane. Worker hz4 throughout, numpy 2.5.2 live in the same
invocation, harness crates/fnp-python/examples/h2h_concat_floor.rs, ELEVEN dtypes x up to seven
sizes x two seeds, interleaved ABBAABBA with dual A/A nulls and the incumbent-spread criterion.

THE FINDING. Every native concatenate route engaged at EVERY size. At n=64 per input, BEFORE:
  f64 1.63x (+803 ns)   f32 4.65x (+4618)   i64 4.68x (+4671)   c128 7.69x (+9255)
  c64 4.62x (+4705)     f16 4.68x (+4675)   i32 4.69x (+4722)   i16 4.71x (+4641)
  i8  4.70x (+4623)     u8  4.72x (+4620)   bool 4.72x (+4638)
TEN OF ELEVEN DTYPES LOSE 4.6-7.7x, AND THEY ALL LOSE BY THE SAME ~4650 ns. That equality is the
whole diagnosis: it is the try_zerocopy_bytes_concatenate ENTRY, not any dtype's kernel. c128 is
worse still (+9255) because at itemsize 16 the byte mover refuses it too and it lands in the cold
extract/rebuild. f64 alone was cheap (+803) because it has its own dedicated helper.

THE CROSSOVER IS IN OUTPUT BYTES, NOT ELEMENTS, and that is the transferable part. Across
itemsizes 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 the sign flips at the SAME 8 MiB of output every time: f64/f32/i64
lose at 4 MiB and win at 8; i32/i8/u8/bool lose at 2 MiB and win at 8; f16/i16/c64 lose at 4 MiB
and win at 16. A gate in ELEMENTS would have needed a different constant per itemsize. This is
regime-gating by what the loss actually varies with.

complex128 IS BARRED OUTRIGHT: 1.202x at 2 MiB, 1.107x at 4, 1.101x at 8, 1.032x at 16, 1.017x at
32 - six sizes, two seeds, NOT ONE A WIN. A floor alone would have left it engaged and losing.

AFTER, same worker, same seed, per-call excess at n=64:
  f64 +803 -> +815 (RESTORED)   f32 -3161   i64 -3176   c128 -7973   c64 -3195   f16 -3242
  i32 -3294   i16 -3192   i8 -3189   u8 -3183   bool -3193
and at n=2^16: c128 +12117 -> +2082, c64 +11634 -> +2167, i64 +8390 -> +2330, f32 +6278 -> +2046.
WINS ABOVE THE FLOOR ALL PRESERVED OR BETTER, which is the check that matters for a gate: f64 2^20
0.276x -> 0.265x, i64 2^20 0.347x -> 0.294x, c64 2^20 0.316x -> 0.240x, i16 2^22 0.711x -> 0.344x,
bool 2^22 0.806x -> 0.410x, i8 2^22 0.786x -> 0.591x.
Tests: conformance_concat_append 33/33, conformance_block_concat 15/15, conformance_stack 26/27
(the failure is the pre-existing np.row_stack one, deadlock-audit-nq438).

*** THE GATE'S PLACEMENT WAS ITSELF A MEASURED DECISION, AND THE FIRST PLACEMENT WAS WRONG. ***
Put ABOVE both helpers with a blanket floor, it made small f64 concatenates 291 ns SLOWER
(1.632x -> 1.862x, +803 -> +1094). The reason is worth carrying: DELEGATING IS NOT FREE. Our
delegate still pays this function's own argument handling and then NumPy's call on top, so for a
route that is already cheap the floor is a regression. Moving the gate BELOW the f64 helper
restored f64 to +815 while keeping every other dtype's win. Caught because the after-measurement
was run on the SAME worker as the before - a different worker would have hidden it.

REFINEMENT TRIED AND REJECTED, recorded so it is not re-attempted blind: hoisting the gate back
above the f64 helper but EXEMPTING f64 from the floor, so small non-f64 operands would also skip
the f64 helper's decline. It compiles, tests pass (33/33, 15/15), and it is a REDISTRIBUTION, not
a win - it buys perhaps 400 ns on non-f64 small operands and costs f64 the four getattrs of the
profitability walk it currently does not pay. Three attempts to measure it landed on hetzner2,
hetzner2 and vmi1227854 rather than hz4, and this campaign does not license a cross-worker
comparison. REVERTED rather than shipped unmeasured. RETRY PREDICATE: only re-attempt with a

numpy call, i.e. fnp.concatenate's own entry (pyo3 argument handling, the kwargs walk, the axis
parse, the profitability walk, then the fallback's PyDict and call). And untouched entirely:

title: probe hygiene: a RAW-BYTE parity probe must special-case longdouble - x86 float128 is 80-bit in a 16-byte slot with 6 UNINITIALISED pad bytes
description:
CLOSED, BlackThrush, 2026-09-01, commit 2f29abe0. The rule is stated AND executable.

STATING IT WAS NOT ENOUGH. Forty-odd conformance suites hand-roll
`result.tobytes() == expected.tobytes()` inside their Python snippets, so a comment in one
helper would not have reached the place the comparison is actually written.
`support::fnp_script` now defines `parity_equal` in EVERY generated script:

    RAW BYTES, because a value comparison cannot see a NaN's SIGN BIT or payload - EXCEPT
      * longdouble / clongdouble (char 'g'/'G'): x86 stores an 80-bit value in a 16-byte slot
        and the other 6 bytes are UNINITIALISED, differing between two independently allocated
        results. That is this bead's finding: 34 phantom divergences from padding alone.
      * object / any `hasobject` dtype: the bytes are POINTERS; two correct results hold
        different ones.
    Both fall back to a VALUE comparison.

EXERCISED before shipping, against numpy 2.4.3, exactly as the generated script defines it:

    f64 equal                      True     NaN sign differs               False
    -0.0 vs 0.0                    False    longdouble independent allocs  True
    object arrays                  True     dtype differs                  False

The two rows in the middle column are precisely what `np.array_equal(equal_nan=True)` gets
WRONG, which is the whole reason the byte rule exists.

A SECOND FINDING WHILE PLACING IT: `tests/common/mod.rs`, the conformance matrix's shared
comparator, is VALUE equality (repr plus `array_equal(equal_nan=True)`). It is therefore blind
to the NaN sign bit AND to `-0.0` vs `0.0` for every case that runs through the matrix. That
is not a defect to fix blindly - the matrix's Close mode wants tolerance - but it was
undocumented, and the note now says so, along with the two exceptions any future upgrade to
bytes must carry.

VERIFIED on hz4 (rch --job): conformance_sqrt, around, arithmetic still green with the new
preamble (51, 17, 15 passed, 0 failed). The suites still using their own `tobytes()` inherit
`parity_equal` as they are converted by
[[deadlock-audit-propagate-extension-resolver-to-135-suites-9l3c0]].
close_reason: Shipped as an executable predicate (parity_equal in every generated script) with both dtype exceptions, exercised against 2.4.3; also documented that the conformance matrix's own comparator is value-level and blind to the NaN sign bit

title: [bug][ledger] masked_sum WIN row uses non-canonical result class 'structural-gap' and its incumbent-arm tokens are split across lines, so no valid class passes the gate
description:
## Symptom

`cargo test -p fnp-conformance --test ledger_hygiene` fails
`new_keep_rows_declare_one_campaign_result_class` on docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md:64:

    ## 2026-08-02 - WIN (LANDED): fused `a[mask].sum()` in one parallel pass,
       no gathered temporary - 17.9x/20.9x REPLICATED
    **Campaign result class:** structural-gap

`structural-gap` is not one of the two canonical values. The gate accepts only
`maintenance-self-speedup` and `incumbent-win`.

This is the SECOND of two independent causes of the ledger_hygiene red; the first
(the `is_keep` classifier misreading 'no production ship') is
deadlock-audit-p126d and is fixed separately.

## Why it cannot simply be relabelled 'incumbent-win' (tried, measured, reverted)

The row IS an incumbent win by content — live NumPy 2.4.3 arm, 17.911x / 20.925x
replicated, A/A nulls disjoint from the effect, 22.25x-vs-1.00x cpu/wall engagement
proof. But changing the marker to `incumbent-win` just moves the failure to
`incumbent_win_rows_carry_the_complete_same_invocation_contract`, because
`has_incumbent_win_contract` reads its tokens from the MARKER'S OWN LINE
(`marker_entry_value`), and this row spreads them across lines:

    **Legacy incumbent arm (same invocation):** name=NumPy version=2.4.3 spelling=`a[mask].sum()`
    measured_ratio=20.925x                      <- next line, so measured_ratio= is NOT seen

    **Incumbent isolation proof:** candidate=fnp.masked_sum incumbent=`a[mask].sum()`
    shared_timed_component=none                 <- next line, so isolation is NOT seen

Missing on the incumbent-arm line: `artifact_sha256=` (NumPy's, and it must differ
from the executing ELF sha), `invocation_id=`, `measured_ratio=`.
Also, `incumbent=` in the isolation proof must name a `numpy.*` SYMBOL; the row
gives the SPELLING `a[mask].sum()`, which the gate rejects by design.

## What is needed

Whoever holds that run's provenance (bead deadlock-audit-v94ol, ELF sha256
2716f8d4..., host Threadripper PRO 5975WX 32P/64L, NumPy 2.4.3) should:

1. Put `name=`, `version=`, `artifact_sha256=`, `invocation_id=` and
   `measured_ratio=` on the single **Legacy incumbent arm** line.
2. Put `candidate=`, `incumbent=<a numpy.* symbol>` and
   `shared_timed_component=` on the single **Incumbent isolation proof** line.
3. Then set `**Campaign result class:** incumbent-win`.

Do NOT resolve this by adding `structural-gap` to the accepted class list. The
two-class taxonomy is the thing that stops a self-speedup being quoted as a
competitive claim; 'structural gap' describes WHY this win exists (the row's own
next section is titled 'WHY THIS IS A GAP AND NOT A SHARED COST'), not what class
of campaign result it is. Widening the enum to make a red go away is a loosening.

Note the direction: `incumbent-win` is the STRICTER classification — it is the one
that triggers the full same-invocation contract, which `structural-gap` bypassed
entirely. So this row has never been checked against that contract.

title: perf(rayon): 95 sites spawn num_threads tasks regardless of n, plus a second shape the grep misses - 2 of 2 measured were badly mistuned, the other 94 are UNMEASURED
description:
A VEIN, NOT A CLAIM. Two members measured, both badly mistuned; the other 94 are unmeasured.

TanBridge, thinkstation1, 2026-08-26. Opened by `deadlock-audit-w9po3` and `deadlock-audit-wnpqg`.

## THE PATTERN

    grep -c 'div_ceil(rayon::current_num_threads())' crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs
    95

Every one of those computes a chunk as `n / num_threads`, i.e. spawns **exactly `num_threads` tasks
regardless of n**. On this 64-thread box that is 64 tasks however small the work is. rayon's pool
must WAKE FROM SLEEP for each task on every call whenever the op is interleaved with other work -
which is what real callers and the bench contract do (ledger amendment `062e58d8`).

**THERE IS A SECOND SHAPE THIS GREP DOES NOT FIND.** `vander` used
`par_chunks_mut(cols).zip(data.par_iter())`: one task per ROW, i.e. `rows` tasks, independent of the
pool entirely. Any `par_chunks*` whose chunk width is a natural unit of the data (a row, a lane, a
field) rather than a measured quantum has the same disease. Grep for `par_chunks_mut(` and
`par_chunks(` too, and read what the width is.

## THE TWO MEASURED MEMBERS

```
  deadlock-audit-w9po3  transcendental_map_f64   floor 8192 elems/task
        default-thread log contract  0.711/0.743 REGRESSION -> 1.051/1.065 parity-to-win
        family-wide sweep effect: total suite headroom 2443 us -> 886 us

  deadlock-audit-wnpqg  try_zerocopy_f64_vander  floor 65536 elems/task
        contract 1.86x LOSS -> DECIDABLE_WIN 4.605964 / 4.648663
        fnp 380401 -> 43222 ns
```

Two for two. That is suggestive, not conclusive - and it is exactly the kind of pattern that invites
a blind sweep, which is why this bead exists instead of one.

## WHY THIS MUST NOT BE SWEPT BLIND

1. **THE FLOOR IS PER-KERNEL AND CANNOT BE COPIED.** 8192 for a libm call, 65536 for a
   multiply-and-store - an 8x difference driven by per-element cost. A single repo-wide constant
   would mistune most sites in the other direction.
2. **A TIGHT-LOOP PROBE POINTS AT THE WRONG OPTIMUM.** `vander`'s old code reads 0.39x in a tight
   loop and 4.20x interleaved at the same size. Any measurement backing a change here must
   interleave.
3. **SOME SITES MAY ALREADY BE FINE.** A site whose n is always large has enough work per task
   regardless. Changing it spends risk for nothing.
4. **AGENTS.md forbids script-driven edits** to this repo, and 95 hand edits without per-site
   measurement is exactly the "many instances" case it warns about.

## HOW TO WORK IT

Per site, in this order: (a) find a real cell that reaches it, from the loss sweep ranked by
ABSOLUTE headroom; (b) confirm the site is on that cell's hot path; (c) same-session A/B of two
builds differing only in the constant, INTERLEAVED, across thread counts and sizes; (d) contract at
the DEFAULT thread count. Bank per site. Do not batch a constant across sites that were not each
measured.

A shared helper (`fn parallel_chunk(n: usize, min_elems: usize) -> usize`) would make each site a
one-line change and make the floor explicit at every call site rather than implicit in a division.
That refactor is worth doing FIRST, with the existing two floors preserved exactly, so later sites
are cheap and uniform - but it must land as a no-op change with the two measured cells re-contracted
to prove it.

## ACCEPTANCE

Per-site contracts as above. This bead closes when either every site is measured or the remainder is
argued to be unreachable/irrelevant with the sweep ranking as evidence.

title: correctness(convolve/correlate): the gather/FFT paths are NOT bit-exact against numpy 2.4.3 despite three source comments claiming they are - 45 cells diverge, max|delta| 2.2e-16 to 1.1e-12
description:
FOUND BY TanBridge 2026-08-26 while guarding deadlock-audit-6kn1k; NOT introduced by it (exact multiset diff of the divergence sets before and after: 0 introduced, 0 fixed).

## THE CLAIM

`try_zerocopy_conv_corr_f64`'s header comment says the gather is 'per-output sum in numpy's tap order = bit-exact'. `convolve`/`correlate` carry similar 'Bit-exact' claims on the int and f16 routes. For f64 the claim is FALSE against the installed numpy 2.4.3 on thinkstation1.

## THE EVIDENCE

Probe: 14 length pairs x 3 modes x {correlate, convolve}, compared on RAW BYTES, plus dtype/layout/edge cases. 45 of them differ. A sample, with max|delta| over the output:

  convolve[3x8, full/same/valid]        2.220e-16   <- THREE TAPS. Not a big-N effect.
  correlate[256x128, full]              1.421e-14
  convolve[256x128, full]               1.776e-14
  correlate[5000x4096, full]            8.527e-13
  convolve[5000x4096, full]             1.137e-12
  correlate[2^20 x 4097, valid]         1.450e-12

The 3x8 case is the one that matters: at three taps there is no parallel reduction and no FFT, so this is not a tree-order artifact of size. It is a summation-order or FMA-contraction difference in the innermost loop.

## WHY IT MATTERS EVEN THOUGH IT IS ULP-LEVEL

1. Three comments assert bit-exactness as the JUSTIFICATION for engaging instead of delegating. If a future cycle trusts that claim to skip a byte-level parity probe, it will pass a broken route.
2. The harness's own raw-bit checksums (the mechanism that caught a NaN-sign regression earlier this session) will flag any bench that compares these routes byte-wise.
3. Per the standing note that float reduction trees are VERSION-DEPENDENT, the right claim is 'matches to N ULP on this build', not 'bit-exact'.

## WHAT IS NOT KNOWN

Whether numpy or fnp is the more accurate of the two - neither was compared against a higher-precision reference. Do NOT 'fix' this by matching numpy's order without first checking which is closer to the exact sum.

## SUGGESTED DISPOSITION

Either (a) correct the three comments to an accuracy claim with a measured ULP bound, or (b) if bit-exactness is actually required by a caller, find the order difference in the 3x8 case first - it is the smallest reproducer and needs no parallelism to trigger.

Probe: scratchpad/conv_parity.py, sha of the ELF it ran against: 27d051518198 and c4d47519d184 (identical results).
