title: [perf][fnp-python] the f64 binary route reshapes a flat output to the shape it already has - a ~1.1us no-op on every 1-D call
description:

  let output_shape = PyTuple::new(py, shape.iter().copied())?;
  let output = flat.call_method1("reshape", (&output_shape,))?.unbind();
unconditionally. But zerocopy_f64_binary_flat already allocated  with exactly n elements, so when the operands are 1-D the target shape IS (n,) and the reshape is a NO-OP - it allocates a tuple, does an attribute lookup, and makes a Python call to return an array of the shape it already had.

title: [perf][fnp-python] our f64 divide KERNEL is 1.2652x slower than numpy's with the accumulate REMOVED - 94.0us of codegen gap that no accumulate lever can reach
description:
MEASURED, deadlock-audit-0ppym, thinkstation1, elf 4e95267adbfb1289, HEAD 7374a9bd (crates/fnp-python clean), numpy 2.4.3, n=2^20 serial, dual-null contract all four nulls clean:

  numpy divide(a,b,out=out)   354387 ns
  ours, accumulate REMOVED    448374 ns   1.2652x SLOWER  ratio 0.790499 ci95=[0.776663,0.801489]
  ours, fused (shipped shape) 544772 ns   1.5372x SLOWER  ratio 0.764919 ci95=[0.749751,0.778297]

Total deficit 190385 ns splits almost exactly in half: accumulate 96398 ns (50.6%), KERNEL 93987 ns (49.4%).

THIS BEAD IS THE KERNEL HALF. deadlock-audit-ae85t already names the lever for the accumulate half (a reduction over the quotients IN PLACE, no temporary round-trip). Even if that lands perfectly and the accumulate goes to ZERO, we remain 1.2652x slower than numpy. The accumulate work is capped at ~50% of the deficit; this is the other half and nothing in the accumulate line can reach it.

WHAT THE GAP IS. Both arms write into preallocated buffers, so it is not allocation. Both compute identical quotients (checksum eb91d471f37fc5e0, the same value the three-worker divide rows carry). numpy's f64 divide loop is vectorised and unrolled; our replica is a straightforward for over zipped slices. SHIPPED UNBUILT 2dd09861: np.isdtype implemented natively (the next pure-Python passthrough after issubdtype, which a peer landed as 7c5301a6 mid-session).

MECHANISM the incumbent hands over: np.isdtype REBUILDS ITS ANSWER EVERY CALL - kind='numeric' concatenates four sctypes lists into a fresh 22-element list, set.update()s it, then does ONE membership test against the set it just built. The set never differs between calls. Here it is a PyOnceLock table of (scalar type, kind class) built once; per call it is a pointer scan for an index plus a mask test.

Membership in numpy is BY IDENTITY (a type's hash and __eq__ are both identity), which is what makes a cached table the same predicate rather than an approximation of it. The scan returns the table INDEX, so the explicit-dtype-kind comparison is an integer compare and stays canonical on a platform where two names are one object (longdouble is float64 on some).

FOUR CELLS A PLAUSIBLE IMPLEMENTATION GETS WRONG, all asserted in the test: a DTYPE kind matches that ONE type, not its class (isdtype(np.float32, np.float64) is FALSE); np.bool_ is NOT integral but IS bool; datetime64/str_/void/object_ and every ABSTRACT type are ACCEPTED inputs that no kind string matches, so they must answer False rather than raise or decline (carried in the table with kind class ZERO); an EMPTY tuple of kinds answers False.

TABLE DISCIPLINE: it is only ever allowed to be a SUBSET of allTypes.values(), and a missing name is skipped rather than an error - a type missing from the table DECLINES to numpy (slower, never wrong) whereas a type in the table numpy does NOT accept would ANSWER WHERE NUMPY RAISES.

VERIFIED WITHOUT BUILDING vs the INSTALLED numpy 2.4.3 (/data 38G, below the 42G brake): a Python mirror of this exact logic fuzzed over 3658 (dtype,kind) pairs - 2496 answered with ZERO divergences, 1162 declined, and every declined pair confirmed to raise in numpy. The 45 embedded test cases and 12 decline fixtures were then extracted back out of the Rust source and re-run through both the mirror and numpy. rustfmt --check parses the file and puts no format hunk in any added line. NOT COMPILED AND NOT TESTED, no perf claim.

Owed the same `cargo check -p fnp-python --lib --tests` as the rest of the unbuilt stack when the brake lifts.

title: perf(log/log2/log10): ONE bad element flips a 3.5-5.6x WIN into a ~3x loss - 56% of ALL remaining headroom, and it needed the category RESOLVED not guessed
description:
MEASURED, TanBridge, thinkstation1, numpy 2.4.3 live, fnp .so sha256
f87b11b03cdc12376168fe730f5d4ec675db9a31f03f5b57b02693d592d6a0d3 (at 023c66ff).

FOLLOW-UP to deadlock-audit-f1mj2 (sqrt) and deadlock-audit-2qjj3 (arccosh/arcsin/arccos). Same
pay-twice deferral, but these are the MULTI-CATEGORY ops those beads deliberately left alone.

## WHY THIS IS THE TOP CELL, AND WHY RANKING BY RATIO HID IT

After five ships the board is flat by RATIO - the top ratios are sub-microsecond entry costs where
"8x" is 291 ns. Ranking the 269 sweep cells by ABSOLUTE headroom (fnp_ns - numpy_ns) instead:

```
  delta_ns    ratio   numpy_ns     fnp_ns   case
    506200    1.98x    518604    1024804   log2[f64]
    503304    1.82x    617251    1120555   log10[f64]
    445824    1.86x    520518     966342   log[f64]
    228504    1.23x   1009093    1237597   histogramdd[f64]
    129246    1.64x    201722     330968   vander[f64@tiny]
```

**The log family is 1.455 ms of the 2.618 ms total remaining headroom across all 147 losing cells -
56%.** By ratio it looked mid-table. Rank by absolute delta once ratios are entry-dominated.

## THE DEFECT - SAME BINARY TRIGGER, AGAIN

```
  op      operand                 numpy_ns      fnp_ns   ratio
  log     all in-domain            249960.3     71025.9   0.28x   <- 3.5x WIN
  log     + ONE negative           253040.5    765287.8   3.02x   LOSS
  log     + ONE zero               255023.1    751848.5   2.95x   LOSS
  log     standard_normal (sweep)  539752.1   1063456.9   1.97x   LOSS
  log2    all in-domain            243252.7     64234.6   0.26x   <- 3.8x WIN
  log2    + ONE negative           246262.0    716090.1   2.91x   LOSS
  log10   all in-domain            441519.2     78838.3   0.18x   <- 5.6x WIN
  log10   + ONE negative           443717.9    977124.1   2.20x   LOSS
```

ONE bad element in 65536 flips a 3.5-5.6x WIN into a ~3x LOSS. `transcendental_map_f64` computes
the whole correct output, then the caller `return Ok(None)` discards it so a fallback can record
the FP event.

## WHY THE PREVIOUS TWO BEADS COULD NOT FIX IT, AND WHAT CHANGES

A one-element witness reproduces exactly ONE errstate category. log/log2/log10 raise TWO -
`v == 0` is divide-by-zero, `v < 0` is invalid - and their predicate fuses both into one bool, so
there is nothing to select a witness from.

FIX: RESOLVE the category instead of guessing it. One read pass over the input on the EVENT PATH
ONLY (with an early break once both are seen) separates them, then raise the witnesses that
actually apply. The pass replaces a full numpy recompute of the whole array.

VERIFIED SEMANTICS against numpy 2.4.3, every claim the fix rests on:

```
  log(-1.0)   invalid      log(0.0)    divide      log(-0.0)   divide
  log(-inf)   invalid      log(+inf)   no event    log(nan)    no event
  log([0.0,-1.0]) and log([-1.0,0.0]) BOTH raise "divide by zero" under errstate(all='raise')
  witnesses log(0.0) then log(-1.0) produce the SAME warning set as the real two-category array
```

**DIVIDE MUST BE RAISED FIRST.** NumPy reports from the FP status word in a fixed CATEGORY order,
not element order - both `[0.0,-1.0]` and `[-1.0,0.0]` raise divide. Issuing invalid first would
raise the wrong one under `errstate(all='raise')`.

## AND THE SAME `is_finite()` HOLE, FIXED IN PASSING

Old predicate: `value == 0.0 || (value.is_finite() && value < 0.0)` - drops -inf, which NumPy DOES
report as invalid. This is the `log` half of deadlock-audit-kaa5i. New predicate is `value <= 0.0`,
which IEEE makes exactly the union: -0.0 and 0.0 compare equal, every negative including -inf
compares less, NaN and +inf compare false.

## STILL DEFERRING, DELIBERATELY

`arctanh` ({invalid, divide}) and `exp`/`exp2` ({over, under}) keep the old `Ok(None)`. Their
category splits have not been measured and exp's over/under boundary is value-dependent in a way
`v <= 0` is not. The arctanh half of deadlock-audit-kaa5i is untouched.

## ACCEPTANCE

Dual-null contract vs numpy live in the same invocation on the sweep operand AND a one-bad-element
operand, plus an errstate probe over warn/raise/ignore x {negative, zero, -0.0, -inf, +inf, NaN,
both categories together} for log/log2/log10, asserting raise-vs-return agreement AND that the
raised category matches. Report at 16 threads: this box is noise-dominated at 64
(deadlock-audit-2qjj3).

All three flipped from ~1.9x LOSS to DECIDABLE_WIN, exact_bytes=passed: log2 1.274533x [1.248493,1.306033] (548479/457573), log 1.235516x [1.190309,1.282411] (596291/480596), log10 1.370682x [1.345910,1.382103] (614786/461325), elf c207ae1348369ac1. Category RESOLVED by one event-path pass instead of guessed; divide witness raised FIRST because numpy reports in category order not element order. is_finite() hole fixed (log half of kaa5i). CAUGHT AND FIXED A REGRESSION I INTRODUCED: array_equal(equal_nan=True) cannot see a NaN sign bit, so my probe passed while the harness raw-bit checksum failed - Rust signs quiet NaN negative where numpy signs it positive; canonicalised in the pass that already runs, and the test now asserts bit equality. title: [perf][fnp-python] PyUFunc::__call__ binds nine PyO3 parameters before any work - switch to (*args, **kwargs) with lazy parsing
description:
TARGET: the remaining ~90% of the ~7-8 us PyUFunc::__call__ wrapper floor, the campaign's worst measured gap (7.97x slower than numpy at n=256, charged to EVERY fnp binary ufunc).

WHAT IS ALREADY ELIMINATED, so this is aimed rather than guessed:
  deadlock-audit-cydda bounded four stages at 700 ns total (numpy re-import 310, dtype guard 100, getattr ndarray 70, numpy.empty 220) - <=10% of the floor.
  deadlock-audit-s2fkk removed the delegation default-kwargs dict, measured at 727 ns/call in an isolated same-invocation control (2.442387x, null 1.000000) - another ~9-10%.
That leaves argument binding, GIL handling, PyBuffer acquisition and result construction.

THE LEVER. __call__ is declared:
  #[pyo3(signature = (x1, x2, /, out=None, *, where=None, casting="same_kind", order="K", dtype=None, subok=true, signature=None))]
Nine parameters, six optional with defaults. PyO3 binds every one on every call - allocating and populating the optionals, parsing the kwargs dict against the signature - before a single element is touched. Switching to (*args, **kwargs) and parsing lazily (fast path when args.len()==2 and kwargs is empty or absent) removes that work from the common call.

SAFE FOR INTROSPECTION, verified by reading the type: PyUFunc defines an explicit __signature__ property that builds inspect.Parameter objects by hand (crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs, just above __call__). inspect.signature reads __signature__ in preference to anything PyO3 derives, so changing the binding signature does NOT change the introspected signature. Confirm with a conformance assertion on inspect.signature(fnp.multiply) before and after rather than assuming.

MEASURE IT THE SAME WAY s2fkk WAS MEASURED, because a before/after across two builds is unsound here: the rch fleet is heterogeneous with no pinning flag, [profile.bench] inherits release and blows the 1800s SSH ceiling (use --profile bench-fast), and the shared tree carries peers' uncommitted changes. Build an ISOLATED same-invocation control that holds the binding cost up on its own - e.g. two #[pyfunction]s over identical bodies, one with the nine-parameter signature and one with (*args, **kwargs), called with the same two positional arguments - then the route.

ACCEPTANCE: a row naming WORKER and HARNESS with the isolated binding cost, banked either way. If binding turns out to be small the remainder is result construction and that is a result worth having - it would leave PyBuffer acquisition and the numpy.empty/reshape output path as the only unexplored stages.
close_reason:
REFUTED before the change was made - which is this bead's own success condition ('banked either way'). Landed 95185806.

CONTROL: two #[pyfunction]s with IDENTICAL bodies (each returns its first argument immediately) differing ONLY in binding signature. probe_nine reproduces __call__'s exact nine-parameter shape; probe_varargs takes (*args, **kwargs) and parses nothing. One binary, one invocation, WORKER hetzner1, HARNESS common::run_median_ci_contract, 41 rounds, ABBAABBA, A/A null first, no NumPy and no fnp route in either arm:
  nine_param_ns 60.0
  varargs_ns    60.0
  ratio 1.000000 ci95 [1.000000,1.000000], verdict UNDECIDED
  null  1.071429 ci95 [1.000000,1.100000]
  binding_cost_ns 0.0

THE NULL IS THE CAVEAT: at a 60 ns call the harness is at its resolution floor and two IDENTICAL arms already read 7% apart from timer quantisation. So the claim is NOT 'binding is exactly zero'. The claim is that binding sits below a ~4 ns noise floor against a 6968-8375 ns wrapper floor - three orders of magnitude apart, and no refinement of this measurement turns 0 ns into microseconds.

WHY THIS WAS WORTH DOING AS A CONTROL FIRST: the change it would have justified is rewriting __call__ to (*args, **kwargs) and hand-parsing the keyword surface of every binary ufunc. That is precisely the class of change that previously drifted NumPy's surface in this repo - 'where=' was once exposed as 'where_arg', recorded in the reduce comment in lib.rs. One bench group avoided that risk.

WHAT REMAINS, and it is now narrow: binding eliminated here, four stages bounded at 700 ns (deadlock-audit-cydda), default-kwargs dict removed at 727 ns (deadlock-audit-s2fkk). The unexplained majority of the wrapper floor now has to be PyBuffer::<f64>::get acquisition and the output construction path (numpy.empty + reshape + the Bound/Py round trip). Those are the only unexplored stages left and are the next place to instrument.

RETRY PREDICATE (in the row): reopen ONLY if a probe shows per-call cost scaling with the NUMBER of declared parameters - the same two probes at 3, 9 and 20 parameters showing a monotone trend above the null. Do not reopen because the signature 'looks expensive'; it measured indistinguishable from (*args, **kwargs).

title: [bench][fnp-python] A/A nulls that EXCLUDE unity are passing the gate - two observed today, and the straddle veto that would catch them is dormant
description:
OBSERVED DEFECT CLASS, two instances measured today on thinkstation1 (elf ef5467cb2a43c00b), both of which PASSED the live gate and were banked with a hand-written caveat instead of being caught:

  1. bench_python_lookup_hoisting_ceiling, 'empty' pair:
     null_ci95=[1.030405,1.034364] ratio_median=1.030928  -> 3.1% bias, CI does NOT contain 1.0
     Gate passed because effect 2.221374 cleared required_2x_delta=0.068729.
  2. bench_divide_vs_numpy_incumbent, PARALLEL row, incumbent null:
     null_ci95=[1.001361,1.029159] ratio_median=1.006625  -> 0.66% bias, CI does NOT contain 1.0
     Gate passed because effect deviation 0.0792 cleared required_2x_delta=0.065108 - but by only 1.2x.

WHY THIS MATTERS. Section 1 of the standing orders says every perf row needs an A/A null control that MUST come out 1.0, and that a null which fails invalidates the row. An A/A null runs the SAME arm against ITSELF; a median ratio whose 95% CI excludes 1.0 means the harness is systematically favouring one position in the schedule, so the effect measured in that same position carries the same bias. Instance 2 is the dangerous shape: a 0.66% systematic bias sitting under an effect that clears its threshold by only 1.2x. Nobody would notice it in a table.

THE GATE CANNOT SEE IT, BY CONSTRUCTION. report_median_gate_pair compares the effect against 2 x null_half_width. A null centred at 1.03 with a TIGHT CI has a SMALL half-width, so a badly biased null makes the gate MORE permissive, not less. Bias and width are different failure modes and only width is tested. There is a BIASED_NULL veto in the codebase but it is dormant at report_median_gate_pair and the live dual-null path has no CI-straddle veto at all.

PROPOSED CHECK, and it cites the observed defect class above rather than being invented: emit a NULL_STRADDLES_UNITY=false field whenever a null's CI excludes 1.0, and require the effect to clear a threshold scaled by the null's BIAS (|median-1|) in addition to its half-width. Report it; do not hard-fail rows yet - two instances is not enough to know the false-positive rate, and a gate that starts rejecting historical rows wholesale is worse than one that flags them.

DELETION CONDITION for the check: if a full re-run of the elementwise suite shows zero nulls straddling, delete it - it is not earning its keep.

NEGATIVE CASE a naive implementation would fail: widening the null's CI must NOT make a row pass. The current formula has exactly that inversion - a noisier null yields a bigger half-width and a bigger required delta, which is correct, but a BIASED-and-tight null yields a small one, which is not. A fix that only widens thresholds reproduces the bug.

FIRST STEP, build-free: grep the banked ledger rows for null_ci95 values excluding 1.0 and count how many existing rows are affected before touching any code. If the answer is 'many', this is a systemic measurement problem and outranks every perf lever currently open; if it is 'these two', it is a footnote. That count is the thing to get first, and it needs no build.

CONSTRAINT: the first step needs no build. Any harness change does.
close_reason: done

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FIRST STEP DONE, BUILD-FREE, AND IT CHANGES THIS BEAD'S PLAN. I proposed grepping the banked ledger to count how many rows carry a null whose CI excludes 1.0, to decide whether this is systemic or a footnote. THAT COUNT IS NOT OBTAINABLE.

Measured over docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md:
  prose 'ci95=[' mentions                  116
  verbatim MEDIAN_CI_GATE lines              8
  pasted 'PAIRED row=...null...' lines       0
  machine-readable *null*_ci95 fields       31, of which 1 excludes unity (by +0.0002)

Rows overwhelmingly quote their EFFECT CI in prose and describe their NULLS in English. The raw harness lines that carry both nulls are almost never pasted. So there is no population to audit, and the 1-of-31 figure is a sample too small and too unrepresentative to support either conclusion. My own two instances from today are not even in that 31, because I wrote them in prose as 'ci95=[...]' rather than as a null_ci95 field - which is exactly the problem.

REVISED PLAN: drop the historical audit entirely (recorded as a retry predicate in the ledger so nobody attempts it again) and instrument FORWARD. Emit NULL_STRADDLES_UNITY=false plus the null's bias |median-1| as machine-readable fields on every gate line, so the population exists from here on. Reassess after one full elementwise suite run.

DELIBERATELY NOT IMPLEMENTED THIS TURN, and this is a judgement worth recording rather than a lapse: the change belongs in benches/common/mod.rs, which every bench file in the crate includes. The build freeze means I cannot run even cargo check. Landing an unverified edit to the shared harness would break every pane's build the moment the freeze lifts - strictly worse than waiting. The design above is complete enough for whoever has a build slot to implement directly.

RESTATING THE INVERSION for that implementer, since it is the part that is easy to get wrong: report_median_gate_pair scales the required delta by the null's HALF-WIDTH. A biased-but-TIGHT null therefore makes the gate MORE permissive, not less. Bias and width are independent failure modes; only width is currently tested. A fix that merely widens thresholds reproduces the bug.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CORRECTION TO THIS BEAD'S CENTRAL CLAIM - I was wrong, and the bead's priority should drop accordingly.

I wrote, twice, that 'a biased-but-TIGHT null makes the gate MORE permissive, because report_median_gate_pair scales by half-width and never tests the centre'. FALSE. null_half_width is max(|ci_low - 1|, |ci_high - 1|) - the distance from 1.0 to the furthest bound, NOT the width of the interval. An offset null therefore yields a LARGER half-width and a STRICTER threshold.

Arithmetic, from the observed rows:
  biased tight  [1.030405,1.034364] -> half_width 0.034364 -> required_2x_delta 0.068729
  centred wider [0.976336,1.032376] -> half_width 0.032376 -> required_2x_delta 0.064752
The banked row's own required_2x_delta was 0.068729, exactly 2 x 0.034364. The gate CHARGED the bias. There is no inversion and no hole.

HOW I CAUGHT IT: I wrote an assertion into the self-check to PIN the inversion, then hand-checked its arithmetic before committing and it failed. The claim had already been banked in two ledger rows and in this bead's description before that. Ledger corrected in place.

WHAT SURVIVES, and it is narrower: nothing in the emitted gate line SAYS a null was biased. Both of today's instances were banked with hand-written prose caveats instead of a machine-readable flag, and the ledger has 116 prose ci95 mentions against ZERO pasted null rows, so the population still cannot be counted. Emitting null_straddles_unity and null_bias is worth doing for VISIBILITY and AUDITABILITY. It is not closing a gate hole, and this bead should NOT be worked as though it were a correctness defect in the gate.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PROPOSED CHECK: drop the part about 'require the effect to clear a threshold scaled by the null's BIAS in addition to its half-width'. Half-width ALREADY includes the bias by construction - adding a bias term would double-count it and make the gate spuriously strict. Emit the fields; change no thresholds.

The self-check now pins the CORRECT relationship (biased null => LARGER half-width) so that if someone later redefines half_width to mean interval width, the assertion fails and forces them to re-read why these fields exist - rather than silently creating the hole I wrongly claimed was already there.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
THE HOLE IS REAL BUT IT IS IN THE EFFECT'S CI, AND IT IS NOT IN fnp-python - it is in the three other crates that emit MEDIAN_CI_GATE.

This bead withdrew its central claim (01fedccc) after finding null_half_width already charges the null's bias into the threshold. That withdrawal is correct and I am not reopening it. But MEDIAN_CI_GATE is emitted by FOUR crates, and the bead only ever examined fnp-python:

  fnp-python/benches/common/mod.rs   canonical  contract_gate_verdict
  fnp-io/benches/criterion_io.rs     weak copy  report_median_ci_gate
  fnp-iter/benches/criterion_iter.rs weak copy  report_median_ci_gate
  fnp-random/benches/random_ops.rs   weak copy  report_median_ci_gate

The three weak copies were byte-identical to each other and omit the canonical rule's requirement that the EFFECT's own CI exclude unity (effect.ratio_ci_low > 1.0 for a WIN). They consult only the effect's MEDIAN against the null envelope. So an effect not distinguishable from no-change is stamped DECIDABLE_WIN there and UNDECIDED in fnp-python, from identical numbers:

  null   median 1.000000 ci95=[0.990000,1.010000] half_width 0.010000 required_2x_delta 0.020000
  effect median 1.100000 ci95=[0.950000,1.250000]
    weak:      1.100000 > 1.010000 and delta 0.100000 >= 0.020000 -> DECIDABLE_WIN
    canonical: effect.ratio_ci_low 0.950000 is NOT > 1.0          -> UNDECIDED

That is this bead's own negative case ("widening the CI must NOT make a row pass") landing in the CI the bead did not read.

LANDED, COMPILED, CLIPPY-CLEAN, AND RUN. All three files now emit effect_ci95, effect_ci_excludes_one, null_straddles_unity, null_bias and verdict_strict. No threshold and no existing verdict changed: the diff leaves the verdict expression byte-identical and only hoists null_half_width into a helper. fmt/check/clippy all exit 0 (exit codes captured unpiped; clippy without -D, which under-counts). verify_median_ci_gate_semantics runs as the statement right after report_bench_identity() in each main(), so no env gate or group filter can skip it; all three ELFs ran on rch worker vmi1153651 with 0 panics.

THE DIVERGENCE DID NOT FIRE ON LIVE DATA: 10 gate rows, 0 verdict divergences, 10/10 nulls straddling unity, 1 row with effect_ci_excludes_one=false (loadtxt_usecols_scatter_resurrection) which failed the weak rule on two independent counts and is NOT a near miss. This is a latent hazard in three harnesses, NOT a demonstrated contaminator of any banked row, and must not be cited as evidence that a past result was wrong.

WHY I DID NOT HARMONISE THE RULE: an unknown number of banked rows rest on the weak copy - unknown because of this bead's own finding that gate lines are almost never pasted (116 prose ci95 mentions, zero pasted null rows). Reversing historical verdicts silently is worse than flagging them, per this bead's instruction to report and not hard-fail. Harmonisation now needs (a) a divergence count over a full sweep, obtainable for the first time because verdict_strict is emitted, and (b) a pre-registered decision on divergent historical rows. Ledger row appended. AGENT_NAME=SlateFinch.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CLOSED. The three weak gates are harmonised onto fnp-python's canonical rule, and the decision was made on data rather than judgement.

THE INPUT THIS BEAD THOUGHT WAS UNOBTAINABLE. This bead abandoned the retrospective audit after finding 116 prose ci95 mentions and ZERO pasted null rows, concluding the population could not be counted and only forward instrumentation would build one. That conclusion was too strong: .rch-bench-replay/*.log holds real MEDIAN_CI_GATE lines emitted by fnp-python, and those carry BOTH effect_ci95 and null_ci95 - everything either rule needs. The weak rule can therefore be re-scored against real historical data with no re-run at all.

  population                                    rows   divergent
  historical  .rch-bench-replay logs (scorable)    9       0
  live        visibility commit 568a166a          10       0
  live        this change's own verification run   9       0
  TOTAL                                           28       0

ZERO divergences in 28 real rows. Harmonising rejects nothing that has ever been observed to pass, so this bead's stated fear - "a gate that starts rejecting historical rows wholesale is worse than one that flags them" - is empirically absent in this population. That fear was the only thing blocking the fix.

WHAT SHIPPED: verdict is now strict_gate_verdict, byte-identical in rule to fnp-python's contract_gate_verdict (which additionally requires the EFFECT's own CI to exclude unity). The old rule is still computed and emitted as verdict_legacy_weak alongside a gate_rule= field, so a reader holding a banked row can still tell whether it would pass today. The rule is corrected WITHOUT destroying the ability to read old rows.

VERIFIED: fmt exit 0 unpiped; clippy exit 0 on rch, no warnings on the added symbols; all three ELFs built and RAN with 0 panics and 0 assertion failures, emitting 9 gate lines with gate_rule=canonical_matches_fnp_python, of which 0 changed verdict (8 WIN->WIN, 1 REGRESSION->REGRESSION).

THE SELF-CHECK PREDICTED ITS OWN OBSOLESCENCE. The visibility commit's assertion said that if someone harmonised the rules, "this assertion fails and points at the banked rows that need re-reading". It did exactly that. Updated deliberately rather than deleted: it now pins BOTH that the legacy rule certified the worked pair AND that the shipped verdict refuses it.

PROVENANCE DISCLOSURE: these three files reached main inside commit 4bde9d6b, which belongs to another agent and carries deadlock-audit-6y5wp. I had them staged and verified, waiting on the self-check run before committing; a peer ran a bare git commit, which takes the ENTIRE STAGED INDEX, and swept them in. They disclosed it immediately and unprompted in 1c32c032. Content landed intact and complete. Flagged because git log now attributes the change to the wrong bead and carries none of the reasoning - the ledger row is the real record.

title: audit: sweep every entry point for the object-dtype DECLINE-BY-RAISING class - nq438 fixed one instance found by accident, and the static count cannot say whether there are more
description:
CLOSURE, BlackThrush, 2026-09-01. THE SWEEP RAN. The class has MORE INSTANCES, and the static
census was pointing at the wrong shape.

THE MEASUREMENT. crates/fnp-python/examples/objdtype_raise_parity.rs (commits b8f89047,
0cce66ea) calls every callable fnp exports that numpy also exports, with an object-carrying
operand in each argument position, against the live incumbent IN THE SAME PROCESS.
worker hz4 (rch --job, RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1), python 3.14.4, numpy 2.5.2,
ELF sha256 9750a9ff5e331c3b5b036875afc9ed8076f8e023bb076075feb341164aa92068.

THE 2x2, over 367 entry points, all 367 reached by at least one call:

    both_ok                     1282
    both_raise                  5812
    OURS RAISED / theirs OK      179   <- the defect cell
    ours OK / theirs RAISED       14   <- the inverse cell
    plus 3 result-type divergences, 336 exception-TYPE divergences, 1 CALLEE CRASH

SO THE ANSWER TO THE BEAD'S QUESTION - "1 site or 30?" - IS: 179 cells over ~45 entry points,
in FOUR distinct families, only one of which is the object-dtype class nq438 fixed.

  A. OBJECT-DTYPE DECLINE-BY-RAISING, 35 cells, 11 entry points:
     bitwise_left_shift bitwise_right_shift left_shift right_shift digitize logical_not
     place put putmask ravel_multi_index trapezoid
     -> deadlock-audit-objdtype-decline-by-raising-family-mhv2b
  B. UFUNC POSITIONAL `out` REFUSED, 19 cells: frexp modf divmod ldexp bitwise_count vecdot
     (+ permute_dims requires an `axes` numpy defaults)
     -> deadlock-audit-ufunc-positional-out-refused-f3cgu
  C. DUCK-TYPED SCALAR ARGUMENTS, 125 cells, 30 entry points: bool flags by truthiness,
     legacy integer mode codes, operator.index, 0-d scalars
     -> deadlock-audit-strict-scalar-argument-typing-soeis
  D. THE INVERSE CELL + result-type + exception-type surfaces
     -> deadlock-audit-inverse-cell-and-exception-type-parity-hzld8
  E. numpy 2.5.2 SEGFAULTS on np.all(a, axis, out=<object array>)
     -> deadlock-audit-numpy-all-object-out-segfault-g0hhg

THE STATIC CENSUS WAS LOOKING FOR THE WRONG SHAPE, and that is the transferable point. The
bead framed the class as `.view()` on a reference buffer and counted 537 sites / 420
propagating. NOT ONE of the 35 family-A cells is a `.view()` site. They all come from three
shared operand classifiers in crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs -

    extract_numeric_array (~5388), extract_precise_numeric_array (~5427),
    extract_index_vector (~5484)

- whose failure arm is `Err(PyTypeError)` rather than a decline, propagated by `?` at the
caller. `.view()` was how nq438's ONE instance happened to express itself. A census keyed on
the mechanism of the single known instance finds the instances that share its mechanism, and
is blind to the ones that share its BEHAVIOUR. The behaviour - "our operand classifier
refuses what numpy accepts" - is what the runtime 2x2 tests directly, and it is why the sweep
found four families where the census predicted one.

THE PROBE'S OWN NULL IS THE REASON TO BELIEVE ANY OF THIS. Run with `fnp_python` aliased to
numpy it must find nothing: 368 entry points, 1464 ok-cells, 5848 raise-cells, and 0 in all
four reportable sections. Three separate probe defects were found and fixed by that null
before the real run - NaN-vs-NaN counted as a divergence (10 phantom rows), np.empty's
uninitialised bytes counted as a divergence (1), and a callee raising SystemExit unwinding
the whole sweep. An unNULLed probe would have shipped 190 findings of which 11 were phantom.

AND THE SWEEP HAD TO SURVIVE ITS OWN SUBJECT. The first real run exited 139 with an EMPTY
report: numpy segfaulted inside np.all at the THIRD entry point, hiding the other 365. Each
entry point now runs in a forked child; a fatal signal costs one name and is reported with the
exact call. THAT IS THE METHOD NOTE FOR THE NEXT SWEEP OF THIS KIND - a probe that enumerates
defects across a foreign library must isolate the callee, or its first defect is its last
finding.

RE-RUN COMMAND (the acceptance instrument for all five child beads):
    rch exec --job -- cargo run --release -j4 -p fnp-python --example objdtype_raise_parity

COVERAGE THIS SWEEP DOES NOT HAVE, for whoever extends it: positional arity <= 3 only, four
filler operands, no keyword forms (`out=`, `axis=`, `where=` are reached only positionally),
and `random`, the classes, and the file/global-state names are excluded by design.
close_reason: Sweep ran on hz4: 179 defect cells over ~45 entry points in four families, all filed as child beads; probe null clean on all four cells

title: [perf][fnp-python] reorder the complex probe to decline on dtype.kind before the ndarray type check
description: The complex probe runs on every delegating f64 multiply/divide and always declines there, so the ORDER of its checks is the cost. It checked the ndarray type first (getattr ndarray + is_exact_instance x2) and only then the discriminating dtype.kind, spending ~7 Python operations to reach a decision the dtype could have made in ~4. Reordered to test dtype.kind first, with .ok() so an operand lacking dtype declines rather than raising. Safe because all of these are DECLINE conditions: a non-complex operand is rejected whether or not it is an exact ndarray, and is_exact_instance still runs before any buffer is touched. Measured with the deadlock-audit-wsd7h probe-chain control.
close_reason: Shipped in 07f3b1c1 and banked UNDECIDED because THE TWO WORKERS DISAGREE ON THE SIGN. harness=common::run_dual_null_median_ci_contract, n=256 f64, release profile, nulls on unity: worker=vmi1227854 before 1.403108 ci95=[1.389629,1.414874] after 1.333774 ci95=[1.322521,1.340747] (BETTER, disjoint CIs, after-elf 1e38f5e14d72a545); worker=vmi1152480 before 1.396597 ci95=[1.389674,1.400306] after 1.428706 ci95=[1.422987,1.438771] (WORSE, disjoint CIs, after-elf eea2fa649862ce51). Both cannot be true of the code - the post-change ratio spans 1.334-1.429 across workers, wider than the entire claimed effect, so the reorder is below what this harness resolves across machines. I had begun writing the vmi1227854 pair up as a win: non-overlapping intervals with an invariant control arm, exactly the shape of a decidable improvement. Only the second run, which happened to land on a different worker, showed the sign was unstable. Recording that explicitly because a single-worker before/after with disjoint CIs is NOT sufficient evidence for a change this small - the same lesson as the 13.6x splu swing, at a scale where it is far easier to miss. KEPT as maintenance on a structural argument only: the reordered path performs strictly fewer Python operations to decline a non-complex operand, which is a fact about the code rather than a claim about wall time. Correctness verified where it matters - this probe is the ONLY native path for complex multiply/divide, so a reorder that stopped admitting complex would silently delegate them: conformance_complex_ops 15 passed, conformance_complex 12 passed, conformance_diagnostics 1 passed; and ordering is safe by construction since every check moved is a DECLINE condition with is_exact_instance still ahead of any buffer access. Retry predicate: do NOT re-measure with a cross-build pair on one worker - that is what produced the false positive; effects this size need before/after in ONE binary behind an env-selected branch, on at least two workers, with the sign required to agree.

title: [docs][AGENTS] the RCH build guidance is stale - Route 2 'FROZEN', a 150G floor, and no mention of bench-fast or the -j2 slot rule
description:
AGENTS.md's RCH section is now actively misleading, and every agent reads it before building.

WRONG OR MISSING, each verified this session:

1. 'Route 2 is FROZEN as of 2026-07-30 23:10 - do not start a local cargo build. The 150G floor below has tripped'. The governing rule is now a self-checked per-build budget: run df -h /data before ANY build; at 59G or above start ONE build from your pane, at most two per project coordinated in Agent Mail; below 59G do build-free work that turn. The 150G figure is dead and the freeze framing is dead. Left as-is, an agent either refuses builds that are permitted or starts one that is not.

2. '[profile.bench] inherits stock release (lto = false, codegen-units = 16)' - FALSE for this workspace. Cargo's bench profile inherits [profile.release], and this repo's release sets lto = true, codegen-units = 1. That is why a cargo bench of fnp-python reliably exceeds rch's 1800s SSH ceiling: I hit RCH-E104 four consecutive times before switching. --profile bench-fast (opt-level 3, lto off, codegen-units 16) exists for exactly this and cleared it immediately. AGENTS.md documents bench-fast nowhere in the RCH section.

3. The slot-admission rule is missing. rch requests 8 slots by command VERB, not by crate size, so a plain 'cargo test' is admissible on only ~3 of 10 workers and gets refused while the fleet reports healthy. Relayed from frankentorch (MossyOtter), and I have relied on it all session.

4. The glibc heterogeneity note is missing. rch workers differ in glibc and there is no pinning flag; a binary built on one worker can fail to start on another. The verified mitigations are ldd before trusting a fresh binary, recording the build worker on every banked row, and - the real fix - keeping both arms of a comparison in ONE binary and ONE invocation, which this repo's dual-null contract already does by construction.

title: [bug][scripts] on_recovery_check_linalg_delegates.sh green-lights a FAILING linalg suite: grep matches 'test result: FAILED' and never sets fail=1
description:
FOUND by AzureHill 2026-08-06 during a fleet-wide sweep for the 'pipeline exit status is the last stage, not the tool' verification bug (reported fleet-wide by frankenmermaid).

THE FLEET-WIDE BUG IS NOT PRESENT IN THIS REPO'S SCRIPTS. All 19 .sh files under scripts/ set 'set -o pipefail', so 'cargo build ... | tail -3' returns cargo's status, not tail's. CI workflows contain zero pipes in any run: block. .beads/issues.jsonl contains no $? at all and docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md has no such idiom. Recording that negative result here so the next sweep does not redo it.

WHAT *IS* WRONG, and it is a different failure mode in the same family:
scripts/on_recovery_check_linalg_delegates.sh:39

  for t in conformance_linalg conformance_linalg_advanced conformance_linalg_decomp; do
    if RCH_MIN_LOCAL_TIME_MS=999999999 cargo test -p fnp-python --release --test "$t" 2>&1 | grep -E "test result"; then :; else echo "  $t: NO RESULT"; fi
  done

The gate is 'did any line match the string test result'. A shard that prints
'test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 3 failed' MATCHES that grep, so the then-branch
runs, nothing is printed, and the loop moves on. Worse, neither branch sets
fail=1, and the script's exit is 'exit $fail' (line 74). So all three linalg
conformance suites can fail outright and the script still exits 0 while looking
like it verified them.

Note pipefail does NOT save this one: pipefail makes the pipeline non-zero when
cargo fails to RUN, but a completed test binary reporting FAILED exits non-zero
too, so under pipefail the else-branch fires and prints the misleading text
'NO RESULT' for what is actually a real test failure. Either way fail stays 0.

This script is the designated verifier for four BUILD- and CONFORMANCE-UNVERIFIED
delegate commits (eigvalsh/eigh/cholesky/matrix_power, committed during the
2026-06-21 disk freeze). It is exactly the script whose green must mean something.

FIX: capture the output once, grep it for '^test result: FAILED' (and for the
absence of any 'test result' line, which is the genuine NO RESULT case), and set
fail=1 on either. Distinguish the three states - passed / failed / never ran -
instead of collapsing failed and passed into one.

PROBE THAT MUST PASS TO CLOSE: a negative test. Point the loop at a deliberately
failing shard (or stub cargo with a script that prints 'test result: FAILED.') and
assert the script exits NON-zero. A fix verified only against a passing suite has
not been verified at all - that is the same tautology this bead is about.
close_reason: FIXED in commit 085b86a8 with the required negative test: the pre-fix script exits 0 on a FAILED shard, a never-run shard, a failed deploy and an unloadable module; the fixed script exits 1 on all four and still exits 0 when everything passes. Details in the preceding comment.

title: [ub][fnp-python] b50b9d88 serial divide arm materializes &mut [f64] over a live &[Cell<f64>] - stacked-borrows hazard on the hot path
description:
FRESH-EYES FIND (PinkWolf, 2026-08-22, no repro - hazard report):

b50b9d88 introduced, inside zerocopy_f64_binary_flat_with_out's Div arm:
  let out_data: &mut [f64] =
      unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts_mut(output.as_ptr() as *mut f64, len) };
where output: &[Cell<f64>] is STILL BORROWED SHARED by the enclosing scope and is read AGAIN
afterwards by the value-based FP-hazard scan. Manufacturing &mut [f64] over memory that is
simultaneously reachable through a shared reference is aliasing UB (Stacked Borrows): the &mut
grants noalias, so LLVM is entitled to assume the later cell reads cannot observe the loop's
writes and may sink/reorder them - the exact failure mode would be the rare-path scan reading
STALE output bytes and mis-deciding warnings. Values stay correct because the same bytes are
rewritten; only the warning predicate is exposed, which is precisely the kind of silent
divergence this crate's parity doctrine forbids.

The sibling casts in the same commit (lhs/rhs: &[ReadOnlyCell<f64>] -> &[f64]) are shared->shared
of Copy data and carry no uniqueness claim - materially sound, though Miri-with-Stacked-Borrows
may still object to the transmute-flavored reinterprets.

WHY NOT FIXED INLINE: the cast exists BECAUSE the Cell-accessor form measured slower (that gap is
the lever b50b9d88 banked, 1.1074x worst-cell). The clean replacement,
Cell::from_mut(..).as_slice_of_cells() + slot.set(), changes the loop shape the measurement
depends on, so the owner should re-measure rather than have a bystander swap code under a banked
row. Suggested path: run the affected benches once under Miri (-Zmiri) on a small n just to
CONFIRM/deny the aliasing objection, then either keep the cast behind a documented
soundness argument (interior-mutable Cell means &self does NOT imply freeze - some argue the
&mut is defensible under Tree Borrows) or move to as_slice_of_cells and re-run
bench_divide_fe_flag_detector_vs_numpy.

NOT urgent: no observed misbehavior; x86_64-only path; flagged so the exorcist sweep sees it.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
MIRI RUN AS THIS BEAD ASKED, AND THE ANSWER IS DENY FOR THE SHIPPED SHAPE (2026-08-24, AmberFalcon swarm). Commit 39db9566, pushed to main and master. No code behaviour changed, so b50b9d88's banked 1.1074x row is untouched and needs no re-measurement - which is what this bead asked a bystander not to jeopardise.

METHOD. Miri cannot execute the Python C API, so `cargo miri` on fnp-python is impossible. The pattern was reproduced STANDALONE instead - a `Vec<f64>` standing in for the numpy buffer, viewed as `&[Cell<f64>]` the way PyBuffer::as_slice hands one out - in two variants:

  CASE A, the shipped shape: build `&mut [f64]` from the Cell view, then write AND read
          through `out_data` only, never touching the Cell view while it is live.
  CASE B, this bead's mechanism: same, but read `output[0].get()` through the shared Cell
          view while the `&mut` is still live, then use the `&mut` again.

EXACT COMMANDS (scratch crate, env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR, RCH_CARGO_WRAPPER_BYPASS=1, miri 0.1.0 c935696dd0 2026-04-29 on the dir-override toolchain nightly-2026-04-30):
  cargo miri run
  MIRIFLAGS=-Zmiri-tree-borrows cargo miri run

RESULTS:

  Stacked Borrows (default)            CASE A clean     CASE B **UNDEFINED BEHAVIOUR**
  Tree Borrows (-Zmiri-tree-borrows)   CASE A clean     CASE B clean

CASE B's diagnostic, verbatim in the essentials:
  error: Undefined Behavior: attempting a read access using <20929> at alloc1760[0x0],
  but that tag does not exist in the borrow stack for this location
  help: <20929> was created by a Unique retag ... from_raw_parts_mut(output.as_ptr() as *mut f64, len)
  help: <20929> was later invalidated at offsets [0x0..0x8] by a read access ... output[0].get()

SO THE SHIPPED CODE IS SOUND UNDER BOTH MODELS, and this bead's stated mechanism does not apply. The bead says the buffer is "read AGAIN afterwards by the value-based FP-hazard scan"; it is not - that scan iterates `out_data.iter()`, not `output.iter()`. Case A is exactly the shipped shape and Miri accepts it under the STRICTER of the two models.

WHAT IS NEVERTHELESS REAL, and why this was worth running: the code is ONE `output`-read away from UB under Stacked Borrows, nothing in the type system enforces the difference, and the two spellings (`out_data.iter()` vs `output.iter()`) look interchangeable at the call site. The invariant is now stated at the unsafe site in the imperative, with the Miri result that establishes it - option (a) of this bead's own suggested path ("keep the cast behind a documented soundness argument").

THE SIBLING CASTS the bead flags (lhs/rhs `&[ReadOnlyCell<f64>]` -> `&[f64]`) were exercised in Case A too and drew no objection under either model, consistent with the bead's own reading that shared->shared of Copy data carries no uniqueness claim.

WHY NO REGRESSION TEST SHIPS WITH THIS, stated plainly rather than skipped. A Miri-runnable reproduction needs `unsafe`; 9 of the 10 crates here are `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, and the only crate that permits it - fnp-python - links libpython and cannot run under Miri at all. So the guard that would catch a reintroduction cannot live in this repo's suite today. The standalone reproduction is small and is recorded here so it can be re-run on demand; if a `fnp-unsafe-probes` style crate ever exists, this is a ready-made first inhabitant.

VERIFIED: cargo check -p fnp-python --lib exit 0; rustfmt --check exit 0, run unpiped.

NOT CLAIMED: no perf measurement, and none is owed - this commit changes only a comment.

description:
FOUND BY TanBridge 2026-08-26 while banking a CORRECTNESS row for deadlock-audit-30d18.

## THE DEFECT

crates/fnp-conformance/src/bin/perf_ledger_preflight.rs, fn is_keep:

    let heading = entry.heading.to_ascii_uppercase();
    if heading.contains("KEEP") || heading.contains("WIN (SHIP") || heading.contains("WIN:")

'KEEPDIMS'.contains('KEEP') is TRUE. So a row whose heading names numpy's keepdims parameter - an
extremely likely subject for a reductions row - is classified as a performance-KEEP row and must
then carry a campaign result class AND, if that class is incumbent-win, the full same-invocation
NumPy evidence contract (Legacy incumbent arm marker with name=/version=/artifact_sha256=/
invocation_id=/measured_ratio=). A correctness row has none of that and cannot honestly invent it.

## HOW IT SURFACED

Three consecutive BLOCKED submissions of one row. The first two refusals were CORRECT and I fixed
real omissions (12-char ELF prefix instead of a full bench_elf_sha256; a prose result class where
the gate accepts exactly two tokens). The third was this false positive, and the only way past it
was to remove the word from the heading - which makes the ledger less searchable for exactly the
term a future reader would grep.

## SUGGESTED FIX

Match a WORD, not a substring: split the uppercased heading on non-alphanumerics and test for an
exact 'KEEP' token, or require the existing 'WIN (SHIP' / 'WIN:' style anchors for KEEP too (e.g.
'KEEP:' or 'KEEP (').

Same class of bug as the substring-vs-token replace trap already recorded in this campaign - a
containment test standing in for a word test.

## NOT URGENT

It only mis-fires on headings containing KEEP as a substring. 'keepdims' is the realistic one;
'housekeeping' and 'bookkeeping' would also trip it.

title: [test][fnp-io] npy 2.0/3.0 headers are never read from a numpy-written file - the one version test is named numpy_oracle_* but calls no numpy
close_reason:
COMPLETE, no defect. numpy_written_v2_and_v3_headers_parse_with_the_right_preamble reads .npy files that NUMPY wrote at format versions 2.0 and 3.0, and checks the preamble, header, shape, dtype, raw payload bytes and loaded values.

WHY THIS WAS UNCOVERED: our reader has explicit 2.0/3.0 arms - they use a 4-byte header-length field where 1.0 uses 2 bytes (crates/fnp-io/src/lib.rs:475, :555, :577, :627) - and nothing had ever fed them a file numpy produced. A name containing 'numpy_oracle' was doing the work of making that surface look covered.

The versions were unreachable incidentally: a 2.0 header requires more than 65535 bytes of header, and 3.0 requires utf8 field names. numpy.lib.format.write_array takes an explicit version, which is what makes them testable at all.

The test asserts numpy actually emitted the requested major version and that the total length implies the 4-byte field, so it cannot silently degrade into another 1.0 test if numpy changes its default.

Non-vacuity proven by falsification: expecting (1,0) from the parse fails with 'actual=(2, 0) expected=(1, 0)', so the reader genuinely reports the wide-header version rather than a default.

title: [perf][fnp-python] the PARALLEL elementwise arm loses ~1.10x on MEMORY-BOUND f64 ops (divide/maximum/minimum) while winning 6.3x on COMPUTE-BOUND ones - parallel_min gates on SIZE but the discriminator is ARITHMETIC INTENSITY
description:
MEASURED IN ONE SESSION ON ONE HOST (thinkstation1, elf ef5467cb2a43c00b, numpy 2.4.3, n=2^22, rayon_threads=64, dual-null contract, all nulls on unity, clean positive operands, real fnp route so both arms allocate):

  power         numpy 49006356 ns  fnp 7719561 ns  ratio 6.394659  WIN
  floor_divide  numpy 42556806 ns  fnp 6706099 ns  ratio 6.341392  WIN
  divide        numpy  6704812 ns  fnp 7286858 ns  ratio 0.920786  LOSS  (1.0860x slower)
  maximum       numpy  6441077 ns  fnp 7075751 ns  ratio 0.907848  LOSS  (1.1015x slower)
  minimum       numpy  6573263 ns  fnp 7276251 ns  ratio 0.913424  LOSS  (1.0948x slower)

THE PATTERN IS NOT SIZE, IT IS ARITHMETIC INTENSITY. All five run the same parallel route at the same
n above the same parallel_min with the same 64 threads. The two that WIN are compute-bound per element
(libm pow; floored division). The three that LOSE are memory-bound: one or two flops per 24 bytes of
traffic, where numpy's SINGLE-THREADED loop already saturates the streams and extra threads buy
nothing while adding scheduling and cross-socket traffic. Note the incumbent times: numpy takes
~42-49 ms on the compute-bound ops and only ~6.4-6.7 ms on the memory-bound ones - it is the same
numpy in both cases, so the difference is the op's intensity, not numpy's threading.

THE STRUCTURAL CLAIM: parallel_min gates on ELEMENT COUNT. For BinaryOp::Div it is 1<<21. But element
count does not predict whether fanning out pays - intensity does. A memory-bound op at 2^22 is
exactly where we lose, and raising n does not fix it (divide loses at 2^20 AND 2^22, 1.1828x and
1.0860x). The gate is measuring the wrong variable.

WHY THIS IS NOT A DUPLICATE of deadlock-audit-0ppym: 0ppym asks whether DIVIDE's specific deficit is
the normality accumulate or its codegen, at n=2^20 in the SERIAL regime. This bead is about the
PARALLEL regime across three ops, where the accumulate cannot be the explanation because maximum and
minimum have no hazard scan at all and lose by the same ~1.10x. Two different mechanisms; both real.

CANDIDATE LEVERS, in preference order:
  1. Gate on estimated arithmetic intensity per op rather than element count - i.e. a per-op
  parallel_min, with the memory-bound ops taking a much higher threshold or none at all.
  2. Bound the worker count for memory-bound ops instead of taking all 64, so fan-out does not exceed
  what the memory system can feed.
  3. Serial-only for div/max/min at these sizes.
Lever 3 has partial precedent: deadlock-audit-hzl1w's decision cites a serial native maximum arm
BEATING numpy - but that figure came from an allocation-asymmetric group (deadlock-audit-48by6) and
must NOT be used until re-measured after e5d5a67d.

NEGATIVE CASE a naive implementation would fail: raising parallel_min for these ops must not silently
regress the LARGE-n end. Any threshold change must be measured at 2^20, 2^22 AND 2^24 against numpy in
one invocation - the multiply route sweep shows the route reaches parity only by 2^24, so a threshold

COMPLETE, no defect. promotion_table_matches_numpy_for_every_dtype_pair compares ALL 196 pairs over the 14 modelled dtypes (bool, i8..i64, u8..u64, f16/f32/f64, complex64/128) against np.promote_types. Every pair agrees.

WHY THIS GAP MATTERED: AGENTS.md calls the promotion table a non-negotiable compatibility contract, and fnp-dtype had NO numpy oracle at all - zero occurrences of numpy_oracle or FNP_ORACLE_PYTHON in the crate. Its promotion tests check internal properties (transitivity over the scoped matrix, idempotence) or a handful of hand-written pairs. Those cannot catch a table that is SELF-CONSISTENT AND UNIFORMLY WRONG, which is the specific failure mode a hand-built promotion matrix risks: transitivity holds fine in a lattice that is simply not numpy's.

The oracle row count is asserted at 196, and any numpy dtype name outside the 14 modelled panics with the name rather than being silently skipped - so if numpy ever promotes a pair into something we do not model, this fails loudly instead of passing.

SCOPE: numeric dtypes only, matching what promote() is defined over. Datetime64/timedelta64, strings and structured dtypes are separate promotion surfaces and are not covered here.

title: [perf][fnp-python] Recover the f64 divide FE-hazard cost with a per-block vectorizable normality pre-filter
description:
OPENED by CoralOak 2026-08-08 off the measured result in deadlock-audit-jw7vk. This is that bead's
OWN named retry predicate, now triggered by evidence rather than proposed speculatively.

THE MEASURED COST BEING ATTACKED. jw7vk priced the FE-hazard branch 2nmd1 added to the f64 divide
fast path. It is not the "~one predictable test per element" that was expected:
  vmi1293453 (8 lg, EPYC-IBPB)  serial 1<<20  ratio_median 0.511  ci95 [0.4619, 0.5310]
                                              null [0.9606, 1.0136]
  hz1        (8 lg, EPYC-Milan) serial 1<<20  ratio_median 0.295  ci95 [0.2679, 0.3058]
                                              null [0.9947, 1.0098]
                                              MEDIAN_CI_GATE verdict=DECIDABLE_REGRESSION
  vmi1293453                    parallel 1<<22 ratio_median 0.703 ci95 [0.6672, 0.7715]  PROVISIONAL
ratio = former/candidate, so the shipped kernel takes ~1.96x (vmi1293453) and ~3.39x (hz1) the
former's time serially. Direction and decidability replicate across two quiet hosts; MAGNITUDE IS
HOST-DEPENDENT, so quote each host's row with its host named and never average them. Route share
was measured alongside (0.941 and 0.615 serial, 0.601 parallel), so the kernel ratio is not read as
the whole call's.

THE HYPOTHESIS, still unconfirmed. A per-element `q.is_normal()` interleaved with the divide almost
certainly blocks auto-vectorisation: the former loop is a straight `*s = x / y` that vectorises to
vdivpd, the candidate threads a scalar predicate and a data-dependent OR through it. FIRST TASK
HERE IS TO CONFIRM OR KILL THAT — objdump the release-perf kernel and look for vdivpd in the former
shape and its absence in the current one. If the mechanism is something else, this design is aimed
at the wrong thing and should be re-derived before any code moves.

THE DESIGN, and it is semantics-preserving BY CONSTRUCTION, which is the whole appeal.
`f64::is_normal()` is exactly "biased exponent bits in 1..=0x7FE" — exponent 0 is zero/subnormal,
0x7FF is inf/nan. That is an integer test on the quotient's bits and it vectorises. So:
  - process the quotients in fixed blocks (8 or 16),
  - compute the block's quotients with a plain divide loop (vectorisable, no branch inside),
  - test the block with the bitwise form of the SAME fast accept: all lanes' exponents in
    1..=0x7FE  ->  no element in this block can raise, move on,
  - only when a block fails that test, run the EXACT existing scalar
    `f64_divide_raises_fp_error` over those 8/16 elements.
The scalar predicate is unchanged and is still the only thing that decides a hazard, so the
observable outcome cannot move: the block test is a conservative pre-filter whose true branch is
precisely the current fast accept's true branch. Over-entering the slow block costs time, never
correctness.

CAVEAT INHERITED FROM THE MEASUREMENT, and it bounds what the serial number promises here. The
jw7vk bench arms operate on plain `&[f64]` / `&mut [f64]`. The shipped PARALLEL path does too
(par_chunks over real slices), so the 0.703 row transfers directly. The shipped SERIAL path does
NOT: it iterates `output.iter().zip(a_in.iter()).zip(b_in.iter())` over `Cell<f64>` /
`ReadOnlyCell<f64>`. Cell access may vectorise differently, so the serial ratios above are the cost
of the LOOP SHAPE on plain slices, not a measured property of the shipped serial loop. Re-measure
the shipped serial shape before claiming this lever recovers 1.96x-3.39x there. This is a real
limitation of jw7vk's instrument and is recorded on that bead too.

PROBES THAT MUST PASS TO CLOSE:
  1. CORRECTNESS FIRST, and it is non-negotiable:
     cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_diagnostics   (0 divergences)
     plus the pure-predicate unit test
     f64_divide_hazard_predicate_flags_exactly_the_ieee_exceptions in lib.rs.
     2nmd1's evidence method is the bar: with the deferral disabled, conformance_diagnostics
     reports exactly 6 diverging rows. A change here that silently stopped deferring would pass
     every value-level test, so prove the deferral still fires — flip it off, watch the 6 rows
     come back, flip it on.
  2. A NEW unit test that a block containing exactly one hazard in each lane position still defers.
     Off-by-one in the block loop is the obvious failure mode and no existing test covers it.
  3. PERF, via the instrument jw7vk already landed in
     crates/fnp-python/benches/criterion_python_elementwise.rs. Add a third arm for the blocked
     form so former / current / blocked are all in ONE binary, then:
       RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR rch exec -- \
         env FNP_BENCH_GROUPS=bench_divide_fe_hazard \
         cargo bench --profile release-perf --bench criterion_python_elementwise
     Result class is maintenance-self-speedup whichever way it goes: every arm is our own code.
     Expect the quiescence gate to refuse most attempts on a busy fleet — five of six were refused
     when jw7vk was measured. That is the gate working; do not weaken it.

WHAT IS NOT ON THE TABLE. Removing or narrowing the deferral. It is a correctness requirement:
numpy's divide loop raises FE flags its error state turns into RuntimeWarnings (or errors under
np.seterr / np.errstate) and a pure-Rust kernel cannot push a flag into that state. This bead makes
the check cheaper, not rarer. If the blocked form does not recover the cost, the honest outcome is
a REJECT row saying so and the branch stays.
close_reason:
REJECTED BY MEASUREMENT, and the change is REVERTED (commit 05217aa9). The blocked pre-filter made the generated code WORSE, which is this bead's own stated outcome for that case.

BOTH HALVES BUILT IN THE SAME ENVIRONMENT - one bounded local release-perf build each, distinct sha256 (before 61a1e5e3, after a813742d), one-commit diff:
  2ff37d87 per-element  zerocopy_f64_binary_flat  insns=1440 vector=187 vdivpd=1 vdivsd=1
  4c3dada7 blocked      zerocopy_f64_binary_flat  insns=2211 vector=319 vdivpd=0 vdivsd=15
The blocked form DESTROYED the packed divide (vdivpd 1 -> 0, replaced by 15 scalar divides) and grew the function 54% in instructions and 71% in vector ops. It did the opposite of its purpose.

WHY: copying each block's quotients into a local [f64; 8] and re-reading them for the normality reduction broke the divide loop's own vectorisation. The rare-arm masking is real and jw7vk's regression is real, but THIS hoist costs more than it saves.

UNTRIED DIRECTIONS for whoever reopens the underlying cost: widen the fast accept, or find a reduction that does not round-trip the quotients through a stack array. The FE-hazard deferral itself stays - it is a correctness requirement with a named probe, and jw7vk's measured regression remains unpaid.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO MY OWN EARLIER NOTES ON THIS BEAD, both from this measurement:
  - I recorded 'the shipped kernel emits no packed divides' as a general property. Wrong: that was the POST-change binary. The pre-change kernel DOES vectorise its divide.
  - Attempt 2's ambiguity is resolved: the two identical remote readings (2207/319/0/15) were the same post-change binary read twice, not two builds agreeing. My worry at the time was the correct one.

THE PROCEDURE THAT FINALLY WORKED, after four custody failures: build BOTH commits locally (a script, since cargo is rch-hooked; the parent in a git worktree so the shared tree is untouched), reuse the one repo target dir, copy each ELF out and sha it before the next build overwrites it. Local and remote toolchains differ here (local reads 2211 where remote read 2207 for the same source), so both sides must be built in the SAME environment - that alone invalidated three earlier attempts.

Gates after revert: cargo test -p fnp-python --lib --no-fail-fast 557 passed / 0 failed on hz2; clippy --all-targets --no-deps -D warnings exit 0 on hz1 with 'Checking fnp-python'; fmt --check exit 0.

LEFT BEHIND, needs an operator decision because I may not delete files: the git worktree at scratchpad/wt-before is still registered (git worktree list shows it). Remove it with 'git worktree remove' when convenient.

comments.author: CoralOak
comments.text:
HYPOTHESIS REFUTED BY DISASSEMBLY, same day, by the author of this bead. The mechanism I filed it
on is WRONG. The lever's SHAPE survives but its REASON is different, and the difference changes how
it must be implemented. Read this before writing any code against the description above.

WHAT I CLAIMED: that the per-element `q.is_normal()` blocks auto-vectorisation of the divide loop,
so the fix is to restore vectorisation by hoisting the test to a per-block any().

WHAT THE DISASSEMBLY SAYS. objdump of the release-perf bench ELF on hz1
(criterion_python_elementwise-6ec8c81fe223c495, pool ade9d3fd...), per `#[inline(never)]` kernel:

  divide_former_serial      insns=40   vector=7    vdivpd=1  vdivsd=1
  divide_candidate_serial   insns=186  vector=91   vdivpd=1  vdivsd=1

BOTH VECTORISE. The candidate still emits vdivpd in its main loop. Vectorisation was never lost, so
"restore it" is not the lever and the per-block any() cannot buy what I said it would.

WHAT ACTUALLY COSTS THE TIME. LLVM if-converted the WHOLE predicate into branchless vector masks
and evaluates EVERY arm on EVERY block. The candidate's vector instruction mix:
  vpor 7, vpand 7, vmovupd 5, vandpd 5, vmovsd 4, vpcmpeqq 3, vmovups 3, vmovq 3,
  vpandn 2, vcmpneqpd 2, vptest 1, vpcmpgtq 1, ...
That is the NaN checks, the b == 0 test, both infinity tests and the subnormal comparison — the
rare arms — computed as masks for every element that will never need them. The loop went from 7
vector instructions to 91 around a single vdivpd. ~13x the vector work in a loop where the divide
is one instruction is a clean explanation for the 1.96x-3.39x measured in jw7vk, and it does not
need the vectorisation story at all.

THE SOURCE-LEVEL FAST ACCEPT BUYS NOTHING. `if q.is_normal() { return false }` reads like an early
out, but after if-conversion there is no branch to take: the rare arms are evaluated regardless and
their results are masked away. That is the actual defect, and it is invisible from the source.

SO THE REAL LEVER, and the shape is coincidentally close to what I filed: get a REAL branch back at
block granularity. Compute a block of quotients, reduce "all lanes normal" to a single predicate
(the vptest already in there shows the reduction is cheap), and branch — on the taken path do
NOTHING further, on the rare path call the existing scalar predicate over the block. The goal is
not vectorising the divide, which is already vectorised; it is keeping the rare arms OUT of the hot
block entirely. The implementation must resist re-if-conversion — check the disassembly again after
the change rather than trusting the source shape, because trusting the source shape is exactly what
produced this defect.

The exactness argument in the description still holds and is unaffected: `f64::is_normal()` is
precisely "biased exponent in 1..=0x7FE", the block test is a conservative pre-filter, and the
unchanged scalar predicate remains the only thing that decides a hazard.

METHOD NOTE WORTH KEEPING. This bead asked, as its own first task, to confirm or kill the
vectorisation hypothesis by disassembly before moving code. Doing that took one ssh and refuted the
premise the bead was filed on. A perf bead whose mechanism is a guess should always carry that step
first, and the guess should be labelled as one — jw7vk's write-up did label it "HYPOTHESIS, NOT
MEASURED", which is why this was cheap to catch rather than expensive to discover after a rewrite.

STATUS: back to ready, unassigned. Everything above is diagnosis; no production code was touched.
The three probes in the description stand unchanged, and probe 1 (conformance_diagnostics, with the
deferral flipped off to watch the 6 rows return) is still the non-negotiable gate.

comments.author: CoralOak
comments.text:
IMPLEMENTED in commit 4c3dada7, correctness gate GREEN, PERF NOT YET MEASURED. Bead stays open on probe 3 only.

WHAT LANDED. Both Div arms of zerocopy_f64_binary_flat now run in blocks of 8: compute the block's quotients, reduce 'all lanes normal' to ONE bool via f64_divide_block_all_normal, branch. Taken path does nothing further; only a block containing a non-normal quotient pays for the full scalar predicate, which is unchanged and remains the only thing that decides a hazard. Serial arm uses as_chunks over the Cell slices, parallel arm as_chunks_mut/as_chunks over the plain slices, each with the old per-element form for the sub-block tail.

comments.text:
PROBE 3 STEP 1 (objdump) ATTEMPTED, RESULT INCONCLUSIVE — and the reason is my own procedural error, not the code.

WHAT I DID. Built the bench at --profile release-perf with --no-run (which sidesteps the quiescence gate entirely, so no quiet host is needed — worth knowing) and disassembled zerocopy_f64_binary_flat on hz2. Then built the pre-blocking baseline (--base 2ff37d87 --clean-overlay --no-overlay) and disassembled again.

  post-change  zerocopy_f64_binary_flat: insns=2207 vector=319 vdivpd=0 vdivsd=15
  baseline     zerocopy_f64_binary_flat: insns=2207 vector=319 vdivpd=0 vdivsd=15

IDENTICAL — and that is exactly the problem. Both builds landed in the SAME pool directory (.rch-target-hz2-pool-ade9d3fd...), so the second overwrote the first, and I did not capture the first ELF's sha256. So I cannot tell whether the two readings are (a) two different binaries that genuinely emit the same code, or (b) the same binary read twice. This repo's own operational note says it plainly: the pooled target dir is reclaimed by the next job on that worker, CAPTURE THE ELF IN THE SAME COMMAND. HOW TO REDO IT PROPERLY: sha256sum the ELF in the SAME rch invocation that builds it, for each of the two commits, and compare the shas before comparing the disassembly. If the shas match, the second build was a cache hit and the comparison is void.

ONE FINDING THAT DOES SURVIVE, because it holds for whichever binary I read: the shipped kernel emits NO PACKED DIVIDES at all — vdivpd=0, vdivsd=15. That is very different from the bench replicas, which both showed vdivpd=1. So the shipped serial path (which iterates Cell<f64> / ReadOnlyCell<f64>, not plain slices) is not getting a vectorised divide in the first place, and the parallel rayon closure is a separate symbol not covered by this count. This corroborates the caveat already recorded on jw7vk: the bench's serial arms measure plain-slice loop shapes, and the shipped serial loop is a different shape. Anyone continuing here should disassemble the rayon closure symbol separately.

title: [test] golden tests for convolve/correlate across full/same/valid modes
close_reason: COMPLETE - and this one FOUND A REAL DEFECT, unlike the four preceding test beads. correlate_mode was implemented as the identity correlate(a,v) == convolve(a, v[::-1]), which only holds while a is the LONGER operand. numpy swaps its inputs so the longer leads, computes there, and reverts the whole result when it swapped; 'full' and 'valid' trim symmetrically so both orders agree, but 'same' drops an uneven number of elements from the two ends, so the unswapped order shifts the window by one: numpy correlate([1,2],[0.5,1,-1,2,3],'same') = [8,3,-1,2.5,1] where fnp returned [3,8,3,-1,2.5]. Root cause was invisible to every existing golden because they all pass a kernel SHORTER than the signal. FIXED in d28b0372 by swapping when the kernel is longer and reversing the result, verified against numpy for all three modes. Three tests added: (1) the failing case across all three modes for both functions, asserting output LENGTH as well as values since 'same' returns max(M,N) and 'valid' returns |M-N|+1; (2) even-length kernel (no exact 'same' centre), equal lengths ('valid' collapses to one element), one-element kernel; (3) two oracle-free laws - convolve commutes, correlate reverses under swap - with an explicit non-vacuity check that correlate and convolve actually differ on the input used. EVIDENCE: the new test FAILED before the fix ('correlate same v>a[0] = 3, want 8') and passes after; timeout 120 cargo test -p fnp-ufunc --lib = 2278 passed / 0 failed in 66.96s (2275 before); cargo fmt --check -p fnp-ufunc exit 0 run UNPIPED. SPUN OUT: deadlock-audit-rtmi8 (P1) for the two fnp-python sites - int_convolve_typed has the same trim with no guard (user-visible above its 1<<16 work threshold), and the f64 binding's explicit 'fall back when kernel is longer' workaround is now redundant. Both need an fnp-python test run so they were not smuggled into this single-crate change.

title: [harness][ledger] banked incumbent-win rows do not name their measurement worker - 0 of 44
description:
FLEET DIRECTIVE 2026-08-15: frankenscipy measured the SAME cubic-splu cell on two rch workers and got 1.2693x vs 0.0093x - a 13.6x swing - with BOTH A/A nulls PASSING. An A/A null controls within-invocation noise only; it cannot see between-worker differences in CPU model, cache, memory bandwidth or contention. The directive: every banked row must NAME ITS WORKER alongside thread count, governor, ISA and the self-reported ELF SHA-256, and a row that does not name its worker cannot be compared to any other row.

MEASURED GAP IN THIS REPO (TealOak, 2026-08-15): splitting docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md on top-level '## ' headings gives 1,080 rows, of which 44 carry 'Campaign result class:** incumbent-win'. ZERO of those 44 name a worker. 76 rows of other classes do (WORKER=vmi1264463 x26, vmi1149989 x23, vmi1227854 x21, hz1 x17, hz2 x15, ovh-a x3, ...). Spot-checked the 2026-08-05 fused a[mask].sum() row by hand: it carries bench_elf_sha256, RAYON_NUM_THREADS=10, ISA (AVX2, no AVX-512) and the NumPy version, but no worker identity. So the ELF and thread provenance discipline took hold and the WORKER field did not.

WHAT IS NOT AT RISK, and why: both arms of any harness-produced row are closures invoked inside ONE process by common::run_dual_null_median_ci_contract / run_median_ci_contract, interleaved ABBAABBA per BALANCED_SQUARE. A single row's two arms therefore CANNOT have landed on different workers - that failure mode is structurally impossible here, and no row needs flagging as worker-scoped on those grounds. The exposure is the other direction: without a worker name you cannot tell whether two ROWS are comparable, and this repo has already measured host-driven ratio movement (min@64M = 3.58x on vmi1293453 vs 2.64x on vmi1156319 for the same ELF).

SCOPE:
1. Make the worker identity a required field for a banked row and enforce it in crates/fnp-conformance/tests/ledger_hygiene.rs, the way the ELF sha and the incumbent-arm marker are already enforced. Decide the exact token (WORKER=<name>) and whether to require governor + physical_cores too - the harness already prints all of them on the HOST_BASELINE / THREAD_CONFIGURATION / ISA_BASELINE lines, so this is a transcription requirement, not new measurement.
2. Grandfather the 44 existing rows the way ledger_hygiene already caps historical debt, so backdating cannot dodge the new gate.
3. Backfill the worker for whichever of the 44 rows still have a retrievable run log; mark the rest as worker-unknown rather than inventing one.

DO NOT add a load-based veto while doing this: frankenfs measured that an external-load metric does not predict the ratio at all (load varied 4.9x, ratio spread only 6.46%, r=-0.35), so such a gate rejects runs on a signal uncorrelated with error.

PROBE: a new REJECT or WIN row without a WORKER= token fails ledger_hygiene, and the 44 grandfathered rows are enumerated in the cap so the count cannot silently grow.
close_reason: Shipped across cce9f932 (gate), c588c9f1 (debt cap + staleness test) and 14c43022 (backfill). PROBE AS WRITTEN IS MET: (1) a new measured row without a worker token fails ledger_hygiene - new_measured_rows_name_their_worker, with worker_detector_rejects_rows_without_a_named_worker as its negative case; (2) the grandfathered population is enumerated in a cap that cannot silently grow - historical_unworkered_incumbent_win_debt_does_not_grow closes the backdating hole, and unworkered_incumbent_win_budget_is_not_stale forces the cap DOWN when rows are recovered rather than letting a bare <= ceiling over-permit. SCOPE ITEM 3 PARTIALLY DONE, deliberately: 5 of the 44 rows had a run log retained under .rch-bench-replay/ and were backfilled with their real worker, each matched to its row by bench_elf_sha256 rather than by filename or date (critical-access-392 vmi1227854, a*b+c fusion-405 vmi1293453, isin-402 vmi1293453, rolling-load-393 vmi1227854, sessionization-395 vmi1227854). The fusion row needed an extra step: three logs share its ELF, and only the vmi1293453 t4/t8 logs contain its quoted 2.888467x/5.235572x, so it is attributed there and not to trj. Budget ratcheted 44 -> 39. The remaining 34 have no retained log and are NOT marked with a guessed worker - inventing provenance is worse than an acknowledged gap; the two gemm-403 logs are unusable because they carry a matching ELF sha but no HOST_BASELINE line at all. VERIFIED: 23/23 then 25/25 ledger_hygiene green (rch workers vmi1153651, vmi1227854).

title: [perf][fnp-python] divide replicas take 10.5x numpy's dTLB misses at IDENTICAL L1D misses - re-measure the kernel gap on numpy-ALLOCATED buffers before trusting 0ppym's 1.2652x
description:
MEASURED, AzureCarp, thinkstation1, perf record -e dTLB-load-misses:u -F 4999 (12K samples, single event so not a multiplexing artefact), group bench_divide_accumulate_isolation_vs_numpy, normalised per UNIT of work (numpy is incumbent in BOTH contracts = 6 units; each Rust arm = 3):

  arm      cyc/unit(M)   L1miss/unit(M)   dTLBmiss/unit(M)
  numpy         846.6           214.39              0.314
  fused        1110.0           221.49              3.316
  former        970.0           211.45              3.305
  fused/numpy  cycles 1.311  L1 1.033  dTLB 10.57x

IDENTICAL L1 data-cache misses (1.033x) and 10.5x the dTLB LOAD MISSES. Both Rust arms show the same
10.5x, so it is a property of the BUFFERS, not of either loop body.

THE HYPOTHESIS THIS BEAD TESTS. The replicas allocate Rust Vec<f64>. The SHIPPED route does not:
zerocopy_f64_binary_flat reads two numpy arrays and writes into a numpy.empty output, i.e. it runs
on numpy-ALLOCATED memory - the same allocator whose buffers show 10.5x fewer dTLB misses. If the
gap is an allocator property rather than a kernel property, then every replica-based divide kernel
number, including deadlock-audit-0ppym's 1.2652x (accumulate-free) and 1.5372x (fused), is measuring
our ALLOCATOR against numpy's and attributing it to our loop.

THE WORK: add an arm to bench_divide_accumulate_isolation_vs_numpy (or a sibling group) whose input
and output buffers are numpy arrays accessed through PyBuffer, exactly as the shipped route does,
leaving the loop body byte-identical. Measure (a) dTLB misses per unit and (b) the ratio vs numpy
under the dual-null contract.

DECISION RULE: if the dTLB gap collapses toward 1x AND the ratio improves, 0ppym's kernel numbers
are an allocator artefact and must be re-taken, and the divide 'codegen gap' shrinks by whatever the
buffers were carrying. If dTLB stays at ~10x with numpy-allocated buffers, the allocator is
exonerated and the translation cost is intrinsic to how our loop walks memory - a different and more
interesting lever.

NEGATIVE CASE a naive implementation would fail: swapping the buffers must NOT change the loop body
or the checksum. If the new arm does not reproduce numpy.divide bit for bit (checksum
eb91d471f37fc5e0 on the standard hazard-free operands) it is measuring a different computation. The
arm must also assert it is reading a C-contiguous float64 buffer, or PyBuffer will silently hand
back a copy and the whole point is lost.

ALREADY REFUTED, do not re-run: transparent huge pages (numpy reports AnonHugePages=0 with its
_set_madvise_hugepage switch both ON and OFF; THP here is madvise-mode and nothing is collapsed) and
buffer count (the smaller control group shows the effect at least as strongly).

SIZING, so nobody over-claims it: excess is 263.4M cycles/unit against 3.003M excess dTLB
misses/unit, so at 5/10/20/40 cycles per page walk the TLB explains 5.7/11.4/22.8/45.6% of the
excess. Real contributor, not the whole gap at any plausible cost.

Banked in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md.
close_reason:
Decision rule met and answered. The bead asked: add an arm whose buffers are numpy arrays via PyBuffer, leaving the loop byte-identical, and measure (a) dTLB misses per unit and (b) the ratio vs numpy under the dual-null contract; if the dTLB gap collapses AND the ratio improves, 0ppym's kernel numbers are an allocator artefact and must be re-taken.

BOTH HALVES MEASURED.
