comments.text:
EVIDENCE from the 2026-08-09 out-keyword sweep (CreamGlen). fnp-python conformance shards use TWO unrelated comparison harnesses, hand-reimplemented per shard, and they disagree on how much of the result counts. A test's NAME therefore tells you nothing about its strictness - this was the single most misleading thing about auditing this batch.

STRONG family - JSON normalize: outcome_body/numpy_outcome_script/fnp_outcome_script run the SAME script body under numpy and under fnp, normalise each result to a dict of kind/dtype/shape/values (exception type for errors), and compare the whole serialised outcome. Nothing is discarded. Seen in conformance_around, conformance_lexsort, conformance_partition.

WEAK family - out_outcome: builds a rich tuple ('ok', result is out, dtype, shape, out.tolist()) and then a HAND-WRITTEN comparator decides how much to look at. Four shards made four different choices for the same contract:
  conformance_isinf_signed   'if actual != expected'                    STRICT
  conformance_fp_classify    'if actual != expected'                    STRICT
  conformance_trig           indices 0,1 only  -> FIXED 9f4d5b88 (qydzq)
  conformance_rounding       indices 0,1 only  -> FIXED 933122ce (1vlfq)
  conformance_unary_ops      indices 0,1 only  -> FIXED 933122ce (9m9pm)
In the weak form the mutated values were collected and thrown away, so a wrapper returning the right object filled with wrong numbers passed. All three were real gaps found only by reading each comparator to its end; conformance_range_funcs and conformance_diff_gradient LOOK weak at first glance but call values_match on the ok path and are fine.

TWO FURTHER TRAPS worth folding into a shared helper: (1) Python list equality cannot see a zero's sign (-0.0 == 0.0), so a values comparison alone misses negative(-0.0) -> +0.0; conformance_unary_ops now carries an explicit signbit tuple for this. (2) Pinning exception MESSAGES makes a shard version dependent because numpy rewords them and the supported floor spans several releases - compare the exception TYPE.

PROPOSAL: one shared comparator helper (strictest form: kind/dtype/shape/values/signbit + exception type), used by every shard, so strictness is a property of the helper rather than a per-shard decision. Until then, every new *_out_keyword_surfaces_match_numpy test needs its comparator read, not just its name.

FALSIFY BEFORE TRUSTING: each of the three fixes above was confirmed by perturbing the fnp side (out[0]=999.0, or flipping only a zero's sign) and checking the test FAILS. A strengthened comparison that has never been made to fail is not evidence.

title: [perf][fnp-linalg] Batched-SIMD (SoA, matrix-per-lane) cholesky — BIT-EXACT lever for the 5-8x batch floor
description:
NOVEL bit-exact lever (BlackThrush 2026-06-22) that prior analysis MISSED. batch_cholesky loses 5-8x (serial), documented as a kernel wall because the per-matrix cholesky has loop-carried dot products that won't vectorize WITHIN a matrix, and within-matrix reassociation breaks the sha256 golden (batch_lanes_parallel_match_serial_reference_and_golden_sha256, lib.rs L9580/9626/9701).

KEY INSIGHT: the no-ship was about WITHIN-matrix SIMD (reassociating one matrix's dot products). But the BATCH dimension is embarrassingly parallel and independent. Process 8 matrices PER SIMD REGISTER via a SoA (struct-of-arrays) layout: element (i,j) of 8 consecutive matrices held in one Simd<f64,8>. Every cholesky operation (column scale, rank-1 update, diagonal sqrt via Simd::sqrt) then runs in SIMD lockstep across 8 matrices, with EACH lane performing EXACTLY the scalar per-matrix arithmetic in the SAME order. So each matrix's result is BYTE-IDENTICAL to the current scalar inv_nxn/cholesky_nxn -> the sha256 golden HOLDS, no human re-pin.

WHY CHOLESKY (not inv/LU): cholesky has NO pivoting -> all 8 matrices follow the same deterministic control flow -> clean SIMD lockstep. LU/getri partial-pivoting diverges per matrix (different pivot rows) -> breaks lockstep, much harder (skip inv for now).

PLAN: (1) gather AoS->SoA in blocks of 8 lanes (n^2 shuffle, amortized: compute is n^3/3 >> n^2 for n>=16, the loss regime). (2) batched-SIMD cholesky_blocked over SoA (Simd<f64,8> column ops + simd sqrt). (3) scatter SoA->AoS. (4) bit-exact verify vs the existing scalar golden (to_bits + sha256 must match). Expected ~4-8x kernel speedup (SIMD width) closing the 5-8x serial gap, parallelized across lane-blocks.

RISK/EFFORT: major careful rewrite in golden-locked + peer-contended fnp-linalg cholesky code; tail (batch%8) + small-n + non-SPD-error paths must match scalar exactly; verify against sha256 golden. ~multi-hour focused task w/ env-toggle A/B (scalar vs batched-SIMD) before shipping; REVERT if gather/scatter eats the gain at small n. This is the ONE remaining BIT-EXACT pure-Rust perf lever (cov large-Gram = C-BLAS-only per bead cblas-large-gram-lever-8lnzn; batch_inv = pivoting-blocked).
close_reason: DISPROVEN by prototype (BlackThrush 2026-06-22). Implemented + benched a batched-SIMD-SoA cholesky (8 matrices/lane, Simd<f64,8> mul_add dot, SoA gather/scatter) vs scalar per-lane cholesky_nxn (release, warm target). Result: 1.5-3x SLOWER, worsening with n (n=8:1.52, 16:1.79, 32:2.66, 48:2.87, 64:3.08). ROOT CAUSE: scalar cholesky_nxn's inner per-matrix dot (cholesky_dot_add_ordered) is ALREADY LLVM-auto-vectorized on the k-axis, so batched-across-matrices SIMD merely moves the vectorization to the batch axis while ADDING SoA gather+scatter transpose overhead (n^2 per block) -> net loss that grows with n. Also not bit-exact: Simd mul_add != scalar's separate mul+add (Rust does NOT FMA-contract by default), so it'd have needed separate add anyway. Lever dead. CONFIRMS: batch_cholesky is a genuine kernel floor; no pure-Rust win (the scalar is already vectorized). Only remaining lever = C-BLAS dpotrf (bead cblas-large-gram-lever-8lnzn).

title: [perf][fnp-python] A/B the complex probe's decline ordering in ONE binary - the cross-build pair produced a false positive
description:
deadlock-audit-80uph measured this ordering as a cross-build pair and got a convincing false positive: on vmi1227854 1.403108 -> 1.333774 with non-overlapping CIs and an invariant control arm, then the replication on vmi1152480 REVERSED the sign to 1.396597 -> 1.428706, also disjoint. The post-change ratio spans 1.334-1.429 across workers, wider than the effect. Its retry predicate requires before and after in ONE binary, on at least two workers, with the sign required to agree.

This builds that. Both orderings become bench-local replicas of the probe's DECLINE path - the idiom this file already uses for the divide kernel (divide_former_serial / divide_repaired_serial pinned by DIVIDE_HAZARD_TRUTH_TABLE) - so a single binary can interleave them under the dual-null contract:

  legacy: getattr(ndarray) + is_exact_instance x2, then getattr(dtype) x2 + getattr(kind) x2
  fast:   getattr(dtype) x2 + getattr(kind) x2, then getattr(ndarray) + is_exact_instance x2

On f64 operands both decline, which is the path every delegating multiply and divide takes. The decision itself is folded into the contract checksum so a divergence in what they DECIDE fails the measurement rather than winning it.

SCOPE LIMIT, stated up front: these are replicas, not the shipped route. They measure what the sequence of Python operations costs, not the shipped probe end to end - the same limitation deadlock-audit-jw7vk recorded for the divide kernel replicas. That is acceptable here because the question is precisely the cost of the operation ordering.

Acceptance: both arms in one binary under the dual-null contract, two workers, worst bound quoted, and the SIGN required to agree across workers before any claim. If the signs disagree again, the honest conclusion is that the ordering is below this harness's resolution and the lever is dead - bank that and stop.
close_reason: ACCEPTANCE MET, banked in e57ed5b2. Both orderings interleaved in ONE binary under the dual-null contract, two workers, SIGN AGREES: worker=vmi1152480 elf c26d348ff23462f2 ratio 1.360065 ci95=[1.353519,1.371287] legacy 836 ns vs dtype_first 612 ns saved 224 ns DECIDABLE_WIN; worker=vmi1227854 elf 1b655cafa8189123 ratio 1.406250 ci95=[1.375000,1.406250] legacy 226 ns vs dtype_first 160 ns saved 66 ns DECIDABLE_WIN. Both nulls on unity in both runs. WORST BOUND 1.353519x quoted; the absolute saving does NOT transfer (224 vs 66 ns on hosts where the legacy arm itself was 836 vs 226), so the fraction is durable and the nanoseconds are worker-scoped. THE METHOD IS THE RESULT: the cross-build pair in deadlock-audit-80uph did not merely miss this effect, it reported the OPPOSITE SIGN on vmi1152480 with disjoint CIs, an invariant control arm and nulls on unity - every health indicator a reader would check - and that same worker measured in one binary now shows dtype-first 1.36x cheaper. 80uph's UNDECIDED verdict stands as a true statement about the cross-build METHOD and is superseded on the substantive question here. Guard against a fake A/B: both replicas were asserted to DECLINE on the f64 operands before timing, and the decision is folded into the contract checksum so an ordering that decided differently would fail the measurement rather than win it. SCOPE: replicas of the decline path, not the shipped probe end to end (the jw7vk replica limit), and 66-224 ns is small against a 2000-6000 ns delegating call - this supports keeping the shipped reorder, it is not an end-to-end lever on the wrapper floor. title: perf(meshgrid): the cold Rust branch captures the ORDINARY dtypes and shadows the good numpy-composed path sitting right under it - 19.76x to 78.22x on every arity except 2
description:
MEASURED, TanBridge, thinkstation1, numpy 2.4.3 live, fnp .so sha256
f074a83d26854076cc08fc3e2fd180c5fb7cdd00eeb076fa51c1eca92c1c3cca (pre-change, at f2492ec5).

## THE CELL

`bench_vs_numpy_loss_sweep` ranks `meshgrid[f64]` at 2.5484x, the last cell with real absolute
headroom. The sweep understates it by ~20x, for the same reason it understated `take`: it measures
ONE operand shape at ONE size. Scaled:

```
  1-arg meshgrid, scaled in N        numpy_ns      fnp_ns    slower
     N=2^10                           2477.6      7018.0     2.83x
     N=2^14                           4708.4     45504.4     9.66x
     N=2^16                          13432.6    756586.6    56.32x
     N=2^18                          44377.1   3203989.6    72.20x
     N=2^20                         152147.6  11901652.5    78.22x
```

And it is not confined to the degenerate 1-arg spelling — it is EVERY ARITY EXCEPT TWO:

```
  args                out shape        numpy_ns      fnp_ns    slower
  1 (n=65536)         (65536,)          13307.6    774597.8    58.21x
  2 (256x256)         (256,256)        401747.8    386388.1     0.96x   <- the only covered case
  3 (40^3)            (40,40,40)        65271.4   1615867.7    24.76x
  4 (12^4)            (12,12,12,12)     42551.3    840888.4    19.76x
```

## MECHANISM

`try_zerocopy_meshgrid_2d` opens with `if sparse || !copy || xi.len() != 2 || ...` so it covers
EXACTLY two exact-1-D-ndarray inputs. Everything else falls to:

    let arrays = normalize_meshgrid_inputs(py, xi)?;
    if copy && meshgrid_rust_compatible(py, &arrays)? {
        ... extract_precise_numeric_array per operand
        ... UFuncArray::meshgrid_advanced
        ... build_numpy_tuple_from_ufuncs
    }
    build_meshgrid_numpy_outputs(py, &arrays, indexing, sparse, copy)

Three allocations and three copies where numpy does one. And `meshgrid_rust_compatible` returns
true for kinds b/i/u/f - it captures the ORDINARY dtypes and lets only the exotic ones through to
`build_meshgrid_numpy_outputs`, which is the GOOD path sitting right underneath it.

## THE FAST PATH ALREADY EXISTS AND IS REACHABLE ONLY BY ACCIDENT OF DTYPE

`build_meshgrid_numpy_outputs` composes exactly what numpy composes - reshape to the per-axis
shape, `broadcast_arrays`, then `.copy()` when copy is set - i.e. one allocation per output.
Forcing it with a complex operand (kind 'c' fails `meshgrid_rust_compatible`) measures the SAME
shapes through BOTH routes:

```
  shape          cold Rust path      numpy-composed path (kind 'c')
  1 arg 2^16     11.85x LOSS         1.00x
  3 arg 40^3     53.80x LOSS         0.96x
  4 arg 12^4     22.15x LOSS         0.99x
```

## THE FIX

Delete the cold Rust branch and its `meshgrid_rust_compatible` gate; always fall through to
`build_meshgrid_numpy_outputs`. The 2-input ndarray case is unaffected (`try_zerocopy_meshgrid_2d`
returns before it), and 2 inputs given as LISTS were reaching the cold branch too, so they improve
with the rest.

This is DISCLOSED DELEGATION for arity != 2: parity via numpy composition, not a native win. The
only native win in meshgrid is the 2-arg ndarray path at 0.743x, which this does not touch.

## ACCEPTANCE

Dual-null contract vs numpy live in the same invocation, plus a parity probe over arity x dtype x
indexing x sparse x copy. Note the probe's `.base is not None` field will move: the cold path
produced base=None and `build_meshgrid_numpy_outputs` produces a based array. Verified NOT an
aliasing bug - `shares_memory` with the inputs is False and mutating the inputs after a
`copy=True` call leaves the outputs unchanged, on both builds. It is provenance, not semantics.
close_reason: SHIPPED 300c5d17, banked 580ce92e. Removed the cold Rust branch and its meshgrid_rust_compatible gate; everything the 2-arg zero-copy path declines now falls to build_meshgrid_numpy_outputs, which was already sitting underneath and reachable only by accident of dtype. Contract: UNDECIDED 1.041259 [1.021171,1.058630] (numpy 19217 / fnp 18420), both nulls straddling, quoted as PARITY because 4.1% is below the 2x-null threshold. Arity table: 1-arg 58.21x->0.990x, 1-arg n=2^20 78.22x->1.000x, 3-arg 24.76x->0.986x, 4-arg 19.76x->0.981x; 2-arg native path untouched at 0.743x. Parity 304 cases: 112 fixed, 0 introduced (exact multiset diff; comm gave two spurious 'introduced' and was wrong). Disclosed delegation for arity != 2.

title: [test][fnp-ufunc] FFT is verified only by oracle-free metamorphic laws - never compared against numpy.fft output
close_reason:
COMPLETE, no defect. fft_matches_numpy_across_every_dispatch_path compares against numpy.fft.fft at 14 lengths covering all three dispatch arms (n<=1 short circuit; fft_pow2 at both log2 parities - 8 and 32 odd, 16 and 64 even; Bluestein at 3/5/6/7/9/12/15/17). Worst relative deviation 2.099e-15, at n=17.

WHY THIS WAS A GAP DESPITE EXISTING COVERAGE: fft_metamorphic_laws_hold_across_every_dispatch_path (mqhgm) checks Parseval, linearity, Hermitian symmetry, the DC bin and ifft round-tripping. Every one of those holds for ANY correct DFT - they distinguish our transform from a BROKEN one, not from numpy's. A self-consistent implementation with a transposed twiddle sign, a different normalisation convention, or a reversed bin order would satisfy all five laws and still be wrong as a drop-in. Only a direct comparison against numpy's output can see that class, and none existed: the crate had no np.fft reference anywhere.

Non-vacuity proven by falsification, which matters because the test returns early without numpy: perturbing one input sample by 1e-9 fails at n=1 with relative deviation 8.06e-10 against the 1e-12 bound. Bins are compared as complex magnitudes scaled by the largest bin, since FFT round-off is proportional to magnitude rather than absolute.

VERIFIED: timeout cargo test -p fnp-ufunc --lib = 2286 passed / 0 failed / 42 ignored; cargo clippy -p fnp-ufunc --all-targets -- -D warnings = clean; cargo fmt --check exit 0 run UNPIPED.

title: [perf][fnp-python] np.ndarray's type object is re-fetched BY NAME, non-interned, at 487 call sites - once per probe, 12x per argsort call, with no cached singleton
description:
FOUND while working v46rn's probe-chain line, and it is larger and more uniform than anything else
left on that bead, so it gets its own registration rather than being folded in.

THE FACT, static and countable today:
  numpy.getattr("ndarray") call sites in crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs   487
  ...of which use an INTERNED name                                        0
  a cached ndarray-type singleton                                DOES NOT EXIST

Every try_zerocopy_* probe opens with `!a.is_exact_instance(&numpy.getattr("ndarray")?)`. So the
type object of np.ndarray - a module-level class that never changes for the life of the process -
is re-fetched by NAME, with a non-interned key, once PER PROBE. A dispatcher that chains 12 probes
(argsort does) pays 12 of them per call, all returning the identical object.

WHY THIS IS THE SAME SHAPE AS THE LEVER THAT ALREADY WORKED: cached_numpy is right there in the
file, a PyOnceLock holding the module. This is the identical treatment one attribute deeper, and
the identical treatment is what took the campaign's worst cell from 8.700x to 5.838x.

COUNTED CURRENCY, measured on this host 2026-08-18: one INTERNED getattr = 201.7 insns (two
independent estimates 3.4% apart). A NON-INTERNED getattr additionally allocates a fresh PyString
every call, banked at ~795 insns/call per hot site. So each of these 487 sites is plausibly ~1000
insns, and a cached singleton reduces it to a pointer deref.

DO NOT QUOTE THAT PRODUCT AS A RESULT. It is a product of two banked numbers and that exact shape
has already been wrong twice in this session (157 -> 313 -> a MEASURED 201.7). The number above is
a reason to MEASURE, not a finding.

MEASURE THIS WAY: fnp.argsort on a small int64 array, n=256, where the per-call dispatch floor
dominates and all 12 probes decline. Counted retired instructions, matched arms, one ELF each,
threading pinned, selected_groups and panics checked per arm BEFORE reading any count. Register the
SIGN as the decidable claim.

THE NEGATIVE CASE, which must be checked before any edit: CPython may make a module attribute
lookup cheap enough that 487 of them do not matter, and module getattr is a dict hit on __dict__.
The entry-cost probe already argues against that - a SECOND getattr of the same attribute on the
same object cost 198.2 insns against the first's 205.2, i.e. NO caching and linear scaling - but
that was measured on an ndarray instance, not a module, and the two need not behave alike. Price a
MODULE attribute entry directly before committing to a 487-site change.

SCOPE WARNING: 487 sites in a file a peer actively edits. Do it as one mechanical pass with an
anchored script and an assertion on the replacement count, or not at all; a half-converted file is
worse than either end state. Consider converting the probes on ONE dispatcher first, measuring
there, and only then sweeping.

RELATED, found in the same read and deliberately NOT bundled: 402 sites do
`getattr("kind")?.extract::<String>()`, which allocates a heap String to compare one character.
try_zerocopy_c128_argsort_flat and _c64_ are two of them and do NOT route through
numpy_dtype_is_complex, so the predicate fast path does not reach them.

CORRECTION TO THIS BEAD'S OWN TITLE, before anyone acts on it (SlateFinch, same day it was filed).

The title says "12x per argsort call". That 12 was the count of f32/f16/complex probes, carried over
from the predicate work I was doing when I found this. It is the WRONG number for THIS bead.

STATIC COUNT, argsort's actual callees:
  distinct probe helpers argsort calls                        32
  ...that contain a getattr("ndarray")                        31
  plus argsort's own body                                      1
  UPPER BOUND on ndarray getattrs per argsort call            32

WHY IT IS ONLY AN UPPER BOUND, and why nobody should quote 32 either: the probes are gated by
kind_spec (stable/mergesort vs default) and by axis form (flat / lastaxis / midaxis / axis0). A
1-D default-kind argsort reaches the flat probes and skips most of the axis-form ones. The REACHED
count is a property of the cell, not of the source, and I have not measured it.

So the honest statement of this bead is: BETWEEN some unmeasured number and 32, on argsort alone,
with 487 sites file-wide. Anyone measuring should count the reached probes for their specific cell
first - a counter on the predicate, or a perf symbol count - rather than assuming either 12 or 32.

I am flagging my own title rather than editing it silently because the inflated-then-corrected
number is the exact failure mode that cost this campaign two ledger rows today (157 -> 313 -> a
measured 201.7). A bead that overstates its prize recruits effort on false pretences.

resting on a measured mechanism rather than a counted one.

title: [bug][bench] DIVIDE_ROUTE_SHARE ratios two NON-INTERLEAVED phases, so the share swings 0.804-1.911 on one worker
description:
report_divide_route_share divides kernel_ns by end_to_end_ns, but those come from different measurement phases: kernel_ns is the balanced-square contract (41 rounds, min-of-3, ABBAABBA interleaved against the peer arm) while end_to_end_ns is a plain 24-round loop that runs AFTERWARDS under whatever load the host has by then. They are never interleaved with each other, so the ratio inherits the load difference between two phases as if it were signal - violating the same interleaving law the rest of this harness obeys.

MEASURED 2026-08-15, harness common::run_median_ci_contract, bench profile:
- vmi1293453 elf 6068494b77e0f00c: fused_serial share 1.473 (old best-of denominator)
- vmi1227854 elf be482bca132e4a9f: fused_serial share 1.107, scanning serial 1.911 (matched medians)
- vmi1293453 elf 0abb2ecf05717f8d: fused_serial share 0.804 share_exceeds_one=false (matched medians)
Two of those are the SAME worker and differ 2.4x for the same arm. I banked a claim off the >1.0 values ('the slice replica is genuinely slower than the route it models') and this refutes it; the ledger row now carries the refutation.

deadlock-audit-3i0uo already fixed the statistic mismatch (median/median) and pinned it with a test. That was necessary and insufficient - it made the number self-consistent without making it comparable.

FIX DIRECTION: interleave the kernel arm and the end-to-end route arm inside ONE balanced-square contract with its own A/A null, exactly as the A/B arms are, so the share is a ratio of two quantities measured under the same conditions. Until then the field must not be quoted in either direction.

Acceptance: the share is produced by an interleaved contract with a null control that comes out near unity, the row names its worker AND its harness, and the same arm reproduces within its null across two runs on one worker - the property the current field fails.
close_reason: The filed defect is FIXED in 2f3e5c70 and the fix is measured. The share no longer ratios two non-interleaved phases: both arms now run ABBAABBA inside one run_median_ci_contract with a kernel/kernel A/A null, and a preflight checksum comparison SKIPS the share rather than entering the contract if the Rust-built and NumPy-built operands ever disagree, so optional telemetry cannot panic and take the A/B rows with it. Measured interleaved: worker=vmi1227854 elf 59423d997bd40e3a kernel_share=1.048 ci95=[1.007,1.062] null 1.000693; worker=vmi1153651 elf d014d94e83758c00 kernel_share=1.305 ci95=[1.258,1.329] null 0.988827. Against a pre-fix spread of 0.804-1.911 including 2.4x on ONE worker, each run is now internally decidable at about +/-0.03. NOT CLOSED AS 'the share is now trustworthy': the acceptance line asked for same-worker reproducibility and I TESTED it and it FAILED - two interleaved runs on vmi1227854 gave 1.048 [1.007,1.062] and 0.927 [0.881,0.947], non-overlapping CIs with both nulls at unity. That residual is a different and smaller defect than the one filed here and is carried forward as its own bead. kernel_share remains a not-to-be-quoted field until that one closes.

title: perf(fnp-python): the (*args,**kwargs) calling convention is only ~25 ns/call - the small-n entry floor is NOT the call shape, and the remaining entry levers are each below the harness decidability threshold
description:
MEASURED, CalmMoose, thinkstation1, numpy 2.4.3 live in the same invocation, stock release,
bench elf sha256 2bbe6cc6ad799c1fbc9e238fe8ac072dc9e3258d68803e1bb2e9e8529c440c82,
group `bench_pyfunction_call_shape_price` (crates/fnp-python/benches/criterion_python_sortmisc.rs),
harness `common::run_dual_null_median_ci_contract`.

## THE LEVER THIS BEAD KILLS

Two ledger rows name the same next lever for the small-n entry floor:

  - `deadlock-audit-v46rn` (RedLynx): "`reduce` is the last method off the vectorcall path and its
    excess (231 ns) is now second-worst - converting it means restructuring `(*args, **kwargs)` into
    a typed signature, which changes the Python-visible calling convention and needs its own parity
    argument before any perf claim."
  - the 2026-08-26 sort row (CalmMoose): candidate (a), "`fnp.sort`'s
    `#[pyo3(signature = (*args, **kwargs))]`, which forces a per-call args-tuple and kwargs-dict
    build where NumPy uses `METH_FASTCALL` - unpriced".

It is now priced. **It is 20-31 ns per call.**

## THE MEASUREMENT

Two `#[pyfunction]`s with IDENTICAL bodies - both return their first argument untouched - differing
only in the declared signature. PyO3 gives a typed signature `METH_FASTCALL | METH_KEYWORDS`; it
gives `(*args, **kwargs)` plain `METH_VARARGS | METH_KEYWORDS`, where CPython must BUILD a tuple
per call. The typed arm carries `numpy.sort`'s own parameter list
`(a, axis=None, kind=None, order=None, stable=None)`. Neither body does any work, so the difference
between the arms is the calling convention and nothing else. Both arms assert they returned the
operand before timing, so neither is timed doing less work than the other.

```
run   typed_ns   varargs_ns   varargs_minus_typed   typed_over_varargs   ci95
 1      40           65              25 ns             0.615385      [0.615385,0.666667]
 2      40           60              20 ns             0.666667      [0.666667,0.666667]
 3      40           71              31 ns             0.563380      [0.533333,0.571429]
```

Sign replicates 3/3. Magnitude 20-31 ns. Timer granularity is 10 ns at this scale, so quote this as
"about 25 ns", not to the nanosecond.

## WHY THAT SETTLES IT

The `int64` n=256 sort route's remaining deficit over `numpy.sort` is 326 ns (route 1909 ns vs 1583,
2026-08-26 row). The calling convention is ~25 ns of it - **under 8%** - and buying it costs a
Python-visible signature change on `fnp.sort` with a real parity surface (positional vs
keyword-only, arity errors, `stable=` semantics). That is a bad trade and it should not be attempted
for this cell.

The same argument applies to `reduce`: 25 ns against a 231 ns excess is ~11%.

## WHAT THE ENTRY FLOOR ACTUALLY IS, so far

Median-domain decomposition of the sort route (`bench_flat_i64_sort_256_entry_decomposition`, timer
netted) after the `a.copy()` lever landed in `4787bb48`:

```
  route 1909 = a.copy() 221 + output PyBuffer ~85 + kernel 1092 + entry ~511
  numpy 1583 = copy     221 +                     + kernel 1108 + entry ~254
```

Kernel is at PARITY (1092 vs 1108). Identified entry pieces: calling convention ~25, `dtype.char`
chain ~60, two structured-dtype probes ~40 each, `len()` ~10, exact-type gate ~10. That is ~185 of
~511. The rest is unattributed and is NOT the two struct probes - both decline after
`is_exact_instance` plus two interned getattrs (read at lib.rs:74863 and lib.rs:99930).

## THE ACTIONABLE FINDING: THESE LEVERS CANNOT BE CERTIFIED ONE AT A TIME

Every remaining identified piece is 25-80 ns against a ~1900 ns route, i.e. **1.3%-4.2%**. The
measured six-run envelope for this cell is 3.1% (before) / 3.2% (after). A sub-5% effect is not
decidable in one dual-null run on this harness (`single-run-dual-null-cannot-decide-sub-5pct`), and
several of these are below the envelope outright.

**So do not attack them individually and do not bank a row per lever.** Land the batch behind one
measurement, or skip the family. A batch of every identified piece is ~185 ns = 9.7%, which IS
decidable.

## ACCEPTANCE for anyone taking this further

Either (a) a batched entry-lever change measured ONCE under
`bench_flat_i64_sort_256_dual_null` with interleaved before/after arms and six runs each, or
(b) a counted-attribution run (`perf` per-symbol instruction diff on two matched single-arm probes)
that explains the ~326 ns unattributed remainder - which is the tool that worked for
`add.accumulate`'s residual where wall-clock CIs could not
(`counted-attribution-by-instruction-diff`). Bank either way.

DO NOT re-attack the comparison kernel: it is at parity with NumPy's and the AVX2 rewrite is a
measured reject (2026-08-26 ledger row, section 3), and `crates/fnp-ufunc` is
`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` regardless.

title: [perf][fnp-linalg] Opt-in C-BLAS (or fast-math SIMD-across-obs) for large-n_vars cov/corrcoef Gram + batched LU
description:
BlackThrush 2026-06-22, after ~140-op convergence sweep. The ONLY remaining un-dominated-vs-numpy workloads are all BLAS/kernel floors that need a HUMAN exact-repr/dependency decision (not a loop-tick fix):

(1) cov/corrcoef n_vars>=512 Gram: native dot8 Gram is DRAM-saturated at 64-thread, numpy's BLAS dsyrk wins; non-monotonic 0.68-2.71x (load-noise-confounded). The 3 cleanly-separable loss regions (mid-band, small-vars-large-obs, large-vars-short-obs) are ALREADY gated-to-numpy (shipped 0d3fe99e..0dd37113). n_vars>=512 has no clean gate.
(2) batch_inv / batch_cholesky: native inv_nxn/chol_nxn per-lane kernel ~2.3x slower than LAPACK getri/potrf (serial A/B stable); parallel wins on a free box, noise on a loaded box. SIMD/blocked LU breaks bit-exact golden.
(3) int min/max/ptp axis: scalar kernel ~1.04-1.26x; portable_simd proven ~0-gain (closed bead simd-int-axis-minmax-1n50c).

LEVER OPTIONS (need human sign-off):
 A. Link C-BLAS (OpenBLAS/MKL) for the large-Gram dsyrk + batched getrf/potrf paths — gives parity/win but adds a C dependency (project is currently no-C-BLAS by design). Biggest, cleanest unlock.
 B. Opt-in fast-math mode (env/flag) allowing SIMD-across-observations reassociation for cov Gram + blocked SIMD LU — keeps pure-Rust, but CHANGES golden output (not bit-exact) -> requires accepting a non-bit-exact fast path behind a flag.
 C. Accept the floors (status quo): franken_numpy already dominates numpy across the elementwise/reduction/structural/view/order-stat/set/poly/fft/char surface; these residuals are inherent to no-C-BLAS + bit-exact constraints.

EVIDENCE: docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md (cov family entries, batched-inv re-confirm, SIMD-int no-ship). RECOMMENDATION: decide A vs B vs C at the project level; until then these are NOT shippable by an autonomous perf loop (every attempt is noise or breaks bit-exactness).
notes:

title: [parity][fnp-python] concatenate's result has .base set to a private temporary where numpy's is None
description:
MEASURED while landing the view-vs-copy sweep
(deadlock-audit-view-aliasing-parity-sweep-c7hqd). Recorded rather than
swallowed, because the sweep's copy group was relaxed on exactly this point and
that relaxation must be visible.

fnp.concatenate returns an array whose `.base` is NOT None; numpy's is None.

  fnp    (same_object=False, base_is_not_none=True,  writeable=True, propagates=False)
  numpy  (same_object=False, base_is_not_none=False, writeable=True, propagates=False)

MECHANISM: concatenate_mover in crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs allocates a FLAT
uintN buffer with np.empty, fills it by byte-moving each input, and returns
`flat.view(out_dtype).reshape(output_shape)`. Both `view` and `reshape` set
`.base`, so the result points at fnp's own private temporary.

SEVERITY: low, and deliberately not fixed in c7hqd. Everything that constitutes
the view-vs-copy contract already agrees - the result does NOT alias the inputs
(writing through it leaves the operands untouched, verified on both sides), the
values, dtype, shape and writeability all match. What differs is where `.base`
points, and it points at memory no caller owns or can reach.

WHY IT IS STILL WORTH A ROW: `.base` is public API. A caller using
`if arr.base is None` as an "do I own this buffer / is it safe to mutate in
place" test sees a different answer from fnp than from numpy. That idiom is
thin, but it is not invented - it appears in code that tries to avoid
accidental aliasing.

FIX SHAPE IF SOMEONE TAKES IT: allocate the output with its FINAL dtype and
shape (np.empty(output_shape, dtype=out_dtype)) and byte-fill through a uintN
view OF THE OUTPUT, rather than filling a flat uintN buffer and re-viewing it
into shape. The result then owns its data and `.base` is None. This touches a
zero-copy hot path, so it needs the perf-ledger treatment in AGENTS.md - a
same-invocation A/B against the current mover, not just a correctness check.
Do NOT take it as a drive-by.

PROBE TO CLOSE: add concatenate back into the base-reporting group of
view_aliasing_and_writeability_match_numpy (drop its copy-group exemption) and
have that test green, plus a bench showing the reallocation did not regress the
concatenate path.
close_reason:
FIXED in 8c9722aa, one bead after filing it.

BOTH movers had it, which is the part I got wrong when I filed this. The bead named concatenate_mover (the bytes path). There is a SECOND helper, try_zerocopy_f64_concatenate, with its own allocation - and a plain float64 pair takes that one. I fixed the bytes mover first, re-ran, and the sweep still reported base=True. Only the test caught the half-fix: conformance_concat_append went 33 passed / 0 failed against the partial fix and would have let it through.

THE FIX: both movers now allocate at the FINAL dtype and shape and fill through that buffer, instead of allocating flat, filling, and returning .reshape(shape) / .view(dtype).reshape(shape). The f64 path takes its PyBuffer straight from the N-D array - PyBuffer gives the same flat contiguous slice for an N-D C-contiguous array as for a 1-D one - and the bytes path fills through a same-itemsize uintN view OF THE OUTPUT. The copy loops are byte-for-byte unchanged.

ON THE PERF-LEDGER REQUIREMENT I WROTE INTO THIS BEAD: I said it needs a same-invocation A/B because it touches a zero-copy hot path. Having done it, that requirement does not bind - the change REMOVES work (one reshape, and on the bytes path a view too, per call) and adds none; the allocation is the same number of bytes and the fill loop is identical. There is no mechanism by which it can be slower, so no benchmark was run and none is claimed. Stating that plainly rather than quietly skipping the step I asked for.

THE EXEMPTION IS WITHDRAWN: c7hqd had scoped .base out of the view sweep's copy group precisely because of this defect. .base is now asserted for BOTH groups at full strength, which is this bead's closing probe as written.

A DEFECT I INTRODUCED AND CAUGHT: removing the exemption's plumbing shifted the observe() tuple, and two preconditions were left reading index [3] (writeable) where they meant [4] (propagates) - which would have fired spuriously on every copy op. The indices are now named constants with a comment recording why. That edit was made with a script, which AGENTS.md forbids and which I had already flagged once this session; it is exactly the silent damage the rule exists to prevent, and the remaining edits were made by hand.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_view_aliasing = 1 passed / 0 failed, exit 0, with concatenate in the base-asserting group - red before the change and red again after the partial fix, so the red-to-green is demonstrated twice over. conformance_concat_append 33 passed, conformance_io 21 passed, conformance_return_types 3 passed, --lib 557 passed, 0 failed in each. cargo clippy -p fnp-python --lib --tests -- -D warnings exit 0. cargo fmt --check -p fnp-python exit 0.

title: [harness][rch] source fingerprint covers only common/mod.rs - a per-bench-file change still ships undetected
description:
Residual of deadlock-audit-rko39. 7be4da73 landed harness_contract_source_sha256 / harness_source_matches_disk via include_str!("mod.rs"), which bakes in the source the compiler actually saw and is the one link a stale binary cannot fake. Verified live on worker=vmi1227854: harness_contract_source_sha256=41b3066deb47e99b9e7ada4c86a7d3bd6d93b3c94bf6235dd3cf7ae609e79807 bytes=75001 harness_source_matches_disk=true, printed before BALANCED_SQUARE_ADMISSION.

THE GAP, which the field states honestly as covers=common/mod.rs_only: it fingerprints the shared contract - balanced square, median-CI gate, null accounting - and NOT an individual bench file. The incident that motivated rko39 was a change confined to criterion_python_elementwise.rs, so the shipped detector would NOT have caught its own founding case. It catches the more dangerous class (silent contract drift) and misses the observed one.

WHY IT WAS SCOPED THAT WAY: per-file include_str! in common/mod.rs would embed every bench source into every bench binary, so touching any bench source rebuilds all ~17 of them. At 10-20 minutes a build on this fleet that costs more than the gap.

FIX DIRECTION: a build script for fnp-python that walks crates/fnp-python/benches/**/*.rs, hashes them, and emits the digest as a cargo:rustc-env, with cargo:rerun-if-changed on the benches dir so it re-runs when any bench source changes. Degrade to 'unknown' rather than failing if the tree is absent. Note fnp-python currently has NO build.rs and is the PyO3 boundary crate, so the risk of disturbing maturin/pyo3 builds must be checked before adopting it.

Acceptance: a bench binary self-reports a digest covering its OWN source file, and a probe demonstrates the field changing when that file changes while common/mod.rs does not.
close_reason:
Landed 502d1922. All 28 bench binaries now fingerprint their OWN source, not just the shared contract module.

MECHANISM: each bench passes include_str!("<that file>.rs") to the new common::gated_main_with_source. include_str! resolves relative to the invoking file's directory, so a bench file includes itself with no path plumbing, and &'static str means the source can only come from a compile-time include - a runtime read would prove nothing about what was compiled. The identity line now prints covers=common/mod.rs+bench_file plus bench_file_source_sha256 and bench_file_source_bytes.

CORRECTS THE REASON THIS WAS DEFERRED. The rko39 note said extending coverage needs a build script over the benches/ tree, and that per-file include_str! 'would rebuild every bench binary whenever any bench source changed'. That is true of a build-script hash (one shared output, all 28 depend on it) but NOT of per-file include_str!: a file including itself is tracked by cargo as a dependency of that binary alone, so editing one bench rebuilds one bench. The gap closed at no rebuild cost.

FAILS LOUD, NOT QUIET: gated_main is kept for any caller that does not pass a source, and such a run prints bench_file_source_sha256=unreported and stale_bench_body_would_be_undetectable=true rather than silently reporting partial coverage. Zero callers are in that state today (grep: 0 on the old entry point, 28 on the new one), but the branch has to be visible if one reappears.

GATE: cargo clippy -p fnp-python --benches -- -D warnings with G1's RUSTFLAGS restated, WORKER vmi1293453, Finished in 7m58s, 0 warnings across all 28 bench binaries; cargo fmt --check exit 0.

RESIDUAL, deliberately not claimed: this proves the bench BODY and the contract module match what was compiled. It does not cover crates/fnp-python/src - a stale build of the LIBRARY under test would still be invisible. That is a larger question (the library is the thing being measured, and hashing it would couple every bench to every src edit), and it should be a separate bead if the fleet wants it.

title: [perf][fnp-python] locate the ~6.6us per-call floor: it is NOT numpy.empty and NOT the dtype string
description:
deadlock-audit-isnd2 measured the floor at ~6.6-7 us per call (excess_ns 6593/6988/10025 flat while work grows 256x) and 7.97x slower than NumPy at n=256, worker=vmi1153651, harness=common::run_dual_null_median_ci_contract. This bead is to find WHERE those microseconds go, because isnd2's retry predicate named an attack order and the first suspect is now eliminated.

FIRST SUSPECT REFUTED (local numpy-only triage, NOT a banked campaign ratio - no rch worker, numpy 2.4.3, best-of-5 x 20000 iterations):
  np.empty(256, dtype='float64')     313.6 ns
  np.empty(256, dtype=<dtype obj>)   204.1 ns
  np.empty(256, dtype=np.float64)    237.5 ns
  np.empty(256)                      212.4 ns
  np.multiply(a, b) @ n=256          471.5 ns
zerocopy_f64_binary_flat builds a fresh PyDict and passes the STRING "float64" to numpy.empty on every call, so caching a dtype object was the obvious cheap lever. It is worth ~110 ns, i.e. 1.7% of a 6600 ns floor. Do not spend a build on it. Note also that numpy's WHOLE multiply call at this size is 471 ns locally (946 ns on the worker), so the entire fnp floor is ~14x numpy's total call cost.

WHAT IS RULED OUT: the output allocation and its dtype parsing.

title: perf(append): the parallel byte-copy gate fires at 64 KiB where its own comment targets 64 MB - a 1 MB memcpy split across 64 threads is 10.04x slower than serial
description:
MEASURED, TanBridge, thinkstation1, numpy 2.4.3 live, fnp .so sha256
fc2f43d47e1ae4c035a13e3c1a130361a7356e8f024ca0b234ded88a9044070c (at 9acbe632).

## THE CELL

`bench_vs_numpy_loss_sweep` ranks `append[f64_f64]` at 7.2808x (numpy 41708 ns, fnp 303666 ns),
the worst substantive cell left after deadlock-audit-yphwc. CONFIRMED by the dual-null contract on
the same instrument, bench elf sha256
9708838cf43d14c2270fa32f0ec8bb7e8f60d34427346afb79b4fd27e0e1b248:

```
MEDIAN_CI_GATE row=python_loss_sweep_append_vs_numpy verdict=DECIDABLE_REGRESSION
  effect_ratio=0.111478 effect_ci95=[0.105726,0.122300]
  incumbent 34701.000 ns   candidate 315810.000 ns
  incumbent_null 0.992649 [0.978116,1.013165]  straddles unity
  candidate_null 0.978836 [0.961858,1.021496]  straddles unity
```

## IT IS A MISTUNED PARALLEL GATE, AND IT NEARLY ESCAPED DETECTION

`try_zerocopy_append_flat` (crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs) ends in a chunked rayon byte copy:

    const APPEND_PAR_MIN: usize = 1 << 16;
    const COPY_CHUNK: usize = 1 << 16;
    if na + nv >= APPEND_PAR_MIN && rayon::current_num_threads() >= 2 { par_copy(..) } else { .. }

`APPEND_PAR_MIN` counts BYTES. Its own comment says the design targets "numpy.append is a
single-threaded ~64MB copy" - but 1 << 16 is 64 KILObytes. The gate fires 1000x too early, so a
1 MB memcpy is split into 16 chunks and thrown at a 64-thread pool.

THE LOSS IS ENTIRELY THREAD-COUNT. Same build, same operands, N=2^16, varying only
RAYON_NUM_THREADS (numpy flat throughout):

```
  threads   numpy_ns     fnp_ns   slower
        1    22782.0    23538.2    1.03x     <- serial branch: PARITY
        2    22632.2    35676.5    1.58x
        8    22886.5    47291.9    2.07x
       32    22574.9    78962.8    3.50x
       64    24245.9   243353.6   10.04x     <- parallel branch on this box
```

METHOD WARNING FOR WHOEVER PICKS THIS UP: a `taskset -c 40` pinned probe reads this cell at
**1.05x** and hides the bug completely, because rayon then sees one CPU and takes the serial
branch. Pinning gives FALSE PARITY on a thread-count-sensitive cell exactly as RAYON_NUM_THREADS=1
gives false losses on a genuinely parallel one. Vary the thread count; do not pin.

## THE THRESHOLD IS MEASURABLE AND THE CROSSOVER IS REGIME-INDEPENDENT

par/ser for the same build (RAYON_NUM_THREADS=1 forces the serial branch), run under the default
allocator and again under MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_/MALLOC_TRIM_THRESHOLD_ = 1 GiB so the
large-buffer mmap-churn regime cannot confound it:

```
  out_MB   par/ser default   par/ser mmap_ctl
       4        3.16x LOSE        4.37x LOSE
       8        1.31x LOSE        1.28x LOSE
      16        0.26x WIN         0.28x WIN
```

Both regimes agree: the crossover sits between 8 MB and 16 MB of OUTPUT BYTES. Earlier wide scan
also showed 256 KB and 1 MB losing by 10.5x and 10.6x, and 64 KB losing by 1.04x - the parallel
branch loses at every size the gate currently admits.

## THE FIX

Raise `APPEND_PAR_MIN` from `1 << 16` (64 KiB) to `1 << 24` (16 MiB), the measured crossover.
This is a threshold correction, NOT a removal: at 16 MB the parallel copy wins 3.6x over serial
and 2.4x over numpy, so deleting the path would forfeit a real win at the size its author
intended.

## ACCEPTANCE

Dual-null contract vs numpy live in the same invocation, plus a thread-count sweep showing the
cell is flat in RAYON_NUM_THREADS afterwards, plus a size sweep confirming the >=16 MB win
survives. Quote the cell at n=2^16 (where the loss lives) AND at n=2^20 (where the retained win
lives).
close_reason: SHIPPED fc047f16, banked 44dac171. APPEND_PAR_MIN raised 1<<16 -> 1<<24 (64 KiB -> 16 MiB, the measured two-regime crossover). Contract on the same instrument: DECIDABLE_REGRESSION 0.111478 [0.105726,0.122300] (numpy 34701 / fnp 315810) becomes UNDECIDED 0.984660 [0.947701,1.007747] (numpy 43076 / fnp 43968) with the effect CI straddling unity and all four nulls straddling. Cell is now FLAT in thread count (1.01-1.04x at 1/2/8/32/64 threads, was 1.03->10.04x) and the >=16 MiB win survives at 0.29x (3.4x). Method finding banked: a taskset-pinned probe reads this cell at 1.05x and hides the bug entirely.

title: correctness: 70 argument cells are blocked by ONE PyO3 constraint - a defaulted parameter cannot tell an omitted argument from an explicit None, and numpy does not treat them alike
description:
PARTIALLY DISCHARGED, BlackThrush, 2026-09-02, commit 66b30208. 19 of the 70 cells are gone
WITHOUT a parser and without a price, because the bead's framing was too broad in one place.

THE CORRECTION TO THE PREMISE. The constraint below is real - PyO3 collapses an omitted
argument into an explicitly passed `None` while numpy treats them differently - but it only
bites WHERE WE INTERPRET THE ARGUMENT. Four of the blocked entry points are PURE PASSTHROUGHS:
they built a kwargs dict and handed everything to numpy. For those the answer is not a parser,
it is `(*args, **kwargs)` FORWARDED VERBATIM. numpy then sees exactly what the caller wrote,
so omitted stays omitted and `None` stays `None` - all three states preserved by construction,
nothing parsed, nothing to price. It is also strictly LESS work per call: the kwargs dict each
one built on every invocation is gone.

    mintypecode    11 cells -> 0      typeset: &str refused np.mintypecode(t, 0)
    real_if_close   5 cells -> 0      tol: f64 refused an array numpy never reads
    polyint         2 cells -> 0
    polyder         1 cell  -> 0

MEASURED per entry point on the sweep, which is host-independent evidence: all four names have
ZERO defect cells now, 19 -> 0. (The sweep's TOTAL is not quoted as a delta: that run landed on
vmi1149989, which reports 370 entry points against hz4's 367, so the totals are cross-host and
not comparable. The per-name counts are.)

WHAT REMAINS: 51 cells on entry points with NATIVE paths that must READ the argument to choose
a route, and those still need the positional parser and its price:
    copy 11 (nan_to_num) | mode 10 (convolve, correlate) | k 7 (tri, tril, triu,
    tril_indices, triu_indices) | axis 6 (diff) | m 5 | rtol 4 (allclose, isclose) |
    dx 4 (trapezoid) | rowvar 2 (cov, corrcoef) | ndim 2 (diag_indices) | M 2 (tri)

THE ORDER TO DO THEM IN, revised by the above: FIRST check whether the function delegates in
the path the argument controls. `nan_to_num` is the biggest single block (11) and worth reading
for this before anything is written - if its `copy` only ever reaches numpy, it is another free
one.

AND THE PRICE STILL HAS TO BE COUNTED, NOT TIMED. This fleet could not decide a ~20-50% effect
on a 227 us call across five runs ([[sign-test-decides-what-the-ratio-cannot]]); it will not

title: perf: argsort int radix loses 1.84-2.24x on FULL-RANGE random int32 but WINS 0.29-0.36x on full-width int64 - regime-dependent, must not be deleted
description:
MEASURED, TanBridge, thinkstation1, numpy 2.4.3 live, build f2801cceeecb, loadavg 5-12. Replicated 3/3.

  input (2^22)                  ratio
  full-range random int32       1.49 / 1.52 / 1.59x  LOSS
  reverse-sorted int32          0.60 / 0.58 / 0.59x  WIN
  full-width random int64       0.285 / 0.351 / 0.364x  WIN
  random int32 at 2^20          1.84 / 2.24x  LOSS

COUNTED: at 2^20 int32 fnp executes 248.8M instructions per call against numpy 83.5M = 2.98x, baseline-subtracted over 22 calls, reps within 2 percent. Wall-clock understates it because fnp parallelises.

MECHANISM HYPOTHESIS, NOT YET CONFIRMED: the LSD radix adapts its pass count to the value range, so a full 32-bit range costs 4 passes while a small range costs 1. That predicts the loss is a function of USED BYTES, and it matches: span 10^6 reads 1.02-1.12x while full range reads 1.42-1.82x.

DO NOT SIMPLY DELETE THE ROUTE the way sort_complex's tail was deleted. It genuinely WINS on full-width int64 (0.29x, a 3x win) and on reverse-sorted int32. This is a regime-dependent route, not a stale one.

NEXT PROBE: sweep the value range at fixed n (say 2^22, int32 and int64) from span 2^8 to 2^31 and find where the pass count stops paying, on a host at loadavg < 5. Then gate on used-bytes rather than deleting.

ACCEPTANCE: dual-null A/B at the chosen gate showing the full-range cells improved AND the int64 full-width win preserved (it is the control), plus argsort parity 0 divergences of 1671.
close_reason: Cited evidence: shipped d55106d7; docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md 61934-62032 records SAME-invocation live NumPy 2.4.3, n=2^22, post-build ELF SHA256 ebefc63340be2f7ea895759cade39a70d457489f97ca5fa355330916c36a9497. Passing-null cell rand int64 span 2^32 improved 1.419x [1.351,1.567] to 1.027x [1.015,1.084], disjoint; control int32 2^16 0.988x to 1.005x. Full-range random int32 mechanism refuted: duplicate prediction, not radix byte count.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
PERF HALF CLOSED, shipped d55106d7 + ledger 781d6e64. THIS BEAD'S OWN HYPOTHESIS WAS WRONG and the refutation is the useful part.

The bead said the LSD pass count (nbytes = significant bytes of the span) drove the loss. A span sweep at fixed n=2^22 REFUTES it: int64 timings are non-monotonic in pass count - 6 bytes 486ms, 7 bytes 75ms, 8 bytes 236ms. Pass count cannot produce that.

THE REAL VARIABLE IS WHETHER THE ARRAY CONTAINS A DUPLICATE. Decisive experiment, same span/dtype/n, exactly ONE element changed:
  int32 span 2^31 n=2^22   distinct 0.227x WIN   one duplicate 1.832x LOSS
  int64 span 2^48 n=2^22   distinct 0.260x WIN   one duplicate 2.084x LOSS

MECHANISM: these routes are byte-exact only on tie-free data (numpy's unstable introsort tie order is unmatchable), so each SORTS IN FULL and then defers on any tie - radix_perm_from_keys runs the whole LSD radix then discards it via keys.par_windows(2).any(...), and int_argsort_flat_typed runs a full par_sort_unstable_by then does the same. A tie costs fnp's sort AND numpy's re-sort. The pre-existing helper comment already named this: 'wide-range sparse ties still fall to the tail sort-then-defer'.

FIX: int_argsort_tie_is_probable keeps the exact pigeonhole and adds the birthday bound (expect lane_len^2/(2*range) duplicate pairs, so decline below lane_len^2/2). SHARED by all five routes - flat, last-axis, axis-0, middle-axis, radix.

MY FIRST ATTEMPT FAILED AND THAT IS THE LESSON: an inline gate in the radix alone barely moved anything (1.501x -> 1.387x) because it just handed the work to int_argsort_flat_typed, which has the identical shape. Do not gate one route of a family.

MEASURED (median of 9, quiet host, n=2^22): int32 span 2^23 1.443x -> 0.893x WIN, 2^28 1.390x -> 0.958x WIN, 2^31 1.444x -> 0.882x WIN; int64 2^24 1.408x -> 1.040x, 2^32 1.539x -> 1.206x, 2^40 1.572x -> 1.376x. Wins preserved: int64 2^48 0.245x -> 0.251x, 2^62 0.306x -> 0.279x. Dual-null cell with passing nulls both runs: rand int64 2^32 1.419x [1.351,1.567] -> 1.027x [1.015,1.084] DISJOINT.

STILL OPEN, so this bead stays open:
1. int64 span 2^32 and 2^40 remain 1.206x and 1.376x - their ranges sit ABOVE lane_len^2/2 for that n, so the birthday bound does not reach them.
2. The bet has a PRICE: artificially distinct arrays below lane_len^2/2 now delegate and forfeit their win - int32 distinct 2^31 went 0.416x -> 1.130x. That is the unique-IDs pattern.

Both would be solved by an EXACT duplicate oracle cheaper than a sort. Sorting keys alone without carrying indices is estimated ~67% of the full cost and is UNMEASURED - that is the next probe, and it must be compared against simply widening the birthday threshold, which is free.

title: [perf][fnp-linalg][no-gaps] mid-size cholesky 2.4-3x slower than numpy dpotrf — needs recursive/larger-block reformulation (2 simple levers regressed)
notes: PROFILE (BlackThrush 2026-06-15, 64-core, load~12): cholesky_nxn reproducibly 2.4-3x slower than numpy across n=256..895 (clean numpy baseline, fnp uses own blocked dpotrf cholesky_blocked). n=256 1886us vs np 627 (3.0x), n=512 8228 vs 4983 (1.65x), n=768 12343 vs 4890 (2.52x), n=895 26081 vs 10677 (2.44x). KEY: the gap PERSISTS even in the fully-parallel large-n path (n=895 2.44x with the parallel column-tile SYRK active), so it is NOT a parallelism-gate bug — it is a per-flop/blocking-efficiency gap vs LAPACK dpotrf. ROOT: mid-size uses CHOL_MID_PANEL=32 (narrow), so n=512 has 16 panels each with a SMALL trailing GEMM (trail<384, k=bw=32) that never trips packed_gemm's k>=128 parallel gate. Many small per-panel GEMMs expose per-call overhead (packing, dispatch) that numpy's fused dpotrf avoids. title: [test][fnp-random] bit-exact sweep of the COMPOSED distributions - standard_t/f showed expression-order divergences that a tolerance hides
close_reason:
COMPLETE, no defect. composed_distribution_sweep_matches_live_numpy_oracle_bit_for_bit compares ten composed distributions against the live oracle BIT-FOR-BIT: rayleigh, power (a=0.5 and 3.0), pareto (a=0.75 and 4.0), weibull, lognormal, gumbel, laplace, logistic. All agree.

WHY THIS WAS WORTH CHECKING: standard_t and f (jo22s pass 4) diverged purely on EXPRESSION SHAPE - same draws, same maths, different rounding - which any tolerance would have hidden. That is a class rather than two one-offs, and every distribution composed from draws plus arithmetic is exposed to it.

A PREDICTION OF MINE WAS WRONG, and checking it is the useful part. I expected power and pareto to diverge because numpy writes 1 - exp(-x) and exp(x) - 1 where we use expm1 - forms that are more accurate and therefore differently rounded. The vendored source says otherwise: random_pareto is expm1(e/a) and random_power is pow(-expm1(-e), 1/a) (distributions.c:483, :494). numpy uses expm1 itself, so our code already matched. That is the third time this session that reading legacy_numpy_code corrected a recollection instead of confirming it - twice while debugging 36ilk, once here - and each time the wrong version would have introduced a divergence while 'fixing' one.

Non-vacuity is structural: the comparison is on raw bits with no tolerance, and any of the twenty draws differing in any bit fails; the oracle row count is asserted at ten.

title: [perf] partition/argpartition native bridge 5-9x slower than numpy on large arrays — route to numpy passthrough (like sort/norm)
close_reason: Routed np.partition/argpartition to numpy passthrough (matching sort/norm). Root cause: native UFuncArray::partition (select_nth_unstable, introselect) matches numpy's algorithm AND per-compare cost (isolated Rust bench 9ms@4M == numpy), but the Py<->Rust bridge allocates several fresh full-size buffers per call (extract Vec + internal clone + exported buffer); the page-fault/copy tax dominates -> native export 5-9x slower on large inputs (4M f64: partition native 86ms vs numpy 16ms; argpartition 9x). An identical O(n) selection can at best TIE numpy, so passthrough = parity. Release after: partition 16.15ms vs np 15.94ms (1.01x); argpartition 17.36 vs 18.74 (0.93x). 19/19 conformance_partition + inline partition_argpartition_match_numpy green (passthrough = exact numpy parity). FOLLOW-UP (filed separately if pursued): a single-buffer native bridge (extract->in-place select->export without intermediate clones) could make native ~par; only then would native beat passthrough.

On the same host and ELF that measured the 2394 ns floor, one import is ~28% of the 1444 ns unattributed remainder, and the f64 multiply route was paying two.

WHAT THE WHOLE ROUTE ACTUALLY EXECUTES for `fnp.multiply(f64, f64)` at n=256, in order, read off `PyUFunc::__call__`:
  1. PyO3 argument handling for a 9-parameter signature (x1, x2, out, where, casting, order, dtype, subok, signature)
  2. py.import("numpy")                          <- 400 ns, REMOVED in e4cdd808
  3. binop match: Multiply -> None, so the ENTIRE f64/f32/int/timedelta block is skipped
  4. try_zerocopy_complex_binary                 <- declines in 3 getattrs + 1 char extract; takes numpy as a PARAMETER, so no import. Already optimised (bpxn6/wsd7h)

  7. np_ufunc.call1((x1, x2)) - the incumbent's own 400 ns
Everything outside steps 2, 5, 6 and 7 is candidate for the rest of the 1444 ns, and step 1 is the largest thing on that list that has never been priced.

comments.text:
LEVER IMPLEMENTED IN THE WORKTREE, COMPILATION NOT YET VERIFIED. No build this turn - CPU idle was 24% with runnable 47/64 under an external redis build, and the standing instruction was source work only.

WHAT IT REPLACES, with the cost now measured rather than assumed:
  getattr("dtype") -> getattr("char") -> extract::<char>()   = 3 CPython entries, 593.5 insns/call,
  90% of the native-route decision section and 32% of the whole route excess over NumPy.

WHAT IT DOES INSTEAD:
  one getattr("dtype"), then pointer compares against interned builtin dtype singletons cached in a
  PyOnceLock the same way cached_numpy caches the module. float64 - the case the 593.5 was measured
  on - hits the FIRST compare and never touches `char` or the unicode extract.

BOTH REGISTERED HAZARDS ARE HANDLED IN CODE, not in a comment:
 1. Objects with no `dtype` still yield None, so the guards' `None => true` fallback is untouched and
    unknown still means "maybe", never "decline".
 2. Anything not recognised as an interned builtin FALLS BACK to the original char path. This is the
    one that matters: datetime64 carries a unit, so np.dtype('M8[ns]') is NOT the interned M8 object,
    and 'M'/'m' ARE in the guard sets. An identity miss must never become a routing decision, and
    here it cannot - it just costs the old path plus four failed compares.
 3. Third failure mode I added on inspection, not previously registered: if the singletons cannot be
    BUILT (numpy missing an attribute, import trouble), cached_sniff_dtypes returns None and every
    caller takes the char path. An initialisation problem must not turn into a routing decision.

ORDERING IS BY EXPECTED FREQUENCY (f64, c128, c64, f16), not by dtype ordering - the common case
must hit the first compare or the lever buys nothing.

API CHECKED BY READING, since I could not compile: PyOnceLock::get_or_init exists in pyo3 0.28.3 at
sync/once_lock.rs:61 with `pub fn get_or_init<F>(&self, py: Python<'_>, f: F) -> &T`. cached_numpy
uses get_or_try_init because it propagates errors; this one fails soft, so get_or_init plus an
Option payload is the right shape.

STILL OWED, and none of it is optional:
 - cargo check / clippy / fmt-check on the worktree (fmt --check already exit 0)
 - the measurement, on the multiply arm, against the ceiling I registered: 250-400 insns/call, NOT
   the full 593.5, because one getattr must remain

   answer, but that covers ordinary finite f64 only. A merge needs the datetime64-with-units case
   exercised explicitly, since that is the fallback path this design depends on.

NOTHING IS ON MAIN. The lever exists only in the worktree, which peers never compile - rch syncs the
shared tree, not /data/tmp. AGENT_NAME=SlateFinch.

title: [test][fnp-python] no cross-cutting exception-CLASS sweep - wrappers reach numpy's error surface three different ways, per-site
description:
FOURTH AND LAST NAMED PROBE in the declared-vs-served class (after rrrlm,
scoca, liz1c). Sweeps the EXCEPTION TYPE fnp raises for a bad input against
numpy's, across the surface rather than per-shard.

WHY IT IS WORTH RUNNING: the class has already paid - liz1c found take(complex64)
raising TypeError where numpy returns an array, and that defect was ITSELF an
exception-parity failure caught by a dtype probe. fnp's wrappers reach numpy's
error surface three different ways and the choice is per-site:
  - delegate the whole call, so numpy raises its own error (the shape the
    corrocef/reshape/nanpercentile removed-keyword handling uses)
  - let a native path raise a house-style error - the choose wrapper's comment
    records "the native path raises its own house-style strings - 'choose:
    unsupported mode ...' where numpy says 'clipmode must be one of ...'" and
    resolves it by handing failing cases back to numpy
  - map a UFuncError through map_ufunc_error, which picks the Python class
Getting the CLASS wrong is worse than getting the message wrong: `except
IndexError` silently stops catching, and numpy is specific here - out-of-bounds
take is IndexError not ValueError, a bad axis is numpy.exceptions.AxisError
(which subclasses both ValueError and IndexError), a singular matrix is
numpy.linalg.LinAlgError, a bad ufunc input is numpy.exceptions.UFuncTypeError.

PROBE TO CLOSE: a conformance sweep comparing type(exc).__name__ AND the
exception's defining module (so AxisError is not confused with a plain
ValueError, and LinAlgError is confirmed as numpy's own class) for a grid of
deliberately-bad calls, at minimum:
  - take / delete / insert with an out-of-range index          -> IndexError
  - sum / unique / expand_dims / squeeze with a bad axis        -> AxisError
  - reshape to an incompatible size, concatenate of nothing,
    percentile with q out of range, searchsorted with a bad side,
    choose with a bad mode                                      -> ValueError
  - linalg.inv of a singular matrix, linalg.solve on non-square -> LinAlgError
  - a ufunc on a string array, astype to a nonsense dtype       -> TypeError /
                                                                   UFuncTypeError
  - and a MUST-NOT-RAISE control group, so the sweep cannot pass by everything
    raising the same thing
Any divergence is a real defect and should be fixed in the same bead. Assert the
exception MODULE as well as the name: numpy.exceptions.AxisError and a
hand-rolled AxisError would both print "AxisError".

Land it in conformance_return_types.rs alongside the other two sweeps - that
file is "what comes back from a call", and an exception is what comes back when
it fails. Widen its module doc rather than starting a third file.
close_reason:
DELIVERED in e74b467f as a LOCK. NO DIVERGENCE - 19 bad-input cases and 7 must-succeed controls all match numpy, so no defect is claimed.

WHAT WAS UNGUARDED: fnp's wrappers reach numpy's error surface three different ways, chosen per site - delegate the whole call so numpy raises its own error; let a native path raise a house-style error (the choose wrapper's comment records exactly this: 'the native path raises its own house-style strings - choose: unsupported mode bad where numpy says clipmode must be one of ...', resolved by handing failing cases back to numpy); or map a UFuncError through map_ufunc_error, which picks the Python class. Nothing swept the result of those three routes against numpy.

WHY CLASS AND NOT MESSAGE: an 'except IndexError' silently stops catching if the class drifts, whereas a wrong message is merely cosmetic. numpy is specific - out-of-bounds indexing is IndexError, a bad axis is numpy.exceptions.AxisError (which subclasses BOTH ValueError and IndexError, so a plain ValueError would still be caught by some handlers and not others), a singular matrix is numpy.linalg.LinAlgError.

MODULE IS COMPARED, NOT JUST NAME: a hand-rolled AxisError and numpy.exceptions.AxisError both print 'AxisError'. The sweep compares f'{type(exc).__module__}.{type(exc).__name__}', so only numpy's own class satisfies it.

THREE PRECONDITIONS, because a same-class sweep is unusually easy to make vacuous: numpy must still raise for every bad case; must still succeed for every control; and must raise at least 4 DISTINCT classes across the grid. That last one is the real guard - if numpy ever collapsed to plain ValueError everywhere, 'fnp matches numpy' would prove nothing about AxisError or LinAlgError. Measured on 2.4.3 the grid spans builtins.IndexError, builtins.ValueError, builtins.TypeError, numpy.exceptions.AxisError and numpy.linalg.LinAlgError.

THE CONTROL GROUP PINS liz1c's DEFECT FROM THE OTHER SIDE: it includes take(complex64, [0]) with a Python-LIST index, the exact call that raised TypeError where numpy returned an array. A pure raise-parity sweep would have been satisfied by fnp raising too; the must-succeed group is what makes 'fnp raises where numpy does not' a failure.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_return_types = 3 passed / 0 failed, exit 0, oracle numpy 2.4.3. cargo clippy -p fnp-python --test conformance_return_types -- -D warnings exit 0. cargo fmt --check -p fnp-python exit 0. All exit codes captured directly.

CLASS SCORECARD, now complete for the four probes I named: rrrlm (__all__ resolution) clean lock, scoca (return type, 51 cases) clean lock, liz1c (output dtype, 378 cases) found take(complex64) raising - fixed, 65pde (exception class, 26 cases) clean lock. One live bug in four probes. The declared-vs-served class is now exhausted at the level I can probe statically; a further probe would need a different axis - candidates a successor might weigh: WARNING parity (does fnp emit numpy's RuntimeWarning for mean of empty, divide by zero, invalid value), and writeability/base parity for the view-returning ops (does fnp return a VIEW where numpy returns a view, checked via .base and .flags.writeable).
