title: [test][fnp-python] datetime64/timedelta64/structured/void dtypes are itemsize-8 or width-colliding like complex64 was in liz1c - no sweep exists
description:
NINTH PROBE, and the one with the strongest mechanical prior of those left.

THE PRIOR IS liz1c, EXACTLY: take's residual guard read
`itemsize == 8 || kind == "b"`, and complex64's itemsize is 8 - the same width as
f64/i64/u64 - so it satisfied a guard written for the numeric widths, reached
extract_numeric_array, which cannot represent complex, and raised TypeError
where numpy returned an array. I fixed that ONE site by adding `kind != "c"`.

datetime64 and timedelta64 are ALSO itemsize 8, with kinds 'M' and 'm'. Any
other guard in the tree spelled as a WIDTH test rather than a KIND test has the
same hole for them. Structured/void ('V') and unicode/bytes ('U'/'S') have
variable itemsize and can collide with 1/2/4/8 just as easily - a
dtype([('a','i4')]) is itemsize 4, and '<U2' is itemsize 8.

These are precisely the families the numeric extract path CANNOT represent at
all, so every wrapper must delegate them in every case. That makes the expected
behaviour easy to state (fnp must equal numpy, including when numpy raises) and
makes any divergence unambiguous.

PROBE TO CLOSE: a conformance sweep over the exotic dtype families -
  datetime64[D] and datetime64[ns], timedelta64[D],
  a structured dtype [('a','i4'),('b','f8')] and a plain void,
  unicode '<U3' and bytes 'S3',
  object,
  plus float64 as the control
crossed with the operations whose guards are width-shaped or which have a
documented cold-extract residual: take, compress, concatenate, repeat, tile,
sort, unique, argsort, searchsorted, flip, ravel, reshape, where, count_nonzero,
nonzero, min/max/sum (which legitimately raise for some of these), isnan,
signbit, equal, astype. Compare dtype, shape, values AND exception class,
because for several of these pairs numpy itself raises and reproducing the raise
is the contract.

Assert a precondition that the exotic dtypes really are exotic - that
np.dtype('datetime64[D]').itemsize == 8 and the structured dtype's kind is 'V' -
so the sweep cannot pass by silently testing float64 seven times.

Any divergence is a real defect; fix it in the same bead.
close_reason:
DELIVERED in 7eb9b3f7 as a LOCK. THE BEAD'S PREDICTION WAS WRONG and that is the main finding: 176 comparisons, all match, so the width-collision hole was confined to the single site liz1c fixed. No defect is claimed.

WHAT I PREDICTED AND WHY: liz1c's defect was a WIDTH test standing in for a KIND test - take's residual guard read 'itemsize == 8 || kind == "b"', complex64 is itemsize 8, so it satisfied a guard written for f64/i64/u64, reached extract_numeric_array (which cannot represent complex) and raised TypeError where numpy returned an array. I fixed that ONE site by adding 'kind != "c"'. datetime64 and timedelta64 are also itemsize 8, kinds 'M' and 'm', so the obvious inference was that other width-shaped guards have the same hole for them - and structured/'<U2' collide on other widths, so it would not be confined to 8 bytes. The mechanism generalised; the bug did not. Worth recording because the inference was reasonable and still wrong, and the next person will be tempted by it again.

THE SWEEP: 8 dtype families x 22 operations = 176 comparisons of dtype, shape, values AND exception class. Families: float64 (control), datetime64[D], datetime64[ns], timedelta64[D], structured [('a','i4'),('b','f8')], '<U3', 'S3', object. Operations chosen for being width-guarded or having a documented cold-extract residual: take with a LIST index and with an ARRAY index (the two spellings that took different paths in liz1c - the list index is what reached the residual), compress, concatenate, repeat, tile, sort, argsort, unique, flip, ravel, reshape, where, count_nonzero, nonzero, min/max/sum, equal, isnan, signbit, astype.

EXCEPTION CLASS IS COMPARED ALONGSIDE VALUES, which matters more here than in the other sweeps: for several of these pairs numpy ITSELF raises (sum of '<U3', isnan of object), and reproducing the raise is the contract. A sweep that only compared successful returns would score every one of those as agreement without testing anything.

PRECONDITIONS assert the exotic dtypes really are exotic AND really do collide on width - datetime64[D] and timedelta64[D] itemsize == 8, structured kind == 'V' - plus at least 150 comparisons run. The itemsize assertions are the load-bearing ones: if numpy ever changed those widths the sweep would still pass while no longer probing the collision it was built for.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_return_types = 6 passed / 0 failed, exit 0, oracle numpy 2.4.3, 176 comparisons. cargo clippy -p fnp-python --test conformance_return_types -- -D warnings exit 0. cargo fmt --check -p fnp-python exit 0. All exit codes captured directly.

TALLY, nine probes: rrrlm, scoca, 65pde, bikey, succi, kue5j clean locks; liz1c found take(complex64) raising (fixed); c7hqd found concatenate's .base (fixed in st00f). Two live bugs in nine, and the last four probes were all clean - including the two I rated most likely to find something (0-stride views in succi, width collisions here). I would read that as the cross-cutting-sweep vein being close to exhausted rather than as evidence the surface is defect-free; a successor looking for defects should probably switch from sweeping ATTRIBUTES to sweeping INTERACTIONS (out= combined with axis and keepdims, where= combined with dtype=, etc.), which no probe so far has crossed.

title: perf(sqrt): f64 sqrt is a 1.8x WIN on positive input and a 16.67x LOSS when the input contains negatives - a 30x swing on SIGN alone
description:
MEASURED, TanBridge, thinkstation1, numpy 2.4.3 live, fnp .so sha256
1eb6a00d75ca74de3d5364a1806bd7300e48c5bb5dd34665e7926920946fcd3c (at fc047f16).

## THE CELL, AND WHY IT HID

`fnp.sqrt` on f64 is a 1.8x WIN when every element is positive and a 16.67x LOSS when the input
contains negatives. Same size, same dtype, same call — a 30x swing on SIGN ALONE. n=2^16:

```
  input                              numpy_ns      fnp_ns   ratio
  standard_normal (50.1% negative)    69195.0   1153755.7   16.67x  LOSS
  abs(...)+0.5     (all positive)     67617.5     37982.2    0.56x  WIN 1.8x
```

`bench_vs_numpy_loss_sweep` ranks `sqrt[f64]` at 5.9024x and its LADDER draws `f64` from
`rng.standard_normal(N)`, so the sweep has been measuring the negative branch all along. Anyone
who re-measures with a positive operand — the natural thing to reach for when benchmarking sqrt —
sees a WIN and concludes the sweep is wrong. It is not; the operand is the variable.

**Register the operand, not just the op.** This is the second cell this session whose true ratio
was invisible under the obvious probe (the first was `append`, hidden by CPU pinning:
`deadlock-audit-dc6mz`).

## WHAT IS NOT YET KNOWN

The mechanism. 1153755 ns against 37982 ns for the positive path is a 30x gap on the SAME kernel
size, which is far more than a decline-and-delegate would cost (delegation would land near numpy's
69195 ns, i.e. ~1.0x). So it is not simply "detects negatives, hands off to numpy". Candidates,
none verified:

  - a per-element scalar libm path taken once any NaN-producing input is present
  - FP exception state handling (`feclearexcept`/`fetestexcept`) per element or per chunk — see
    the f64-divide FE-hazard predicate in the CI-gate ledger row for the shape of this
  - a pre-scan for negatives that then still runs the full native kernel AND the fallback
  - NaN handling forcing a denormal/exception slow path in the hardware

FIRST STEP IS ATTRIBUTION, NOT A FIX: matched single-arm probes at 100% positive vs 100% negative
vs mixed, and a `perf` per-symbol instruction diff between them. A 30x gap will be obvious in the
symbol profile. `counted-attribution-by-instruction-diff` is the tool that has worked for this
class before.

## SIBLING GATE WORTH CHECKING IN THE SAME PASS

`SQRT_PARALLEL_MIN: usize = 1 << 17` (crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs). Unrelated to the sign
defect, but the positive path does degrade with thread count in a way that looks like the
`APPEND_PAR_MIN` bug's smaller cousin — measured on positive input, ratio vs numpy:

```
  threads   n=2^16   n=2^18   n=2^20
        1    0.55x    0.55x    0.55x
        8    0.56x    0.21x    0.19x
       64    0.54x    0.50x    0.30x
```

At n=2^18 the win is 0.21x on 8 threads but only 0.50x on 64 — the parallel path is LOSING half
its advantage as threads scale, which is the same fork/join-over-a-bandwidth-bound-loop shape.
That is a lost win, not a loss, so it ranks below the sign defect.

## ACCEPTANCE

Dual-null contract vs numpy live in the same invocation on the NEGATIVE-containing operand (the
one the sweep uses), plus the counted attribution that explains the 30x. Quote the cell at its
worst operand, and state the positive-operand ratio alongside it so the next reader is not misled
the way the obvious probe misled me.
close_reason: SHIPPED f2492ec5, banked 2b9af381. Contract on the sweep's own instrument: sqrt[f64] goes from rank-3 LOSS (5.9024x) to DECIDABLE_WIN 1.794117x [1.785108,1.800244], numpy 68228 ns vs fnp 37836 ns, both nulls straddling unity, exact_bytes=passed. Ratio is now FLAT in operand sign (0.541-0.552x for all-positive / 6-negatives / 50%-negative / -inf) where it swung 30x. Mechanism was pay-twice: the fused loop computed the whole correct output then discarded it via Ok(None) so a fallback could record numpy's invalid event - and that deferral delivered NONE of the three parities it charged 12.69x for (no raise under errstate raise, warned under ignore, missed -inf). Fixed by keeping the buffer and reproducing the event with a 179.6 ns one-element same-ufunc probe, plus widening the detector to v<0.0. SQRT_PARALLEL_MIN=1<<17 deliberately NOT touched; noted in the ledger retry predicate as a lost-win, not a loss.

title: [perf][sort] Re-decide the flat f64 unique AVX2 surrender (sibling of the sort regate) with a tie-density sweep
description:
## The same surrender, one function over

`try_zerocopy_f64_unique_flat` (crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs, ~L92080) opens with the
identical blanket AVX2 refusal that `try_zerocopy_f64_sort_flat` carried, and its own
comment names the kinship: "Stale-basis regate (2026-07-14, sibling of the flat f64 sort
regate)".

```rust
if numpy_f64_qsort_is_simd() {
    return Ok(None);
}
```

Its recorded evidence is `0.995x on distinct data and 0.547x on dense ties`.

## Why it needs re-deciding, and why it is NOT a copy of the sort fix

The sort regate turned out to be a CORE-COUNT result generalized to an ISA check: the
gate's own numpy arm (121.1ms at 8M) reproduced almost exactly on thinkstation1
(126.07ms) while its native arm (202.3ms) was 5.5x the 36.6ms the same kernel turns in
on 32 cores. `unique` was sampled in the same campaign, on the same class of small
worker, so the same confound is likely.

But the dense-ties number is NOT explained by core count alone. numpy's unique is
sort + flags + compress, and on dense ties the compress output collapses to a handful of
values; the candidate is par_sort + Vec::dedup + a right-sized copy. That is a genuinely
different mechanism from the flat value sort and it deserves its own measurement rather
than an inherited verdict. Regime-gate on what the loss VARIES WITH (tie density), not on
the ISA.

## Method that settled the sort case

1. Measure live numpy on the target host and confirm cpu/wall ~1.0 (no threading layer).
2. Sweep the candidate kernel standalone across RAYON_NUM_THREADS 2/4/8/16/32 against that
   fixed single-threaded incumbent, at several sizes AND at several tie densities.
3. Set the floor where the margin clears the route's own overheads, not where the ratio
   first crosses 1.0.
4. Prove engagement: a deferred route returns numpy's own answer and measures 1.0 by
   construction, so a decidable ratio IS the engagement proof.

## Related, same shape, also unmeasured at high core count

- `F64_AXIS_SORT_SIMD_MIN_THREADS = 16` (axis sort) - different economics (fan-out PER
  LANE against numpy's efficient per-lane SIMD basis), so 16 may be right; unverified.
- `I32_FLAT_SORT_SIMD_MIN_THREADS = 16` (int32 flat sort) - explicitly says it "mirrors
  the measured f64 SIMD-sort family gate", i.e. it inherited the number that the flat f64
  measurement has now moved to 8.
- avx512f hosts: the flat f64 arm still surrenders unconditionally. The one sampled
  avx512 data point was a WASH (numpy 92.9ms vs 96.1ms native at 8M) on a small box, so a
  many-core avx512 host is unmeasured in both directions.
close_reason: RE-DECIDED AND SHIPPED. Gate change dc4a40dc, ledger row 2fa3921e, harness 8784bd35/8761e792/ebaa17e4. BOTH halves of the surrender's basis ('0.995x on distinct data and 0.547x on dense ties') are REFUTED - it was a core-count result generalized to an ISA check, same defect as the flat-sort sibling. Blanket is_x86_feature_detected!(avx2) refusal replaced by F64_UNIQUE_SIMD_MIN_THREADS=8; avx512f keeps the prior surrender (unmeasured either direction). MEASURED vs live NumPy 2.4.3 same-invocation dual-null median-CI, thinkstation1 32P/64L AVX2: uniform 4M 1.040/1.525/1.885/2.18 at 4/8/16/32T; uniform 16M 1.326/1.492/1.51 at 8/16/32; uniform 64M 1.677/1.76 at 16/32; 16M-from-1M-distinct 1.611/1.868/1.95; 16M-from-64 1.012UND/1.094/1.101/1.21; 64M-from-64 1.313/1.313/1.302; 16M-from-2-distinct 0.999UND/0.996UND/1.030UND/1.159DW. TWO MECHANISMS: compute-bound rows scale with workers, bandwidth-bound dense ties are FLAT (64-distinct at 64M is 1.313/1.313/1.302 across 8/16/32). FLOOR=8 is the measured knee: 5 of 6 corpora DECIDABLE_WIN at 1.09-1.61x there, the 6th a WASH not a loss; at 4 both tie corpora are UNDECIDED and the only deciding row is 1.040x. THE 2-DISTINCT CORNER IS BANKED AS PARITY, NOT A WIN (UNDECIDED at 4/8/16, decided once at 32 unreplicated, 1.03-1.17 run-to-run spread on a second ELF). INCUMBENT TOPOLOGY measured before any candidate existed: numpy.unique is single-threaded cpu/wall 0.997-1.000 at every size and tie density; its sort is 73% of the job distinct / 87% dense. ENGAGEMENT PROVEN: OBSERVED_THREAD_ACTIVITY numpy=1 thread vs fnp=33 in the same invocation; conformance test prints NATIVE_ARM_REACHABLE and was verified BOTH ways on this host (true at 32 workers, false at 4 with every corpus still byte-exact). HARNESS TRAP CAUGHT BEFORE ANY NUMBER WAS BANKED: integer-drawn tie corpora are claimed by try_zerocopy_f64_unique_binary_grid BEFORE the sort route, so every tie row would have timed the bucket path under the wrong route name; tie pools are now uniform doubles and each row asserts its corpus is off the 1/16 grid. TESTS: flat_f64_unique_woken_route_is_byte_exact_and_defers_correctly covers engage (distinct, dense ties, all-same, single-sign +0.0 and -0.0, inf/subnormal/max, 2-D ravel) and defer (NaN, both signed zeros, strided, below the 1<<20 gate); 37 targeted tests over the unique/setop/sort surface pass; clippy -p fnp-python --lib -D warnings clean; ledger_hygiene 18 passed with the single remaining failure being the unrelated masked_sum row tracked as deadlock-audit-6j4o8. PROVENANCE: three release-perf ELFs differing only in bench corpus order - 5ccb8d9c (distinct), dd0c0a04 (ties), eda72f90 (floor sweep); numpy artifact 2e0027bb; max observed host busy 0.167 vs the 0.200 ceiling. Shipped constant is 8 while the measurement ELFs carried 2 so every width could reach the arm; at >=8 workers they are the same route. RETRY PREDICATE: reopen for a many-core avx512f host, a widening to another dtype/layout/axis, a decided row for the 2-distinct corner, or if numpy.unique gains a threading layer.

INCUMBENT TOPOLOGY (measured first, before any candidate existed): numpy.unique is SINGLE-THREADED at every size and tie density sampled - cpu/wall 0.997-1.000 at n=4M/16M/64M crossed with 4M/1M/64/2 distinct. Its np.sort is 73% of the job on distinct input and 87% on dense ties. Dense ties do NOT buy numpy a threading layer; they only make its sort cheaper in absolute terms.

RESULT, distinct-uniform, 32 threads, TWO independent invocations of the same ELF:
  4M   2.293x / 2.253x   (CI [2.220,2.306] / [2.209,2.272])
  16M  1.516x / 1.506x   (CI [1.506,1.533] / [1.495,1.527])
  64M  1.766x / 1.757x   (CI [1.750,1.770] / [1.746,1.788])
All six rows DECIDABLE_WIN. All four nulls per row in 0.975-1.025. The surrender's recorded '0.995x on distinct data' is REFUTED at 32 workers - same core-count-vs-ISA confound as the flat-sort sibling.

ENGAGEMENT PROVEN, not inferred: OBSERVED_THREAD_ACTIVITY in the same invocation reads arm=numpy threads_actually_used=1 vs arm=fnp threads_actually_used=33. A deferred route would have read 1 on both and ~1.0x.

PARITY: exact_bytes=passed on every corpus reached, including the tie corpora (2-distinct and 1M-distinct at 16M).

HARNESS TRAP FIXED BEFORE MEASURING (commit 8784bd35): the first corpora were rng.integers(...).astype(np.float64), which try_zerocopy_f64_unique_binary_grid claims BEFORE the sort route - every ties row would have timed the O(n+range) bucket path while printing candidate_route=try_zerocopy_f64_unique_flat. Tie pools are now uniform doubles indexed by random integers, and each row asserts its corpus is off the 1/16 grid.

STILL OPEN: no timed row for ANY tie corpus. Cause is host exclusivity, not the lever: the harness re-checks quiescence before EVERY contract and this box is shared with ~12 agents, so four runs so far cleared the process preflight and were killed mid-sweep (blocked with cpu16 at 50-83%, plus 3-10 other CPUs over the 20% ceiling). Corpus order was changed to ties-first (commit 8761e792, ELF-B sha256=dd0c0a048542a4a658822cb900c7aeca3cefdcaaeca30a28f566836e43b8c23b) so a short-lived run yields the rows that are still missing rather than re-measuring the banked ones.

DO NOT SHIP A GATE CHANGE ON THE DISTINCT ROWS ALONE. The surrender's other half is '0.547x on dense ties', and that is a different mechanism (numpy's sort+flags+compress collapses when the output is a handful of values) rather than an inherited verdict. Enabling the route unconditionally without that number risks shipping a regression on tie-heavy off-grid f64 input.

That was based on an is-ascending check reporting lanes=[], and that check is BLIND to the failure mode - it excludes NaN from ordering, and it was reached only after an earlier branch had already bailed out. IT IS NOT GONE. It is alive on numpy 2.4.3.

MINIMAL REPRO, pure numpy, no fnp loaded, WORKER hz2:
  import numpy as np                      # numpy 2.4.3, py3.14.4
  rng = np.random.default_rng(20260716)
  _   = (rng.standard_normal(200000)*2).astype(np.float16)   # consume in order
  a   = (rng.standard_normal(2000003)*2).astype(np.float16)
  e   = np.unique(a)
  e.size                                   -> 24403
  e.size - np.unique(e.view(np.uint16)).size -> 2        # TWO DUPLICATES
  np.all(np.diff(e.astype(np.float32)) > 0)  -> False    # NOT ASCENDING
  np.unique(a.astype(np.float32)).astype(np.float16).size -> 24401   # correct

ISA IS THE AXIS, AND A STANDING NOTE IS WRONG: hz2 is the fleet's ONLY avx512f host. Verified from /proc/cpuinfo today: hz1 avx512f=0 (EPYC-Milan, Zen 3 - no AVX-512 at all), hz2 avx512f=1 (EPYC-Genoa, Zen 4). Neither has avx512fp16. title: [perf][sort] Flat f64 sort surrenders to NumPy on EVERY AVX2 host - make the ISA gate thread-count-aware
description:
## The surrender

`try_zerocopy_f64_sort_flat` (crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs:62694) opens with:

```rust
if numpy_f64_qsort_is_simd() {
    return Ok(None); // numpy's SIMD (avx2/avx512) qsort owns the flat f64 basis here
}
```

`numpy_f64_qsort_is_simd()` is `is_x86_feature_detected!("avx2")`. That is TRUE on
essentially every x86-64 host in the fleet, including thinkstation1. So the entire
parallel flat-f64 sort route is dead code on every measurement host: `np.sort` on a
flat f64 array is 100% NumPy passthrough, single-threaded.

The gate encodes a real measurement — a Rayon fan-out loses to NumPy's vectorized
qsort on a SMALL AVX2 box (the comment cites 0.579x on "the sampled small AVX2
worker"). It then generalizes that to ALL AVX2 hosts regardless of core count.

The sibling axis-sort gate 20 lines above already gets this right:

```rust
const F64_AXIS_SORT_SIMD_MIN_THREADS: usize = 16;
fn f64_axis_sort_native_is_profitable() -> bool {
    !numpy_f64_qsort_is_simd() || rayon::current_num_threads() >= F64_AXIS_SORT_SIMD_MIN_THREADS
}
```

The flat path never got the same treatment.

## Why this is the biggest single line item

Flat f64 sort is the largest entry in the 2026-07-31 reduction/ordering
time-on-the-table map (sort 1086 ms at 64M, vs cumsum 462, var/std 384, sum 28).
Re-measured on thinkstation1, live NumPy 2.4.3:

| n | np.sort wall | cpu/wall |
|---|---|---|
| 16M | 274.7 ms | 1.00x |
| 64M | 1780.3 ms | 0.99x |

cpu/wall ~1.0 confirms NumPy has no threading layer for sort — this is the
"incumbent cannot follow" class, not a bandwidth-bound wash like the elementwise
family (which the 2026-07-27 `greater` row and the a*b+c 1.5x traffic ceiling
already closed at ~1.0-1.5x).

## Standalone kernel probe (scratchpad, 32 physical cores, not yet a shippable ratio)

| n | dist | numpy | par_sort (the code already in the repo) | sample sort |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16M | uniform[0,1) | 274.7 ms | 65.0 ms (4.2x) | 51.9 ms (5.3x) |
| 64M | uniform[0,1) | 1780.3 ms | 357.9 ms (5.0x) | 211.2 ms (8.4x) |
| 16M | wide dynamic range | - | 86.0 ms | 59.9 ms |
| 64M | wide dynamic range | - | 365.4 ms | 217.5 ms |

REJECTED DESIGN, recorded before anyone rebuilds it: MSD radix partition on the
TOP bits of the order-preserving u64 key collapses on float data. Uniform [0,1)
doubles share sign+exponent, so the top 11 bits take ~30 distinct values and one
bucket holds half the array, leaving a serial tail — measured 0.8 GB/s, WORSE than
par_sort. Any flat-float partition on high bit-prefixes is distribution-fragile.
Sample sort (splitters drawn from the data) is distribution-independent and is the
variant that holds up on both distributions above.

## Plan

1. Gate fix only: replace the blanket AVX2 surrender with the thread-count-aware
   predicate the axis-sort sibling already uses. Reuses the existing kernel and its
   existing `f64_sort_values_defer` (NaN + mixed signed zeros), so correctness
   properties are unchanged — ISA has nothing to do with values. ~10 lines.
2. Measure vs live NumPy same-invocation under the dual-null gate. Keep or revert.
3. Only then consider the sample-sort kernel as a second, larger step.

Deferral predicate is already correct for both designs: it defers on any NaN and on
inputs carrying BOTH -0.0 and +0.0, which are exactly the cases where a value sort's
tie order is algorithm-specific.
notes:
LAND-TIME TODO: a tree-wide cargo fmt (peer, for the red G1 gate) reformatted my
criterion_python_sortmisc.rs AFTER commit 190b2bed, so that commit holds the UNFORMATTED
version and would fail CI's fmt check. Fold the whitespace-only diff in before pushing
(git commit --amend --only -- crates/fnp-python/benches/criterion_python_sortmisc.rs).
Deliberately NOT done now: the peer currently has 6 files staged in the shared index
(.beads/issues.jsonl, criterion_python_median_gate.rs, src/lib.rs, conformance_all.rs,
conformance_any.rs, docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md) and amending risks disturbing their staging.
No cost to deferring - nothing is pushed.

MEASURED (same-invocation dual-null, live NumPy 2.4.3, thinkstation1, quiescence clear):
  distinct uniform  4M: 1.725158x @32w / 1.645758x @8w  DECIDABLE_WIN

title: fleet: workers do not run the same numpy - one is on 2.3.5 from the distro package while others are on 2.5.2, so bit-exactness verdicts AND the exported surface differ by host
description:
THE FLEET IS NOT RUNNING ONE NUMPY, and every oracle-relative result on this campaign is
measured against whichever one rch happened to pick.

MEASURED 2026-09-02, from inside the runs themselves:

    worker fixmydocuments (rch alias ovh-a)   numpy 2.3.5
        umath = /usr/lib/python3/dist-packages/numpy/_core/_multiarray_umath...so
        cpu baseline = ['SSE', 'SSE2', 'SSE3']
    worker hz4                                numpy 2.5.2
        umath = <user site-packages>/numpy/_core/_multiarray_umath...so
        cpu baseline = ['X86_V2']
    installed interpreter, thinkstation1      numpy 2.4.3   baseline ['X86_V2']

So one worker runs the DISTRO package out of /usr/lib, two minor versions behind, built for a
generic SSE baseline, while the others run a user-site build at X86_V2.

WHAT IT ALREADY BROKE, both observed rather than predicted:

  1. A MUST-class bit-exactness clause is GREEN on hz2/hz4 and RED on ovh-a with NO source
     difference - `log(-1.0)` is a negative NaN in 2.3.5 and a positive NaN in 2.4.3/2.5.2
     ([[deadlock-audit-log-nan-sign-differs-by-worker-elz1p]], closed). `cargo test -p
     fnp-python --lib` is the regression check every agent runs before landing, and its
     verdict is currently a coin flip on worker selection. It cost one full diagnostic cycle
     to find that out, and would cost the next agent the same.

  2. THE EXPORTED SURFACE DIFFERS. `objdtype_raise_parity` reports 370 entry points on the
     2.3.5/2.5.2-era workers against 367 on hz4, so a before/after cell count taken on
     different workers is not a comparison at all. This session had to discard one such delta
     for exactly that reason and fall back to per-name counts.

AND THAT SAME WORKER HAS NO `perf`. Nine consecutive attempts to take an instruction count
(`examples/count_entry_shape_insns`) all landed on it, and `perf stat -e instructions` produces
no countable line there. It is now the least-loaded worker, so rch routes everything to it -
which means the one host where an oracle-relative measurement is untrustworthy is also the one
host where the counted alternative cannot run. Both fallbacks are closed at once.

AND ROUTING IS NOT UNIFORM ACROSS JOB SHAPES, which is what makes the above hard to work
around. Measured back-to-back in the same window:

    light `python3 -c` jobs        -> hz4              (numpy 2.5.2, perf AVAILABLE)
    `cargo run --example` jobs     -> fixmydocuments   (numpy 2.3.5, perf ABSENT)

Fourteen inventory probes went to hz4; six builds of the same example, issued minutes later,
all went to fixmydocuments. So you cannot reach a perf-capable host by retrying a BUILD, and
the probe that tells you which host has perf is exactly the shape that goes somewhere else.
The documented escape is AGENTS.md's "Route 1": build anywhere, scp the ELF to a host you
choose, verify sha256 both ends, and run it there.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TESTS. This repo's standing rule is that the vendored oracle leads every
release ([[vendored-numpy-oracle-is-ahead-of-every-release]]) and that results are confirmed
against the INSTALLED interpreter. Neither rule survives a fleet where the oracle differs by
host: a parity claim, a dtype-promotion audit, a raise-parity 2x2 and any bit-exactness gate
all mean something different depending on where they ran.

WHAT TO DO, in order of cheapness:
  1. INVENTORY. One `rch exec --job -- python3 -c "import numpy, sys, os; print(os.uname()
     .nodename, numpy.__version__, numpy.__file__)"` per worker - repeated until every worker
     has been sampled, since selection follows load and cannot be steered.
  2. DECIDE THE PIN. Either every worker gets the same numpy as the installed interpreter, or
     the campaign states which version is the oracle and every measured row names it.

title: perf(take): a CONTAINER index still copies the whole source - 19.44x at list10, and the obvious normalise-and-retry fix is a MEASURED REJECT
description:
FOLLOW-UP to deadlock-audit-yphwc, which fixed the SCALAR half of the same defect.

MEASURED, TanBridge, thinkstation1, numpy 2.4.3 live, pinned `taskset -c 40`, fnp .so sha256
fc2f43d47e1ae4c035a13e3c1a130361a7356e8f024ca0b234ded88a9044070c (at 9acbe632), all A/A nulls
PASS.

## WHAT IS LEFT

```
  cell             numpy_ns     fnp_ns   slower
  list10             1169.2    23255.1   19.443x
  idx1k_i64          1528.6     3437.6    2.250x
  2d_T_scalar      109922.9   111015.6    1.013x   (parity; transposed, declines by design)
```

Same root cause as the scalar half: `try_zerocopy_f64_take` / `try_zerocopy_int_take` require
`indices` to be an EXACT int64 ndarray, so a Python list, a tuple, or an int32 index array
declines every fast path and reaches the residual, which calls `extract_numeric_array` and copies
THE ENTIRE SOURCE. The tiny operand decides the route; the huge one pays.

## THE OBVIOUS FIX IS MEASURED AND IT DOES NOT WORK

"Normalise the indices to int64 and re-enter the existing gather" is the natural move. Priced
against the installed interpreter:

```
  np.asarray(l10, dtype=np.int64)          470.0 ns
  i32.astype(np.int64)                     300.3 ns
  np.take(a, l10)   <== the WHOLE incumbent 1169.2 ns
```

The conversion alone is 40% of numpy's entire budget for the call, before any gather runs and
before fnp's own ~120 ns entry. A normalise-and-retry lands at parity at best. Confirming this
from the other side: `np.take(a, np.asarray(l10, np.int64))` is 1354.8 ns, i.e. SLOWER than
`np.take(a, l10)` — numpy's own take already absorbs the conversion more cheaply than a separate
`asarray` can.

## SO THE ONLY LEVER THAT CAN WIN IS A NATIVE SMALL-INDEX GATHER

Read the index elements directly in Rust (PyList/PyTuple/typed buffer), bounds-check, gather from
the borrowed source buffer, and build the output — never materialising an intermediate int64
index ARRAY. Budget to beat: 1169 ns for 10 indices, 1529 ns for 1024.

DO NOT re-attempt the normalise-and-retry design. It is a measured reject.

## TRAPS (verified against numpy 2.4.3)

1. A BOOL ARRAY IS AN INDEX LIST, NOT A MASK: `np.take(a, np.array([True,False]))` yields
   `[1., 0.]`, i.e. elements 1 and 0. Do not route it to boolean-mask indexing.
2. u64 indices: `np.uint64(2**63+5)` wraps to a negative i64 and numpy's OWN take reports
   `IndexError index -9223372036854775803`, so the wrap is observable behaviour, not a bug to
   fix here — but any conversion must reproduce it rather than diverge.
3. Out-of-range must fall through so numpy owns the message.
4. `mode='clip'/'wrap'` change index resolution and are NOT `__getitem__` semantics.

## SEPARATE PRE-EXISTING CORRECTNESS BUGS FOUND IN THE SAME PROBE — NOT FIXED, NOT MINE

A 2300-case probe (25 sources x 23 index spellings x 4 kwarg sets) leaves 134 divergences after
deadlock-audit-yphwc. The one that is a wrong VALUE rather than a wrong error:

  `mode='clip'` WITH A NEGATIVE INDEX RETURNS THE WRONG ELEMENT. numpy clamps -1 to 0
  (`np.take(np.arange(10), -1, mode='clip')` yields 0.0); fnp returns 9.0, i.e. it applies the
  negative-from-end wraparound that clip is defined NOT to do. Silent wrong answer, 6+ cases.

`subclass` sources account for 37 of the 134. These deserve their own bead; they are
correctness, not performance.

title: [perf][fnp-linalg] multi_dot 4-6x slow on skinny-intermediate chains — small-k GEMM path (DP already correct)
description: np.linalg.multi_dot is 6.18x slower than numpy on an order-sensitive chain (1500,2)(2,1500)(1500,2)(2,1500): numpy 2.30ms vs fnp 15.46ms; 4.62x on a 5-matrix chain. ROOT CAUSE: NOT the chain order — fnp's multi_dot (fnp-linalg:4717) ALREADY does the optimal-parenthesization DP correctly (verified: parity True, same FLOPs as numpy). The gap is mat_mul_rect for SKINNY matrices: the optimal order's dominant matmul is (1500x2)@(2x1500), k=2, and the cache-blocked packed GEMM's B-pack/A-pack + k-loop micro-kernel is pure overhead when k is tiny (output 2.25M, memory-bound). LEVER: add a small-k direct path (k <= ~8) — for each output row, out[i,j]=sum_{p<k} a[i,p]*b[p,j] as k SAXPYs over the contiguous j-row (autovectorizes), parallel over rows; skip packing. Bit-identical (same ascending-k accumulation) or tolerance. Isolate to multiply_range (or a mat_mul_smallk helper) to avoid touching the shared GEMM. CAUTION: fnp-linalg/src/lib.rs had a peer's UNCOMMITTED change in the working tree (git-trap risk) — do this in a quiet window or via isolated worktree per the disjoint-region-commit discipline. Target Score >= 2.0 on skinny chains; verify on typical (non-skinny) chains for no regression.

The gap is NOT packing overhead; it's deeper: the (1500x2)@(2x1500) op writes an 18MB output and fnp pays a build_numpy_array copy + cold page faults + the skinny-GEMM regime, all compounding. This is GEMM-microkernel/BLAS-class territory (8vdtg), not a quick kernel-regime patch. Tried via isolated git worktree (fnp-linalg had peer contention); reverted. comments.text:
G1's FMT STEP IS THE LIVE BLOCKER AGAIN, AND `cargo fmt --check` HIDES IT (BlackThrush, 2026-08-30, thinkstation1).

The title blocker is long gone (chunks_exact_to_as_chunks, fixed by a4166754) and I found NO clippy
blocker today: RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec -- cargo clippy -j2 -p fnp-python --all-targets -- -D warnings
-> exit 0, worker vmi1153651, 164.4s, zero diagnostics.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY RED: rustfmt ABORTS while cargo fmt --check reports success.

  cargo fmt --check  ->  exit 0, but stderr carries:
  'memory allocation of 64537337760 bytes failed' (60.1 GiB) in rustfmt_diff::make_diff

That is the SAME make_diff blowup this bead recorded on 2026-08-22 (116 GiB). It was not a one-off
input: it recurs whenever ANY drift appears in a very large file, because the allocation scales with
FILE size, not diff size. The abort happens while RENDERING the diff, so the offending filename is
never printed AND the wrapper still exits 0. Piping is not required to hide it - I redirected to a
file and it still exited 0. Anyone running the workspace command sees success.

METHOD THAT FOUND IT (this bead's own 08-22 plan, executed):
  1. per-file `rustfmt --edition 2024 --check <f>` under `ulimit -v 4000000` over all crates/**/*.rs.
     Exit 134 (SIGABRT) = the OOM file; exit 1 = ordinary drift.
     -> crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs = 134;  crates/fnp-ufunc/src/lib.rs = 1
  2. `rustfmt --emit stdout` piped to diff instead of `--check`, which skips make_diff entirely and
     renders the drift without the blowup.

THE DRIFT WAS FOUR SITES TOTAL, all pure line-wrapping, no semantics:
  crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs       2 sites (an ISNAN_MASK_BYTE_LUT index chain; a
                                     numpy_default.call_method0 chain in a keepdims test)
  crates/fnp-ufunc/src/lib.rs        1 site (an assert_eq! in the all-NaN percentile test)
  crates/fnp-conformance/src/bin/perf_ledger_preflight.rs   1 site (an assert! message)
A 180k-line file with 2 wrapping defects was enough to demand 60 GiB to print them.

Fixed BY HAND, never `cargo fmt -p <crate>` - the standing lesson is that crate-formatting this
accumulated multi-agent lib.rs once rewrote 11 files / 3040 lines of other agents' code.

AFTER: cargo fmt --check -> exit 0, ZERO 'Diff in' lines, ZERO abort lines, EMPTY output
(before: 1 'Diff in' line + the 60 GiB abort). Run UNPIPED.

comments.author: BlackThrush
comments.text:
THE make_diff ABORT RECURRED WITHIN HOURS, AND THIS TIME IT MASKED MY OWN DRIFT (BlackThrush, 2026-08-30, second report). Commit 9b97b383.

Earlier today I cleared this and verified `cargo fmt --check` exit 0 with empty output. Hours later
it was aborting again at 60 GiB in rustfmt_diff::make_diff - and in between, several of my own
commits landed with fmt drift, because the gate reported exit 0 and ZERO 'Diff in' lines the whole
time. One of the three sites I just fixed was mine (an over-100-column predicate I wrote).

THAT IS THE POINT WORTH RECORDING: this is not a one-off pathological input that can be "fixed
once". The allocation scales with FILE size, not diff size, so ANY new drift appearing in
crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs (180k lines) re-triggers it, and from that moment the workspace gate
silently stops reporting drift for the whole workspace. On a shared tree with a dozen agents
committing into that file, the expected time to recurrence is hours. Between recurrence and
discovery, `cargo fmt --check` is not a gate at all - it is a green light that means nothing.

THE ONLY RELIABLE CHECK, and it should probably be what CI runs:
  ( ulimit -v 4000000; rustfmt --edition 2024 --check <file> )
    -> 0 = clean, 1 = ordinary drift, 134 (SIGABRT) = the OOM file
  and to READ the drift without triggering make_diff:
    rustfmt --edition 2024 --emit stdout <file> | diff - <file>
  (strip rustfmt's leading filename line; it follows `mod` declarations, so trailing "hunks" may
   just be the next module's contents)

Three sites this round, all pure wrapping, zero semantics: my `ordered_batch` predicate, a peer's
`assert_same_outcome` closure parameter list, and a peer's `expected_array.getattr` chain. Peer
hunks fixed as my own per the standing rule - never `cargo fmt -p`, which once rewrote 11 files /
3040 lines of other agents' code here.

AFTER: per-file rustfmt --check on fnp-python/src/lib.rs exits 0 (not 134); cargo fmt --check exits
0 with ZERO bytes of output and zero abort lines. Both checks, because either alone can lie.

STILL UNSATISFIED: this bead's named probe is a real CI run showing G1 success and G2-G8 not

title: correctness(flip family): flipud/fliplr/flip stripped an ndarray SUBCLASS - and the fix is to stop converting, not to delegate, because subclass[slices] already returns the subclass

title: [test][fnp-linalg] eig_nxn has no randomised/property sweep - it underpins every polynomial *roots, one of which was silently wrong
close_reason:
COMPLETE, no defect. eig_nxn_recovers_known_spectra_across_randomised_triangular_matrices pins the eigenvalue engine that every polynomial *roots sits on - the one whose companion-matrix caller (chebroots) was silently wrong at degree >= 5 until a randomised differential caught it (xb1ue).

TWO HALVES, deliberately, because the first one alone would have been misleading:
  TRIANGULAR (28 matrices, n = 2..10): a triangular matrix's eigenvalues ARE its diagonal, exactly and by construction, so this needs no oracle and no tolerance on the expected values. It also asserts a real spectrum - a non-zero imaginary part would itself be a defect. Worst deviation 0e0.
  GENERAL (18 matrices, n = 2..8, vs numpy.linalg.eigvals): worst deviation 1.688e-14, both spectra lexsorted by (real, imag) since eigenvalues carry no inherent order.

THE 0e0 IS WHY THE SECOND HALF EXISTS. A triangular matrix is ALREADY in real Schur form, so the Francis iteration converges immediately and reads the diagonal off unchanged - the triangular half pins the contract but exercises none of the solver. I noticed the exactly-zero result was too clean to be meaningful and added the general-matrix half rather than banking it. The test now asserts worst_general > 0.0 explicitly, so if that half ever starts matching numpy exactly it fails, on the grounds that it would mean the iteration is no longer being reached.

Also fixed a bug in my own oracle while writing it: f'{z.real!r}' emits np.float64(...) under numpy 2.x, which does not parse as a float. Caught by the test failing, not by inspection.

title: perf(histogramdd): a 1-D ndarray sample is read as 65536 axes - 1332x vs live numpy
description:
Live-NumPy loss cell found by the new broad sweep (bench_vs_numpy_loss_sweep, criterion_python_loss_sweep).

TRIAGE RANK 0 of 267 comparable cases, and worst in the campaign by ~12x over the runner-up:
  case=histogramdd[f64]  numpy_ns=1004404  fnp_ns=1338462369  ratio_numpy_over_fnp=0.000750
  i.e. 1.338 SECONDS against NumPy's 1.0 ms on a 65536-element f64 sample.
Triage statistic only (interleaved min-of-25, no A/A null); the contract row is the decision.

MECHANISM, read from source and not inferred: `histogramdd`'s dispatcher classifies its
`sample` argument into NumPy's two spellings. An (N, D) ndarray takes `is_array_form`; a
sequence of D per-axis arrays takes an `else if ... sample.try_iter()` branch. A 1-D
ndarray is ITERABLE, so it fell into the sequence branch and was read as 65536 axes of one
sample each -- the loop then called `numpy.histogram_bin_edges` once per element before the
attempt failed and the call delegated to NumPy anyway. Every one of those 1.338 seconds was
wasted in front of a result NumPy produced regardless.

NumPy's actual rule: an ndarray is never the sequence spelling. It unpacks `sample.shape`
into two names and, when that fails, normalises with `np.atleast_2d(sample).T` -- so a 1-D
(N,) array is (N, 1), ONE axis of N samples. A 3-D ndarray raises even after that retry.

SCOPE: `fnp.histogramdd` sample-form classification only. Bind a 1-D ndarray as the single
column NumPy's own normalisation produces (which also lets the existing counting kernel
serve it natively), decline any other non-2-D ndarray so NumPy's error is reproduced
verbatim, and keep ndarrays out of the sequence branch entirely.

ACCEPTANCE: exact counts/edges/dtype parity for 1-D, 2-D and the error type for 3-D; and a
dual-null median-CI contract row against live numpy in the same invocation, with both A/A
nulls straddling unity, reported whether it wins or loses.

NOT IN SCOPE and owned elsewhere: sort/argsort/searchsorted (franken_numpy-ixs5y.409 and
deadlock-audit-9g7u0).

title: [bug][fnp-python] corrcoef accepts ddof/bias, which numpy REMOVED in 2.4 - the supported floor now spans two incompatible numpy behaviours
description:
FOUND by CoralOak 2026-08-07 while landing the last item of deadlock-audit-keqog. It was HIDDEN
BEHIND that item: cov_corrcoef_python_container_keyword_outcomes_match_numpy asserts case-by-case
in a loop, so it aborted at case 2 ('cov y ddof', the FMA/ULP one) and never reached case 6.
Fixing case 2 is what exposed this. Same shape as the repo's standing 'waking a dormant route
exposes regressions hiding in its body' finding.

THE DEFECT. fnp.corrcoef ACCEPTS a ddof keyword and returns a result. Concretely, on
vmi1152480 (rch pool a97f68be..., commit 178b3fed):
  numpy: {"message": "corrcoef() got an unexpected keyword argument 'ddof'",
          "status": "err", "type": "TypeError"}
  fnp:   {"result": {"dtype": "float64", "kind": "ndarray", "shape": [2, 2],
          "values": [[1.0, -1.0], [-1.0, 1.0]]}, "status": "ok"}
Panic at crates/fnp-python/tests/conformance_statistics.rs:384, case
'corrcoef y ddof compatibility'.

THE VERSION MATRIX, measured on three real environments rather than inferred:
  numpy 2.3.5 (hz2, over ssh)  ACCEPTS ddof, emits DeprecationWarning
                               "bias and ddof have no effect and are deprecated", returns the
                               value. With warnings promoted to errors it raises that warning.
  numpy 2.4.3 (this box)       RAISES TypeError - the parameter is GONE.
  numpy 2.4.x (vmi1152480)     RAISES TypeError, as above.
  vendored oracle              legacy_numpy_code/numpy is 2.5.0.dev0 and its signature at
                               numpy/lib/_function_base_impl.py:2900 is
                               'def corrcoef(x, y=None, rowvar=True, *, dtype=None)'.
                               No ddof, no bias.
So upstream did not merely deprecate this - it FINISHED removing it. numpy 2.3 is the laggard,
not the target.

WHY THIS IS NOT KEQOG AND NOT 1jqrw-AS-WRITTEN. The declared supported oracle floor is numpy
>= 2.3 (deadlock-audit-1jqrw). That floor was built for cases where the OLD numpy was the outlier
and fnp matched the newer one. Here the supported range itself spans two INCOMPATIBLE behaviours
for the same call: 2.3 accepts-and-ignores, 2.4+ rejects. No single fnp behaviour satisfies a
live-oracle exact comparison on both. The floor has an upper end and nobody has declared it.

THE DECISION SOMEONE HAS TO MAKE - I deliberately did not make it drive-by, because both options
have a cost and one of them turns a currently-green host red:
  (a) Follow upstream: drop ddof/bias from fnp.corrcoef so it raises TypeError. Matches numpy
      2.4.x and 2.5.0.dev0. COST: goes RED on hz2, where numpy 2.3.5 still accepts. Needs either
      a floor raise to >= 2.4 or a documented row in docs/DIVERGENCES.md saying fnp is ahead of
      2.3 on purpose.
  (b) Keep accepting it. Matches 2.3 only, diverges from every numpy anyone will actually install
      from here on, and contradicts the vendored oracle. Needs a DIVERGENCES.md row too.
(a) is the better engineering and is where upstream has already landed. It is still a decision
about the SUPPORTED RANGE, not about this test.

WHAT NOT TO DO. Do NOT version-key the expectation inside conformance_statistics.rs. The doc
comment on numpy_oracle_meets_the_supported_version_floor
(crates/fnp-python/tests/conformance_module_metadata.rs) names that explicitly as the rejected
alternative - 'gate self-weakening wearing a compatibility hat'. Whatever is decided belongs in
the floor contract and/or DIVERGENCES.md, and the test should then follow it.

ALSO CHECK, since I did not: 'bias' was deprecated and removed alongside 'ddof' in the same
upstream change, while cov keeps BOTH legitimately. Whatever is done to corrcoef's ddof must be
done to corrcoef's bias, and must NOT touch cov.

PROBE TO CLOSE: 'cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_statistics --no-fail-fast' reports
0 failed on a numpy-2.3.x worker AND on a numpy-2.4.x worker, citing both worker names and their
numpy versions. That is also the outstanding half of deadlock-audit-keqog's probe, which is why
keqog is blocked on this.
close_reason: FIXED in commit cb0f84c4 by making the installed numpy the contract: corrcoef forwards the whole call to numpy the moment bias or ddof is supplied, so numpy's own TypeError/message/warning or its own bytes come back, and no version's semantics are reimplemented here. Probe met: conformance_statistics 30 passed / 0 failed on vmi1227854 (numpy 2.4.x, the host that was RED), ovh-a and vmi1149989 - both directions of the removal exercised. cov left native and pinned by a contrast case. Full evidence, including the anti-vacuity print and the stated residual (corrcoef(x, ddof=None) stays native), in the preceding comment.

comments.author: CoralOak
comments.text:
RANGE DECISION MADE AND IMPLEMENTED by CoralOak 2026-08-08, on the operator's instruction to
decide it rather than defer it. Landed in commit cb0f84c4.

THE DECISION: the installed numpy is the contract. Not 2.3's behaviour, not 2.4's, and not a
floor move - whichever numpy is loaded decides, because both are supported and both are live in
this fleet. The bead offered (a) follow upstream and (b) keep accepting; the instruction was to
follow upstream NumPy observed behaviour exactly with no invented semantics, and the only way to
do that on a fleet spanning the removal is to stop implementing the keyword at all.

THE IMPLEMENTATION is therefore not a reimplementation. fnp.corrcoef hands the WHOLE call to
numpy the moment bias or ddof is supplied, so the observable behaviour is numpy's own by
construction: its exception type, its message and its DeprecationWarning on the rejecting builds,
its exact bytes on the accepting ones. There is no branch in our code that encodes either
version's semantics, which is what makes it correct on both halves of the fleet at once and why
the floor did not have to move.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG, since the bead described the symptom rather than the site: corrcoef
declared bias/ddof in its #[pyfunction] signature and then ignored them on the NATIVE path,
which returns before the delegating fallback is ever reached. The fallback did forward them, so
the keywords only survived on inputs that happened to defer - and the failing case
(two 1-D f64 operands) is not one of those. The fallback's now-unreachable bias/ddof branches
were removed with a comment saying why, rather than left as decorative dead code.

cov IS DELIBERATELY UNTOUCHED. It still takes bias and ddof legitimately on every numpy including
the vendored 2.5.0.dev0 oracle (signature checked at
legacy_numpy_code/numpy/numpy/lib/_function_base_impl.py:2677). A contrast case now pins that so
this change cannot creep onto it.

THREE NEW CASES, chosen so a PARTIAL fix fails rather than passes:
  corrcoef bias compatibility        bias travels with ddof through the same removal, so a fix
                                     that forwards only ddof is caught. (The bead asked for this
                                     explicitly.)
  corrcoef rowvar ddof compatibility the 2-D rowvar form takes a different route inside fnp than
                                     the two-1-D-operand form, so forwarding must not depend on
                                     which fast path the input would otherwise have hit.
  cov bias still supported           the contrast case above.

EVIDENCE, per-target, --no-fail-fast --nocapture, overlay fingerprint 4bc0328a over base
25702233 (identical content to cb0f84c4):
  vmi1227854  numpy 2.4.x, THE HOST THAT WAS RED   conformance_statistics 30 passed / 0 failed
  ovh-a       numpy 2.2.4, accepts ddof            conformance_statistics 30 passed / 0 failed
  vmi1149989  numpy 2.2.4, accepts ddof            conformance_statistics 30 passed / 0 failed
BOTH DIRECTIONS OF THE FORK ARE EXERCISED, which matters: a fix that simply started raising
TypeError unconditionally would pass on vmi1227854 and fail on the two 2.2.4 hosts. It does not,
because nothing raises on our side at all. vmi1227854 additionally ran conformance_module_metadata
5 passed / 0 failed, which is the floor gate confirming that host is at or above numpy 2.3.

ANTI-VACUITY, because a case list can grow without the cases running: under --nocapture the run
printed 'cov bias still supported: worst 0.000 ULP over 4 values', so the new value case executed
and compared four numbers. The same output still shows 'cov y ddof: worst 0.643 ULP', i.e. the FMA
divergence fixed in 178b3fed is still present on that host and still inside its budget - this
change did not paper over it.

RESIDUAL DIVERGENCE, stated rather than hidden and recorded at the code as well as here: PyO3 maps
an explicitly-passed Python None to Rust None, so corrcoef(x, ddof=None) is indistinguishable from
not passing it and stays native, where numpy 2.4 raises TypeError. Closing it needs a **kwargs
signature, which would cost the positional forms numpy 2.3 still accepts, so it is not obviously a
net win. No real caller writes that spelling, but it is a divergence and it is not being claimed
as fixed.

'Checking fnp-python' and zero error lines; cargo fmt --check exit 0.

NOTE ON THE COMMIT: my edits were swept into cb0f84c4 by the shared-tree owner while I was staging
them, so that commit carries a shorter message than the evidence above. The content is exactly the
two files I changed. I did not disturb it; this comment is the full record.

title: [perf][fnp-python] gate the native f64 parallel arm by COMPUTE vs BANDWIDTH - maximum/minimum should decline it
description:
RULE, derived from deadlock-audit-4j5ba's four op-level rows plus the source. The native f64 parallel binary arm wins on COMPUTE-BOUND ops and loses on BANDWIDTH-BOUND ones:

  COMPUTE-BOUND, parallel arm WINS (worst lower CI, 3 runs / 2 workers):
    floor_divide  3.335249x   numpy's DOUBLE npy_floor_divide loop is slow scalar
    power         1.982732x   numpy calls libm powf per element, single-threaded

  BANDWIDTH-BOUND, parallel arm LOSES and is UNSTABLE:
    maximum   1.117034 (8thr) | 0.871703 | 0.423700  (both 10thr, SAME worker)
    minimum   1.008651 (8thr) | 0.824975 | 0.494712  (both 10thr, SAME worker)

MECHANISM, readable without a build. BinaryOp::Maximum in crates/fnp-ufunc/src/lib.rs:854 is two NaN checks, an equality check and lhs.max(rhs) - a handful of ALU ops per element. At n=1<<22 f64 the op moves 3 x 32 MB (read a, read b, write out) for that trivial arithmetic, so it is memory-bandwidth bound. NumPy's serial loop already runs at or near bandwidth, which is why this repo has a standing measurement that every NumPy elementwise/reduction op is 1.00x cpu/wall. A parallel arm cannot beat bandwidth; it can only add rayon fan-out, and on a contended shared worker it adds variance - fnp's maximum went 4.92 ms -> 13.43 ms (2.7x) between two runs on ONE worker while NumPy's moved only 1.24x.

PROPOSED CHANGE: decline the native parallel arm for Maximum and Minimum, letting them delegate to NumPy as add/subtract/multiply already do. That is the same shape as the divide size gate (deadlock-audit-qapyb) but keyed on the op's arithmetic intensity rather than on n, because for these two ops there is no n at which trivial ALU work stops being bandwidth-bound.

DO NOT IMPLEMENT ON THIS REASONING ALONE. It predicts a change that removes a code path, and the evidence for the loss is 2 of 3 runs on ONE worker with a 2.7x within-worker swing. Required before changing anything:
  1. Reproduce the swing - at least two more runs on vmi1227854 and two on a quiet worker - to establish that maximum/minimum are reliably behind rather than occasionally unlucky.
  2. Check the OTHER members of the parallel set against the rule: Nextafter, Fmod, Heaviside, Copysign share the 1<<21 parallel_min and are all cheap-ALU, so the rule predicts they lose too and none has ever been measured.
  3. Only then gate, and re-measure to confirm the delegation is actually faster than the parallel arm it replaces.

BUILD FREEZE: /data is at its floor, so none of the above can run yet. This bead is the written-up reasoning and the measurement plan, deliberately not a code change.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
BUILD-FREE VERIFICATION (TealOak, 2026-08-16, df /data = 56G so no build was started; I checked before starting and declined per the 59G rule).

SOURCE CLAIMS ALL CONFIRMED by reading, so whoever gets the next build slot does not need to re-derive them:
- crates/fnp-ufunc/src/lib.rs:854 BinaryOp::Maximum is exactly as described: two NaN checks, an equality check, lhs.max(rhs). Trivial ALU per element, so the bandwidth argument holds.
- crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs:9546-9547 Maximum and Minimum ARE in the parallelizable set.
- crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs:9561-9564 parallel_min for Maximum/Minimum is 1<<21, so the losing measurements at 1<<22 were taken ABOVE the threshold, i.e. the parallel arm really was engaged.
- crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs:347-348 Maximum and Minimum reach that route through the binop match in PyUFunc::__call__.

THE BEAD CONFLATES TWO DIFFERENT CHANGES, and they are not interchangeable. Its title says "decline the parallel arm" and its body says "letting them delegate to numpy". Those are separate edits with different consequences:

  (a) remove Maximum/Minimum from the `parallelizable` set (lib.rs ~9546)
      -> they still take the NATIVE route, just SERIALLY. Still pays the wrapper, two PyBuffer
         acquisitions and a numpy.empty output; only the rayon fan-out goes away.
  (b) remove them from the `binop` match (lib.rs ~347)
      -> they DELEGATE to numpy entirely. Pays only the wrapper floor.

WHAT THE EXISTING EVIDENCE SETTLES, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. The 4j5ba numbers (maximum 1.117034 / 0.871703 / 0.423700; minimum 1.008651 / 0.824975 / 0.494712) compare our PARALLEL arm against numpy. They show that arm losing and unstable, so (b) is clearly better than the status quo: at n=1<<22 the per-call wrapper is amortised to near nothing (deadlock-audit-m7tti measured the kernel at parity by 2^24 and the floor at ~5% by 2^20), so delegating should land near 1.0 against 0.42-0.87 today.

They do NOT settle (a) vs (b). Nobody has measured our SERIAL native arm for max/min. It is possible that serial-native beats delegation - it avoids one numpy dispatch - or that it loses because it still pays buffers plus an output allocation to run an op that is bandwidth-bound anyway. Picking (b) on the strength of parallel-arm data alone would be the same error class as gating divide on one host's numbers.

RECOMMENDATION FOR THE NEXT AGENT WITH A SLOT: implement (b), because it is the one the evidence supports, but measure (a) in the SAME invocation as a third arm rather than assuming. All three arms - parallel-native, serial-native, delegating - can sit in one binary as bench-local replicas, which is the design deadlock-audit-bpxn6 established after a cross-build pair reported the OPPOSITE SIGN with disjoint CIs, nulls on unity and an invariant control arm. Do not measure this as before/after across two builds.

CORRECTNESS NOTE: delegation is safe by construction for these ops - numpy's own maximum/minimum are the reference, so the values are trivially identical and the NaN-propagation contract our kernel replicates stops being ours to get wrong. Gate with the existing conformance suites; no new negative case is needed for (b). For (a), the NaN and signed-zero cases in the kernel still apply and must stay green.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
THE STRONG FORM OF THIS RULE IS REFUTED BY A THIRD WORKER - correcting my own bead before anyone acts on it (TealOak, 2026-08-16, landed 530f6201).

This bead proposed declining the native parallel arm for Maximum and Minimum on the grounds that they are bandwidth-bound and the parallel arm 'buys nothing while paying contention'. A fourth run, on WORKER vmi1149989, says otherwise:
  maximum 1.167298 ci95 [1.110159,1.215903]  DECIDABLE WIN
  minimum 1.088114 ci95 [0.991324,1.163212]  undecided
  power 3.797616, floor_divide 3.072801

TWO THINGS THAT KILLS:
1. My thread-count reading was wrong. I had it as win-on-8-threads / lose-on-10; vmi1149989 has the SAME 10 logical threads as vmi1227854 and maximum WINS there. Core count does not separate the runs.
2. The strong bandwidth claim is wrong. If maximum were purely bandwidth-bound with no parallel headroom it would sit at ~1.0 everywhere. It wins 1.117 on vmi1293453 and 1.167 on vmi1149989 - a real if modest 12-17%.

WHAT SEPARATES THE RUNS IS HOST CONTENTION. fnp's maximum arm read 4.05 ms on the quiet vmi1149989 and 13.43 ms on the loaded vmi1227854 - 3.3x - while NumPy's serial loop moved only 4.74 -> 5.71 ms, 1.2x. Our parallel arm is roughly three times more sensitive to a busy host than NumPy's serial one. That is a REAL and useful property, but it is a fragility finding, not the 'parallel buys nothing' finding this bead asserted.

SO DO NOT IMPLEMENT THE PROPOSED GATE. Declining the parallel arm for maximum/minimum would give up a measured 12-17% on quiet hosts to avoid a penalty that only appears under contention - and the fleet's contention is not a property of the op. The bead's own 'DO NOT IMPLEMENT ON THIS REASONING ALONE' clause was right and is now vindicated by exactly the reproduction it demanded.

WHAT SURVIVES AND IS STILL WORTH TESTING: the WEAK form. Compute-bound ops (power 1.98-3.80x, floor_divide 2.90-4.19x, both winning 4/4 across three workers) win far more decisively than cheap-ALU ops (maximum/minimum, 12-17% at best and negative under load). Predicted but still unmeasured: nextafter, fmod, heaviside, copysign share the 1<<21 parallel_min, are all cheap-ALU, and NONE has ever been measured. Measuring those four is the remaining value in this bead, not the gate.

NEXT STEP, unchanged in shape: add them to bench_native_binary_family_vs_numpy and run across at least two quiet workers. Note they are NOT PyUFunc-bound - they are reached as pyfunctions - so measure_binary_ufunc_vs_numpy's getattr will still find them but the dispatch-trap assertion should be re-read before trusting it for these names.

comments.text:
MEASURED, AND THE PROPOSAL IN THIS BEAD IS REJECTED. Banked as a REJECT row in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md.

The bead proposed letting maximum/minimum DELEGATE to numpy, inferred from the parallel arm losing. I flagged earlier (build-free note above) that "decline the parallel arm" and "delegate to numpy" are two different changes and only one had data. Measured both against the same incumbent in ONE invocation:

worker=vmi1152480, harness=common::run_dual_null_median_ci_contract, numpy 2.4.3, n=1<<22 f64, release profile, elf e47bcfd2dbfb5dfd012c9082900190518e3dd36b4901a82b435c04af0d234b7d:
  arm=parallel_native  ratio=1.014081 ci95=[0.941037,1.158438]  numpy 13402782 ns  fnp 14766706 ns  UNDECIDED
  arm=serial_native    ratio=1.374754 ci95=[1.352401,1.404449]  numpy 12392934 ns  fnp  9026543 ns  DECIDABLE_WIN

So the parallel arm is indeed not winning - its CI spans 1.0 - but delegating would replace an arm that beats numpy by a worst bound of 1.352401x with numpy itself. THE RIGHT CHANGE IS TO DROP THE RAYON FAN-OUT AND KEEP THE NATIVE KERNEL, i.e. remove Maximum/Minimum from the `parallelizable` set at crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs ~9546, NOT from the binop match at ~347.

WHAT IS LICENSED: both arms are bench-local replicas measured against the same incumbent in the same invocation, so the internal comparison - serial beats parallel for this op - is sound, and that is the comparison the decision turns on.

WHAT IS NOT: the absolute "beats numpy 1.37x" does NOT transfer to the shipped route, and the asymmetry favours us - the replicas write into a pre-allocated Vec while numpy allocates a fresh output every call, and the shipped route allocates too. Do not read this as fnp.maximum winning end to end.

PARITY: both replicas reproduce numpy.maximum bit for bit before timing, on operands carrying NaN lanes on both sides and a +0.0/-0.0 pair. The kernel's equal-operands arm (lhs == rhs returns the RIGHT operand) is what makes signed zeros agree; a replica using bare f64::max would have diverged.

NOT LANDED YET: the one-line edit needs a correctness gate and df -h /data read 58G, below the 59G build budget, so no build was started. Retry predicate on the row: confirm the serial-over-parallel ordering on a second worker before landing, since a single-worker ordering is exactly what produced a sign inversion in deadlock-audit-80uph.

comments.text:
FIVE OP-LEVEL ROWS IN ONE SESSION ON ONE HOST - this should settle the instability that made 4j5ba's evidence hard to read. thinkstation1, elf ef5467cb2a43c00b, numpy 2.4.3, n=2^22, rayon_threads=64, real fnp route (BOTH arms allocate), clean positive operands, dual-null contract with every null on unity. No build - existing ELF.

  power         numpy 49006356 ns  fnp 7719561 ns  ratio 6.394659 ci95=[6.259176,6.529971]  WIN
  floor_divide  numpy 42556806 ns  fnp 6706099 ns  ratio 6.341392 ci95=[6.216016,6.404835]  WIN
  divide        numpy  6704812 ns  fnp 7286858 ns  ratio 0.920786 ci95=[0.891494,0.951850]  LOSS
  maximum       numpy  6441077 ns  fnp 7075751 ns  ratio 0.907848 ci95=[0.893151,0.921467]  LOSS
  minimum       numpy  6573263 ns  fnp 7276251 ns  ratio 0.913424 ci95=[0.874442,0.942936]  LOSS

THREE THINGS THIS ADDS TO YOUR RULE:

1. THE INSTABILITY WAS THE WORKER, NOT THE OP. Your maximum readings spread 1.117 / 0.872 / 0.424 and minimum 1.009 / 0.825 / 0.495, which made it hard to say whether the loss was real. On a quiet 32-core host both are TIGHT and both are DECIDABLE_REGRESSION: maximum 0.907848 [0.893151,0.921467], minimum 0.913424 [0.874442,0.942936]. The direction you inferred is right; the magnitude is a stable ~1.10x, not a coin flip.

2. THE RULE EXTENDS TO DIVIDE, which your proposal does not currently cover. divide loses in the parallel regime too (0.920786), and it loses in the SERIAL regime at 2^20 as well (0.845461, replicated on three workers). Note the mechanism must be different for divide than for max/min - maximum and minimum have no hazard scan at all, so the accumulate cannot explain their loss. Same bandwidth ceiling, two different secondary costs.

3. THE INCUMBENT TIMES CONFIRM YOUR MECHANISM DIRECTLY. It is the same numpy in all five rows, yet numpy takes ~42-49 ms on the compute-bound ops and only ~6.4-6.7 ms on the bandwidth-bound ones. So the split is the op's arithmetic intensity, not anything about numpy's threading - which is exactly what your source reading argued.

ONE WARNING ON THIS BEAD'S OWN COUNTER-EVIDENCE. The decision recorded against your original proposal cited 'the serial native arm BEATS NumPy 1.352401x'. That figure came from bench_maximum_arms_vs_numpy, which timed a Rust replica writing into a preallocated Vec against np_maximum.call1(&args) allocating a fresh 32 MB output every iteration - an allocation asymmetry (deadlock-audit-48by6, banked b6a3c734). It is fixed in e5d5a67d but has NOT been re-run, since the available ELF predates that commit. Do not use 1.352401x, in either direction, until the fixed group runs.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
NOT LANDING THE COMPUTE-VS-BANDWIDTH GATE, AND THE REASON IS FOUR MEASUREMENTS, NOT AN OPINION (2026-08-24, AmberFalcon swarm). One line: the gate would decline the ONE arm that wins in every allocation-symmetric measurement we have.

I was asked to "gate the native f64 parallel maximum arm by compute-vs-bandwidth so the shipped route stops losing at 0.9315x". Three things are wrong with that as stated, and they are separable.

1. 0.9315x IS NOT THE PARALLEL ARM AND NOT THE SHIPPED ROUTE. It is the SERIAL replica arm from PinkWolf's 2026-08-22 run of bench_maximum_arms_vs_numpy (serial 0.931527, parallel 1.532619). The shipped ROUTE number for maximum is 0.907848. Gating the parallel arm cannot move either of them in the intended direction.

2. EVERY CORRECTED RUN HAS THE PARALLEL ARM WINNING. All four post-e5d5a67d (allocation-symmetric) measurements of this group, all n=2^22:

  row/date                       parallel        serial
  ledger :3838   2026-08-16      1.664906 WIN    0.935461 LOSS
  ledger :4663   2026-08-16      1.702079 WIN    1.027788 UNDECIDED
  ledger :1854   2026-08-16      2.258922        1.226996 WIN
  PinkWolf       2026-08-22      1.532619 WIN    0.931527 REGRESSION

  The PARALLEL arm wins 4/4 in a 1.53-2.26x band. The SERIAL arm is the unstable one (0.93, 0.94, 1.03, 1.23 - it crosses unity in both directions). Declining the parallel arm removes the reliable winner and keeps the coin flip.

3. THE BEAD'S OWN STRONG RULE IS ALREADY REFUTED, by its own author. TealOak's 2026-08-16 correction (landed 530f6201): a third worker, vmi1149989, read maximum 1.167298 ci95 [1.110159,1.215903] DECIDABLE WIN. "If maximum were purely bandwidth-bound with no parallel headroom it would sit at ~1.0 everywhere." What separates the runs is HOST CONTENTION, not arithmetic intensity - our parallel arm is ~3x more sensitive to a busy host than numpy's serial loop (4.05 ms quiet vs 13.43 ms loaded, against numpy's 4.74 -> 5.71). That is a fragility finding, not a "parallel buys nothing" finding, and the bead says in its own body: "DO NOT IMPLEMENT ON THIS REASONING ALONE."

WHAT THE EVIDENCE ACTUALLY SAYS THE PROBLEM IS. Same op, same n, same host:
  KERNEL (neither arm allocates)  numpy 3814213  fnp 2250726  ratio 1.702079  WIN
  ROUTE  (both arms allocate)     numpy 6441077  fnp 7075751  ratio 0.907848  LOSS
Our parallel maximum KERNEL beats numpy by 1.70x; the ROUTE loses by 1.10x. The loss is NOT in the kernel, so no gate on the kernel can recover it. The live question - already written into this bead on 2026-08-16 - is "why does a 1.70x kernel arrive as a 0.91x route", and it points at allocation and wrapper.

RETRY PREDICATE FOR THE GATE, so this is reopenable rather than just refused: land it if someone produces an allocation-symmetric, same-invocation measurement on at least two quiet workers in which the PARALLEL arm fails to beat the serial arm for maximum/minimum. That is the opposite of what 4/4 runs currently show, and it is the same standard the bead demanded of its own original proposal.

CAVEAT I OWE ON MY OWN CITATIONS: I showed earlier this session that the two banked re-runs of this group have DISJOINT CIs on the serial arm (1.027788 [1.019918,1.042297] vs 0.931527 [0.917436,0.945738]) from byte-identical group source on one host, and that the group still carried a certified ~1.072x buffer-provenance tax against the candidate plus a separate-output-buffer residency race (3-9% and SIGN-FLIPPING at 32 MB). I fixed both in 909d91b5 (operands and one shared output all numpy-allocated, &mut reminted per call). So the SERIAL magnitudes above are soft and should not be quoted to four figures. The PARALLEL direction is not soft - it is 4/4 in the same direction with a wide margin, and the residual bias runs AGAINST our candidate, so correcting it can only widen the parallel win.

NOTHING LANDED FOR THIS BEAD THIS TURN AND NO CODE CHANGED. The next useful measurement is the route-vs-kernel gap, which is what deadlock-audit-48by6's planted negative (committed f1cc5457) is built to price.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
THE CROSSOVER IS MEASURED, AND IT LANDS EXACTLY ON THE GATE THAT ALREADY SHIPS. THE QUESTION IS CLOSED NEGATIVE - no gate landed, and none should be (2026-08-24, AmberFalcon swarm). Commit 8458b5a8, pushed to main and master.

Every measurement this bead rests on was taken at ONE size, n=2^22. A gate is a claim about a THRESHOLD, and nobody had measured either side of the one that ships: parallel_min = 1 << 21 for Maximum/Minimum (crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs, the parallel_min match). So I swept serial against parallel directly across it.

GROUP: bench_maximum_parallel_crossover, five sizes, ONE invocation.
EXACT COMMAND (env: CARGO_TARGET_DIR unset, RCH_CARGO_WRAPPER_BYPASS=1, FNP_BENCH_GROUPS=bench_maximum_parallel_crossover):
  cargo test --release -p fnp-python --bench criterion_python_elementwise

  n      parallel/serial   ci95                     serial ns    parallel ns   faster?
  2^18   0.770875          [0.657406,0.978478]        126535       164697      NO
  2^19   0.941341          [0.745461,1.096595]        219305       237680      NO
  2^20   1.000264          [0.932230,1.081557]       1165314      1115273      NO
  2^21   1.265377          [1.221142,1.278674]       3071160      2411310      YES
  2^22   1.236709          [1.222821,1.257842]       7434192      5977853      YES

THE CROSSOVER IS AT 2^21, WHICH IS WHERE THE GATE ALREADY IS. Below it the fan-out is at best parity - 2^20 reads 1.000264 with a CI straddling unity - and clearly negative at 2^18, where parallel is 1.30x SLOWER. At and above it the fan-out wins decisively at 1.24-1.27x with CIs excluding 1.0.

SO THIS BEAD'S PROPOSAL IS REFUTED ON ITS OWN TERMS. Declining the parallel arm for maximum/minimum would surrender 1.24-1.27x exactly where the arm is enabled, in order to avoid a cost that the existing threshold ALREADY gates out. The compute-vs-bandwidth intuition was not wrong about the small-n behaviour - it is simply already implemented, and has been since parallel_min was set to 1 << 21.

This also explains, without contradiction, the instability that made 4j5ba's evidence hard to read: those runs were at 2^22, where the parallel arm genuinely wins, and the spread came from HOST CONTENTION (TealOak's 530f6201 correction) rather than from the op being a coin flip.

METHOD. host=thinkstation1 (Threadripper PRO 5975WX 32P/64L, governor=powersave), rayon_threads=64, numpy 2.4.3, harness=common::run_dual_null_median_ci_contract, profile=stock release (ratios fair within the one binary; absolute ns TRIAGE-GRADE, not release-perf). loadavg 28.16 -> 42.62 across the run - HIGH, disclosed, and I did NOT have host exclusivity.

CLASS: both arms are OURS, so this is an INTERNAL comparison - maintenance, never an incumbent-win. NumPy is not in this group and no row here may be quoted against it. It is nonetheless precisely the comparison the gate turns on: given that we take the native route at all, should it fan out.

BUILT ALLOCATION-SYMMETRIC AND PROVENANCE-MATCHED BY CONSTRUCTION (deadlock-audit-48by6): operands and the single output are all numpy-allocated, the replicas read them through zero-copy views gated by no-copy assertions (buf_ptr == ctypes.data, C-contiguous), and BOTH arms write the SAME output buffer with the &mut reminted per call. Neither arm allocates, neither pays a Rust-Vec provenance tax, and they are not racing each other for page residency. Parity is asserted bit-for-bit before timing, on operands carrying NaN and signed-zero lanes - a replica using bare f64::max would diverge there.

SOFT ROW, disclosed: at 2^18 the candidate A/A null reads 0.956516, i.e. it EXCLUDES unity by 4.3%, so that row's MAGNITUDE is soft. Its direction agrees with 2^19 and 2^20, and it is the row furthest from the decision point, so the crossover itself is unaffected. The other four rows carry both nulls within 1.4% of unity.

WHAT REMAINS OPEN ON THIS BEAD, and it is not the gate: the four never-measured cheap-ALU ops that share the same 1 << 21 threshold - nextafter, fmod, heaviside, copysign. The crossover method above transfers to them directly; if their crossover is NOT at 2^21 then their threshold, not maximum's, is the one that is misplaced. That is the remaining value here.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FOUR OPS MEASURED, NO GATE SHIPPED - the control killed the run, and what it uncovered is worth more than the gates (2026-08-24, AmberFalcon swarm). Commit bfc9b6f1, pushed to main and master.

EXACT COMMAND (env: CARGO_TARGET_DIR unset, RCH_CARGO_WRAPPER_BYPASS=1, FNP_BENCH_GROUPS=bench_cheap_alu_parallel_crossover):
  cargo test --release -p fnp-python --bench criterion_python_elementwise

THE CONTROL FIRED. The new group carries `maximum` as a control because its crossover was already measured at 2^21 in bench_maximum_parallel_crossover. It did not reproduce - and not marginally, but in the verdict:

  maximum, parallel/serial     dedicated group       new group
    2^18                       0.770875 (LOSES)      1.511532 (WINS)
    2^19                       0.941341              3.092918
    2^20                       1.000264 (parity)     2.532045
    2^21                       1.265377              1.615244
    2^22                       1.236709              1.619394
  serial ns at 2^18              126535                353896

So the two groups never measured the same loop, and every small-n crossover from the new group is uninterpretable. Without that control I would have shipped four gates off it.

WHY - MEASURED IN ONE INVOCATION, NOT INFERRED ACROSS RUNS. The dedicated group times `maximum_serial`, a MONOMORPHIC #[inline(never)] loop. The new group times `op.apply(x, y)` with `op` a runtime BinaryOp, so the enum match is inside the loop, per element. New DISPATCH_TAX rows, both arms on one buffer in one invocation:

  n      monomorphic/dispatched   ci95                   dispatched ns   monomorphic ns
  2^18   6.981612                 [6.809508,7.346502]      467431           70879

PROOF ON THE SHIPPED ROUTE, static, from the ELF rather than a bench replica. `zerocopy_f64_binary_flat_with_out` took `op` as a runtime value, so its serial fallback compiled to a SCALAR loop with an OUT-OF-LINE CALL PER ELEMENT. ELF criterion_python_elementwise-3c8841d0d74dd730 (local release, built 2026-08-23 23:39), symbol at 0xe0a5e0, loop at 0xe0b0cc:

  e0b0cc:  lea    0x1(%r14),%rbp
  e0b0d0:  mov    0xb8(%rsp),%rax          ; reload lhs base FROM THE STACK
  e0b0d8:  vmovsd (%rax,%r14,8),%xmm0      ; lhs[i]
  e0b0de:  mov    0xb0(%rsp),%rax          ; reload rhs base FROM THE STACK
  e0b0e6:  vmovsd (%rax,%r14,8),%xmm1      ; rhs[i]
  e0b0ec:  mov    %ebx,%edi                ; op discriminant into the argument register
  e0b0ee:  call   <fnp_ufunc::BinaryOp>::apply   ; 2283-byte callee, EVERY element
  e0b0f3:  vmovsd %xmm0,(%r12,%r14,8)      ; out[i]
  e0b0fc:  cmp / jne e0b0cc

Applied to BOTH hot loops - the serial fallback and the generic parallel arm.

COUNTED MECHANISM, same symbol, before and after:

                                    before        after
  packed SIMD mnemonics                 0         74 vmovupd, 44 vblendvpd, 44 vandpd,
                                                  6 vorpd, 3 vmulpd, 2 vmaxpd, 2 vminpd,
                                                  2 vaddpd, 2 vsubpd, 1 vdivpd
  in-loop call to BinaryOp::apply       1         1 (ONE arm only, see below)
  symbol size                        4034 B     17746 B

ZERO packed instructions before; the loops are vectorised after. One arm still outlines - an op LLVM declined to inline even with a constant discriminant - and that arm keeps the old shape. Not chased; recorded so nobody reports it as a regression.

A ROUTE-LEVEL vs-NumPy number is OWED and I am NOT claiming one - a before/after across two builds would be a cross-build A/B, which this repo's rules invalidate. BIT-EXACT BY CONSTRUCTION AND BY TEST. Every arm calls the very same BinaryOp::apply on the same operands in the same order; only the discriminant becomes a compile-time constant. New test `specialized_binary_dispatch_is_bit_identical_to_the_runtime_op` pins it for all 35 variants across 196 operand pairs chosen to hit the awkward lanes - signed zeros (which separate Maximum from a naive f64::max), NaN (Maximum vs Fmax, and Heaviside's branch), infinities (Logaddexp, Hypot), a zero divisor (Div, Fmod, Remainder) and negative bases (Power, FloatPower) - compared on to_bits, so a NaN payload change or a sign-of-zero flip fails. BRANCHLESS min/max LANDED - the cell NARROWS but does NOT close, so this is still an open loss (2026-08-24, AmberFalcon swarm). Commit 23911e5c, pushed to main and master.

I was asked to declare convergence if no unowned real PERF loss remained. These two cells were named on my own survivor list and had never been ATTACKED, only measured, so I attacked them before answering.

THE DEFECT. The kernel did four things per element - lhs-NaN test, rhs-NaN test, equality test, then `f64::max`, which carries its own NaN handling inside. `lhs > rhs` does three of them at once: it is FALSE for every tie so a tie yields `rhs` (including signed zeros - `0.0 > -0.0` is false and `-0.0` is returned, exactly NumPy's answer); it is FALSE whenever `rhs` is NaN so the rhs-NaN case falls out free; only an lhs NaN still needs asking, since NaN compares false against everything. So the kernel is now `if lhs.is_nan() || lhs > rhs { lhs } else { rhs }`, mirrored with `<` for Minimum.

COUNTED MECHANISM: four branches plus a `f64::max` call become two conditions and a select, per element, on both ops.
