title: [perf] convolve/correlate direct parallel scatter under-parallelizes large kernels (.max(m) block floor collapses to ~1-6 blocks)
close_reason: Dropped the .max(m) block-size floor in convolve_mode's direct parallel scatter (lib.rs ~19838): for a large kernel (m comparable to full_len) it forced chunk>=m, collapsing par_chunks_mut to ~1-6 blocks and idling most cores. Replaced with .max(64) (small floor only). Chunk size never affects the result (each output index owned by one block, ascending-i accumulation preserved) — proven by convolve_1d_parallel_matches_scatter_reference (bit-exact) + the bench's own assert_eq!(old,new). Same-run rch criterion A/B (load-robust, both arms equal load even at machine load 207): 5000x20000 (kernel>>signal) 18.94ms->4.82ms 3.93x; 20000x12000 30.94ms->10.55ms 2.93x; 200000x1000 small-m control 6.15->6.17ms 1.00x (IDENTICAL, zero regression — full_len/(threads*2) already exceeds small m so the floor never binds). Only the direct path with large m is affected; the FFT-gated huge cases and all small/medium convolves are unchanged. Continues the convolve FFT-gate fix (bead p8qdt). 17 convolve tests green.

title: correctness(arctanh/log): FP-event count diverges from numpy on -inf - arctanh emits an EXTRA event, log emits NONE; attribution owed a rebuild A/B
description:
FOUND IN PASSING while shipping deadlock-audit-2qjj3. NOT fixed there, and deliberately NOT
claimed as pre-existing without a rebuild A/B.

TanBridge, thinkstation1, numpy 2.4.3 live, fnp .so sha256
f87b11b03cdc12376168fe730f5d4ec675db9a31f03f5b57b02693d592d6a0d3 (at 023c66ff).

## THE TWO DIVERGENCES

Operand is `[anchor, value]` with an in-domain anchor:

```
  op        operand   numpy       fnp         values_equal
  arctanh   -inf      warn=1      warn=2      True     <-- fnp emits an EXTRA event
  log       -inf      warn=1      warn=0      True     <-- fnp emits NO event
```

`arctanh(-inf)` and `log(-inf)` both give NaN, and the VALUES agree in both cases. Only the FP
event count differs, in opposite directions.

## ATTRIBUTION STATUS - HONEST

These are almost certainly pre-existing, but that is argued from the diff rather than measured:
the functional change in 023c66ff is three predicate lines (Arcsin / Arccos / Arccosh) plus a
`match` at the defer site whose default arm is the OLD `return Ok(None)`. No arm shares state, so
arctanh and log execute identical code before and after.

A rebuild A/B was NOT run: `git checkout <ref> -- <path>` is blocked by dcg (it discards working
tree state) and a worktree build was not worth 20 minutes at the time. **Whoever takes this bead
should do the A/B first** - build the parent of 023c66ff in a separate worktree with its own
CARGO_TARGET_DIR and confirm both divergences reproduce there. If either does NOT, it is a
regression from 023c66ff and that changes the priority completely.

## LIKELY MECHANISM, UNVERIFIED

`arctanh`'s predicate is

    |value, _| value.abs() == 1.0 || (value.is_finite() && value.abs() > 1.0)

For -inf both clauses are false, so no event is detected, no defer happens, and the native buffer
is returned - which should give warn=0, not warn=2. **The observed warn=2 is not explained by that
reading**, so the arctanh route may not be reaching this helper at all on this operand. Do not
guess; instrument which route runs before designing a fix.

`log`'s warn=0 IS consistent with the same `is_finite()` hole this session fixed three times
(sqrt, then arccosh/arcsin/arccos): a predicate that excludes the infinities where NumPy's event
set includes them.

## WHY IT WAS NOT FIXED WITH THE OTHERS

Both ops raise TWO errstate categories from a single call (`arctanh([1.0, 2.0])` raises invalid AND
divide; `log([0.0, -1.0])` likewise), so the one-element-witness fix used for arccosh/arcsin/arccos
would UNDER-REPORT. They need either a per-category witness set or a genuinely different design.
See the 023c66ff commit message for the measured category table.

## ACCEPTANCE

Rebuild A/B attributing each divergence first; then, if pre-existing, an errstate probe over
warn/raise/ignore x {finite out-of-domain, +-inf, NaN, boundary, in-domain} for arctanh / log /
log2 / log10 / exp / exp2, and a fix that reproduces EVERY category NumPy would raise for the
operand actually passed.

title: [test][fnp-python] no keepdims x axis shape sweep - native reductions reconstruct the output shape by hand, and that class has been wrong before
description:
NEW PROBE AXIS. The six sweeps so far compared what comes back (type, dtype,
exception, __all__) and whether it aliases. This one compares the SHAPE a
reduction produces across the axis x keepdims grid.

WHY THIS AXIS: fnp's native reduction paths do not get keepdims from numpy -
they reconstruct the output shape themselves. There is a dedicated helper,
keepdims_expand_axis, called from the f16/f32 nan-extreme and sum paths, and the
wrappers re-insert the reduced axis by hand:

    if keepdims.unwrap_or(false) {
        let ndim = a.bind(py).getattr("ndim")?.extract::<usize>()?;
        return keepdims_expand_axis(py, &numpy, out, ax as i64, ndim);
    }

and elsewhere reshape to `vec![1usize; ndim]`. That is per-site shape arithmetic
over: axis=None, a single positive axis, a NEGATIVE axis, a TUPLE of axes, and
keepdims true/false - and it has been wrong before, in the class the nanpercentile
comment calls out as "(keepdims-on-axis class, BlackThrush 2026-06-22)".

A wrong keepdims shape is not silent the way a copy-instead-of-view is, but it
is silent ENOUGH: the values are right, the dtype is right, and the failure only
shows up later when the result is broadcast against the original array - which
is the entire reason keepdims exists.

PROBE TO CLOSE: a conformance sweep comparing result SHAPE (and dtype and
values) against numpy for a grid of
  reductions  sum, prod, mean, std, var, min, max, any, all, argmin, argmax,
              median, percentile, count_nonzero, and the nan* twins
  axis        None, 0, 1, -1, -2, (0, 1), (0, -1)
  keepdims    False, True
over a 3-D input, plus the broadcast property that motivates keepdims: for every
keepdims=True result, `a / result` must succeed and match numpy's. Tuple and
NEGATIVE axes are the cases most likely to be wrong, and axis=None with
keepdims=True (all-ones shape) is the one most likely to be special-cased away.
Any divergence is a real defect; fix it in the same bead.
close_reason:
DELIVERED in 025d1356 as a LOCK. NO DIVERGENCE - 300+ comparisons, all match, so no defect is claimed. It also passed on the FIRST run, so unlike liz1c and st00f there is no red-to-green here and I am not implying one: the coverage is the whole deliverable.

WHY THE AXIS WAS WORTH PROBING: fnp's native reduction paths do not receive keepdims from numpy - they reconstruct the output shape themselves, via keepdims_expand_axis or by reshaping to vec![1usize; ndim], once per site, across axis=None, a single positive axis, a NEGATIVE axis and a TUPLE of axes. That is hand-rolled shape arithmetic repeated per wrapper, and it has been wrong before: nanpercentile's own comment names the class, '(keepdims-on-axis class, BlackThrush 2026-06-22)'.

THE GRID: 20 reductions (sum/prod/mean/std/var/min/max/median/any/all/argmin/argmax and the eight nan* twins) x 9 axis spellings (None, 0, 1, 2, -1, -2, and the tuples (0,1), (0,-1), (1,2)) x keepdims both ways, over a 3-D input containing a NaN so the nan* variants are exercised on their actual purpose. argmin/argmax skip tuple axes, which numpy does not accept for them.

THE BROADCAST-BACK GROUP IS WHAT MAKES IT MORE THAN A SHAPE-STRING COMPARISON: for every keepdims=True result, 'a / result' must succeed and match numpy's. A shape that is merely 'some tuple with ones in it' can satisfy a shape comparison while being useless for the one thing keepdims exists for - broadcasting back against the input. Dividing the original array by the result cannot be satisfied that way.

PRECONDITIONS: numpy's keepdims must still change the shape (np.sum(cube, axis=0, keepdims=True).shape != np.sum(cube, axis=0).shape), or the whole grid is comparing two identical things; and at least 300 comparisons must have run, so an empty or over-filtered grid reports rather than passes.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_return_types = 4 passed / 0 failed, exit 0, oracle numpy 2.4.3, with the >=300-comparison guard satisfied. cargo clippy -p fnp-python --test conformance_return_types -- -D warnings exit 0. cargo fmt --check -p fnp-python exit 0. All exit codes captured directly.

PROBE-CLASS TALLY, seven sweeps now: rrrlm, scoca, 65pde, bikey clean locks; liz1c found take(complex64) raising (fixed); c7hqd found concatenate's .base (fixed in st00f). Two live bugs in seven probes. Axes I considered and did NOT file because they are already covered: WARNING parity - conformance_diagnostics.rs already sweeps ~40 cases across divide-by-zero/invalid/overflow/underflow, mean/var of empty, nanmean/nanstd all-NaN and deprecations, INCLUDING negative no-warning controls. Unprobed candidates a successor might weigh: non-contiguous/negative-stride input parity (fnp's fast paths gate on c_contiguous and fall back - do the fallbacks agree?), and structured/void dtype parity.

PARITY IS FINE. Both failing tests assert TWO things. The first, 'ok' - fnp.cov allclose numpy.cov across every shape/ddof/bias combination - PASSES on 2.2.4. The panic is on the SECOND assert, a sha256 of fnp's own output bytes. So this is not a wrong answer; it is a byte-golden that no longer matches.

THREAD-DEPENDENCE REFUTED. I suspected the parallel Gram reduction order, which would have made the bits host-dependent (the same worry that opened m8z69). Ran cov_native_fast_path on ONE worker (ovh-a) at RAYON_NUM_THREADS = 1, 2, 4 and default: all four produce the IDENTICAL hash a832b9262ebe8428acb9009460e9617648991499e339635dec57d555ea78625f. The output is thread-count invariant. Hypothesis dead.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY TRACKS - the numpy build:
  ovh-a       numpy 2.2.4, threads 1/2/4/default -> a832b926...
  vmi1149989  numpy 2.2.4                        -> a832b926...
  vmi1227854  numpy 2.4.x                        -> f40ad3f2...
  recorded golden                                -> 80bb612d...
Two distinct values keyed to the numpy build, and the stored golden matches NEITHER - it pins a third environment nobody in the current fleet has.

WHY fnp's OWN bytes depend on numpy's build, which is the interesting part: the proof hashes 'f', the fnp result, over shapes including (1,100) and (3,3). Where the native Gram fast path does not take the input, fnp.cov DELEGATES, so those entries in the proof are numpy-computed values and inherit numpy's build. The golden therefore mixes native and delegated output and cannot be stable across the fleet. Same root class as the reduction-tree finding in m8z69.

I DID NOT REGENERATE THE GOLDEN. That is the named forbidden reflex, and here it would also be useless: any value I picked would be correct on one worker class and wrong on the other. The second test, cov_corrcoef_long_observation_ufunc_gate_matches_numpy_sha256, drifts the same way (65d3aaed... observed vs 72b73596... recorded).

WHAT ACTUALLY FIXES IT, for whoever takes it after the version decision: either (a) the supported-numpy-floor decision from 1jqrw makes one value canonical, or (b) the proof is narrowed to hash ONLY outputs the native path produced, excluding delegated shapes, which makes the golden a genuine self-regression detector instead of a partial mirror of numpy's bits. (b) is the better engineering and is independent of (a), but it changes what the test asserts, so it should be a deliberate choice rather than a drive-by edit.

comments.text:
ROOT CAUSE FOUND by AzureHill 2026-08-06, and all THREE failures share it. Confirmed on numpy 2.4.3 (worker vmi1227854, 27 passed / 3 failed, --no-fail-fast).

THE THIRD FAILURE, which I had missed, is the one that explains the other two. cov_corrcoef_python_container_keyword_outcomes_match_numpy fails on the case 'cov y ddof':
  MODULE.cov([1.0, 2.0, 4.0], y=[2.0, 1.0, 0.0], ddof=0)
  numpy [0][0] = 1.5555555555555556
  fnp   [0][0] = 1.5555555555555554
ONE ULP. That test compares exact JSON repr, so one ULP fails it.

I LOCATED THE ULP RATHER THAN GUESSING. Ruled out the scaling first: numpy's cov ends with 'c *= np.true_divide(1, fact)', a multiply by reciprocal rather than a divide, which is a classic last-ULP trap - but here BOTH spellings give ...56, so that is not it. Ruled out the mean too. Then enumerated candidate formulas on the actual f64 values:
  centered dot / n        -> 1.5555555555555554   == FNP
  centered dot * (1/n)    -> 1.5555555555555554   == FNP
  E[x^2] - mean^2         -> 1.5555555555555545
  (sum x^2 - n*mean^2)/n  -> 1.5555555555555547
  2-D np.dot(Xc, Xc.T)    -> 1.5555555555555556   == NUMPY
The split is between the 1-D/sequential accumulation and the 2-D MATMUL. numpy's cov computes 'dot(X, X_T.conj())' as a 2-D matmul, which goes to BLAS dgemm and is FMA-contracted; our cov_gram_from_centered accumulates in plain no-FMA Rust. Same math, different last bit.

WHY THIS EXPLAINS THE TWO GOLDEN FAILURES AS WELL. Both sha256 goldens hash fnp's OWN output bytes over a shape sweep. If our Gram differs from numpy's BLAS Gram in the last ULP, and some shapes in that sweep delegate to numpy while others take the native path, the proof is a MIXTURE of our bits and BLAS's bits - which is exactly why the recorded golden 80bb612d... matches neither worker class and why the value tracks the numpy build rather than our code. One cause, three symptoms.

THIS IS A STRUCTURAL CONSTRAINT, NOT A TYPO. We cannot bit-match dgemm without linking BLAS (forbidden by the suite premise) or replicating its exact FMA order. Note cov_native_fast_path_matches_numpy_across_shape_ddof_bias ALREADY encodes that: its own comment says 'Reassociated dot sums -> allclose, not bit-exact', and its allclose assert PASSES. So the codebase holds TWO CONTRADICTORY CONTRACTS for cov - allclose in one test, exact-repr and byte-golden in the others. That contradiction is the bead.

FIX OPTIONS, and this is a decision with a perf cost, so I am not making it drive-by:
  (a) Gate the native Gram to shapes where it is a measured win and DEFER the rest. Small inputs like this 2x3 case gain nothing from it anyway, and deferring makes them bit-exact by construction. Cost: the goldens must be re-derived once, and the gate needs a measurement to place.
  (b) Accept allclose as cov's contract everywhere: relax the exact-repr comparison for cov cases and narrow the byte-goldens to natively-computed outputs only. Cost: cov's exactness claim weakens, deliberately and in writing.
(a) is the better engineering and is consistent with 'defer what you cannot reproduce'. (b) is honest but weaker. Either way the two goldens must stop hashing a native/delegated mixture.

DO NOT regenerate the goldens to green this. The drift is a symptom; regenerating pins whichever worker ran last and re-breaks on the other class.

Still NOT the 1jqrw version class - all three are red on 2.4.3.

comments.text:
CONTRACTS RECONCILED in commit 0043ec2f, per the operator design call. Probe FIRST, then the change.

THE PROBE PASSED, so the exact contract does not stand. If it had failed the defect would have been ours. numpy's cov computes dot(X, X.T) as a 2-D matmul -> BLAS dgemm -> FMA-contracted inner loop. On the failing case cov([1,2,4], y=[2,1,0], ddof=0) entry [0][0], with identical centred operands both sides:
  separate multiply+add (our kernel): 4.666666666666666 -> /3 = 1.5555555555555554  == fnp
  math.fma accumulation (dgemm loop): 4.666666666666667 -> /3 = 1.5555555555555556  == numpy.cov
One rounding per term versus two, and nothing else. I ruled out the alternatives before concluding: numpy's 'c *= true_divide(1, fact)' reciprocal-multiply gives the SAME answer as a divide here, and the mean is identical, so neither explains the ULP.

AND THE TARGET IS NOT A FIXED ONE. An explicit 1x3 dot of that same data yields the NO-FMA value while cov's internal 2x3 dot yields the FMA one - BLAS picks micro-kernels BY SHAPE. So the 'correct' bytes vary with shape, with the BLAS build and with the host, which is exactly why the recorded goldens matched NEITHER worker class. Bit-equality here is not merely unachieved, it is not well-defined.

CHANGE: both sha256 pins replaced by COV_FMA_RELATIVE_BOUND = 1e-12, documented at the constant with the probe above. It is ~4 orders ABOVE the accumulated contraction difference at these sizes and ~3 orders BELOW the 1e-9 allclose already in use, so a wrong formula (1e-2..1e-1, not 1e-15) still fails loudly. Both tests now PRINT the observed worst relative deviation, so drift toward the bound is visible - the goldens' one real service kept without their impossible demand. The parity assertion against numpy is untouched and still runs.

EVIDENCE: conformance_statistics 30 passed / 0 failed on hz2, up from 27 passed / 3 failed. clippy --no-deps -D warnings exit 0 with zero error lines and the log showing it reached the crate; rustfmt --check exit 0.

I changed nothing in it, and it failed on vmi1227854 while PASSING on hz2 - confirming it is host/BLAS-dependent in precisely the same way and will flake by worker. Its cov numeric cases belong under the same bound, but it also covers error surfaces and dtype outcomes where exact comparison is CORRECT, so splitting value cases from outcome cases is its own change and should be decided as one. title: [test][fnp-python] keyword INTERACTIONS never crossed - out= shape is a function of axis and keepdims, and each was only verified alone
description:
TENTH PROBE, and the first to cross PARAMETERS rather than sweep one attribute.

WHY NOW: nine probes have swept a single dimension each - return type, dtype,
exception class, __all__ resolution, keepdims shape, input layout, exotic
dtypes, aliasing. The last four were clean, including the two with the strongest
priors. That pattern says the single-dimension vein is close to exhausted, not
that the surface is clean, so this one crosses dimensions instead.

WHY INTERACTIONS ARE THE RIGHT NEXT CUT: every keyword this session touched is
handled per-site by hand. out= forces delegation in one wrapper and is forwarded
in another; keepdims is reconstructed by keepdims_expand_axis at some sites and
by reshaping to vec![1usize; ndim] at others; where= gates the native path in
five reductions and is forwarded in the rest; dtype= forces an accumulator type.
Each was verified ALONE. Their combinations were not, and the combination is
where the hand-rolled arithmetic actually has to agree:

  out= 's REQUIRED SHAPE IS A FUNCTION OF axis AND keepdims. A wrapper that
  computes the reduced shape correctly for its own return, but computes the
  out= shape check (or the write) from a different expression, is wrong only in
  the crossed case - and every existing test passes one keyword at a time.

PROBE TO CLOSE: a conformance sweep crossing, over a 3-D input:
  - out= x axis x keepdims, with the out buffer allocated at the shape NUMPY
    says the result should be, asserting `result is out`, out's contents, and
    the exception when the out shape is deliberately wrong for that
    axis/keepdims pair
  - where= x axis x keepdims, including where= with keepdims=True (the mask
    broadcast and the output shape interact)
  - where= x dtype=, and where= x initial= x axis
  - dtype= x axis x keepdims
across sum/prod/mean/min/max/any/all and the nan* twins that take each keyword.
Compare dtype, shape, values and exception class on both sides.

Assert as a precondition that the crossed cases genuinely differ from the
single-keyword ones - specifically that numpy's required out shape for
(axis=0, keepdims=True) differs from that for (axis=0, keepdims=False) - or the
cross is not actually crossing anything.

Any divergence is a real defect; fix it in the same bead.
close_reason:
DELIVERED as a LOCK, landed in 1c4b42c8. NO DIVERGENCE - 358 crossed comparisons, all match, so no defect is claimed.

WHY CROSS RATHER THAN SWEEP: the previous nine probes each varied ONE dimension, and the last four came back clean including the two with the strongest priors. That pattern says the single-dimension vein is near exhausted, not that the surface is clean. Every keyword this session touched is handled per-site by hand - out= forces delegation in one wrapper and is forwarded in another; keepdims is rebuilt by keepdims_expand_axis at some sites and by reshaping to vec![1usize; ndim] at others; where= gates the native path in five reductions and is forwarded in the rest; dtype= forces an accumulator type - and each was verified ALONE. The combination is where the hand-rolled arithmetic actually has to agree, because OUT='S REQUIRED SHAPE IS A FUNCTION OF axis AND keepdims. A wrapper that computes its own return shape correctly but derives the out= check or the write from a different expression is wrong only in the crossed case, which no single-keyword test can reach.

FOUR CROSSES, 358 comparisons: out= x axis x keepdims with the buffer allocated at the shape NUMPY says the result has for that pair (plus a deliberately WRONG buffer both sides must reject identically); where= x axis x keepdims; where= x dtype= x axis; dtype= x axis x keepdims x out=.

A PROBE ARTIFACT CAUGHT BEFORE LANDING, the third this session: the first run reported four failures whose fnp and numpy lines were character-identical, NaN included. nan != nan, so a tuple compare fails whenever BOTH sides legitimately produce NaN - which where= on a fully-masked position does for mean. Reading the printed values rather than the failure count is what caught it; had I trusted '4 failures' I would have gone looking to 'fix' correct code. The comparison now substitutes NaN first, as the keepdims sweep already did for the same reason. The three artifacts this session (r.reshape(-1) copying for transposed views in c7hqd, the shifted tuple index in st00f, NaN inequality here) were all in the PROBE, not the subject - which is its own finding about this style of test.

PRECONDITIONS assert the cross actually crosses: numpy's required out shape must differ between keepdims True and False, and the where= mask must change the result. Without those, every out= case collapses into the single-keyword case earlier sweeps already cover, and the sweep would pass while testing nothing new.

Content verified intact (the test function and the NaN-substitution comment are both present in HEAD). Same thing happened to succi in f6c9c280. Flagging it because the ledger should not imply I authored a commit I did not, nor that the work is missing because my commit is absent.

title: [bench][fnp-python] stage attribution counts import_numpy_ns as accounted, but the route no longer executes it - accounted_fraction 0.763 overstates by 410ns
description:

title: [parity][fnp-python] Window/tile/tri/savetxt parameter names diverge from numpy (M/A/N/X) - keyword calls TypeError
description:
FOUND by a signature audit of all 647 `#[pyo3(signature = ...)]` declarations in
crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs against `inspect.signature(numpy.<name>)` on the
installed numpy (2.4.3, python 3.13.7). 35 declarations diverge; this bead covers
the subset where fnp spells a PARAMETER NAME differently from numpy, so a caller
who passes it by keyword — exactly as the numpy docs write it — gets a TypeError
from fnp where numpy succeeds.

CONFIRMED ON THE NUMPY SIDE (all of these work today):
  np.hamming(M=5) / np.hanning(M=5) / np.bartlett(M=5) / np.blackman(M=5)
  np.kaiser(M=5, beta=2.0)
  np.tile(A=[1, 2], reps=2)
  np.tri(N=3, M=2)
  np.savetxt(buf, X=arr)

fnp declares these as lowercase: bartlett/blackman/hamming/hanning `(m,)`,
kaiser `(m, beta)`, tile `(a, reps)`, tri `(n, m, k, dtype)`, savetxt
`(fname, x, ...)`. numpy's own signatures use the capital spellings, which is
what its docs and every ported call site use.

ALSO IN THE AUDIT, needs verifying rather than assuming: copyto, nanprod,
nanstd and nanvar declare the parameter as the Rust raw identifier `r#where`.
PyO3 may or may not strip the `r#` when it builds the Python-visible name; if it
does not, `fnp.nanstd(x, where=mask)` is broken. Check before touching it — this
may be a non-defect.

FIX: rename the Rust parameters to numpy's spelling (PyO3 takes the Python
keyword straight from the Rust identifier), with #[allow(non_snake_case)] where
the capital spelling trips the lint. CI runs clippy -D warnings, so the allow has
to be explicit and local.

PROBE TO CLOSE: a no-mock conformance test that calls each of these functions
BY KEYWORD with numpy's spelling and compares fnp's outcome against numpy's in
the same interpreter, green on a named worker with its numpy version cited.

The other two classes the same audit surfaced are separate beads: keywords numpy
has that fnp is MISSING (nansum/nanmax/nanmin `initial=`/`where=`, nanmean
`where=`, take/choose/compress/fix `out=`, trim_zeros `axis=`, indices `sparse=`,

title: bug(test): two fnp-python lib tests are RED ON EVERY WORKER and green locally - numpy 2.5.2 removed row_stack and moved register_dlpack_dtype (pre-existing, confirmed on a clean baseline)
description:
CLOSED, BlackThrush, 2026-09-01, commit f05cd0c9. `cargo test --release -p fnp-python --lib`
is GREEN ON A WORKER for the first time: 663 passed, 0 failed, 4 ignored (hz4, rch --job,
numpy 2.5.2). It was 661/2 before.

BOTH FAILURES WERE PRODUCT DEFECTS, not stale test expectations. That is the finding worth
carrying: the bead framed them as "version drift, not logic", and reading them that way would
have led to version-gating two tests and shipping two real gaps.

1. THE dtypes LAZY FALLBACK WAS A HARD-CODED NAME LIST. `fnp.dtypes.__getattr__` gated on a
   frozenset of the 33 DType class names, so it could only ever be as new as the release it
   was typed against. numpy 2.5.2 added `register_dlpack_dtype` to `numpy.dtypes.__all__`;
   the eager copy picked it up FROM `__all__` and the lazy path then refused the same name.
   Any caller who dropped the eager attribute - which is exactly what the test does to
   exercise PEP-562 - hit AttributeError on a name numpy has. It now forwards whatever the
   LIVE `numpy.dtypes` has and raises only when numpy does.

2. `fnp.row_stack` CALLED `numpy.row_stack`. 2.5.2 removed it, so OUR function raised
   AttributeError on every worker - a broken export, not a broken test. `row_stack` was only
   ever an alias of `vstack`, so it falls back to `vstack`: the same function, not an
   approximation. The export is KEPT (2.4.3, the installed interpreter, still has it) and the
   test's oracle resolves the same way, `np.row_stack` where it exists and `np.vstack` where
   it does not.

THE TRANSFERABLE POINT: a test that is red only on the workers is not automatically a test
problem. The oracle there is AHEAD of the installed one
([[vendored-numpy-oracle-is-ahead-of-every-release]]), so a worker-only failure is the first
place a FUTURE numpy's behaviour shows up - it is an early warning, and both of these were.
Any surface built from a baked list rather than from the live numpy has the same shape; the
exceptions submodule next door is worth the same read.
close_reason: Both were PRODUCT defects, not stale tests: the dtypes lazy fallback was a hard-coded name list and fnp.row_stack called a numpy function 2.5.2 removed. --lib is now 663/0 green on hz4 (was 661/2)

title: [bug][fnp-python] fnp.linalg.diagonal/trace return the WRONG ARRAY for ndim>2 - the top-level wrappers are aliased under the linalg names
description:
FOUND by extending the fnp-python signature audit to the SUBMODULES - the
original 35-row audit only walked top-level numpy names. Of 110 mapped
numpy.linalg / numpy.fft bindings, 5 diverge, and two of them are silent WRONG
ANSWERS rather than signature nits.

ROOT CAUSE, at crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs in the linalg registration block:
the `for (numpy_name, flat_name)` table does
`linalg.add("diagonal", m.getattr("diagonal"))` - it registers fnp's TOP-LEVEL
wrapper under the linalg name. But numpy.linalg.diagonal and numpy.linalg.trace
are Array-API variants that are NOT the same function as np.diagonal / np.trace:
they operate on the LAST TWO axes, where the top-level ones use axes 0 and 1.

  a = np.arange(24).reshape(2, 3, 4)
  np.diagonal(a).shape        -> (4, 2)      np.linalg.diagonal(a).shape -> (2, 3)
  np.trace(a)                 -> [16,18,20,22]   np.linalg.trace(a)      -> [15, 51]

So fnp.linalg.diagonal(a) and fnp.linalg.trace(a) return the WRONG ARRAY for any
input with ndim > 2. For 2-D input the two conventions coincide, which is
exactly why this survived.

The registration block's own comment shows the authors hit this class already:
"cross is excluded here because numpy.linalg.cross rejects 2-D vectors while
numpy.cross accepts them; route it directly to numpy.linalg.cross". The same
reasoning was never applied to diagonal/trace/outer/tensordot.

ALL FIVE, verified against numpy 2.4.3 (fnp accepts each call numpy rejects,
because it is exposing the top-level wrapper's wider signature):
  linalg.diagonal   numpy (x, /, *, offset=0)      - rejects a positional offset,
                    rejects axis1=/axis2=; fnp's takes (a, offset, axis1, axis2)
  linalg.trace      numpy (x, /, *, offset=0, dtype=None) - rejects out=,
                    rejects axis1=/axis2=; fnp's takes (a, offset, axis1, axis2, dtype, out)
  linalg.outer      numpy (x1, x2, /) - rejects out=, and REQUIRES 1-D
                    ("Input arrays must be one-dimensional") where np.outer
                    flattens 2-D happily; fnp's takes (a, b, out)
  linalg.tensordot  numpy (x1, x2, /, *, axes=2) - axes is KEYWORD-ONLY;
                    fnp's takes it positionally
  linalg.matrix_rank numpy spells the first parameter A, fnp spells it a, so
                    np.linalg.matrix_rank(A=m) is a TypeError on fnp

FIX: stop aliasing the top-level wrappers for the four that differ. Follow the
pattern already used for cross and vector_norm in the same block - a dedicated
passthrough that delegates to numpy.linalg.<name> at call time (lazily, because
numpy may not be importable during module init). matrix_rank needs only the
parameter rename, since its semantics already match.

PROBE TO CLOSE: no-mock conformance that for ndim > 2 input fnp.linalg.diagonal
and fnp.linalg.trace equal numpy.linalg's (NOT the top-level ones - assert they
DIFFER from np.diagonal/np.trace, or the case cannot fail), that the
signature surfaces above raise the same way numpy does, that linalg.outer
rejects 2-D, and that the top-level np.diagonal/np.trace/np.outer/np.tensordot
are UNCHANGED by the fix. Green on a named worker with its numpy version cited.

numpy.fft: 0 mismatches in the same audit run.
close_reason:
FIXED in df4e9244.

THE BUG WAS A WRONG ANSWER, not a signature nit. The linalg registration table aliased fnp's TOP-LEVEL wrappers under the numpy.linalg names, but numpy.linalg.diagonal and numpy.linalg.trace are Array-API variants over the LAST TWO axes where np.diagonal/np.trace use axes 0 and 1. Measured on numpy 2.4.3 with a = arange(24).reshape(2,3,4): np.diagonal(a).shape (4,2) vs np.linalg.diagonal(a).shape (2,3); np.trace(a) [16,18,20,22] vs np.linalg.trace(a) [15,51]. fnp.linalg.diagonal/trace therefore returned the wrong array for every input with ndim > 2. They coincide at 2-D, which is exactly why it survived.

outer and tensordot differ in accepted SURFACE rather than value: numpy.linalg.outer REQUIRES 1-D ('Input arrays must be one-dimensional') where np.outer flattens 2-D happily, numpy.linalg.tensordot makes axes keyword-only, and neither accepts out=. All four now delegate lazily to numpy.linalg at call time - the pattern this same block already used for cross. Its comment ('cross is excluded here because numpy.linalg.cross rejects 2-D vectors while numpy.cross accepts them') shows the class was already known; it just was not carried across to the other four.

matrix_rank was the fifth: numpy spells the first parameter A, fnp spelled it a, so np.linalg.matrix_rank(A=m) was a TypeError. Renamed with a local allow(non_snake_case), same as the window functions in 9w6uj. Its semantics already matched, so nothing else changed.

HOW IT WAS FOUND: extending the signature audit to the SUBMODULES. The original 35-row audit only walked top-level numpy names, so numpy.linalg and numpy.fft had never been compared. 110 bindings mapped by parsing the registration tables, 5 mismatches, all five real. numpy.fft: zero mismatches.

THE TEST HAS A PRECONDITION GUARD, which matters more than usual here: it asserts np.linalg.diagonal and np.diagonal actually DISAGREE on the 3-D input used, and likewise for trace. Without that, all 20 cases would still pass with the alias in place on any numpy where the two conventions happened to agree - the test would silently stop testing the thing it exists for. It also pins the TOP-LEVEL diagonal/trace/outer/tensordot as unchanged, so the fix is shown not to have moved them.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_linalg_advanced = 34 passed / 0 failed, exit 0, oracle numpy 2.4.3. cargo test -p fnp-python --lib = 557 passed / 0 failed, exit 0. cargo clippy -p fnp-python --lib --tests -- -D warnings exit 0. cargo fmt --check -p fnp-python exit 0. All exit codes captured directly.

title: [bug][linalg] linalg_error_surface_probe fails on main: matrix_rank raises in NumPy but not in fnp
description:
## Symptom

`cargo test -p fnp-python --lib` fails one test on main:

```
thread 'tests::linalg_error_surface_probe' panicked at crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs:116623:13:
LinAlgError divergences detected:
  matrix_rank: ours=OK, theirs raises
test result: FAILED. 544 passed; 1 failed; 1 ignored
```

`ours=OK, theirs raises` means live NumPy raises where `fnp.matrix_rank` returns a value —
an error-surface divergence, not a numeric one.

## Confirmed pre-existing and host-independent

Found incidentally while checking blast radius for the flat-f64-sort gate change
(`deadlock-audit-flat-f64-sort-avx2-surrender-7mh1i`); it is NOT caused by that change.

- With the sort change in tree: fails on `vmi1227854` at `lib.rs:116702`.
- At baseline `f5dba29b` (that commit's parent) with `--clean-overlay --no-overlay`, i.e.
  WITHOUT the change: fails identically on `vmi1153651` at `lib.rs:116623`.

The 79-line offset is exactly what the sort change inserts above it. Two different workers,
same verdict, so it is neither a regression nor a single-worker artifact.

CI does not currently catch it: the red job on main (`30685764934`) is `G1: fmt + lint`, the
pre-existing chunks_exact lint sweep (`deadlock-audit-snvtc`), so this test failure is
sitting behind an already-red gate and is untracked.

## Likely cause to check first

NumPy version. The measurement/build workers do not all carry the same NumPy
(2.2.4 / 2.4.3 / 2.4.6 are all present in the fleet), and `numpy.linalg.matrix_rank`'s
raising behaviour on degenerate input is version-sensitive. Determine the NumPy version on
each worker that reproduces, and whether the divergence tracks it, BEFORE touching
`fnp.matrix_rank` - the fix may be a version-gated expectation in the probe rather than a
change to the implementation.

Do not "fix" it by loosening the probe until that question is answered: the probe exists to
catch exactly this class of divergence.
close_reason: Fixed in f808ea3c. Root cause: numpy's matrix_rank threshold is S.max(axis=-1)*rtol; for zero-size input svd returns an EMPTY S so the max has no identity and raises ValueError (traceback confirmed at _linalg.py:2140 on numpy 2.4.3, reproduced identically on 1.26.4 -> version-INDEPENDENT across the whole fleet, so the bead's version-gated-expectation hypothesis is REFUTED; the vendored 2.5.0.dev0 oracle differs only because upstream main added initial=0). fnp's native <=16-dim path returned 0. Fix defers any zero-length-dimension input to numpy so the observable behaviour tracks the installed numpy. Evidence, local build numpy 2.4.3, cargo test -p fnp-python --lib: tests::linalg_error_surface_probe ok (was FAILING), tests::matrix_rank_zero_size_error_surface_matches_numpy ok (new; covers (0,3),(3,0),(0,0),(2,0,0),(0,3,3),(0,) comparing ok:repr OR err:type:message against live numpy), tests::matrix_rank_matches_numpy_across_tol_rtol_hermitian_and_batched ok; 3 passed 0 failed.

title: bug(conformance): a MUST clause is GREEN ON hz2/hz4 AND RED ON ovh-a with no source difference - log(-1.0) returns a NaN whose SIGN BIT differs from numpy's on one worker
description:
ANSWERED, BlackThrush, 2026-09-02, commit 24527513. IT IS ORACLE DRIFT. The fleet is not
running one numpy, and this assertion was the first thing to notice.

    FAILING  host=fixmydocuments (rch alias ovh-a)   numpy=2.3.5
             umath=/usr/lib/python3/dist-packages/numpy/_core/_multiarray_umath...so
             baseline=['SSE', 'SSE2', 'SSE3']
    PASSING  host=hz4                                numpy=2.5.2
             umath=<user site-packages>/numpy/_core/_multiarray_umath...so
             baseline=['X86_V2']
    local    thinkstation1                           numpy=2.4.3  baseline=['X86_V2']

`log(-1.0)`: numpy 2.3.5 returns 0xFFF8000000000000, numpy 2.4.3 and 2.5.2 both return
0x7FF8000000000000, and fnp returns 0x7FF8000000000000 on every host observed. OUR VALUE IS
THE STABLE ONE. The failing worker runs the DISTRO package out of /usr/lib rather than the
user site-packages every other host uses - a different version, a different install path and a
different SIMD baseline.

SO THERE IS NO fnp DEFECT HERE, and the original framing ("our log returns the wrong NaN
sign") was wrong in the direction that would have cost the most: someone would have "fixed" a
correct log to match a two-releases-old oracle.

HOW IT WAS FINALLY PINNED, because the method transfers. The host split was established in six
clean-baseline runs (hz2 3/3 green, ovh-a 3/3 red), but the diagnostic that would name the
CAUSE could not be landed: rch routed ten consecutive tiny `python3 -c` jobs to hz4, the host
where it passes. Selection follows load, so a probe cannot choose its host, and the failing
host is by definition the one you cannot reach on demand.

    THE FIX WAS TO MOVE THE DIAGNOSTIC INTO THE ASSERTION.

The bit comparison now prints host, numpy version, umath path and CPU baseline at the moment
it fails, so whichever host fails carries its own evidence. The next failing run answered a
question ten targeted probes could not. THAT IS THE GENERAL LESSON: when a failure is
host-dependent and the fleet picks the host, instrument the FAILURE, not the fleet.

WHAT IS LEFT, and it is not this bead's to fix:
  - THE FLEET SHOULD RUN ONE NUMPY. A worker two minor versions behind silently changes what
    every bit-exactness clause, every parity sweep and every oracle-relative measurement on
    this campaign means. `objdtype_raise_parity` already sees it from the other side: on that
    worker it reports 370 entry points against hz4's 367, so even the SURFACE differs. This
    belongs to whoever owns worker provisioning; filed here as the finding, not the repair.
  - THE ASSERTION IS LEFT FAILING THERE ON PURPOSE. It is a true signal, and silencing it
    would hide the drift. It is now self-explaining, which is what it was missing.
close_reason: ORACLE DRIFT, not an fnp defect: the failing worker runs numpy 2.3.5 from the distro package (baseline SSE/SSE2/SSE3) while every other host runs 2.4.3/2.5.2 from user site-packages. numpy 2.3.5's log(-1) is -NaN; 2.4.3, 2.5.2 and fnp all give +NaN. Pinned by moving the diagnostic INTO the assertion

title: [test][fnp-ufunc] einsum RESULTS never compared against numpy - the only live oracle checks the contraction PATH, not the values
close_reason:
COMPLETE, no defect. einsum_results_match_live_numpy_across_subscript_forms compares einsum OUTPUT against np.einsum across ten structurally distinct subscript forms: pure transpose (ij->ji), full reduction (ij->), partial reduction (ij->i), diagonal extraction (ii->i), trace (ii->), outer product (i,j->ij), matmul (ij,jk->ik), batched matmul (bij,bjk->bik), two-index contraction (ijk,jkl->il) and an ellipsis form (...ij,...jk->...ik). All agree within 1e-12 relative.

WHY THIS WAS A GAP DESPITE 75 EINSUM TESTS: the only live-numpy einsum test in the crate is einsum_path_greedy_matches_live_numpy_oracle_when_available, which checks the contraction PATH. A path is a performance decision - it says nothing about whether the contraction produces numpy's numbers. Nothing compared einsum VALUES to np.einsum, so a wrong index mapping in any single subscript form would have been invisible to all 75 tests as long as it was self-consistent. Same shape of gap as the FFT metamorphic laws (c4vfm) and the dtype promotion lattice (9xrd5): strong internal checks, nothing comparing the thing itself to the contract.

Non-vacuity proven by falsification: perturbing the first element of every operand by 1e-6 makes all 10 of 10 forms diverge, so each case is genuinely compared rather than passing on a trivially-satisfied path. Scalar results are compared by element count rather than shape vector, since ours is shape [] where numpy's is [1] after atleast_1d.

title: [bug][bench] the INTERLEAVED route share still moves 13% run-to-run on one worker with nulls at unity
description:
Residual of deadlock-audit-c9rn8, which fixed the defect it was filed for and exposed a smaller one underneath.

c9rn8 removed the phase artifact: the share used to divide a contract median by a separate later loop's median, and swung 0.804-1.911 for one arm including 2.4x on a single worker. After 2f3e5c70 both arms run interleaved ABBAABBA inside one run_median_ci_contract with a kernel/kernel A/A null. Each run is now internally decidable with a CI of about +/-0.03.

WHAT REMAINS, measured on ONE worker (vmi1227854), harness=common::run_median_ci_contract, both runs interleaved, both nulls at unity:
  elf 59423d997bd40e3a: kernel_share=1.048 ci95=[1.007,1.062] null 1.000693
  elf ddf42424be243a7d: kernel_share=0.927 ci95=[0.881,0.947] null 0.998068 ci95=[0.988225,1.026292]
The two 95% CIs DO NOT OVERLAP and the point estimates straddle 1.0. A ~13% move run-to-run on one host, with both nulls saying the host was quiet, is the same signature that condemned the pre-fix field - an order of magnitude smaller but not gone.

CAVEAT: the two ELFs differ (the second carries a peer's print-only edit adding worker=/harness=/rounds=). The kernel and route arms compute the same thing in both, so I read the spread as real, but it is not a byte-identical replication.

CANDIDATES, none tested: asymmetric warm-up between a Rust closure and a PyO3 call; interpreter or allocator state drifting across the 41 rounds; the route arm holding the GIL for its whole slot while the kernel arm does not.

Acceptance: two runs on ONE worker whose kernel_share CIs overlap, or a named mechanism for why they cannot. Until then kernel_share stays a not-to-be-quoted field.
close_reason: CLOSED ON A NAMED MECHANISM, which the acceptance permits as an alternative to overlapping CIs. The two runs this bead rests on used DIFFERENT BINARIES - elf 59423d997bd40e3a giving kernel_share 1.048 ci95=[1.007,1.062] and elf ddf42424be243a7d giving 0.927 ci95=[0.881,0.947] - and the bead itself recorded that caveat at filing time (the second carried a peer's print-only edit). deadlock-audit-bpxn6 has since characterised exactly this failure mode with a controlled experiment: a CROSS-BUILD PAIR on ONE worker reported the OPPOSITE SIGN from the truth, with disjoint CIs, an invariant control arm and nulls on unity - every health indicator a reader would check - where the same question measured with both arms in ONE binary came out decidable and sign-consistent across two workers (worst bound 1.353519x). On vmi1152480 specifically the cross-build pair said 'worse' and the same-binary A/B said 1.36x better. So the 13% non-overlap reported here is fully consistent with being an artifact of the cross-build comparison it rests on, and there is no evidence left that the INTERLEAVED share is unstable within a binary. NOT claiming the residual is proven absent: nobody has run two same-binary repetitions of the share on one worker. That is the actual open question and it is now a one-line variation of the bpxn6 design (same binary, repeat, require overlap), so it does not need a standing bead of its own - the retry predicate on the wsd7h row already tells the next agent to use a same-binary control. kernel_share stays a not-to-be-quoted field until someone does that.

title: [perf][fnp-python] is the binary-ufunc route floor FIXED overhead or PROPORTIONAL kernel cost? size sweep decides
description:
deadlock-audit-1pt96 established a 5-7% route floor: fnp.multiply, which computes no hazard scan, loses to numpy.multiply on two workers (0.931251 on vmi1227854, 0.950794 on vmi1153651), both DECIDABLE_REGRESSION with nulls at unity. That floor is paid by EVERY fnp binary ufunc before any kernel work, and it is now the actionable target - the divide-specific increment did not replicate.

But 1pt96 measured a single size (n=2^20), which cannot distinguish two very different causes:
(a) FIXED per-call overhead - PyO3 dispatch, dtype/contiguity sniffing via Python attribute lookups, numpy.empty output allocation and its first-touch page faults. Constant nanoseconds per call, so the RATIO approaches 1.0 as n grows and is worst at small n.
(b) PROPORTIONAL kernel cost - our loop simply moves less data per cycle than numpy's SIMD ufunc loop. Constant ratio, flat across n.

These call for opposite levers: (a) is attacked at the route (buffer reuse, cheaper sniffing, avoiding a fresh allocation per call - and note the banked finding that large-buffer mmap churn is worth 2.8x repo-wide, collapsing to 1.015x under MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_), (b) is attacked in the kernel and nowhere else.

DESIGN: sweep fnp.multiply vs numpy.multiply across n = 2^16, 2^20, 2^24 in ONE invocation on ONE worker, each cell under the dual-null contract with both A/A nulls, identical C-contiguous float64 operands. multiply is the right probe precisely because it has no hazard scan - it isolates the route.

Acceptance: a row naming WORKER and HARNESS with all three cells and their nulls, plus the excess in NANOSECONDS per cell. Fixed overhead shows a roughly constant excess_ns across three sizes spanning 256x; proportional cost shows excess_ns growing with n while the ratio stays flat. Whichever it is, say which, and say it even if the two smaller cells disagree - a non-replicating answer is the finding, as it was for 1pt96.

title: [bug][fnp-python] masked_sum byte-identity MISMATCH at n>=100k across densities (3 tests RED at HEAD)
description:
Child 2 of deadlock-audit-xdyx7. 3 failing tests in conformance_masked_sum.

masked_sum_is_byte_identical_across_sizes_and_densities reports MISMATCH at (100000, 0.25/0.5/0.75/1.0), (1048575, all four), (1048576, 0.25 and 1.0), (1500000, 0.5/0.75/1.0). Also failing: masked_sum_deferred_inputs_still_match_numpy, masked_sum_parallel_path_handles_skewed_masks.

The sizes cluster at and around 1<<20, and the whole density sweep is affected at the larger sizes - that points squarely at the parallel split logic, not at the summation kernel.

HIGHEST-VALUE THING TO CHECK FIRST: whether the split points depend on rayon::current_num_threads(). If they do, byte-identity becomes HOST-DEPENDENT - a far worse bug than a wrong sum, and one that would make every banked masked-reduction byte-identity claim conditional on the measuring host's core count. The banked 17.9-20.9x masked-reduction result rests on a STREAMED pairwise tree whose split points were supposed to be located from band prefix counts precisely so that every parallel boundary is a REAL tree split. Verify that invariant still holds.

Reproduced at pristine HEAD b86ce6ef via --base b86ce6ef --clean-overlay --no-overlay, so it is not caused by any in-flight work.

PROBE TO CLOSE: 'cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_masked_sum' green, AND green with RAYON_NUM_THREADS forced to at least two different values, since that is the hypothesis.
close_reason:
CLOSED BY THE ORACLE-FLOOR DECISION (1jqrw). The kernel was correct throughout; NumPy 2.2.4 was the outlier.

THIS BEAD'S OWN HYPOTHESIS WAS REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT, not argument. It proposed that the parallel split points depend on rayon::current_num_threads(), which would have made byte-identity host-dependent. Two independent lines killed it: (1) two of the failing sizes, 100000 and 1048575, are BELOW MASKED_SUM_PARALLEL_MIN (1<<20) and never reach the rayon path at all; (2) 'cut' does vary with thread count, but masked_pairwise_parallel and masked_pairwise_streamed apply the SAME split rule, so cut chooses which thread evaluates a subtree, never the accumulation order. masked_locate correctly backs up over duplicate prefix entries and base_sum_simd's bound is exactly numpy's n - n%8.

DECIDED BY AN ARBITER THAT TOUCHES NEITHER ARM. The test now computes numpy's DOCUMENTED pairwise tree in pure numpy and classifies each mismatch OURS_WRONG / NUMPY_DIFFERS / BOTH_DIFFER. I validated that reference against numpy 2.4.3 locally at n = 1000, 4096, 25000, 100000, 250000, 1048575 - identical bits every time. On numpy 2.2.4 the verdict was NUMPY_DIFFERS on ALL 13 failing cells: our kernel reproduces the documented tree bit-for-bit and 2.2.4's own a[mask].sum() departs from it, with the boundary visible in the data (<=4096 selected agree, >=25166 diverge).

That classifier is the durable output here - any future divergence self-reports which side moved instead of leaving the next agent to guess.

EVIDENCE: conformance_masked_sum on vmi1227854 (above floor), 5 passed / 0 failed, --no-fail-fast; was 2 passed / 3 failed on the 2.2.4 class. LEDGER: the banked masked-reduction row was annotated before the decision (byte-identity vs numpy 2.4.3, diverges on 2.2.4 above ~25k selected, plus the note that its bench ELF predates HEAD by three fnp-python changes); under the floor that annotation reads as a scope statement. ledger_hygiene 19/19.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
RESOLVED TO A VERDICT by AzureHill 2026-08-06, commit df58a509. The kernel is CORRECT. NumPy 2.2.4 is what differs. Blocking on the version decision, not on a fix.

THIS BEAD'S OWN LEADING HYPOTHESIS IS REFUTED. I wrote 'check first whether the split points depend on rayon::current_num_threads(), because that would make byte-identity HOST-DEPENDENT'. They do not, and two independent lines of evidence say so:
  1. Two of the failing sizes, 100000 and 1048575, are BELOW MASKED_SUM_PARALLEL_MIN (1<<20). They never reach the rayon path; they run the serial streamed kernel. No thread-count effect can explain them.
  2. 'cut' DOES vary with current_num_threads(), but masked_pairwise_parallel and masked_pairwise_streamed apply the SAME split rule (n2 = n/2 rounded down to a multiple of 8), so cut only chooses which thread evaluates a subtree, never the accumulation order. The comment at that function is accurate. masked_locate correctly backs up over duplicate prefix entries (empty bands), and base_sum_simd's 'i + 8 <= n' bound is exactly NumPy's 'i < n - (n % 8)' including the tail.

HOW IT WAS DECIDED rather than argued. The test now computes NumPy's DOCUMENTED pairwise tree in pure NumPy - under 8 sequential, 8..128 eight accumulators, else split at n/2 rounded down to a multiple of 8 - and classifies each mismatch OURS_WRONG / NUMPY_DIFFERS / BOTH_DIFFER. The reference touches no fnp code, so it arbitrates between the arms instead of assuming one. I first validated that reference locally against numpy 2.4.3 at n = 1000, 4096, 25000, 100000, 250000 and 1048575: identical bits every time, so the reference IS numpy's tree on a modern build.

VERDICT, worker vmi1149989: numpy=2.2.4 verdicts=['NUMPY_DIFFERS'], all 13 cases. Our kernel reproduces the documented tree bit-for-bit; 2.2.4's own a[m].sum() departs from it. The selected counts locate the boundary: <=4096 selected agree, >=25166 diverge. That build changes reduction strategy above a size 2.4.x does not.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PERF LEDGER - someone should act on this. The banked masked-reduction win (17.9-20.9x) claims BYTE-IDENTITY with a[mask].sum(). That claim holds only on the NumPy build it was verified against and is FALSE on 2.2.4. Any ledger row publishing it must name its NumPy build, exactly as the reduction-family memory already warns that NumPy's float reduction tree is version-dependent and bit-exactness is per-BUILD.

WHY THE TEST STAYS RED. We genuinely do not match 2.2.4. Version-keying the assertion is the same operator decision as 1jqrw (declare a supported NumPy floor, or key the expectation, or defer), and making that call inside a test file would be gate self-weakening. Blocked on 1jqrw.

WHAT CLOSES THIS: the version-floor decision. If the floor lands at NumPy >= 2.3 this test is correct as written and closes with no code change. If 2.2.4 must be supported, the only honest option is for masked_sum to DEFER to numpy on builds whose tree it cannot reproduce - which costs the win on those hosts, and is a trade the operator makes, not me.

title: [test][fnp-python] lock the numpy.ma namespace re-export so the linalg alias bug cannot recur where it would hurt most
description:
NEGATIVE AUDIT RESULT PLUS A MISSING LOCK. Extending the submodule signature
audit past linalg (deadlock-audit-linalg-aliases-toplevel-wrappers-mi3k6) to
numpy.ma, numpy.char, numpy.strings, numpy.random and numpy.polynomial found
ZERO real divergences. numpy.random: 29 comparable bindings, 0 mismatches.
numpy.polynomial: 0 comparable. The 16 raw hits the script printed for
ma/char/strings are ALL parser false positives - it matched a numpy submodule
name against an fnp Rust fn of the same name, when the registration does not use
that Rust fn at all.

WHY THEY ARE FALSE POSITIVES, read off the registration block: numpy.ma's core
names are re-exported straight from numpy.ma -

    for name in ma_core_names {
        if let Ok(value) = np_ma.getattr(name) { ma.add(name, value)?; }
    }

plus a module __getattr__ that resolves anything else through `import numpy.ma`.
So fnp.ma.asarray IS numpy.ma.asarray, not fnp's top-level asarray, and the same
holds for cov/corrcoef/ptp/reshape/resize/identity/indices/choose/put/allclose.
The char/strings `count` hits came from the ma table's ("count", "ma_count")
entry bleeding through a fixed-size text window.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY MISSING: nothing asserts that. numpy.ma is precisely where the
linalg mistake would be most tempting to repeat - numpy.ma.cov, numpy.ma.corrcoef,
numpy.ma.reshape, numpy.ma.choose, numpy.ma.ptp, numpy.ma.allclose all share a
NAME with an fnp top-level wrapper while being a DIFFERENT function with
different semantics (masked-aware, and in several cases a different parameter
list: ma.cov is (x, y, rowvar, bias, allow_masked, ddof) where the top-level cov
has fweights/aweights/dtype and no allow_masked; ma.allclose has masked_equal
where the top-level has equal_nan; ma.choose's first parameter is `indices` not
`a`; ma.ptp's is `obj`). If a future change swaps any of them for the top-level
wrapper - exactly what happened in linalg - masked inputs would silently produce
unmasked answers and nothing in the suite would notice.

PROBE TO CLOSE: a no-mock conformance test that, for the ma names which collide
with an fnp top-level wrapper, asserts (a) fnp.ma.<name> behaves as
numpy.ma.<name> on MASKED input, (b) the answer DIFFERS from the top-level
function on that same input, so the case cannot pass on an alias, and (c) the
ma-only keywords numpy documents (allow_masked, masked_equal) are accepted.
Same precondition-guard shape used in the linalg test. Green on a named worker
with its numpy version cited.

This bead is a LOCK, not a fix - no production defect is claimed for ma, and the
audit line for submodules is closed by it.
close_reason:
DELIVERED in 71b42f0a as a LOCK. No production defect is claimed for numpy.ma, and this closes the submodule audit line opened by mi3k6.

THE AUDIT RESULT IS NEGATIVE AND THAT IS THE POINT. Extending the signature audit past linalg to numpy.ma / char / strings / random / polynomial found ZERO real divergences. numpy.random: 29 comparable bindings, 0 mismatches - worth stating explicitly given fnp-random is a flagship. numpy.polynomial: 0 comparable bindings (all its wrappers take *args/**kwargs). The 16 raw hits my script printed for ma/char/strings were ALL parser false positives: the bare-quoted-string regex bled across a fixed-size text window, so it matched a submodule name against an fnp Rust fn of the same name when the registration never uses that fn. numpy.ma's core names come straight from numpy.ma via np_ma.getattr(name), with a module __getattr__ resolving the rest through 'import numpy.ma'.

I DID NOT LEAVE THAT AS A READING. The lock test now asserts it at runtime, which matters because the reading is exactly the kind of thing that was wrong twice earlier in this session (nh23c: I read sum's source, concluded the family was fine, and the test found 5 of 9 broken).

WHY ma SPECIFICALLY: it is where the linalg mistake would be most tempting to repeat. ma.cov, ma.corrcoef, ma.allclose, ma.ptp, ma.count and ma.average share a NAME with an fnp top-level wrapper while being different masked-aware functions with different parameter lists (ma.cov has allow_masked and no fweights/aweights/dtype; ma.allclose has masked_equal where the top-level has equal_nan). In linalg the aliasing returned the wrong ARRAY for ndim > 2; in ma it would silently drop the MASK, which is worse because the result still looks like a plausible answer.

TEST ma_namespace_is_numpy_ma_not_the_toplevel_wrappers, 9 surfaces plus preconditions: ma.cov on masked input, ma.cov allow_masked=, ma.corrcoef, ma.allclose masked_equal=, ma.ptp, ma.count, ma.average returned=, and identity checks that fnp.ma.masked IS numpy.ma.masked and fnp.ma.MaskedArray IS numpy.ma.MaskedArray.

PRECONDITION GUARD, same shape as the linalg test: it asserts ma.cov and np.cov actually DISAGREE on the masked input used - measured [[0.5,0.5],[0.5,1.0]] vs [[1,1],[1,1]] - and that np.cov / np.allclose really do reject allow_masked= / masked_equal=. If those ever stop holding, the nine cases can no longer tell numpy.ma's function from the same-named top-level one, and the test reports that rather than passing quietly. That is the failure mode a namespace test is most prone to.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_masked_array_ops = 15 passed / 0 failed, exit 0, oracle numpy 2.4.3. cargo clippy -p fnp-python --test conformance_masked_array_ops -- -D warnings exit 0. cargo fmt --check -p fnp-python exit 0. All exit codes captured directly.

SUBMODULE AUDIT LINE IS NOW CLOSED: linalg had the only real defects (mi3k6, 5 of them, 2 wrong-answer); ma/char/strings/random/polynomial are clean and ma is now pinned.

title: [perf][fnp-python][no-gaps] cov/corrcoef gram dot is single-accumulator latency-bound — register-block to dsyrk-class multi-accumulator
description:
np.cov/corrcoef on (50,1000) f64 are 4.3-4.8x SLOWER than numpy (cov 526us vs 123us); the gap is regime-dependent: (10,1000) 1.47x, (50,1000) 4.28x, (200,1000) 1.38x, (50,10000) 2.41x, (500,500) 0.86x (fnp already wins large).

ROOT: cov_gram_rowvar_f64 (lib.rs ~20717) computes each symmetric-Gram cell as a SINGLE-ACCUMULATOR dot `ci.iter().zip(cj).map(|(a,b)|a*b).sum()`. That is a length-n_obs DEPENDENT FP-add chain (~n_obs cycles latency-bound, no SIMD/ILP), where numpy's BLAS dsyrk uses multiple accumulators + register blocking. At m~50 there is too little row-parallelism to hide the per-dot latency; at m>=200 or m few-vars-many-obs the par_chunks_mut fan-out aggregates bandwidth and the gap shrinks.

LEVER (NO-CEILING, attack the primitive): replace the naive dot with a register-blocked MULTI-ACCUMULATOR dot (e.g. 4-8 partial sums unrolled, combined at the end) — classic dependency-chain break, the dsyrk microkernel structure. Optionally MR x NR register-tile the symmetric Gram (compute a small block of cells against shared centered rows) for reuse. Also fix the triangle LOAD IMBALANCE: par_chunks_mut(n_vars) gives row i only i+1 dots, so row m-1 does m x the work of row 0 — flatten the lower triangle into equal-work cell ranges.

TARGET: >=3x on the (50,1000) regime, no regression on the already-winning (500,500)/(50,10000) regimes. Score>=2.0.

BLOCKERS / OBLIGATIONS:
1. PARITY TEST IS EXACT-REPR. cov_matches_numpy_* and corrcoef_matches_numpy_* use assert_array_matches_numpy = exact tolist() repr compare. Multi-accumulator changes summation ORDER => last-ULP divergence from numpy's BLAS even on small inputs (4-5 obs test cases) once the combine order differs from serial. numpy's cov contract is allclose, so exact-repr is STRICTER than numpy requires. MUST relax cov/corrcoef matchers to np.allclose(rtol/atol) FIRST (or prove small-input bit-stability), as a deliberate parity-contract decision.
2. CLEAN A/B: needs box load < ~8 for reliable measurement (GEMM-microkernel ratios are bandwidth/scheduling sensitive; measured under load 18 here). Use rch criterion same-worker A/B.
3. Keep serial==parallel bit-identical within fnp (each cell still one independent dot); gate fan-out on work as today.

Found via gapsweep2 (2026-06-14); cov/corrcoef were the ONLY vs-numpy gap across ~50 ops swept (3 sweeps) — everything else parity-or-faster (unique/cumsum/searchsorted/median/percentile/nan*/char.*/triu/outer all fnp-faster). This is the next no-gaps lever after the set-op bitmap family (80305403/217d6f27/a6c7122e) shipped 6-65x.
notes:
REFUTED LEVER (2026-06-14, dot8 single-cell multi-accumulator): replaced the naive single-accumulator dot with an 8-lane multi-accumulator dot8() (chunks_exact(8) + 8 independent partial sums, autovectorizing; n<8 stays bit-identical so the exact-repr conformance tests — all <=5 obs — pass unchanged, parity allclose for n>=8). Measured NO improvement: cov (50,1000) 4.28x -> 4.16x (noise), (200,1000) 1.38->1.25x, (500,500) 0.86->0.82x. REVERTED.

WHY IT FAILED / SHARPENED DIAGNOSIS: the (50,1000) gram is MEMORY-TRAFFIC-bound, not dot-latency-bound. centered is row-major (n_vars x n_obs); the lower triangle rereads each cj row once per i>j, streaming ~sum_i (i+1)*n_obs*8 bytes (~10MB for 50x1000) from L2/L3 since the 400KB working set exceeds L2. The dot's dependency chain was never the bottleneck. numpy's dsyrk blocks an MR x NR tile of output cells and reuses each loaded panel of centered rows across the whole tile, cutting memory traffic ~MR-fold.

NEXT ATTEMPT (go straight here, skip dot accumulator tweaks): MR x NR register-blocked symmetric gram — load MR centered rows + NR centered rows into the tile, compute the MRxNR block of dots reusing them (panel-packing optional), only over the lower-triangular block range. Combine with the triangle load-balance fix (flatten to equal-work cell ranges, not per-row). Keep serial==parallel bit-identical. Conformance tests stay green only if the small-input (<8 obs / <tile) path remains the serial left-to-right sum. Needs quiet box for clean rch criterion A/B; target >=3x at (50,1000), no regression at (500,500)/(50,10000).

title: perf(log1p): the SAME pay-twice deferral 7kcz8 fixed for log/log2/log10 - 2.978x -> 1.253x at 2^13 and 1.870x LOSS -> 0.507x WIN at 2^16, plus a per-ufunc NaN SIGN and a dropped -inf event
description:
MEASURED, TanBridge, thinkstation1, numpy 2.4.3 live, fnp .so sha256
6426b4c8a40aa5a73db2783d... built from COMMITTED source at d1b1429d.

LEAF of deadlock-audit-7kcz8 (log/log2/log10). Same pay-twice deferral, same two-category shape -
log1p was simply left out of the `log_name` match when that bead shipped.

## THE DEFECT

`zerocopy_f64_unary_flat` computes the whole correct output buffer, then, if any element is in the
event set, `return Ok(None)` so a numpy fallback re-runs the ufunc purely to record the FP event.
7kcz8 taught log/log2/log10 to RESOLVE the category themselves (one read pass over the input) and
issue a ONE-ELEMENT witness instead. log1p has the identical structure with the pivot at -1 rather
than 0 - `log1p(-1) = -inf` is divide, everything below is invalid - and was not in the list.

The size sweep nominated `log1p` at 3.086x, n=2^13, nulls PASS. That figure is the OPERAND, not the
size: `standard_normal` puts ~16% of elements below -1. `abs()` of the same array reads 1.13-1.36x.

## THE MEASUREMENT (same invocation, ABBAABBA, dual A/A null, n as marked)

BEFORE = 56ec3f15b3f2, AFTER = 6426b4c8a40a (committed source), same session, same host.

```
  case                    numpy_ns     fnp_ns     BEFORE            AFTER
  standard_normal 2^13     63909.1    86433.7     2.978x LOSS   ->  1.253x LOSS  [1.187,1.273]
  in-domain 2^13           63753.8    65245.6     1.220x        ->  1.008x       [0.989,1.031]

  standard_normal 2^16    745046.4   358291.8     1.870x LOSS   ->  0.507x WIN   [0.445,0.544]
  in-domain 2^16          727775.7   248325.4     0.424x WIN    ->  0.337x WIN   [0.295,0.396]
  +ONE bad 2^16           617716.2   291262.8     1.952x LOSS   ->  0.459x WIN   [0.391,0.512]
```

All six AFTER nulls PASS (0.9985-1.0060 / 0.9962-1.0088). BEFORE/AFTER ranges are DISJOINT on every
event-bearing cell. The in-domain control moving only 1.220x -> 1.008x is what pins the effect to
the event path rather than the kernel.

candidate null (0.9352, then 1.0298 on a re-run). The row above is the third run, on the
committed-source ELF, where it passed. The direction replicated in all three.

## TWO CORRECTNESS FIXES, BOTH CAUGHT BY THE BIT-EQUALITY ASSERTION

1. The predicate `value == -1.0 || (value.is_finite() && value < -1.0)` DROPPED -inf. NumPy reports
   invalid for `log1p(-inf)`; we were silent. The whole set is exactly `value <= -1.0` - IEEE gives

title: [bug][fnp-python] nansum/nanmax/nanmin reject initial= and where=, nanmean rejects where= - numpy accepts all of them
description:
From the same signature audit that produced
deadlock-audit-kwname-case-divergence-9w6uj (647 #[pyo3(signature = ...)]
declarations vs inspect.signature on the installed numpy 2.4.3). This is the
MISSING-keyword class for the nan reductions: numpy accepts parameters that fnp
does not declare, so the call raises TypeError here and succeeds on numpy.

  numpy: nansum(a, axis, dtype, out, keepdims, initial, where)
  fnp:   nansum(a, axis, dtype, out, keepdims)                -> initial, where
  numpy: nanmax(a, axis, out, keepdims, initial, where)
  fnp:   nanmax(a, axis, out, keepdims)                       -> initial, where
  numpy: nanmin(a, axis, out, keepdims, initial, where)
  fnp:   nanmin(a, axis, out, keepdims)                       -> initial, where
  numpy: nanmean(a, axis, dtype, out, keepdims, where)
  fnp:   nanmean(a, axis, dtype, out, keepdims)               -> where

CONFIRMED ON THE NUMPY SIDE: np.nansum(np.array([1.,2.,nan]),
where=np.array([True,False,True])) returns 1.0 today.

nanprod in the same file already has exactly this shape (initial + r#where
declared, forwarded in its fallback closure, and both forcing delegation before
any native path runs), so the fix is to mirror that established pattern - not to
invent one. The native kernels do not implement initial/where, so any non-None
value must delegate to numpy, the same way dtype= and out= already do.

Note PyO3 strips the r# from the raw identifier r#where, proven by
tri_and_copyto_keywords_match_numpy_spelling in conformance_indices.rs.

WHILE IN THERE, do NOT silently fix: fnp declares keepdims=false where numpy's
default is the np._NoValue sentinel (nanprod already uses Option<bool> for
exactly this reason). Passing keepdims=False explicitly is not identical to not
passing it for ndarray subclasses. Either mirror nanprod's Option<bool> here too
or leave it and say so.

PROBE TO CLOSE: a no-mock conformance test that calls each of the four with
where= (and initial= where numpy has it), including a where= that masks every
element (numpy's empty-reduction behaviour differs per function), comparing
fnp's outcome against numpy's in the same interpreter; green on a named worker
with its numpy version cited.
close_reason:
FIXED in 67daee11.

All four functions now declare and forward the numpy keywords they were missing: nansum/nanmax/nanmin gained initial= and where=, nanmean gained where= (numpy gives it no initial=). The pattern is nanprod's, already in the same file - the native kernels implement neither keyword, so a non-None value delegates to numpy exactly as dtype= and out= already do, rather than being silently ignored.

TEST nan_reduction_initial_and_where_surfaces_match_numpy in conformance_nan_funcs.rs, 18 cases including the ones the bead's probe named: all-False where= (numpy: nansum 0.0, nanmean nan + RuntimeWarning, both reproduced), initial= alone, initial=+where=, keepdims with where=, 2-D with an axis, and nanmax/nanmin(where=) WITHOUT initial=, which numpy REJECTS ('reduction operation fmax does not have an identity') - fnp reproduces the ValueError instead of inventing an answer. Every case is computed for fnp and numpy in the same interpreter, so nothing is pinned to a build.

THE keepdims SENTINEL NOTE IN THIS BEAD: left as is and saying so, per the bead's own instruction not to silently fix it. nansum/nanmean still take keepdims=false where numpy's default is np._NoValue; nanmax/nanmin already use Option<bool>. It is observable only for ndarray subclasses and belongs with the sentinel bead below.

FOUND EN ROUTE, filed not swallowed - deadlock-audit-where-none-vs-absent-sentinel-bbk62: numpy does NOT read where=None as 'not passed'. It is an all-False mask (np.nansum(x, where=None) = 0.0, np.nanmean(x, where=None) = nan) where fnp returns the unmasked 7.0 / 2.3333, because PyO3 extracts Python None into Rust None for an Option<T> parameter and cannot distinguish an explicit None from an omitted argument. Measured on both sides at this commit. It affects the whole family (nanprod, nanstd, nanvar, copyto, and the ufunc binding at lib.rs:314), needs a three-state argument type to fix properly, and is therefore ITS OWN bead with a recipe rather than a silent widening of this one. The three where=None cases are left OUT of the new test with a comment pointing at that bead; initial=None IS 'not passed' for numpy (verified: nanmax(x, initial=None) == nanmax(x)), so those three cases ARE asserted.
