title: [test][fnp-python] no non-contiguous input sweep - every fast path gates on c_contiguous, so awkward layouts answer from an untested fallback
description:
EIGHTH PROBE. The seven so far varied the RESULT attribute (type, dtype,
exception, shape, aliasing, __all__). This one varies the INPUT LAYOUT and asks
whether fnp's fallbacks agree with numpy.

WHY: nearly every fnp fast path gates on C-contiguity and bails when it fails.
The source is full of it -
    "Non-contiguous (transposed/strided) source ndarrays bail into the cold
     extract; delegate."                                            (take)
    "int/uint canonicalize lossy; non-contiguous bails the fast path into the
     transpose-copy extract (~55x slower). Delegate both to numpy."  (signbit)
    "A size-changing uintN view requires C-contiguous data; otherwise defer."
                                                                (concatenate)
So for awkward layouts the answer comes from a DIFFERENT code path than the one
every contiguous test exercises - either numpy itself, or a cold extract that
rebuilds through a Vec. The contiguous tests cannot see a defect in either.

The layouts that matter, in rough order of nastiness:
  - a BROADCAST view (np.broadcast_to) - 0-stride, read-only. A buffer protocol
    consumer that assumes stride == itemsize reads the same element repeatedly
    or runs off the end. liz1c showed fnp reaching extract paths for dtypes the
    guard did not intend; a 0-stride input is the layout equivalent.
  - a NEGATIVE stride (a[::-1]) - pointer walks backwards.
  - a transposed view, an F-ordered array, and a strided slice (a[::2]).
  - a non-contiguous 2-D slice (a[1:, ::2]).

PROBE TO CLOSE: a conformance sweep over those six layouts crossed with the
operations most likely to have a contiguity-gated fast path - sum, mean, min,
max, argmin, argmax, cumsum, sort, unique, take, compress, count_nonzero,
nonzero, clip, abs, sqrt, negative, flip, ravel, reshape, concatenate, repeat,
diff, where - comparing dtype, shape and VALUES against numpy for each. Include
the C-contiguous layout as a control so a build that got everything wrong the
same way is still caught, and assert the preconditions that the layouts are
actually non-contiguous (a[::-1].flags.c_contiguous is False, broadcast_to's
strides contain a 0) - otherwise the sweep silently tests six spellings of the
same contiguous array.

Any divergence is a real defect; fix it in the same bead.
close_reason:
DELIVERED in 3e70f767 as a LOCK. NO DIVERGENCE - all 210 comparisons match, including every 0-stride case, so no defect is claimed. It passed on the first run; there is no red-to-green here.

WHAT IT COVERS: 7 input layouts x 30 operations, comparing dtype, shape and values against numpy in the same interpreter. Layouts: C-contiguous (control), transposed, Fortran-ordered, a strided row slice a[::2], a NEGATIVE stride a[::-1], a non-contiguous 2-D slice a[1:, ::2], and a BROADCAST view (np.broadcast_to) which is 0-stride and read-only. Operations: the reductions, sort/unique/take/compress/nonzero/count_nonzero, the elementwise ones, and the structural ones (flip/ravel/reshape/repeat/diff/concatenate/where/transpose) - chosen because each is documented in the source as having a contiguity-gated fast path.

WHY THE AXIS WAS WORTH PROBING: nearly every fnp fast path gates on C-contiguity and bails. The source says so at each site - take: 'Non-contiguous (transposed/strided) source ndarrays bail into the cold extract; delegate'; signbit: 'non-contiguous bails the fast path into the transpose-copy extract (~55x slower). Delegate both to numpy'; concatenate: 'A size-changing uintN view requires C-contiguous data; otherwise defer'. So for an awkward layout the answer comes from a different code path than the one every contiguous test exercises - numpy itself, or a cold extract that rebuilds through a Vec - and the contiguous tests are structurally unable to see a defect in either. The broadcast view was the specific bet: 0-stride is where a buffer consumer that assumes stride == itemsize reads one element repeatedly or walks off the end, and liz1c had already shown fnp reaching an extract path for a dtype its guard did not intend. That bet did not pay - the 0-stride cases are clean.

THE PRECONDITIONS ARE THE ANTI-VACUITY MECHANISM, and they are specific to this axis: each layout is checked to BE what it claims - c_contiguous False for the strided/transposed/negative cases, f_contiguous-and-not-c_contiguous for the Fortran one, and a literal 0 in broadcast_to's strides. Without them the sweep could be seven spellings of the same contiguous array and pass exactly as loudly, which is how a layout sweep goes quietly useless.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_return_types = 5 passed / 0 failed, exit 0, oracle numpy 2.4.3, 210 comparisons. cargo clippy -p fnp-python --test conformance_return_types -- -D warnings exit 0. cargo fmt --check -p fnp-python exit 0. All exit codes captured directly.

TALLY, eight probes: rrrlm, scoca, 65pde, bikey, succi clean locks; liz1c found take(complex64) raising (fixed); c7hqd found concatenate's .base (fixed in st00f). Two live bugs in eight. The rate is falling, which is itself information - the remaining unprobed axis I would rank highest is structured/void and datetime64/timedelta64 dtype parity, since those are the dtype families the numeric extract path cannot represent at all and therefore must delegate in every case.

title: [bug][fnp-python] sum/prod/mean/std/var/max/min/any also treat where=None as absent - same defect as bbk62, outside its list
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-08 on numpy 2.4.3 while closing
deadlock-audit-where-none-vs-absent-sentinel-bbk62, which named only copyto, the
nan reductions and the ufunc __call__. The NON-nan reductions have the identical
defect and were not in that list, so they are filed here rather than folded in
silently.

x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]), omitted vs where=None:
  sum   10.0  -> 0.0            prod  24.0 -> 1.0
  mean  2.5   -> TypeError      std   1.118 -> TypeError
  var   1.25  -> TypeError      max   4.0  -> ValueError
  min   1.0   -> ValueError     any   True -> False
  all   True  -> True   (the one that genuinely does not differ)

fnp declares `r#where` as Option<Py<PyAny>> on these, so PyO3 collapses an
explicit Python None into Rust None and each returns the UNMASKED answer instead
of numpy's masked-to-nothing result or its exception.

THE FIX IS ALREADY IN THE TREE AND THIS IS MECHANICAL: bbk62 added
`enum WhereArg { Absent, ExplicitNone, Value }` with its FromPyObject impl and
the `apply` / `is_supplied` / `mask` helpers next to copyto in
crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs. Each site needs three edits, exactly as the nan
reductions took:
  - signature default `r#where=None` -> `r#where=WhereArg::Absent`
  - parameter type `Option<Py<PyAny>>` -> `WhereArg`
  - forwarding `if let Some(w) = r#where.as_ref() { kwargs.set_item(...) }`
    -> `r#where.apply(py, &kwargs)?;`, and any native-path guard
    `r#where.as_ref().is_some_and(...)` / `.is_some()` -> `r#where.is_supplied()`

DO NOT convert the ufunc __call__ binding at lib.rs:314. Measured:
np.add(y, y, where=None) == np.add(y, y), so Option is correct there and
changing it would invent a divergence. bbk62 records the same finding.

Check `all` before changing it - it is the one function measured NOT to differ,
so a where=None case for it must assert the unchanged answer, not an exception.

PROBE TO CLOSE: conformance cases for each of sum/prod/mean/std/var/max/min/any
covering where=None AND the omitted spelling (so the fix is shown to change only
the explicit-None case), plus `all` asserting no change, compared against numpy
in the same interpreter; green on a named worker with its numpy version cited,
and clippy -p fnp-python --lib --tests (NOT bare --lib, which skips cfg(test)).
close_reason:
FIXED in c7b42e3f - and the bead as filed was wrong in two ways, both corrected by measurement.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY BROKEN: five of the nine, not all nine. prod, py_max, py_min, all, any gated their native paths on where_.as_ref().is_some_and(|v| !v.is_none()) - so an explicit where=None FAILED the check, the native path ran, and fnp returned the unmasked answer. Measured against numpy 2.4.3: prod gave 24.0 where numpy gives 1.0 (empty-product identity), max/min gave 4.0/1.0 where numpy RAISES ValueError (fmax/fmin have no identity), any gave True where numpy gives False, all gave False where numpy gives True.

sum/mean/std/var are NOT affected and were left alone: they gate every native path on the kwargs dict being EMPTY, so any supplied where= already delegates regardless of its value. The test asserts their omitted and where=None spellings both match numpy, so that claim is held rather than asserted.

THE FIX IS NOT bbk62's TYPE: these wrappers take **kwargs and read  out of the dict, so the distinction is already present - the key exists. Gating on where_.is_some() rather than on the value being non-None is the whole fix. WhereArg is for wrappers that take where= as a TYPED parameter, where PyO3 collapses Python None into Rust None. Two different mechanisms producing the same defect; using the type here would have been cargo-culting it.

CORRECTION 1 TO THIS BEAD: I wrote that np.all 'is the one function measured NOT to differ'. That was wrong, and wrong in the flattering direction - all(where=None) returns the identity True regardless of input, coinciding with the unmasked answer only when that answer is already True, and my sample was all-nonzero. Re-measured with an input containing a zero: omitted False, where=None True. np.all is in scope, and its conformance case uses an input CONTAINING A ZERO or it would be vacuous. A correcting comment was added to this bead before any code was written.

CORRECTION 2, against my own reasoning: I had read sum's source, seen it gate on kwargs being empty, and concluded the whole family was already correct - I was about to close this bead as a false alarm on that basis. The test disagreed on five of nine. Reading the code is not measuring it, and the only reason the defect was found is that I wrote the cases anyway and ran them.

NON-VACUITY IS DEMONSTRATED, not argued: the new cases went RED naming exactly prod/max/min/any/all (1 failed, 41 passed) before the change and GREEN (42 passed, 0 failed) after. That is the red-to-green I could not produce for the save bead.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_nan_funcs = 42 passed / 0 failed, exit 0, oracle numpy 2.4.3, with the pre-fix red recorded above. cargo clippy -p fnp-python --lib --tests -- -D warnings exit 0. cargo fmt --check -p fnp-python exit 0. All exit codes captured directly.

comments.text:
CORRECTION TO THIS BEAD, before anyone acts on it: the instruction "np.all is the one function measured NOT to differ, so assert its answer is unchanged" is WRONG, and it was wrong because the measurement behind it used all-nonzero sample data.

np.all(x, where=None) returns the reduction IDENTITY, True, regardless of the input - it does not return the unmasked answer. That coincides with the unmasked answer only when the unmasked answer is already True. Re-measured on numpy 2.4.3:

  x = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]   all omitted=True   where=None=True    (looks the same - the trap)
  x = [1.0, 0.0, 3.0]        all omitted=False  where=None=True    DIFFERS

So np.all belongs in the fix with the other eight, and its conformance case MUST use an input containing a zero or the case is vacuous. Nine functions in scope: sum, prod, mean, std, var, max, min, any, all.

General lesson for the other cases too: a where=None case whose input makes the masked and unmasked answers coincide proves nothing. Pick inputs where they differ.

title: bug: np.where with OBJECT-dtype choices RAISES where numpy succeeds - TypeError: Cannot change data-type for array of references
description:
CLOSURE, BlackThrush, 2026-09-01, FIXED AND VERIFIED in commit dd7dbd4c.

ROOT CAUSE, exactly where the bead pointed: try_zerocopy_any_dtype_where. np.object_ has itemsize 8
on this target, so it passed the `matches!(itemsize, 1|2|4|8|16)` width gate untouched and reached
the `.view(uint8)` in as_bytes, where numpy raises

    TypeError: Cannot change data-type for array of references.

and the `?` carried it out of np.where. Confirmed against the INSTALLED interpreter BEFORE any
build - numpy 2.3.5, `np.array(['a','b'],dtype=object).reshape(-1).view(np.uint8)` reproduces the
exact message, `.dtype.itemsize` is 8 and `.dtype.hasobject` is True.

THE FIX DECLINES ON `dtype.hasobject`, NOT ON `kind == 'O'`. hasobject also catches a STRUCTURED
dtype with an embedded object field, which reports kind 'V' and is equally unviewable, so a
kind-shaped fix would have left the sibling standing. Both are barred for a second reason that
holds even where the view would have succeeded: the element bytes are BORROWED PyObject POINTERS,
so a verbatim byte select would hand back an array of references numpy never incref'd. No wider
kernel fixes that - the delegate is the right answer, and the gate returns None to reach it.

PLACEMENT: after the width gate, so the extra attribute read is paid only by operands that already
matched on dtype, shape and itemsize (dtype-only-audit-and-failure-path-placement).

SECOND CHANGE, same commit: `.view()` in as_bytes now DECLINES on any failure
(`let Ok(viewed) = ... else { return Ok(None) }`) instead of propagating. hasobject names the one
dtype class known to throw there; this is the standing guarantee for anything else, because
np.where must never surface an error numpy would not have surfaced.

NO REGRESSION SURFACE. Behaviour changes for hasobject dtypes ONLY, and every one of those
previously raised without exception, so there is no route this can make worse.

VERIFICATION - worker hz4 via rch, RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1, lib.rs sha256
4654ec1c5843931b6398123680a157d4306c85868e35310f7021f6742babbe32:
    cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_searching
    test result: ok. 3 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored
The matrix PANICS on any failing MUST clause, so 3/3 green IS the acceptance criterion met -
searching-where-object-choices and searching-where-mixed-object-choices both pass. The bead's note
about this failure aborting multi-target cargo test invocations is discharged with it.

SIBLING GATES AUDITED, ALL CLEAN: try_zerocopy_where_array_scalar gates kind to f|i|u|c|b before
any view; try_zerocopy_f64_where and try_zerocopy_int_where are dtype-specific. Only the any-dtype
gate - the one whose name promises any dtype - carried the hazard, exactly as the bead guessed.

SUCCESSOR FILED for the general class. A static census over lib.rs counts 537 `.view()` call sites,
420 of which propagate with `?`. THAT NUMBER IS AN UPPER BOUND AND NOT A DEFECT COUNT - most view
an output we just allocated, or an operand already kind-gated - so it licenses a RUNTIME probe, not
a code change.

--- original bead follows ---

PRE-EXISTING, found while regression-testing deadlock-audit-66w2d and VERIFIED pre-existing rather
than assumed.

conformance_searching::conformance_searching_matrix fails one MUST clause:

  searching-where-object-choices (where): ours raised, theirs succeeded:
  TypeError: Cannot change data-type for array of references.

Every other clause in that matrix passes, INCLUDING the three sibling object-dtype clauses
searching-where-object-condition-as-nonzero, -object-condition-select and
-mixed-object-condition-select. So the defect is specifically an object-dtype array in the CHOICE
(x/y) position, not in the condition.

VERIFIED PRE-EXISTING, NOT INHERITED FROM THE ENTRY-TAX WORK. deadlock-audit-2nudi and -66w2d
touched numeric_operand_facts, concatenate, sum's delegate tail and the sort/argsort gate chains -
none of which np.where reaches - but the argument was CHECKED rather than made: the lib.rs from
commit b1e33216 (before ANY source change in this campaign) was put in place and the test run
again. IDENTICAL FAILURE, same clause, same message. The working file was restored and verified by
sha256 (4280c34ba7c3bdfa253a09c11031e47a9218e09ae335fc7c8e98c39bd3db27bc).

The error text is numpy's own - 'Cannot change data-type for array of references' is what numpy
says when you retype an O-dtype buffer - so the likely site is a native where path that views or
retypes the choice arrays without first declining kind 'O'.
try_zerocopy_any_dtype_where is the gate whose name promises any dtype and is the first place to
look.

NOTE FOR WHOEVER RUNS THE SUITE: this failure ABORTS a multi-target cargo test invocation, so a run
that includes --test conformance_searching silently drops every target listed after it. That is how
it was found - two earlier runs reported fewer targets than were requested.

ACCEPTANCE: fnp.where(cond, obj_x, obj_y) returns what numpy returns, or declines to numpy; the
conformance_searching matrix passes 3/3.

title: hazard: numpy 2.5.2 SEGFAULTS on np.all(a, axis, out=<object array>) - it killed the raise-parity sweep at its THIRD entry point and hid the other 365
description:
CLOSED, BlackThrush, 2026-09-01. REDUCED TO FOUR LINES, DETERMINISTIC, and the bead's premise
was wrong about which function it is.

THE REPRO. On worker hz4, numpy 2.5.2, python 3.14.4, plain `python3 -c` - no fnp, no pyo3,
no rlimit, no rayon:

    import numpy as np, gc
    f = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
    out = np.array(7, dtype=object)
    r = np.any(f, 0, out)      # returns array(True, dtype=object)
    del r, out
    gc.collect()               # SIGSEGV

The call SUCCEEDS and returns the right value. The crash comes later, in the collector.

IT IS `np.any`, NOT `np.all`. Same shape, same worker, one subprocess per op:
    any  exit=-11 (SIGSEGV)      all  ok      max  ok      min  ok
And on the INSTALLED interpreter (numpy 2.4.3) `any` and `all` both survive, so this is a
REGRESSION somewhere in 2.5.x and it is confined to one reduction.

WHY THE BEAD NAMED `all`. The original faulthandler traceback showed `np.all` on the stack -
because the corruption from an EARLIER `np.any` call surfaced when a later `np.all` allocated.
A `gc.collect()` after every call moved the crash onto the true culprit and the last line
printed was `any o0d 3 2 ['f64','i0']`. THE CRASH LOCATION IS NOT THE CAUSE when the fault is
a refcount: that is the same lesson the sweep's own first run taught, one level down.

MECHANISM, inferred and consistent with everything above: the reduction stores its `True` into
the object slot without an INCREF (or drops the slot's previous reference), so the array holds
a borrowed or dangling pointer; freeing it later decrefs garbage. Nothing else fits "call
returns the correct value, GC dies".

WHAT WE DO ABOUT OUR OWN np.any: NOTHING, deliberately. Our route delegates - the sweep's
child died inside numpy's frame, our arm never ran - so on 2.5.2 we crash exactly as numpy
does, and on 2.4.3 and on any fixed 2.5.x we behave exactly as numpy does. Special-casing an
object `out` would make us diverge from every numpy that does not have this bug, and we cannot
cheaply detect "this numpy is broken". Matching the incumbent is the contract even when the
incumbent is wrong; the containment belongs in the probe, not in the route.

CONTAINMENT ALREADY SHIPPED (commit 0cce66ea): objdtype_raise_parity forks a child per entry
point, so a fatal signal costs one name and is reported with the exact call instead of taking
the report with it. That is the durable part of this bead.

WORTH REPORTING UPSTREAM: the four lines above are the whole cost. Not filed by this session.
close_reason: Reduced to 4 deterministic lines: it is np.any (not np.all), numpy 2.5.2 only, crash lands in gc.collect() after the call returns correctly; 2.4.3 unaffected. We deliberately keep delegating

title: [test][fnp-python] solve_triangular_complex FAILS (not skips) when scipy is absent - only scipy-dependent test in the crate
description:
Split out of deadlock-audit-xdyx7. NOT a code defect - an oracle-availability defect.

solve_triangular_complex (conformance_linalg_advanced.rs ~560) fails with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'scipy'. Confirmed on TWO workers: vmi1149989 and vmi1227854. It is the ONLY test in the crate that uses scipy as its oracle (rg scipy = 3 hits, all in this one test).

So on any worker without scipy this test is a permanent red that trains everyone to ignore the shard.

FIX SHAPE, and the tension is the point: a test whose oracle is missing must not FAIL, but it must not SILENTLY SKIP either - a silently-skipping oracle test is this repo's documented vacuous-green trap (the fnp-random oracle beads skipped without numpy and looked green). Skip LOUDLY: print a named reason to stderr and make the skip visible in the run, or assert scipy's presence in one place so the absence is reported once as an environment problem rather than as a parity failure.

ALSO WORTH DECIDING: whether scipy belongs as an oracle at all here, given numpy is this project's declared behavioural oracle. If solve_triangular has no numpy equivalent, say so explicitly in the test.

PROBE TO CLOSE: on a worker WITHOUT scipy, 'cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_linalg_advanced' reports 0 failed AND the run visibly names the skipped oracle. Both halves required.
close_reason:
CLOSED in commit 90dd91da - but NOT as filed. The premise was wrong and the loud skip would have hidden a real defect.

THE BEAD SAID test hygiene: 'solve_triangular_complex FAILS instead of skipping when scipy is absent'. The traceback was never at the test's 'import scipy.linalg'. It was at line 9, the fnp.solve_triangular CALL:
    // Complex arrays must fall back to scipy
    if kind_a == "c" || kind_b == "c" { let scipy_linalg = py.import("scipy.linalg")?; ... }
A PUBLIC fnp entry point raised ModuleNotFoundError on every host without scipy, for ALL complex input. scipy is not a declared dependency, it is absent from every worker checked (hz2, vmi1149989, vmi1227854, vmi1152480), and that was the ONLY scipy reference in the crate - one isolated point routing a core linalg operation through LAPACK, against the suite's premise of owning the implementation. Making the skip loud would have dressed up a broken function.

FIXED PROPERLY. native_complex_solve_triangular does forward substitution for lower and back substitution for upper, in complex128 regardless of input width, casting back to promote_types(a.dtype, b.dtype). Complex division uses Smith's algorithm - the same one the elementwise complex path already uses. scipy's documented semantics preserved: only the named triangle is read, unit_diagonal treats the diagonal as 1 without reading it, and a zero diagonal raises numpy.linalg.LinAlgError naming the row rather than returning inf/nan.

ORACLE CHOICE VALIDATED BEFORE RELYING ON IT: for an exactly triangular a, np.linalg.solve, hand-written forward substitution, and scipy all agree on the test system. NumPy - the declared oracle - decides this case alone, so the test no longer needs scipy either.

NINE SUB-CASES now asserted, each of which a naive substitution gets wrong differently: lower/upper 1-D, lower/upper unit_diagonal, lower/upper 2-D rhs (catches a row/column indexing slip), a POISONED opposite triangle that must be ignored rather than read, complex64 dtype preservation, and a singular zero diagonal that must raise.

THE SKIP IS STILL LOUD, as asked, but it is now the SECOND opinion rather than the only one. Where scipy exists it runs; where it does not, the script emits SKIPPED_ORACLE naming exactly what was not compared and the Rust side re-emits it as a stderr banner. Honest limitation stated in the test: libtest captures output for passing tests, so the banner shows under --nocapture, on any other failure in the shard, or to a log scan grepping SKIPPED_ORACLE. The anti-vacuity guarantee is NOT the banner - it is that the numpy arm always runs and always asserts, so the test cannot pass having checked nothing.

ALSO HONEST: the scipy branch is currently unexercised fleet-wide, since no checked worker has scipy. Its logic was verified locally where scipy agrees with np.linalg.solve.

EVIDENCE, hz2 (no scipy), --nocapture: conformance_linalg_advanced 33 passed / 0 failed, up from 32 passed / 1 failed, banner printed. Gates, real exits: cargo check --all-targets 0; clippy --no-deps -D warnings 0 with zero error lines and the log showing it reached the crate; rustfmt --check 0.

title: [bug][fnp-python] multiply_add f16 special values not byte-identical (1 test RED at HEAD)
description:
Child 4 of deadlock-audit-xdyx7. Failing: multiply_add_f16_special_values_are_byte_identical in conformance_multiply_add. Reproduced at pristine HEAD b86ce6ef.

SPECIAL VALUES is the operative word - the f16 path's intermediate narrow is load-bearing (numpy widens f16->f32, operates, narrows), and the fused-vs-unfused question is decided per dtype: numpy's COMPLEX multiply is FMA-contracted while real f64 must NOT be. Check which side of that line f16 multiply_add sits on before changing the kernel, and check it against the INSTALLED numpy rather than assumption.

PROBE TO CLOSE: 'cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_multiply_add' green, citing worker and numpy version.
close_reason:
FIXED in commit 3a1fe6ec. Real kernel defect, fixed on the NEWER numpy, NOT version-keyed.

DEFECT: 8 of 1331 triples in multiply_add_f16_special_values_are_byte_identical, all one case in its sign variants - the invalid product 0 x inf with a NaN addend. Ours 0xfe00, numpy 0x7e00.

DIAGNOSED BY MEASUREMENT, not argument. NumPy's f16 multiply agrees with ours EXACTLY: np.float16(0.0)*np.float16(inf) is 0xfe00 on both sides, the negative default QNaN x86 produces for an invalid product. The whole divergence is in the ADD and it is an operand-order effect:
  numpy (A*B) + C = 0x7e00  <- the addend
  numpy C + (A*B) = 0xfe00  <- still the second operand
Our kernel writes 'product + addend' in the same source order yet got the product's NaN, because Rust lowers a + b to an addss whose operand order is the backend's choice. Which NaN survives is not a language guarantee.

RULE DERIVED BY SWEEPING NUMPY: when BOTH operands of an f16 add are NaN, numpy returns the SECOND operand. Verified over every ordered pair of {0x7e00, 0xfe00, 0x7e01, 0xff00} - second operand every time, payload preserved. With exactly one NaN operand both sides already agree, so only the both-NaN case is special-cased.

THE FIRST FIX WAS WRONG AND THE TEST I ADDED CAUGHT IT. Returning the addend verbatim made the 1331-triple grid pass (31 passed / 0 failed) - but that grid only ever uses np.nan (0x7e00), so it cannot distinguish 'return the addend' from 'return a canonical +qNaN' NOR from 'return a signalling payload untouched'. I added multiply_add_f16_both_nan_keeps_the_addend_payload with distinct payloads and it failed immediately on 7c01/7e01: numpy QUIETS a signalling addend. Correct rule is addend | 0x0200 (no-op when already quiet). Without that test the bug would have shipped looking green.

EVIDENCE, worker vmi1227854, numpy 2.4.x: conformance_multiply_add 32 passed / 0 failed, up from 30 passed / 1 failed at HEAD. Run per-target with --no-fail-fast. Measured on the NEWER numpy, so this is a genuine fix and this bead was correctly NOT blocked on 1jqrw.

INCIDENTAL SELF-INFLICTED BREAK REPAIRED IN THE SAME COMMIT: my earlier commit 7b4f4313 (smr32) added resolve_numpy_submodule with three tail-position 'return' statements, so 'cargo clippy -p fnp-python --all-targets -- -D warnings' had been FAILING on main since - the G1 gate was red and I put it there, because I ran cargo check and targeted tests on that commit but not clippy. Rewritten as match + map_err. Lesson recorded: cargo check passing is not evidence clippy passes.

GATES, real exit statuses: clippy --no-deps -D warnings exit 0, zero error lines, log shows it reached the crate; rustfmt --check exit 0.

DIAGNOSED by AzureHill 2026-08-06, commit 3469e8ab. REAL KERNEL BUG, not the numpy-version class. Staying OPEN for the fix.

The test now prints the diverging triples on raw bits. Verdict on vmi1227854, numpy 2.4.x: exactly 8 of 1331 differ, and they are ONE case in its sign variants - the invalid product 0 x inf with a NaN addend:
  0.0*inf+nan, 0.0*-inf+nan, -0.0*inf+nan, -0.0*-inf+nan,
  inf*0.0+nan, inf*-0.0+nan, -inf*0.0+nan, -inf*-0.0+nan
  ours = 0xfe00 (NEGATIVE quiet NaN)    numpy = 0x7e00 (POSITIVE quiet NaN)
Both are NaN; the SIGN BIT differs. Ours keeps the default QNaN that the invalid 0 x inf produces on x86; numpy ends up carrying the addend's positive NaN.

CRITICALLY, THIS IS NOT VERSION-DEPENDENT. The run was on numpy 2.4.x - the NEWER side of the split that explains 1jqrw, 6nr1a, m8z69 and keqog. So unlike those, this must be FIXED, not version-keyed, and this bead must NOT be blocked on 1jqrw.

SCOPE IS NARROW. The sibling multiply_add_f16_intermediate_narrowing_is_load_bearing PASSES, so the widen->multiply->narrow->add path is right for ordinary values; only NaN selection when the product is invalid is wrong. The fix is in the f16 multiply_add kernel's handling of that case - decide it against the INSTALLED numpy rather than from IEEE first principles, because which NaN survives an add of two NaNs is implementation-defined and x86's answer depends on operand order.

NEXT STEP for whoever takes it: find the f16 multiply_add kernel (fnp-python, the f16 widen path), reproduce 0 x inf + nan in isolation, and match numpy's operand ordering. The 8 cases above are the complete acceptance set.

title: perf(sum/mean): CORRECTED - the sign test does not decide this cell either (5 runs: 3 slower, 1 faster, 1 undecided); what IS stable is std and the >=1.25M band, and the floor was NOT changed
description:
CORRECTED, BlackThrush, 2026-09-01, commit 7f56a4d8. THIS BEAD OPENED ON A CLAIM THAT DID NOT
SURVIVE ITS OWN INSTRUMENT, and the correction is the finding.

WHAT WAS CLAIMED when this bead was opened (from qpylx's closure, commit 98e027f9): a paired
sign test over 21 interleaved rounds decided sum/mean f64 2^20 as SLOWER, replicated on two
runs. WITHDRAWN. Five runs of the SAME cell, SAME worker (hz4), SAME ELF:

    sum f64 2^20    21/21 SLOWER | 19/21 SLOWER | 20/21 SLOWER | 5/21 (p=.027, leaning
                    FASTER, median -64.7%) | 12/21 not decided
    mean f64 2^20   17/21 SLOWER | 19/21 SLOWER | 17/21 SLOWER | 1/21 DECIDED FASTER
                    | 12/21 not decided
    std f64 2^20     0/21 FASTER |  0/21 FASTER |  0/21 FASTER |  0/21 FASTER | 0/21 FASTER

Every A/A control was clean in every run, INCLUDING the run whose verdict reversed. So a sign
test controls WITHIN-run drift exactly as the A/A null does, and is exactly as blind to
run-to-run structure. A decisive p from one run is a statement about that run and nothing more.
Two runs agreeing is not replication - it is two draws from a distribution whose spread we had
not measured. THIS CELL REMAINS UNDECIDABLE, which is where qpylx started.

WHAT IS DECIDABLE, and it is worth having:
  - `std` f64 2^20 is FASTER, 5 of 5 runs, 0/21 every single time. That one is real and is
    already banked (~2.5-2.9x).
  - THE SIZE LADDER IS STABLE ABOVE ~1.25M ELEMENTS: fnp decisively FASTER in 3 of 3 runs at
    1.25M / 1.5M / 1.75M / 2.0M / 2^21 / 2^22, with the margin growing monotonically from
    -73 us to -2.5 ms. The parallel exact-tree route earns its keep well above its floor.
  - Below ~1.1M elements the ladder is UNSTABLE: 2^18 read 3/21 FASTER in one run and 20/21
    SLOWER in the next; the 2^20 ladder row read 20/21, then 6/21, then 14/21.

WHAT I ALMOST SHIPPED, and this is the part to remember. The FIRST ladder run showed a clean
narrow band - a loss at 2^20 only, wins on both sides - which reads exactly like a parallel
floor fitted one size too low (F64_SUM_PARALLEL_MIN_ELEMENTS = 1_000_000, and 2^20 is 4.9%
above it). The obvious next move was to raise the floor to ~1.25M and claim the removal of a
standing loss. Two more ladder runs dissolved the band. A FLOOR FITTED TO THAT FIRST LADDER
WOULD HAVE BEEN FITTED TO NOISE, and it would have looked like a textbook chunk-floor win.

THE FLOOR IS UNCHANGED. No lever is claimed.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY MOVE THIS, in order:
  1. CONTROL THE REGIME BEFORE FITTING ANYTHING. The fixed cell (a settled `f`, calls=30) and
     the ladder row at the same size (a freshly allocated array, calls=4) disagree in the same
     process, minutes apart. Buffer provenance and inner repetition count are not nuisance
     parameters here, they are the experiment
     ([[large-buffer-mmap-churn-dominates-elementwise]], [[deadlock-audit-tjo4w]]).
  2. COUNT INSTRUCTIONS INSTEAD OF NANOSECONDS. ~50-130 us on a ~227 us call is inside the
     noise of this fleet but far outside the noise of a counter
     ([[counted-attribution-by-instruction-diff]]).
  3. ONLY THEN consider a floor change, and require the ladder to replicate 3 of 3.

title: [bug][fnp-python] fnp ufunc objects expose no x1/x2 in inspect.signature - cluster 5 of the RED-main audit, still untracked
description:
FILED by CoralOak 2026-08-07 while working deadlock-audit-keqog. This is CLUSTER 5 of
deadlock-audit-xdyx7 (main is RED at pristine HEAD b86ce6ef). All four of xdyx7's children are
closed and cluster 4 (multiply_add f16) closed under deadlock-audit-oo52g, but cluster 5 never
got a bead at all, so it was the one RED with nobody pointed at it.

FAILING TEST: ufunc_signature_has_x1_x2, crates/fnp-python/tests/conformance_ufunc_edge.rs:165.

WHICH SIDE IS WRONG - measured, not assumed. On numpy 2.4.3 locally:
  inspect.signature(np.add)
  -> (x1, x2, /, out=None, *, where=True, casting='same_kind', order='K', dtype=None,
      subok=True, signature=None)
  'x1' in sig.parameters and 'x2' in sig.parameters -> True
  np.add.__text_signature__ -> None  (so numpy is NOT getting this from a text signature;
  numpy's ufunc type supplies __signature__/parameters some other way - find out how before
  copying an approach)
So the oracle is healthy and the gap is OURS.

WHERE THE ORIGINAL REPORT PUTS THE PANIC: xdyx7 records the failure at conformance_ufunc_edge.rs
:174, which is the 'assert_eq!(fnp_result, np_result)' line, NOT the '.expect(\"fnp\")' on the
oracle call above it. That distinction matters: it means inspect.signature(fnp.add) SUCCEEDS and
simply reports no x1/x2 (almost certainly a generic (*args, **kwargs)), rather than raising. So
this is a missing signature, not a broken callable. VERIFY that on a worker before fixing - I
could not run fnp locally (the .so is built remotely).

SCOPE NOTE: fnp.add is a real PyUFunc object, not a #[pyfunction] - see the memory-of-record trap
that ufunc-named #[pyfunction]s can be dead code while the PyUFunc object is the live route. Fix
the ufunc object, and check whether the fix generalises to every ufunc or only to 'add'.

PROBE TO CLOSE: 'cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_ufunc_edge --no-fail-fast' green,
citing worker name and its numpy version. Run per-target or with --no-fail-fast: a multi-target
invocation aborts at the first failing target and its N-passed is a prefix count.
close_reason:
WITHDRAWN BY ITS AUTHOR (CoralOak, 2026-08-07, ~35 min after filing). I had the direction of the
divergence BACKWARDS. Closing as already-resolved by deadlock-audit-1jqrw, not as fixed.

WHAT I GOT WRONG. I reasoned from the panic being at the assert_eq! line rather than the
.expect() on the oracle call, concluded both arms ran and therefore fnp must be the one printing
'False', and filed it as our missing signature. I never checked the other explanation for the same
panic line: that NUMPY printed False and WE printed True.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE, and it was already written down in the codebase before I filed:
crates/fnp-python/tests/conformance_module_metadata.rs:116, in the doc comment on
numpy_oracle_meets_the_supported_version_floor, lists this exact symptom among the measured
below-floor behaviours - "inspect.signature(np.add) exposes x1/x2 from 2.3 on, not on 2.2.4" -
with the standing finding from 1jqrw that in every one of those cases fnp matched the NEWER numpy
and 2.2.4 was the outlier, never the reverse. My own local probe is consistent: numpy 2.4.3 gives
(x1, x2, /, out=None, ...). The RED at pristine HEAD was on a 2.2.4 worker (vmi1149989).

So cluster 5 needs no fix. Under the declared >= 2.3 oracle floor a below-floor host now fails at
numpy_oracle_meets_the_supported_version_floor with a named reason, which is exactly the mechanism
1jqrw built for this class.

METHOD NOTE, since this is the second time this pattern has cost someone here: an assert_eq!
between an fnp arm and a numpy arm tells you they DIFFER; it does not tell you which one moved.
AzureHill's masked_sum work reached the same conclusion the expensive way and built an arbiter that
classifies OURS_WRONG / NUMPY_DIFFERS / BOTH_DIFFER. I should have looked for the oracle's own
version contract before asserting a side. Grep the floor test's doc comment first - it is the
fleet's list of known below-floor symptoms.

NOT VERIFIED BY ME ON A WORKER: I did not run conformance_ufunc_edge on a 2.2.4 host to watch it
pass the floor gate, because the floor decision already covers it and re-running would only
re-derive 1jqrw's evidence. If a >= 2.3 host ever fails ufunc_signature_has_x1_x2, that IS a real
fnp defect and this bead should be reopened rather than a new one filed.

title: [bug][fnp-python] take/choose/compress/fix reject out=, and numpy puts out BEFORE mode so positional calls mis-bind
description:
From the signature audit behind deadlock-audit-kwname-case-divergence-9w6uj (647
#[pyo3(signature = ...)] declarations vs inspect.signature on the installed
numpy 2.4.3). This is the out= subset of the MISSING-keyword class, and it is
two defects rather than one:

  numpy: take(a, indices, axis=None, out=None, mode='raise')
  fnp:   take(a, indices, axis=None, mode='raise')
  numpy: choose(a, choices, out=None, mode='raise')
  fnp:   choose(a, choices, mode='raise')
  numpy: compress(condition, a, axis=None, out=None)
  fnp:   compress(condition, a, axis=None)
  numpy: fix(x, out=None)
  fnp:   fix(x)

(1) KEYWORD: np.take(a, idx, out=buf) works on numpy and raises TypeError on
fnp. Same for choose/compress/fix.

(2) POSITIONAL ORDER, which is the nastier half: numpy puts out BEFORE mode, so
np.take(a, idx, 0, buf) binds buf to out - on fnp that same call binds buf to
`mode` and fails, or worse coerces. np.choose(a, choices, buf) likewise. Adding
out in numpy's position fixes both at once; adding it at the END would fix only
(1) and leave a silent mis-binding.

CONFIRMED ON THE NUMPY SIDE (2.4.3): take/choose/compress/fix all accept out=,
return the SAME object (result is out), and write through it. np.take with an
out= of a different dtype casts into it rather than raising.

FIX: declare out in numpy's position and forward it; no native path here writes
into a caller-supplied buffer, so a non-None out delegates to numpy exactly as
the nan reductions do for out=. Do NOT invent an out-writing native path.

PROBE TO CLOSE: a no-mock conformance test per function covering out= as
keyword AND in numpy's positional slot, the `result is out` identity, the
written values, a dtype numpy is allowed to cast into, and the error surfaces
(bad out shape), comparing fnp against numpy in the same interpreter; green on a
named worker with its numpy version cited.

Not in scope, tracked elsewhere: trim_zeros axis=, indices sparse=, cov dtype=,
loadtxt quotechar=, identity/tri/ascontiguousarray/asfortranarray like=,
asarray_chkfinite order= (same MISSING class), and the REMOVED-upstream class
(reshape newshape=, save fix_imports=, nanpercentile/nanquantile interpolation=).
close_reason:
FIXED in 0eb189b6.

BOTH HALVES THE BEAD NAMED. take/choose/compress/fix now declare out= and forward it, AND it sits in numpy's own position - take(a, indices, axis=None, out=None, mode='raise'), choose(a, choices, out=None, mode='raise'), compress(condition, a, axis=None, out=None), fix(x, out=None). Putting out at the END would have fixed only the keyword call and left np.take(a, idx, 0, buf) binding buf to `mode`, which is the silent half; the bead called that out and the fix honours it.

DELEGATION, NOT A NEW KERNEL: no native gather/compaction/select/trunc writes into a caller-supplied buffer, so a non-None out delegates whole - the same shape the nan reductions use for out=, and exactly what the bead asked for ('Do NOT invent an out-writing native path').

TEST take_choose_compress_fix_out_parameter_matches_numpy in conformance_compress_choose_diagonal.rs, 16 cases: out= as keyword AND in numpy's positional slot for all four functions; the 'result is out' identity; the values actually written; out= with mode='clip'; out= with axis= for take and compress; an int64 out; an int32 out that numpy casts a float64 result into; and the bad-out-shape ValueError. Every case was verified against numpy 2.4.3 FIRST to confirm it is a surface numpy accepts - so the test cannot pass by both sides failing identically, which is the failure mode a bare fnp-vs-numpy comparison invites.

A METHOD NOTE WORTH KEEPING: six inline unit-test call sites needed the new arity, and 'cargo clippy -p fnp-python --lib -- -D warnings' passed exit 0 while five of them were still broken - clippy --lib does NOT compile cfg(test) code. '--lib --tests' catches them, which is what CI's --all-targets does. A green crate-scoped clippy is not evidence that the crate's own unit tests compile.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_compress_choose_diagonal = 27 passed / 0 failed, exit 0. cargo test -p fnp-python --lib = 557 passed / 0 failed, exit 0. cargo clippy -p fnp-python --lib --tests -- -D warnings exit 0. cargo fmt --check -p fnp-python exit 0. Every exit code captured directly rather than through a pipe.

REMAINING IN THE MISSING-KEYWORD CLASS, semantics already verified against numpy 2.4.3 for whoever takes it next: trim_zeros axis= (2-D trims along an axis), indices sparse= (returns a tuple of broadcastable arrays), cov dtype=, identity/tri/ascontiguousarray/asfortranarray like=, asarray_chkfinite order= (order='F' really does produce an F-contiguous result), loadtxt quotechar=.

title: [test][fnp-python] no cross-cutting output-DTYPE sweep, and the extract path canonicalises to f64 - a missed guard is a silently wrong dtype
description:
THIRD PROBE IN THE DECLARED-VS-SERVED CLASS (after
deadlock-audit-submodule-all-names-must-resolve-rrrlm and
deadlock-audit-return-type-parity-sweep-scoca). This one sweeps OUTPUT DTYPE
against numpy across the dtype grid, rather than per-shard.

WHY THIS ONE HAS THE STRONGEST PRIOR: fnp's generic extraction path canonicalises
to an f64 Vec. The source says so repeatedly, in comments written by whoever hit
it:
  "extract_numeric_array canonicalizes to an f64 Vec element-wise (~49x slower
   than numpy for int32)"                                    (signbit)
  "the cold extract residual below still widens narrow widths, so it is guarded
   to bool/8-byte only"                                      (take)
  "the native path extracted the whole array to a widened-f64 UFuncArray"
                                                             (isposinf/isneginf)
Every one of those is a case where a native path would have returned float64
where numpy returns int8/int32/float32, and each was fixed by adding a guard or
a zero-copy path BY HAND. A missed guard is a silently wrong output dtype -
which downstream code sees as a memory blow-up, a failed `astype` round trip, or
an integer overflow that no longer wraps.

WHAT EXISTS: per-shard dtype assertions in many conformance files, and a few
golden sha256 tests that hash `str(out.dtype)` alongside the bytes. There is no
cross-cutting sweep, so which wrappers lack the check is unknown - exactly the
gap scoca closed for return TYPE, applied to output DTYPE.

PROBE TO CLOSE: a conformance sweep comparing `result.dtype` (as a string)
against numpy for a dtype grid x function grid:
  dtypes  int8/16/32/64, uint8/16/32/64, float16/32/64, complex64/128, bool
  groups  - STRUCTURAL, which must preserve the input dtype exactly:
            reshape, transpose, sort, unique, concatenate, repeat, tile, flip,
            roll, ravel, compress, take
          - ELEMENTWISE, which follow numpy's promotion: abs, negative, square,
            sqrt, sign, add with a python int, add with a python float
          - REDUCTIONS, where numpy's accumulator rules apply (int8 sum -> int64
            on this platform, float16 mean -> float16, bool sum -> int64):
            sum, prod, mean, min, max, cumsum
Any divergence found is a real defect and should be fixed in the same bead; if
none is found the sweep lands as the missing lock. Include bool and float16
deliberately - they are the two the f64 canonicalisation mangles most visibly.

Keep it in the file scoca created (conformance_return_types.rs is about what
comes BACK from a call, and dtype is the same question) or a sibling file; do
not scatter it into per-function shards, which is what left the gap.
close_reason:
FIXED in 412dbf4a. The sweep this bead asked for found ONE real defect in 378 comparisons, and the bead's prior was right about the mechanism if not the dtype.

THE DEFECT: fnp.take on a complex64 array raised TypeError where numpy returns a complex64 array. take's residual guard reads 'if !(dtype_kind == "b" || itemsize == 8) { return fallback(); }' and exists precisely to stop narrow dtypes reaching extract_numeric_array, which canonicalises to an f64 Vec. complex64's itemsize is 8 - identical to f64/i64/u64 - so it SATISFIED the guard, reached extract_numeric_array, which does not accept complex, and the error propagated instead of falling back to numpy. complex128 (itemsize 16) was already excluded by the earlier gate, so complex64 alone was affected. Guard now requires 'itemsize == 8 && dtype_kind != "c"'.

WHY IT SURVIVED: the byte-gather fast paths above the residual DO handle complex64, so the residual is only reached when they decline - e.g. for a Python-list index rather than an int64 index array, which is what the sweep happened to pass. Every existing complex take test evidently used an array index.

THE BEAD'S PRIOR, scored honestly: it predicted the f64-canonicalisation guards would have a hole and named narrow ints and float32 as the likely victims. Those were all clean. The hole was in the same guard, from the opposite direction - a WIDE dtype whose itemsize collides with the allowed ones. The mechanism was predicted, the dtype was not.

THE SWEEP: 378 comparisons of result.dtype against numpy over a 14-dtype grid (int8/16/32/64, uint8/16/32/64, float16/32/64, complex64/128, bool) crossed with 14 structural ops that must preserve dtype exactly, 7 elementwise ops following numpy's promotion, and 6 reductions following its accumulator rules. bool and float16 are in the grid deliberately - they are what an f64 canonicalisation mangles most visibly.

PRECONDITIONS: numpy itself must still return int8 from sort(int8) and float16 from abs(float16), and at least 300 comparisons must have run. Without the first two, 'matches numpy' could be satisfied by the very widening the sweep exists to catch; without the third, an empty grid would pass.

RED TO GREEN DEMONSTRATED: the sweep failed naming structural/complex64 take before the guard change and passes after - the same standard met in nh23c and not met in v0mxm or mi3k6.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_return_types = 2 passed / 0 failed, exit 0, oracle numpy 2.4.3, 378 comparisons, against 1 failed / 1 passed before the fix. cargo test -p fnp-python --lib = 557 passed / 0 failed, exit 0. take's neighbouring shards conformance_compress_choose_diagonal and conformance_indices = 27 and 21 passed / 0 failed. cargo clippy -p fnp-python --lib --tests -- -D warnings exit 0. cargo fmt --check -p fnp-python exit 0.

SIBLING PROBE STILL UNRUN in this declared-vs-served class: exception-CLASS parity - does fnp raise numpy's exception TYPE for the same bad input, swept rather than per-shard. This bead is evidence that class is worth continuing: two of the three probes run so far were clean locks, the third found a live bug.

title: bug: conformance_sqrt cannot run under rch - it dlopens libfnp_python.so as a sibling of its own test binary, which only exists in a target/debug/deps layout (15/15 ImportError)
description:
CLOSED, BlackThrush, 2026-09-01, commits 68040d9c and e6b74fae. The mechanism is fixed and
proved; the remaining work is mechanical and is
[[deadlock-audit-propagate-extension-resolver-to-135-suites-9l3c0]].

ROOT CAUSE CONFIRMED, and it is the one the bead named. The suite computed the module path as
a SIBLING of its own test binary. Measured on worker hz4, the two artifacts land under
DIFFERENT build hashes:

    .rch-target/debug/build/fnp-python/0efa4e6151b9ad04/out/conformance_sqrt-0efa4e...
    .rch-target/debug/build/fnp-python/dfbfae95a8d36650/out/libfnp_python.so

The cdylib IS built - it is a COUSIN of the test binary, not a sibling. That is why
`cargo build --lib && cargo test` in one invocation did not help: nothing was missing, the
path was wrong.

THE FIX. `extension_module_path()` in the new crates/fnp-python/tests/support/mod.rs searches
in order: an `FNP_PYTHON_MODULE` override; the sibling (unchanged for the normal
target/debug/deps layout); each ancestor's `libfnp_python.so` and `deps/libfnp_python.so`;
and, when an ancestor is the package's `build/fnp-python` directory, the NEWEST
`<hash>/out/libfnp_python.so` beneath it. It falls back to the bare file name so a genuine
"not built" still reports the original error text.

    cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_sqrt   on hz4, rch --job
    before: 0 passed; 15 failed        after: 15 passed; 0 failed

SEVEN MORE SUITES were converted as evidence the replacement generalises - abs, allclose,
angle, apply_funcs, arctan2, arithmetic, around - and all are green: 159 cases in total that
could not run at all before.

TWO THINGS WORTH CARRYING FORWARD:

1. THE MODULE'S HOME IS A COMPILE-BUDGET DECISION, not a style one. The first commit put the
   resolver in tests/common/mod.rs; `mod common;` compiles an 800-line pyo3 harness into
   every declaring target, and 142 suites need the resolver while none needs the harness.
   With ~2300 test targets already near rch's 1800s ceiling, that would have been a real
   cost. tests/support/mod.rs depends on `std` alone.

2. THE CLASS WAS NEVER ONE SUITE. 168 files carry the idiom; conformance_hypot was run
   UNMODIFIED on the same worker to confirm it fails identically. 43 further files use
   common's in-process `with_fnp_and_numpy` route and were never affected - that route needs
   no .so on disk at all, and remains the better pattern for anything written new.
close_reason: Root cause confirmed (cdylib is a build-hash COUSIN, not a sibling); resolver shipped in tests/support/mod.rs; conformance_sqrt 0/15 -> 15/15 and seven more suites green (159 cases); 135 remaining files tracked in 9l3c0

title: [test][fnp-linalg] svd_mxn has no randomised shape sweep - reconstruction tests are all fixed-shape, and rank-deficient inputs are untested against numpy
close_reason:
COMPLETE, no defect in svd_mxn. svd_mxn_singular_values_match_numpy_across_randomised_shapes drives ten shapes - square, tall, wide, very thin in both orientations (2x7 and 7x2), and two rank-deficient - against numpy's np.linalg.svd(compute_uv=False). Worst relative deviation 9.34e-16, i.e. machine precision.

WHY SINGULAR VALUES RATHER THAN THE FACTORS: unlike U and Vt they are canonical, carrying no sign or column-order freedom, so a mismatch is a real disagreement rather than a different-but-equally-valid factorisation. The test also asserts the contract properties the existing fixed-shape tests cover only at their own sizes: exactly min(m,n) values, non-negative, and descending.

MY OWN TEST WAS WRONG FIRST, and the failure was informative. I generated rank deficiency by duplicating row 0 into row 1 for every deficient case. That does not work for a TALL matrix: rank is bounded by min(m,n), so for 6x3 the other four rows still span all three columns and the matrix stays full rank - the smallest singular value came back 0.774, not zero. The duplicate has to go along the SHORTER dimension: rows when m <= n, columns otherwise. Fixed, and the assertion that the smallest singular value of a genuinely rank-deficient matrix is a true zero now holds - which is the case where a solver that silently regularises would be caught.

EXISTING COVERAGE this complements: cholesky/qr/svd reconstruction tests exist but at fixed shapes only (2x2, and specific n), and reconstruction is self-consistency - it cannot see a shape nobody wrote a test for, nor a rank-deficient input.

VERIFIED: timeout cargo test -p fnp-linalg --lib = 335 passed / 0 failed / 17 ignored in 149.55s; cargo clippy -p fnp-linalg --all-targets -- -D warnings = clean; cargo fmt --check exit 0 run UNPIPED.

title: [perf][fnp-python] f16 einsum single-operand REDUCTION specs ('ij->j' 27.9ms strided, 'ij->i'/'ij->' 7.3ms @2896^2) - scalar half kernels, portable contract, next crackable vein
description: Ranked #3-5 in the 2026-07-12 einsum surface sweep (einsum_surface_rank_hz1.txt). title: [bug][ci] ledger_hygiene G-gate red on main: is_keep() misreads 'no production ship' as a SHIP verdict, enforcing KEEP evidence on a REJECT row
description:
## Symptom

`cargo test -p fnp-conformance --test ledger_hygiene` is RED on main: 16 passed, 2 failed.

    test new_keep_rows_carry_an_executing_elf_sha256 ... FAILED
    test new_keep_rows_declare_one_campaign_result_class ... FAILED

Both name one offender, docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md:36402:

    ## 2026-08-04 - REJECT (measured, no production ship): RandomState Zipf cache
       retry clears median-CI but misses its historical CV predicate

added by 959b0a0d (franken_numpy-ixs5y.404).

## The row is fine. The CLASSIFIER is wrong.

`is_keep()` takes the heading text after the first ` - `, truncates at the first
`:`, and treats the label as a KEEP if it contains the WORD token KEEP, WIN, or
SHIP — where SHIP is suppressed only when the label contains the literal substring
`NO-SHIP` / `NO SHIP` / `NOSHIP`.

The label here is `REJECT (measured, no production ship)`. It negates SHIP with a
word in between, so the substring guard misses it, the SHIP token counts as
positive, and a row whose verdict is literally REJECT is enforced as a KEEP —
demanded to carry an executing-ELF SHA-256 and a campaign result class.

`is_reject()` classifies the SAME heading as a rejection. Two classifiers that must
be mutually exclusive disagree; that disagreement IS the defect.

## Do NOT fix it by making is_keep return false whenever is_reject is true

That is a LOOSENING and it would be wrong. Seven rows are currently classified as
both, and six of them are legitimately dual-verdict and MUST keep their KEEP
obligations:

    4457  MAINTENANCE KEEP / INCUMBENT REJECT: loadtxt(usecols) ...
    5097  CANONICAL RESURRECTION CLOSEOUT (3 KEEP, 2 REJECT/VALID-AB) ...
    5450  SUPERSEDED PROVISIONAL RESURRECTION/HARNESS (4 KEEP, 1 REJECT) ...
    6916  WIN (SHIP, ARCHITECTURAL) + embedded REJECT ...
    12481 SPLIT (SHIP c64 / REJECT c128) ...
    13422 STALE-REJECT REOPENED (WIN) ...
    36402 REJECT (measured, no production ship) ...   <- the only bad one

## Tight fix + its integrity check

Count the SHIP token as positive only when the label carries no negating NO token
(KEEP and WIN tokens are unaffected). Measured over the whole ledger: 1072
headings, is_keep = 771 before, 770 after — EXACTLY ONE row changes
classification, and it is the one whose heading begins with REJECT. All six
dual-verdict rows keep KEEP status through their own KEEP/WIN tokens, so no row
gains an exemption it should not have.

The exempted row remains bound by the REJECT gate
(new_reject_rows_record_a_null_control_or_counted_mechanism), which it already
passes.

Pin the classification with a unit test over both forms so the next
similarly-worded heading cannot silently flip the gate again.
close_reason: Fixed in aed035f2. DEFECT: is_keep() read the label 'REJECT (measured, no production ship)' as a positive SHIP verdict because its negation guard tested only the literal substrings NO-SHIP/NO SHIP/NOSHIP, so a negation with a word in between slipped through and a REJECT row was enforced as a KEEP; is_reject() classified the same heading as a rejection, and that disagreement between two mutually-exclusive classifiers IS the defect. FIX: suppress the SHIP token on any NO token in the label (subsumes the old substring cases, since NO-SHIP tokenizes to NO + SHIP). Deliberately NOT 'is_keep is false whenever is_reject is true' - that is a LOOSENING: 7 headings satisfy both and 6 are genuinely dual-verdict (MAINTENANCE KEEP / INCUMBENT REJECT, SPLIT (SHIP c64 / REJECT c128), WIN (SHIP, ARCHITECTURAL) + embedded REJECT, CANONICAL RESURRECTION CLOSEOUT (3 KEEP, 2 REJECT), SUPERSEDED PROVISIONAL (4 KEEP, 1 REJECT), STALE-REJECT REOPENED (WIN)) and must keep their KEEP obligations, which they do through their own KEEP/WIN tokens. INTEGRITY CHECK as the gate-change protocol requires: 1072 headings, is_keep 771 -> 770, EXACTLY ONE row changes classification (the one beginning with REJECT), it stays bound by the REJECT gate which it already passes, and the change admits ZERO new wins - it removes a false red only. New test is_keep_reads_negated_ship_verdicts_as_rejections pins both directions on real headings. EVIDENCE: rch exec -- cargo test -p fnp-conformance --test ledger_hygiene: new_keep_rows_carry_an_executing_elf_sha256 FAILED -> ok, new test ok, pre-existing keep_classifier_requires_a_positive_verdict_word still ok, 18 passed 1 failed. The remaining failure is a SECOND, unrelated, TRUE red tracked as deadlock-audit-6j4o8 (NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md:64 declares the non-canonical class 'structural-gap'; relabelling it incumbent-win was TRIED and REVERTED because it only moves the failure to the same-invocation contract test - that row splits its incumbent tokens across lines and names the incumbent by spelling rather than as a numpy.* symbol).

title: [harness][ledger] no gate requires a measured row to name the HARNESS that produced it
description:
FLEET DIRECTIVE 2026-08-15: two sanctioned harnesses differed 2x on ONE worker, both with passing A/A nulls. The null is computed inside whichever harness is running, so it cannot see a difference between harnesses any more than it can see a difference between workers - the same blind spot that motivated the worker gate (deadlock-audit-alold), one level up.

This repo ships several harnesses with materially different semantics:
- common::run_median_ci_contract - ONE A/A null (base/base), then the interleaved effect
- common::run_dual_null_median_ci_contract - incumbent A/A AND candidate A/A, plus the 2x-null-margin gate and effect-CI exclusion
- the legacy common::report_median_gate_pair - reached by 48 arms across 8 groups, carrying a DORMANT BIASED_NULL straddle veto, i.e. a different verdict rule entirely

A ratio produced by one is not comparable to a ratio produced by another, and today nothing records which one ran. cce9f932 added the worker gate; the harness half was never enforced.

MEASURED GAP: of the two rows I banked on 2026-08-15, one named its harness only incidentally inside a prose paragraph and the other did not name it at all - and both passed every existing ledger gate.

Acceptance: measured rows dated on/after the enforcement date must carry an explicit machine-checkable 'harness=<name>' field; prose does not count, for the same reason it did not count for the worker. Negative case: a row carrying worker, ELF sha, an A/A null and a ratio, whose only mention of the harness is prose, must FAIL - that is the row a 'looks well-sourced' check waves through. Forward-only enforcement so no historical row is retroactively failed.
