FAILING, all in crates/fnp-python/tests/conformance_unravel_unique.rs, worker ovh-a:
  unique_values_basic
  unique_values_matches_numpy_set_semantics
  unique_values_strings
Three tests, one shard, one chunk exit 101 out of 28 targets reported.

THIRD RED THE SWEEP HAS FOUND, and like the other two it is not in xdyx7's 18, not in any of its five clusters, and untouched by every targeted shard run this session. The first two (deadlock-audit-vmo78, deadlock-audit-nkvau) are both fixed.

NOT DIAGNOSED. Breadth was the job. Start with:
  RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR rch exec -- \
    cargo test -p fnp-python --no-fail-fast --test conformance_unravel_unique -- --nocapture
and read the assertion WITHOUT a grep filter - filter the captured file afterwards, not the stream. I lost a result to filtering-at-capture twice this session.

STRONG PRIOR, worth one minute before anything else: 'unique_values' is numpy's ARRAY-API name (numpy.unique_values, added in 2.0 alongside unique_all / unique_counts / unique_inverse). Two of this session's three reds were upstream-surface drift of exactly this kind - vmo78 was numpy renaming trapz to trapezoid, and hp9u2 was numpy REMOVING corrcoef's bias/ddof. So check FIRST whether the installed numpy has unique_values at all and what it returns, before assuming the defect is in our implementation. The 'strings' variant failing alongside the basic one also hints at a dtype-coverage gap rather than a rename.

THERE IS A SECONDS-LONG LOCAL REPRODUCER available - see the recipe on deadlock-audit-nkvau: import the cdylib at target/release-perf/deps/libfnp_python.so directly and call fnp.unique_values(...). That turns each iteration from a 6-minute rch round trip into seconds and it is what finally cracked nkvau.

ALSO RULE OUT: which side moved (an fnp-vs-numpy assert proves they differ, not who is wrong), and the worker's numpy version - the fleet spans versions and ovh-a's moved during this session, so keqog's table is stale.

PROBE TO CLOSE: 'cargo test -p fnp-python --no-fail-fast --test conformance_unravel_unique' reports 0 failed, citing worker and numpy version.
close_reason:
FIXED in commit 2574548a. fnp.unique_values SORTED; numpy does not.

np.unique_values([3,1,2,1,3]) is [2,1,3] on numpy 2.4.3, fnp returned [1,2,3]. The shared array-API route returns the sorted set - numpy.unique's contract, not this function's - so fnp diverged on any input whose sorted order differs from numpy's. All three failing tests were that one cause.

WHY DELEGATION RATHER THAN A NATIVE ORDER FIX: the array API leaves unique_values' result order UNSPECIFIED, so reproducing it natively encodes a behaviour upstream has explicitly reserved the right to change. Same doctrine as hp9u2 (corrcoef's removed bias/ddof) and vmo78 (the trapz->trapezoid rename): where the contract says 'unspecified', the installed numpy IS the contract. Delegating is also correct across numpy versions for free.

THE STRINGS CASE PASSING BEFORE WAS COINCIDENCE, not partial correctness - ['a','b'] is both the sorted order and the order numpy produced for that input. Discriminating inputs are the ones where those differ; [3,1,2,1,3] is one, ['b','a','b'] is not.

STATED AND NOT VERIFIED, recorded at the code as well: unique_all, unique_counts and unique_inverse share the same array-API order guarantee AND the same native route. Their tests pass today, but that may only mean their inputs do not discriminate. Someone should check them with a discriminating input rather than assume.

EVIDENCE: conformance_unravel_unique 67 passed / 0 failed on ovh-a, up from 64 passed / 3 failed. clippy -p fnp-python --all-targets --no-deps -D warnings exit 0 on hz2 with 'Checking fnp-python' and no warning lines; fmt --check exit 0.

FOLLOW-UP for vsiir: chunk 5 should be re-run to confirm the whole chunk is green, alongside the outstanding chunk 3 and 4 re-runs.

comments.author: CoralOak
comments.text:
CRUX FOUND IN ONE PROBE, using the local reproducer. fnp SORTS, numpy DOES NOT.

  numpy 2.4.3, has unique_values: True
  ints     np.unique_values([3,1,2,1,3]) = [2, 1, 3]      fnp = [1, 2, 3]
  strings  np.unique_values(['b','a','b']) = ['a','b']     fnp = ['a','b']

So the upstream-drift prior was half right: numpy HAS unique_values, but its ORDER IS NOT SORTED.
numpy's array-API unique_values returns values in an unspecified order (the spec explicitly does not
guarantee sorting, and numpy 2.4.3 demonstrably returns [2,1,3] for that input). fnp returns the
sorted set, which is what numpy.unique does - and unique_values is NOT numpy.unique with the extras
stripped, which is almost certainly the assumption baked into our implementation.

The strings case matching is a coincidence of that input, not evidence: ['a','b'] happens to be both
the sorted order and the order numpy produced. Do not read it as 'strings are fine'.

WHAT I THINK THE FIX IS, stated as a recommendation because it is a contract decision and I did not
implement it: DELEGATE unique_values to numpy. Its order is explicitly unspecified by the array API
and is therefore free to differ by numpy version and by input - reproducing it natively means
encoding a behaviour upstream has reserved the right to change, which is exactly the trap
deadlock-audit-hp9u2 established the doctrine for. The installed numpy is the contract; where the
contract is 'unspecified', the only stable implementation is to ask numpy. Check whether
unique_all / unique_counts / unique_inverse have the same problem - they share the array-API order
guarantee and are likely implemented the same way.

IF SOMEONE PREFERS A NATIVE PATH, the honest alternative is to keep it ONLY where our order provably
matches the installed numpy's, and defer otherwise - but note that makes correctness depend on a
numpy internal, which is why I recommend delegation instead.

VERIFY WITH, seconds per iteration (recipe on deadlock-audit-nkvau): import the cdylib at
target/release-perf/deps/libfnp_python.so and compare fnp.unique_values against np.unique_values on
several inputs INCLUDING ones where sorted order and numpy's order differ - [3,1,2,1,3] is such a
case and [\'b\',\'a\',\'b\'] is not, so pick discriminating inputs.

STATE: bead returned to ready, no code touched. The three failing tests are one cause.

comments.author: CoralOak
comments.text:
CAVEAT RETIRED WITH EVIDENCE: the three siblings are NOT affected, and the asymmetry is real rather than an accident of my test inputs.

My closure said unique_all / unique_counts / unique_inverse share the same array-API order guarantee and the same native route, so they might have the same bug and their passing tests might just mean their inputs do not discriminate. Checked on numpy 2.4.3 with the discriminating input [3,1,2,1,3]:

  np.unique_values(a)          [2, 1, 3]   <-- UNSORTED, the bug this bead fixed
  np.unique_all(a).values      [1, 2, 3]   sorted
  np.unique_counts(a).values   [1, 2, 3]   sorted
  np.unique_inverse(a).values  [1, 2, 3]   sorted
  np.unique(a)                 [1, 2, 3]   sorted

So ONLY unique_values is unsorted. The three siblings match classic np.unique, which is exactly what
fnp's shared native route already returns - they are correct as they stand and must NOT be
'fixed' to match unique_values. Anyone who reads my earlier caveat and delegates all four would
be introducing a bug, not removing one.

WHY THE ASYMMETRY IS PLAUSIBLE, offered as explanation not as verified mechanism: unique_all,
unique_counts and unique_inverse all have to compute indices, inverse or counts, which numpy derives
from a sort it has to do anyway; unique_values needs none of that machinery and is free to skip the
sort. The array API permits it in every case - only unique_values actually exercises the permission.

That leaves the delegation in commit 2574548a correctly scoped to exactly one function. No further
work; this comment exists so the caveat is closed rather than left hanging.

title: tests: 135 conformance suites still cannot run under rch - one identical block replacement each, the resolver they need is already shipped
description:
CLOSED, BlackThrush, 2026-09-01. `grep -l current_exe crates/fnp-python/tests/*.rs` IS EMPTY.
143 of 143 suites resolve the extension through `tests/support`, and none computes the path
itself. Commits 7902a5c2, 78258fa5, 68837f03, 9df649f8, 94d688a3.

WHAT IT RECOVERED. Every one of these suites was 100% ImportError under rch - the only
sanctioned build route here - so their clauses were not running at all. Measured green on
worker hz4 in batches as they were converted: roughly 1450 cases across the tranches that were
run whole, plus one suite per shape at the end.

IT WAS NOT ONE SUBSTITUTION. Four shapes, and the count matters for anyone planning similar
work:
   116  plain swap: `mod support; use support::fnp_script;`
    14  same block under a PER-FILE NAME (fnp_sum_script, fnp_argmax_script, ...) - the name
        and its call sites stay, only the body delegates
     9  needed extra preamble (`numpy.ma`, `io`, `BytesIO`/`StringIO`) or
        `sys.modules[spec.name] = fnp` BEFORE exec_module, which is the behaviour the
        re-export suites assert on -> `support::fnp_script_with(imports, register, body)`
     1  conformance_dtype_sniff_fallback keeps its OWN script and shares only
        `extension_module_path()`, because its prologue defines a `check()` helper and its
        epilogue prints the accumulated mismatches

TWO REAL DEFECTS FELL OUT, which is the argument for having done it rather than filed it:

  1. `fnp.cross` computed a 2-VECTOR cross product that numpy 2.5.2 REFUSES (2.4.3 returns the
     scalar z component; 2.5.2 raises ValueError). It now delegates when either operand's last
     axis is 2, so it tracks whichever numpy is installed. Fixed in 78258fa5. The case exists
     TWICE - conformance_cross and conformance_linalg_basic - and both copies had to learn the
     same lesson, which is what a duplicated test case costs.
  2. My own blanket substitution broke conformance_dtype_sniff_fallback (`NameError: check is
     not defined`) and the run caught it. THE SHAPE CHECK I RAN UP FRONT ASKED WHETHER EVERY
     FILE CALLS `fnp_script`; it did not ask whether the script each one BUILDS is the same
     script. A conversion that is identical in 135 files still needs the last few read
     individually.

METHOD NOTE ON THE FLEET: `cargo test -p fnp-python --tests` (all ~2300 targets) is not a
usable verification here - it exceeds rch's 1800s ceiling and, during this session, admission
refused it outright while reporting 18/56 slots free. Verify in tranches of 10-40 named
targets, with `--no-fail-fast` so one failure cannot hide the rest, and drop to `-j2` with a
single target when admission is tight.

FINAL GATES on the committed tree (worker hz4, rch, RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1):
  cargo clippy -p fnp-python --all-targets   0 warnings, 0 errors  (this is the gate that
      matters after touching 143 test files - G1 treats every clippy warning as an error, and
      an unused `use support::fnp_script;` in any one of them would have tripped it)
  cargo fmt -p fnp-python --check            exit 0, no output
  one suite per shape, both rounds:          8 ok / 175 cases, then 9 ok / 95 cases, 0 failed
close_reason: 143 of 143 suites converted; grep -l current_exe tests/*.rs is empty. Four shapes, not one substitution. Found and fixed fnp.cross computing a 2-vector cross numpy 2.5.2 refuses, and caught my own blanket substitution breaking dtype_sniff_fallback. clippy --all-targets clean

title: [perf][fnp-python] the native f64 divide is WORST just above its own gate - 1.286x at 2^16 vs 1.091x at 2^20, so F64_DIV_NATIVE_MIN_LEN may be admitting a losing band
description:
MEASURED, banked in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md 2026-08-16 (RedLynx), from committed-provenance ELF 6766850940f767eb on thinkstation1, three sizes in one binary, all DECIDABLE_REGRESSION, all six A/A nulls on unity:

  n        path        fnp/numpy   numpy_ns   fnp_ns    excess_ns   excess as % of numpy
  2^8      DELEGATES   3.185x           430      1368         938   218%
  2^16     NATIVE      1.286x         19136     24577        5441    28.4%
  2^20     NATIVE      1.091x        449042    473283       24241     5.4%

THE FINDING: the native f64 divide path is at its WORST immediately above its own gate. deadlock-audit-qapyb set F64_DIV_NATIVE_MIN_LEN = 1 << 14 so 2^8 and 2^12 delegate while 2^16 and 2^20 go native. At 2^20 that pays (5.4% overhead). At 2^16 it costs 28.4% - more than five times worse proportionally.

THE HYPOTHESIS TO TEST: that the gate at 2^14 admits a band where DELEGATING would be cheaper than our native path. If the wrapper cost at 2^16 were near the 938 ns measured at 2^8, delegating at 2^16 would cost ~20074 ns = ~1.049x, substantially better than the 1.286x the native path delivers.

WHY THAT ARITHMETIC IS NOT VALID YET, and this is the point of the bead: the wrapper cost is NOT constant in n. `multiply` delegates at every size here and its excess grew from 836 ns at n=256 to 5190 ns at n=2^20 - a factor of 6.2. So the 938 ns figure CANNOT be carried to 2^16. Subtracting it there would repeat exactly the cross-size subtraction error that overstated deadlock-audit-6twge by 5.5x.

WHAT TO MEASURE, in order:
  1. `multiply` at n=2^16, in the SAME invocation as divide at 2^16. multiply always delegates at these sizes, so its excess IS the delegating control the gate decision needs. The cell does not exist today: bench_percall_floor_across_ops_vs_numpy hardcodes `let n = 1usize << 8`. Parameterise it, or add a sibling group over {2^14, 2^16, 2^18, 2^20}.
  2. Add 2^14 and 2^18 divide cells to LOCATE the worst band rather than inferring it from three points. bench_divide_size_gate_vs_numpy currently runs only {2^8, 2^16} - its own comment explains a four-cell sweep did not fit rch's 1800s SSH ceiling, but the cells are cheap when the ELF already exists and is run locally.
  3. Only then re-decide F64_DIV_NATIVE_MIN_LEN. qapyb's existing REJECT of a gate move was measured on other sizes and does NOT cover this question - read its retry predicate before re-attacking.

MECHANISM LEAD, not a claim: at 2^16 the operands are 512 KB and cache-resident, so NumPy's serial loop is fast while our costs are dispatch-shaped - a rayon fan-out over 64 threads leaves ~1024 elements per thread, where scheduling can plausibly cost more than the arithmetic. At 2^20 the arrays are 8 MB, both sides are DRAM-bound, and the fan-out amortises. That predicts a loss worst in a band just above the gate, shrinking either side - consistent with all three cells and directly testable by step 2.

DECISION RULE, written before the measurement: if delegating at the worst band beats the native path by more than the controlling null half-width, raise the gate to the crossover. If it does not, the gate is right and the lever is the native kernel's fan-out threshold instead - which is a different bead.

CONSTRAINT: df -h /data before building; the ELF for steps 2-3 may already exist, so check before compiling anything.
close_reason: Resolved by 4108c11c raising F64_DIV_NATIVE_MIN_LEN to 1<<21 citing this bead; confirmed independently today: entire swept band now delegates at ~0.99x parity (thinkstation1, provenance-recorded local build), no losing band remains below the gate.

comments.author: RedLynx
comments.text:
CONTROL LANDED, UNBUILT (4c7dd41c): bench_percall_floor_across_sizes_vs_numpy, registered.

Measures BOTH multiply and divide at {2^12, 2^14, 2^16, 2^18, 2^20} in ONE invocation. multiply delegates at every one of them, so its excess IS the wrapper cost at that size; divide goes native above the gate. Every subtraction is therefore WITHIN a size and WITHIN an invocation - which is exactly what the three banked rows could not do, and why I refused to carry the 938 ns n=256 wrapper up to 2^16 in the ledger.

Each cell also emits the counterfactual the gate actually turns on: projected_delegating_fnp_ns = numpy's own divide + the same wrapper multiply pays, and projected_delegating_ratio against the measured native ratio, with delegating_looks_better as a LEAD (a point comparison; both sides carry CIs).

THE METHOD CARRIES ITS OWN NULL, which is the part to check first: at 2^12, below the gate, BOTH ops delegate and pay the same wrapper, so divide_specific_excess_ns must come out near zero. The cell is emitted with is_method_null_cell=true. If it is not near zero the subtraction is contaminated and NO row from this group may be believed - do not report the 2^16 result before checking the 2^12 one.

Steps 2 and 3 of this bead's plan are now covered by step 1's group (four cells above the gate locate the worst band). Step 3, re-deciding F64_DIV_NATIVE_MIN_LEN, still needs the decision rule in the description: raise the gate only if delegating beats native by more than the controlling null half-width. AGENT_NAME=RedLynx.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CONFLICT AT 2^20 - do not drop the native divide path on 3470db0f's evidence yet.

I re-ran bench_percall_floor_across_sizes_vs_numpy on the SAME HOST (thinkstation1) with elf 4e95267adbfb1289, committed HEAD, local build under the exported cargo-shim bypass. Two invocations, all ten A/A nulls straddling unity.

                        3470db0f (elf d285003d)   my run (elf 4e95267a)
  2^20 multiply_ratio          0.992288                0.990259     AGREE (0.2%)
  2^20 divide_ratio            0.890373                1.106503 / 1.099069   OPPOSITE
  2^20 wrapper_ns                  3096                   10084
  2^20 divide_specific_excess    +65294                  -52193
  2^20 delegating_looks_better     true                    false
My 2^20 is DECIDABLE_WIN, effect_ci95=[1.060956,1.121751], replicated across two invocations.

THE SOURCE IS IDENTICAL. All 33 crate commits today touch crates/fnp-python/benches/; NONE touches src/. So no peer landed a divide change between the two builds - this is not a code difference.

WHAT THAT LEAVES: multiply DELEGATES and is insensitive to our codegen, and it agrees to within 0.2%. divide runs NATIVE and is sensitive to our codegen, and it diverges 24%. That pattern points at the BUILD. deadlock-audit-ae85t already recorded this hazard by name: local and remote toolchains here emit different code for identical source (local 2211 instructions vs remote 2207). I can say mine was built locally with the repo's +avx2 config; I cannot establish how d285003d was built, and that is precisely the provenance field neither row records.

SECOND REASON TO DISTRUST EITHER 2^20 CELL: wrapper_ns at 2^20 is multiply_fnp - multiply_numpy, a difference of two ~380000 ns quantities. It reads 3096 in one run and 10084 in the other - a 3.3x swing from inputs agreeing to 0.2%. divide_specific_excess subtracts that noisy term again. The derived columns at 2^20 are cancellation noise regardless of what the raw ratios do. The group's design is sound at small n where the wrapper is a large fraction of the call.

WHAT SURVIVES: at 2^14/2^16/2^18 both runs agree delegating is cheaper, effects are 2947/4037/7164 ns against a method null of 114-135 ns, nulls clean. RAISING F64_DIV_NATIVE_MIN_LEN above 2^14 is justified TODAY. DROPPING the native path outright is not - that conclusion rests on the 2^20 cell, which reverses.

RETRY PREDICATE: settle 2^20 by building both halves in the SAME environment with the build method recorded as a provenance field. Use raw divide_ratio with its CI, not the derived columns.

comments.author: AzureCarp
comments.text:
PREMISE UPDATE, not a re-decision - AzureCarp. Not touching this bead's status; it is IN_PROGRESS and
a peer's. Flagging that its n=2^8 figure is stale by a factor of two.

  this bead (ELF 6766850940f767eb, 2026-08-16)
    n=2^8 DELEGATES  3.185x   numpy_ns 430  fnp_ns 1368  excess 938 ns
  measured today (ELF 8be4764d, 5 runs, one window, all nulls straddling unity)
    n=2^8 DELEGATES  1.5578x  numpy_ns 461  fnp_ns  691  excess 245 ns

  incumbent 430 -> 461 (+7.2%); our arm 1368 -> 691 (-49.5%); excess 938 -> 245 (-73.9%)

The incumbent moved 7% while our arm halved - window noise does not do that, so the comparison
survives being cross-ELF. The cause is every wrapper lever that landed on this route since that row
was taken: axis-default removal, kwargs-dict removal, getattr interning, the vectorcalls, the
probe-to-decline cuts, by several agents.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE. This bead's finding rests on the contrast between below-gate and just-above:
  THEN  below gate 3.185x   vs  just above (2^16 native) 1.286x
  NOW   below gate 1.5578x  vs  just above (2^16 native) 1.286x
That contrast has collapsed from 2.5x to 0.27x. The native band did not improve - nothing landed on
the divide kernel - the DELEGATING side did, by three quarters of its excess. So the question this
bead asks, whether F64_DIV_NATIVE_MIN_LEN admits a losing band, now has to be asked against 1.5578x
rather than 3.185x, and the answer may differ.

WHAT I DID NOT DO: I did not re-measure 2^16 or 2^20 - my runs covered n=256 only. I am NOT assuming
the native band held merely because no kernel lever landed; that is an inference, and stale-cell
inferences are exactly what this note is about. Whoever resumes should re-take those two on a current
ELF before deciding the gate.

Banked in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md.

comments.text:

[0.988425,0.998814], divide_ratio=0.992352 [0.987950,0.997290] - delegation is

title: [bug][linalg] linalg_error_surface_probe fails again on NumPy 2.4.6: matrix_rank ours=OK theirs raises (pdrxy fix does not hold)
description:
Found 2026-08-05 by SilentBadger while running the full fnp-python lib suite on vmi1153651 (AVX2, python 3.13, NumPy 2.4.6). 'cargo test -p fnp-python --lib' = 555 passed, 1 FAILED:

  thread 'tests::linalg_error_surface_probe' panicked at crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs:117692
  LinAlgError divergences detected:
    matrix_rank: ours=OK, theirs raises

PROVEN PRE-EXISTING, not caused by the transcendental-probe work landing alongside it: I reverted crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs to HEAD on that same host (git show HEAD:... piped over) and re-ran the single test - identical failure. So it reproduces on unmodified main.

WHY THIS IS A REOPEN, NOT A NEW BUG: this is the exact symptom of deadlock-audit-linalg-matrix-rank-error-surface-pdrxy, closed 2026-08-04 in f808ea3c (which IS an ancestor of HEAD - verified with git merge-base --is-ancestor). That bead's closing evidence was taken on a LOCAL build against NumPy 2.4.3. This host runs 2.4.6 and the fix does not hold there.

THE CONFUSING PART, which the next agent should start from rather than rediscover: the probe's input is np.zeros((0,3)) and the test comment expects NumPy to raise 'zero-size array to reduction operation maximum'. But a standalone probe of the SAME interpreter on that host shows NumPy 2.4.6 does NOT raise for any zero-size shape - np.linalg.matrix_rank returns 0 for (0,3), (3,0), (0,0), (0,), [0 0] for (2,0,0) and [] for (0,3,3). Yet inside the test process NumPy raised. Same host, same numpy. Resolve that contradiction FIRST - it means either the test process resolves a different numpy than the system python3, or matrix_rank is being called with arguments the standalone probe did not reproduce (tol/rtol/hermitian), or the failing arm is not the input the comment claims. Do not adjust the expectation until you know which.

RELEVANT PRIOR CONTEXT: upstream is mid-change here. The vendored oracle in legacy_numpy_code/numpy is 2.5.0.dev0 and returns 0 for matrix_rank(zeros((0,3))) because upstream main added initial=0 to the reduction, while older releases raise. pdrxy's own close note recorded the raise reproducing identically on 1.26.4 and 2.4.3 and concluded it was version-INDEPENDENT; the 2.4.6 result above refutes that conclusion. Whatever the fix is, it must be validated on at least 2.4.3 AND 2.4.6, because the fleet runs 2.2.4, 2.3.5, 2.4.2 and 2.4.6 simultaneously.

ACCEPTANCE: 'cargo test -p fnp-python --lib -- linalg_error_surface_probe' green on a 2.4.6 host AND on a 2.4.3 host, with the numpy version printed by the test so a pass cannot be silently version-specific.
close_reason: FIXED in 8d746c56. ROOT CAUSE WAS THE TEST, NOT matrix_rank. linalg_error_surface_probe matched on (ours, theirs) with the arm '(Ok(_), _) => ours=OK, theirs raises' - a WILDCARD that also matches (Ok, Ok). So it reported a divergence whenever BOTH sides returned a value, which means it could only pass while NumPy kept raising, and it broke the moment NumPy stopped. The solve(singular) probe below it had the identical defect. Fixed by splitting (Ok, Ok) = agreement from (Ok, Err) = real divergence, and the messages now carry the exception TYPE and TEXT (diagnosing 'theirs raises' cost a whole round trip). title: [perf][fnp-python] gate the native f64 binary route by size: below the crossover it costs MORE than delegating
description:
deadlock-audit-cydda measured, worker=vmi1153651 harness=common::run_dual_null_median_ci_contract elf 8203f255de2174ac n=256: fnp.divide takes the native zerocopy route and costs 13540 ns against numpy's 1092 (excess 12448), while fnp.add/subtract/multiply - which simply DELEGATE to numpy - cost 9197/9302/7930 (excess 8290/8375/6968). Taking our own fast path is about 4 us DEARER than not taking it.

Mechanism: zerocopy_f64_binary_flat has no lower size gate. At 256 elements it acquires two PyBuffers, allocates a numpy.empty output and runs its dispatch to save essentially no compute, because at that size there is almost nothing to compute.

LEVER: decline the native route below a size threshold so small calls delegate to numpy. Safe by construction - delegating IS the incumbent behaviour, so the values are numpy's own and the FE-hazard deferral question does not even arise at those sizes.

SCOPED TO Div DELIBERATELY: the same wrapper cost applies to the other binop ops in that set (remainder, power, maximum, minimum), but those are compute-heavy ops numpy runs single-threaded, so their crossover is likely at a much smaller n and a blanket gate could regress them. Gate only where there is evidence.

The gate must be applied EARLY - before PyBuffer::get on both operands - or it saves nothing, since buffer acquisition is part of what makes the route expensive.

Acceptance: fnp.divide vs numpy.divide measured in ONE invocation across sizes spanning the threshold, naming WORKER and HARNESS, showing the small-n ratio improve and the large-n ratio unchanged. A threshold that improves small n while regressing large n is a REJECT and gets banked as one.
close_reason: Gate SHIPPED in 2efdb79d and its post-state MEASURED AND REPLICATED, banked in 16aec68e. worker=vmi1152480, harness=common::run_dual_null_median_ci_contract, numpy 2.4.3, two runs on that one worker, elfs 7a736c42be5ede45 and 3c378f3dc9eb77bc, all four cells DECIDABLE_REGRESSION with every null on unity: n=256 (below gate, delegates) 0.144221 ci95=[0.143547,0.145417] and 0.148403 ci95=[0.147312,0.150175]; n=65536 (above gate, native) 0.577185 ci95=[0.574512,0.581702] and 0.621716 ci95=[0.614808,0.626028]. Correctness green before landing (conformance_diagnostics 1 passed; its size-1 divide warning rows now delegate and still match NumPy exactly) and the gate's negative test executed green, pinning >= not > at the threshold, remainder/power/maximum/minimum untouched at any size, and no decline when the operand has no size attribute. CLOSED WITH ONE ACCEPTANCE LINE EXPLICITLY UNMET: the acceptance asked to SHOW the small-n ratio improve, and I cannot license that - the pre-gate 0.081557 came from a different worker (vmi1153651) and a different 307MB bench-profile binary, while these are a 49MB release test-mode binary on vmi1152480, so the comparison the acceptance wants is exactly the cross-worker cross-binary one this ledger forbids. The gate is justified by the same-invocation cross-op mechanism in deadlock-audit-cydda, not by a delta. Carrying that forward: licensing it needs pre- and post-gate code in ONE binary on ONE worker, e.g. an env-selected threshold read once at init.

title: [perf][reduction] Parallel exact flat argmin/argmax for float64
description: NumPy runs argmin/argmax single-threaded (measured cpu/wall=1.00x, ~29ms each at 64M f64); fnp delegates both. Sibling of the shipped min/max value routes (deadlock-audit-1aklb, 2.34-3.58x) but the tie convention is OPPOSITE and must NOT reuse that combine: arg* return the FIRST index on ties and the FIRST NaN's index, where the value routes keep a later element. Verified against live NumPy: argmin([3,1,1,5,5])=1, argmax=3; argmin([1,-0.0,0.0])=1 (the -0.0 at index 1 ties with 0.0, first wins); argmin([1,nan,0.5,nan])=1 and argmax=1 (first NaN index, NOT the extremum). Parallel combine must take the lower index on ties, and a NaN anywhere forces the first-NaN index rather than deferring. Empty raises ValueError. Expect the same SIMD treatment that took min/max from ~53 to ~116 GB/s, but index tracking makes the lane reduction harder than a plain simd_min.
close_reason: Shipped parallel exact vectorized flat float64 argmin/argmax: 2.849702x argmax and 2.498365x argmin at 64M, all DECIDABLE_WIN under same-invocation corrected dual-null on vmi1156319; 4M argmin UNDECIDED and not claimed. NO deferral regimes: ties take the FIRST index (opposite of the min/max value routes), signed zeros carry no ambiguity since the answer is an index, and NaN deterministically returns the first NaN index. 11/11 conformance first run. Recorded a FAILED prediction: arg* expected materially slower than min/max due to index bookkeeping, measured essentially equal - the scan is memory-bound not issue-bound.

title: perf: sum/mean f64 2^20 is NOT a decidable loss - 4 measurements span 1.094-1.456x, all VOID; and bit-exactness bars the obvious lever
description:
CORRECTION, same day, after three more runs. THE "SIGNS REPLICATE" CLAIM ABOVE IS WITHDRAWN.
Five runs of this cell on the same worker with the same ELF read:

    sum   21/21 SLOWER | 19/21 SLOWER | 20/21 SLOWER | 5/21 (p=.027, leaning FASTER) | 12/21 nd
    mean  17/21 SLOWER | 19/21 SLOWER | 17/21 SLOWER | 1/21 DECIDED FASTER            | 12/21 nd
    std    0/21 FASTER |  0/21 FASTER |  0/21 FASTER | 0/21 FASTER                    | 0/21 FASTER

Every A/A control was clean in every run, INCLUDING the one whose verdict reversed. A sign test
controls WITHIN-run drift exactly as the A/A null does and is exactly as blind to run-to-run
structure; two runs agreeing was not replication, it was two draws from a spread I had not
measured. THE BEAD'S ORIGINAL CONCLUSION STANDS: sum/mean f64 2^20 is not a decidable cell.
What IS decidable is `std` (FASTER, 5 of 5) and the size ladder above ~1.25M elements (FASTER,
3 of 3). Details and the corrected instrument in commit 7f56a4d8 and in
[[deadlock-audit-order-preserving-sum-lever-9qqqv]].

CLOSED WITH THE MEASUREMENT IT ASKED FOR, BlackThrush, 2026-09-01, commit 98e027f9.
Successor: [[deadlock-audit-order-preserving-sum-lever-9qqqv]].

THE BEAD'S CONCLUSION WAS HALF RIGHT, and the half that was wrong is the useful part. The cell
is NOT decidable by RATIO - four measurements spanning 1.094x-1.456x, every one VOID, and this
session added two more (1.447x, 1.467x for sum; 1.157x, 1.030x for mean; three of the four
VOID). It IS decidable by SIGN.

A SIGN TEST OVER 21 INTERLEAVED ROUNDS, which is the alternative the bead's own acceptance
named. Each round times both arms ADJACENTLY, alternating which runs first, and keeps only
which was faster: a drift that moves both arms together cancels instead of adding noise, and
the statistic is exact - under "no difference" the wins are Binomial(21, 1/2), so 17 of 21 is
p<0.01. Every row carries its own numpy-vs-numpy A/A control and a row whose control is also
decisive would be discarded.

TWO RUNS, worker hz4 (rch --job, numpy 2.5.2, 64 cores), different seeds and invocations:

    sum f64 2^20     21/21 p<1e-5     19/21 p=0.00022     controls 11/21, 9/21   clean
    mean f64 2^20    17/21 p=0.0072   19/21 p=0.00022     controls 14/21, 12/21  clean
    std f64 2^20      0/21 p<1e-5      0/21 p<1e-5        controls  9/21, 9/21   clean

    fnp.sum SLOWER. fnp.mean SLOWER. fnp.std FASTER (~2.9x). All three signs replicate.

MAGNITUDE IS STILL NOT DECIDABLE: +22.5% then +56.8% for sum, +21.3% then +44.1% for mean, on
the SAME worker. That is [[single-run-dual-null-cannot-decide-sub-5pct]] from the other side -
signs replicate where magnitudes do not - and it is why the successor bead says to quote the
direction and a floor, never a ratio.

WHAT THE BEAD ESTABLISHED AND THIS RUN RE-CONFIRMED, both still true:
  - THE ROUTE IS NATIVE. The engagement spy reads 0 numpy.sum and 0 numpy.add calls.
  - WE ARE BIT-EXACT. 0 of 8 cells differ, so numpy's PAIRWISE tree is reproduced exactly and
    every reordering lever - parallel, re-blocked, wider - is BARRED, not merely risky.
  - THE HEADROOM IS SMALL. One full pass over 8 MiB is ~859 us here; numpy.sum is ~227 us,
    already 0.26 of a copy. Our excess is ~50-130 us on a ~227 us call.

THE TRANSFERABLE POINT: "the A/A null passed and the cell still swings 33%" does not mean the
cell is undecidable. It means the RATIO is undecidable. When the question is "which is faster"
rather than "by how much", a paired sign test answers it with an exact p from the same
harness, and it answered a cell six ratio measurements could not.
close_reason: DECIDED by sign test, replicated on hz4: fnp.sum and fnp.mean are slower (21/21 and 19/21; 17/21 and 19/21), fnp.std faster, all A/A controls clean. Magnitude remains undecidable. Lever bead 9qqqv opened with the bit-exactness constraint

comments.author: BlackThrush
comments.text:
INCUMBENT-SPREAD CRITERION IMPLEMENTED AND APPLIED - THIS BEAD IS ANSWERED TWICE OVER (BlackThrush, 2026-08-31). Commit 9a71376a, pushed main+master. Do not close.

The fleet-wide ledger-293 lesson (sweeps must interleave arms AND the effect must exceed the
incumbent's within-run spread) is now enforced by h2h_survey rather than left to the reader.

WHAT WAS MISSING: a dual A/A null says the two arms did not DRIFT apart. It says NOTHING about how
much the incumbent bounces within the same run, and a ratio is only meaningful if the effect
exceeds that bounce. The survey now records numpy's own per-round samples - from the effect
measurement AND from both of its A/A arms - takes the largest min-to-max spread of the three, and
marks a cell actionable only if the nulls are clean AND |ratio - 1| exceeds that spread.

worker=hz4 (64 cores, loadavg 23.6), numpy 2.5.2 live in the same invocation,
in-process ELF cfdaedbcb145b08e076a8aade4aea6535fbee6a4e6f42d0a708fd783c97741d4.

THE BOARD COLLAPSES FROM 18 "DECIDABLE" TO 8 ACTIONABLE:

     1.017x  argmin f64 2^20        incumbent_spread  0.8%
     0.628x  count_nonzero 2^20     incumbent_spread  2.0%   win
     0.515x  std f64 2^20           incumbent_spread 34.9%   win
     0.362x  concatenate f64 2^20   incumbent_spread 14.5%   win
     0.330x  cumsum f64 2^20        incumbent_spread  2.3%   win
     0.283x  cumprod f64 2^16       incumbent_spread  1.1%   win
     0.161x  searchsorted 2^16      incumbent_spread  0.7%   win
     0.074x  unique i64 2^16        incumbent_spread  0.5%   win

SEVEN OF THE EIGHT ARE WINS. The only non-win is argmin at 1.017x - a 1.7% effect over a 0.8%
spread - and 1.7% is not a campaign. THERE IS NO ACTIONABLE LOSS LEFT ON THIS SURFACE.

*** IT CONFIRMS THIS BEAD'S OWN CLOSURE BY A COMPLETELY DIFFERENT ROUTE. *** This bead closed
mean f64 2^20 as not decidable after FOUR dedicated measurements spanning 1.094-1.456x. The
criterion reaches the same conclusion in ONE run and explains it: the incumbent's own arm varied
198.8% within that run. The cell that headed this campaign's loss map was measuring the host. Slow
route and fast route agree, which is the check that matters.

NINE FURTHER CELLS THE OLD BOARD RANKED ARE NOW WITHDRAWN as NOISE>EFFECT:
  sqrt 1.229x against a 30.8% spread; dot 0.721x against 102.6%; sort 0.992x against 35.1%;
  isnan 0.988x against 31.0%; repeat 1.009x against 15.3%; where 1.036x against 4.2%; and others.
EVERY ONE of those would have been a plausible lane to open, and each would have been an effect
smaller than the noise it was measured in. That is the concrete cost this criterion prevents.

KNOWN CONSERVATISM, STATED PLAINLY: the criterion uses full min-to-max spread, not a CI, so it is
strict by construction and excludes cells that are probably real wins - take f64 2^20 at 0.111x and
clip at 0.889x are almost certainly genuine (both banked elsewhere) but fail here on a busy host.
IT ERRS TOWARD INACTION, which is the safe direction for a board whose only job is choosing what to
work on next. A cell excluded here is NOT disproved; it is unranked.

RETRY PREDICATE: do not open a lever on any cell marked NOISE>EFFECT or VOID without re-measuring
it on a quiet host first - that is the entire point of the new column. argmin at 1.017x is the only
actionable non-win and is too small to be worth a fleet slot. The next real perf work needs a WIDER
board - f32, complex, 2-D axis reductions, strided inputs, small-n entry costs - not another pass
over these 24 cells.

title: [bug][parity] Generator.integers rejects int8/int16/uint8/uint16 (numpy supports); needs buffered narrow-width Lemire sampler in fnp-random
description:
Generator.integers(dtype=int8/int16/uint8/uint16) raises 'Unsupported dtype dtype(...) for integers' (validate_random_integer_dtype_bounds in fnp-python lib.rs only handles I32/I64/U32/U64). numpy's Generator.integers supports all of these.

CANNOT be fixed by generating i64 and casting: numpy's narrow-width integers use a DIFFERENT, width-specific bounded-integer stream. Verified empirically: numpy int8 != numpy int64-cast-to-int8 (same seed). fnp.integers IS bit-exact vs numpy for int32/int64/uint32 (fnp-random has bounded_lemire_uint32/uint64 at lib.rs ~3535/3556), so the fix must add the matching narrow-width samplers.

Correct fix (fnp-random core, delicate): add bounded_lemire_uint8/uint16 matching numpy's _bounded_integers.pyx buffered_bounded_lemire_uint8/16 — numpy BUFFERS leftover bytes from a single uint32 draw across consecutive narrow samples, so bit-exact parity requires replicating that buffer state machine exactly. Then width-parameterize integers_shaped/integers_endpoint_shaped to dispatch by dtype width, add I8/I16/U8/U16 arms to validate_random_integer_dtype_bounds (fnp-python lib.rs ~3657) and confirm random_integer_storage handles them. Gate with an oracle differential (capture_numpy_oracle) across widths/ranges/endpoint. Found 2026-06-17 while sweeping Generator dtype parity (the choice/permutation/shuffle/permuted f64-dtype family, beads 4byse/id2c9, is already fixed).
close_reason: Implemented NumPy-width Generator.integers parity for int8/int16/uint8/uint16: fnp-random now has buffered uint8/uint16 Lemire samplers that consume leftover bytes/halfwords from uint32 draws, fnp-python dispatches narrow dtypes to typed storage instead of i64 generation/cast, dtype bounds/storage support narrow integer dtypes, and oracle tests cover signed/unsigned/bounded/endpoint/scalar cases. title: [test][fnp-python] no cross-cutting return-TYPE sweep: numpy scalar vs 0-d ndarray is chosen per-wrapper by hand ~200 times
description:
SECOND PROBE IN THE DECLARED-VS-SERVED CLASS opened by
deadlock-audit-submodule-all-names-must-resolve-rrrlm, after the signature-audit
vein closed. This one compares the RETURN TYPE fnp hands back against numpy's,
across the whole reduction/elementwise surface at once.

WHY IT IS A LIVE TRAP HERE, not a hypothetical: numpy returns a numpy SCALAR
(np.float64, np.int64, np.bool_) for a full reduction, NOT a 0-d ndarray. Same
dtype, same shape, different type - and any caller doing type(x), isinstance,
or `x is np.True_` can see the difference. fnp has a dedicated helper for this,
build_numpy_scalar_or_array, whose whole reason to exist is collapsing the 0-d
case; the choice between it and build_numpy_array_from_ufunc is made
per-wrapper, by hand, ~200 times. The `choose` wrapper's own comment records
getting exactly this wrong ("numpy returns a SCALAR (numpy.int64), while
build_numpy_array_from_ufunc returns a 0-d ndarray - same dtype, same shape,
different type, which any caller reading type() can see", deadlock-audit-41nl1).

WHAT EXISTS TODAY: scattered per-function checks. `grep -l "__name__"
crates/fnp-python/tests/*.rs` hits ~40 shards, each asserting the return type of
its own function - abs, angle, argmax, argmin, all, any, arctan2, argwhere and
so on. There is NO cross-cutting sweep, so WHICH functions lack the check is
unknown, and a wrapper added without one is invisible.

PROBE TO CLOSE: a conformance sweep comparing type(result).__name__ (plus
isinstance-of-ndarray and ndim) between fnp and numpy for, at minimum:
  - full reductions on 1-D float64 and on int64: sum, prod, mean, std, var,
    min, max, ptp, median, average, any, all, argmin, argmax, count_nonzero,
    and the nan* twins
  - 2-D reductions WITH an axis (must stay ndarray - the control that proves
    the sweep is not just asserting "everything is a scalar")
  - 0-d and python-scalar input to an elementwise op (sqrt, abs, negative)
  - linalg.det / linalg.norm, dot and vdot on 1-D
Any divergence found is a real defect and should be fixed in the same bead;
if none is found the sweep still lands as the missing cross-cutting lock.

A new test file is justified here rather than growing a shard: the sweep is
cross-cutting by construction and belongs to no single function's shard. Keep it
one file, one test.
close_reason:
DELIVERED in e3d7fb33 as a LOCK. NO DIVERGENCE FOUND - all 51 cases match numpy, so no defect is claimed. Saying that first because the bead was filed expecting to find one.

WHY IT WAS WORTH PROBING ANYWAY: numpy returns a numpy SCALAR for a full reduction, not a 0-d ndarray - same dtype, same shape, different type, and visible to any caller doing type(), isinstance, or 'x is np.True_'. fnp chooses between build_numpy_scalar_or_array (which collapses the 0-d case) and build_numpy_array_from_ufunc (which does not) BY HAND, once per wrapper, roughly 200 times. That is a per-site decision with no structural enforcement, and the choose wrapper's own comment records having got it wrong (deadlock-audit-41nl1: 'numpy returns a SCALAR (numpy.int64), while build_numpy_array_from_ufunc returns a 0-d ndarray ... which any caller reading type() can see').

WHAT EXISTED: about 40 shards assert the return type of their own function (grep -l __name__ over crates/fnp-python/tests). None of them sweeps, so WHICH wrappers lacked the check was unknown - a wrapper added without one was invisible. That was the actual gap, and it is what this closes.

THE SWEEP: 51 cases comparing type(result).__name__, isinstance-of-ndarray and ndim against numpy in the same interpreter.
  34 full reductions - sum/prod/mean/std/var/min/max/ptp/median/average/any/all/argmin/argmax/count_nonzero/trace, all nine nan* twins, percentile and quantile with a scalar q, dot/vdot/inner on 1-D, linalg.det, linalg.norm
   9 that must STAY ndarray - axis reductions, keepdims, list-q percentile, sqrt on an array, cumsum
   8 scalar-or-0-d inputs to elementwise ops - python float, np.float64, np.int64, a 0-d array

THE MUST-STAY-NDARRAY GROUP IS LOAD-BEARING, not padding. Without it the sweep could pass by asserting 'everything collapses to a scalar', which is the opposite error and equally wrong. Two preconditions back it: numpy's full reduction must NOT return an ndarray, and numpy's axis reduction MUST. If either stops holding, the two groups are no longer testing opposite things and the test says so instead of going slack - the same guard shape used in mi3k6 and 1jlkg.

NEW FILE, deliberately: the sweep is cross-cutting by construction and belongs to no single function's shard. One file, one test, per the bead.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_return_types = 1 passed / 0 failed, exit 0, oracle numpy 2.4.3. cargo clippy -p fnp-python --test conformance_return_types -- -D warnings exit 0. cargo fmt --check -p fnp-python exit 0. All exit codes captured directly.

REMAINING SIBLING PROBES in this declared-vs-served class, still unrun: exception-CLASS parity (does fnp raise numpy's exception type for the same bad input, across the surface rather than per shard) and dtype-PRESERVATION parity (does each wrapper return numpy's output dtype, especially for narrow ints and float32 where fnp's extract path historically widened through f64).

title: [bug][fnp-iter] external_loop F-order chunking ignores unit axes - nditer([1,5], order=F) yields chunks of 1 where numpy yields one chunk of 5
close_reason:
FIXED. plan_external_loop's F arm (crates/fnp-iter/src/lib.rs:1627) now collapses unit axes before choosing the chunk: the inner loop is the extent of the first NON-UNIT axis, with the remaining non-unit axes forming the outer loop, and an all-unit shape falling back to element_count. It previously took shape[0] unconditionally.

RULE TAKEN FROM NUMPY BY MEASUREMENT, not from reasoning - a leading unit axis is not the only shape that matters, and I had been wrong from memory three times earlier this session:
  (1,5) F -> [5]        (1,1,5) F -> [5]       (1,5,3) F -> [5,5,5]
  (5,1,3) F -> [5,5,5]  (2,1,3) F -> [2,2,2]   (1,2,3) F -> [2,2,2]
  (3,1) F -> [3]        (1,1) F -> [1]         (2,3) F -> [2,2,2]
Unit axes drop out wherever they sit - leading, middle or trailing - and the first surviving extent becomes the chunk.

WHY THE REST OF THE STATE MACHINE IS UNAFFECTED, which is what I was worried about when I filed this rather than patching inline: (1) numpy REJECTS external_loop together with multi_index ('Iterator flag EXTERNAL_LOOP cannot be used if an index or multi-index is being tracked'), so multi_index consistency is not a constraint here at all; (2) chunking flows through a single value, chunk_len_for_plan -> plan.inner_loop_len(), and chunk_start is a linear chunk_index * chunk_len over the flat order; (3) the F-order element resolution computes operand_stride = element_count / inner_loop_len, which I checked by hand against the traversal for (1,5,3) (stride 3, chunk [0,3,6,9,12]) and (2,1,3) (stride 3, chunks [0,3],[1,4],[2,5]) - both correct under the new inner_loop_len.

ACCEPTANCE TEST MET: [1,5] F external_loop is back in nditer_matches_numpy_across_shape_order_and_external_loop, which also gained [1,1,5], [1,5,3], [5,1,3], [2,1,3] and [1,1] so unit axes are exercised in every position. The sweep passes against numpy's own nditer.

STILL OPEN, filed on v0p7v and worth doing separately: the bridge validates numpy's chunk length against an expectation derived from OUR plan, so a future divergence of this shape surfaces as PythonBridgeFailure rather than as a value mismatch. That is how this one appeared, and it makes a parity defect look like broken infrastructure.

VERIFIED: timeout cargo test -p fnp-iter --lib = 117 passed / 0 failed; cargo test -p fnp-conformance --test smoke = 7 passed (it exercises the nditer_python bridge); cargo clippy -p fnp-iter --all-targets -- -D warnings = clean; cargo fmt --check exit 0 run UNPIPED.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FOUND by nditer_matches_numpy_across_shape_order_and_external_loop (CreamGlen, 2026-08-09), added under v0p7v. One of 27 swept configurations diverges: shape [1,5], order F, external_loop.

GROUND TRUTH, taken from numpy directly rather than from the bridge's framing:
  shape=(1,5) order=C chunks=[5]      shape=(1,5) order=F chunks=[5]
  shape=(5,1) order=C chunks=[5]      shape=(5,1) order=F chunks=[5]
  shape=(2,3) order=C chunks=[6]      shape=(2,3) order=F chunks=[2,2,2]
numpy COLLAPSES UNIT AXES before deciding the external_loop chunk: (1,5) reduces to (5,) and yields a single chunk of 5.

OURS: plan_external_loop (crates/fnp-iter/src/lib.rs:1627) is
    NditerOrder::C => (Vec::new(), None, element_count),
    NditerOrder::F => (shape[1..].to_vec(), Some(0), shape[0]),
so the F chunk is ALWAYS shape[0], with no unit-axis collapse. For (1,5) that is 1 where numpy gives 5.

WHY IT SURVIVED: (3,1) and (2,3) agree by coincidence - (3,1) has its unit axis in the trailing position where it does not affect shape[0], and (2,3) has no unit axis at all. Only a LEADING unit axis exposes it, and the single pre-existing bridge comparison used shape [2,3,4], which has none. The C arm is unaffected because it already coalesces everything.

NOTE ON THE BRIDGE: it surfaced as PythonBridgeFailure('python bridge emitted chunk length 5, expected 1') rather than as a value mismatch. The bridge validates numpy's chunk length against an expectation derived from OUR plan, so when numpy disagrees the bridge rejects numpy rather than reporting a divergence. That validation encodes our model as the contract and would mask this class in ordinary use - worth fixing alongside, or the next divergence of this shape will look like an infrastructure error too.

SUGGESTED FIX: collapse extent-1 axes before computing the F-order chunk. That makes (1,5)->(5,) chunk 5, leaves (3,1)->(3,) chunk 3 and (2,3) chunk 2 unchanged. It is a state-machine change though: the outer shape, iterindex and multi_index reporting all derive from the same plan, so the collapse has to be consistent across them, which is why it is filed rather than patched inline.

NOT FIXED. The sweep landed with this one configuration excluded and named, so it runs green without pinning the wrong behaviour; re-including [1,5] F external_loop is this bead's acceptance test.

title: [bug][fnp-python] integer correlate 'same' has the unswapped-trim defect fixed in fnp-ufunc d28b0372, with no guard
close_reason: FIXED in d05707e7. Both fnp-python sites named in the bead are closed. (1) int_convolve_typed reproduced the fnp-ufunc defect with NO guard - it sliced the full convolution at (full_len-out_len)/2 regardless of operand order, so integer correlate(a,v,'same') with len(v)>len(a) returned a window shifted one slot from numpy. Because convolution commutes the VALUES were never wrong, only the trim offset, so the fix is one line: the reversed window taken at k_start from the reversed full result equals the forward window taken at full_len-out_len-k_start from ours; a no-op for 'full' (0) and 'valid' (always even), shifting by one exactly in the 'same'+longer-v case. (2) The f64 binding's explicit 'fall back to NumPy for mode=same when kernel is longer' deferral was papering over the same divergence; now redundant, removed, and the shape is served natively again. TEST: correlate_matches_numpy_when_the_kernel_is_longer_than_the_input covers f64 in all three modes (shape AND values), int64 in all three modes above the native gate, the MIRRORED orientation so the fix cannot have moved the defect to the other side, and convolve in both orientations as a commutativity control. NON-VACUITY PROVEN BY FALSIFICATION: reverting the one-line fix makes the test fail with 'correlate int64 same with a longer kernel diverges from numpy', which proves the native integer kernel is actually engaged (n*m = 100*1000 = 100000 >= INT_CONV_MIN_WORK 1<<16, rayon threads >= 2) rather than quietly deferring to numpy. EVIDENCE: timeout 120 cargo test -p fnp-python --lib -- convolve correlate = 2 passed / 0 failed; cargo fmt --check -p fnp-python exit 0 run UNPIPED. Commit d05707e7.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: ROOT CAUSE fixed in fnp-ufunc by d28b0372 (bead aej7h): correlate(a,v) == convolve(a, v[::-1]) only holds while a is the LONGER operand; numpy swaps so the longer leads and reverts the result, and 'same' trims unevenly so the unswapped order shifts the window by one. numpy correlate([1,2],[0.5,1,-1,2,3],'same') = [8,3,-1,2.5,1]; the unswapped identity gives [3,8,3,-1,2.5]. TWO SITES REMAIN IN fnp-python/src/lib.rs. (1) int_convolve_typed computes k_start = (full_len - l)/2 for 'same' with NO is_correlate/longer-v guard, so the integer correlate path reproduces the defect. It is gated behind try_native_int_convolve's INT_CONV_MIN_WORK = 1<<16 and rayon threads >= 2, so a repro needs len(a)*len(v) >= 65536 with len(v) > len(a) - e.g. a of 100 int64 and v of 1000 int64, mode='same' - which is why no small-array test caught it. 'valid' is unaffected there ((6-4)/2 = 1 is correct). (2) the f64 correlate binding carries an explicit workaround, 'Fall back to NumPy for mode=same when kernel is longer than input', which is now REDUNDANT and costs the native path on that shape; remove it and let correlate_mode serve the case. title: [perf][fnp-python] the probe chain is 65% of the delegating route's excess in INSTRUCTIONS - measure its TIME cost with a route-level A/B, not a partition
description:
SUCCESSOR to deadlock-audit-ei9jz, which retired the replica-sum partition after five refusals.

THE QUESTION THAT REMAINS WORTH MONEY: what does the probe chain cost in TIME on the delegating binary-ufunc route? ei9jz established it costs 1189.4 instructions/call (65% of the route's 1830.5-insn excess over NumPy at n=256), but that is an INSTRUCTIONS-ONLY result. It has no time-domain confirmation and, by ei9jz's stop rule, will not get one from a partition.

WHY A PARTITION CANNOT ANSWER IT, so nobody rebuilds one: retired instructions are conserved and additive - every instruction is executed once and counted once wherever it sits - but time is not. A replica measured in isolation runs with different branch-predictor state, cache residency and ILP than the same code embedded in the route, and out-of-order execution overlaps work across the boundaries a replica-sum identity assumes are clean. Summing replica TIMES over-counts, which is why the wrapper residual came out negative in 4 of 4 runs (-19.4 to -56.9 ns) while the instruction-domain residual was firmly +640 insns/call. Five instruments refused it: aggregator choice swung the ratio 1.57<->4.68 on identical runs; a cross-host conversion was withdrawn; the completed partition went negative; the terms were shown to sit 2 timer-ticks above zero; and a resolution-fixed batched harness still returned a negative part.

THE TRACTABLE EXPERIMENT INSTEAD - a route-level A/B, not a partition:

  Build TWO ELFs differing ONLY in whether the probe chain runs on the delegating path, and
  measure the ROUTE (fnp.multiply at n=256) in each. That is a single well-conditioned
  difference of two large, directly-measured quantities - not a residual of five replicas -
  so it is additive-safe in the time domain in a way the partition never was.

  The separator must NOT be casting="unsafe". That flips ONE predicate gating BOTH the probe
  block AND the keyword tail (wsd7h), so the "probe-skipped" arm also pays a PyDict alloc, a
  set_item, pyo3's keyword binding and NumPy's parse - measured at 2719.1 insns/call against
  a probe chain of 1189.4, i.e. the confound is more than twice the signal. Use a build-time
  switch (cfg feature or a const) that removes the probe block and changes nothing else.

REGISTER BEFORE RUNNING: the expected effect. The probe chain is 1189.4 of 1830.5 insns/call
of excess, and the route's whole excess is 288.6 ns by the 400,000-call loop method, so a
proportional expectation is ~187 ns - but per-component IPC varies up to 3x on this route
(measured 4.8 to 14.4 insns/ns), so the time effect could plausibly land anywhere in roughly
60-250 ns. Register a band before measuring, not after.

METHOD CONSTRAINTS, all learned the hard way in ei9jz:
 - Pin OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1. perf stat counts the
   OpenBLAS spinners; unpinned it reads 15.5x high AND proportional to elapsed time, so it
   does not cancel in a matched difference.
 - Batch the timed region over thousands of calls. Instant::now costs 20.0 ns here.
 - Take instruction counts alongside wall clock: they cost nothing extra and carry 0.08%
   spread against wall clock's 4.8-6.1%, so they tell you immediately whether the two ELFs
   differ by what you think they differ by.
 - Verify BENCH_GROUP_SELECTION selected_groups=1 per arm - the selector matches by SUBSTRING.
 - Name the worker and record vmstat idle + runnable-vs-cores, not just loadavg; loadavg 30
   coexists with 87% idle on this 64-core box.

ACCEPTANCE: a route-level ratio between the two ELFs with dual A/A nulls, or an explicit
UNDECIDED. A negative or straddling result is a publishable answer here - the point is to
learn whether removing 65% of the excess instructions buys proportional time, and "it does
not" would be the more interesting outcome.

Filed by SlateFinch on closing ei9jz.
close_reason: done

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
THE CORRECTNESS ARGUMENT FOR THE SWITCH, derived by source reading because no test supplies it.

The switch bypasses every native route in PyUFunc::__call__. Whether that is SAFE is a real question - if any route existed because NumPy would fail, or would give a different answer, then skipping it changes results and the A/B compares two different computations rather than two speeds. Nothing in the test suite asserts this, and I did not want it resting on an assumption.

Routes the switch bypasses (enumerated from the span between the switch and the delegation tail):
  try_zerocopy_f64_binary_into, try_zerocopy_f64_binary, try_zerocopy_f32_binary,
  try_zerocopy_f16_binary_widen, try_native_int_power, try_native_int_remainder,
  try_native_timedelta_remainder, try_zerocopy_complex_binary, try_zerocopy_f64_floor_divide

Their own documentation is consistent on the point:
  - int remainder: "BIT-EXACT: numpy integer wrapping_rem then adding the divisor when the
    remainder is non-zero and its sign differs" - it reproduces NumPy, it does not extend it.
  - timedelta remainder: "numpy returns NaT when either operand is NaT or the divisor is 0, so
    DEFER (zero-copy scans) on NaT (i64::MIN) or zero divisor" - the edge cases are handed BACK
    to NumPy rather than handled differently.
  - f16 widen: a dtype whose kind is not a single character "has no f16 route either, so it must
    DECLINE".
  - complex: "divide defers on a zero complex divisor so numpy's div-by-zero recovery surfaces".
  - f64 floor_divide: "non-finite operands / zero divisors defer in-helper so numpy's
    RuntimeWarnings + NaN payloads surface".

THE ARGUMENT, and it is stronger than "the routes are bit-exact": DELEGATION IS THE REFERENCE.
Every native route in this function exists to reproduce NumPy's answer faster, and each one declines
to NumPy on exactly the inputs where reproducing it is hard. So bypassing them cannot change
correctness RELATIVE TO NUMPY - it can only remove our own opportunity to diverge. With
FNP_DISABLE_NATIVE_ROUTES=1 the wrapper is strictly more conservative than the default path, not
less. That is what makes the A/B a comparison of two speeds computing one answer.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT LICENSE: it is an argument about SEMANTICS, not about the switch being untested
code. The by-reference parameter change in the extraction is still unexercised by any test, and the
gate on it stands. It also says nothing about cells where a native route ENGAGES - there the two
arms run different code and the comparison is not an A/B of the same work, which is why the call
site restricts use to delegating cells.

title: [perf][fnp-python] PyUFunc delegation rebuilds a kwargs dict and forces numpy to parse casting/order/subok on every call
description:
TARGET: the ~7-8 us PyUFunc::__call__ wrapper floor (deadlock-audit-cydda lever (b)), which is the campaign's worst measured gap - 7.97x slower than numpy at n=256 and charged to EVERY fnp binary ufunc including the three that merely delegate.

MECHANISM, read from crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs:552-571. The delegation tail runs on every call that does not take a native route:
  let np_ufunc = numpy.getattr(self.kind.name())?;   // getattr
  let kwargs = PyDict::new(py);                      // allocation
  kwargs.set_item("casting", casting)?;              // ALWAYS set
  kwargs.set_item("order", order)?;                  // ALWAYS set
  kwargs.set_item("subok", subok)?;                  // ALWAYS set
  np_ufunc.call((x1, x2), Some(&kwargs))
out/where/dtype/signature are already omitted when absent, but casting, order and subok are set unconditionally. Their values in the default case are exactly numpy's own defaults ('same_kind', 'K', True), so we allocate a dict and then make numpy parse three keyword arguments to tell it what it would have assumed anyway.

LEVER: when every kwarg is at its default, call np_ufunc.call1((x1, x2)) with NO kwargs dict. Semantically identical by construction - omitting a keyword whose value equals its default cannot change behaviour - and it removes a PyDict allocation, three set_item calls, and numpy's keyword parsing from the hot path.

WHY IT IS AIMED, NOT GUESSED: deadlock-audit-cydda bounded the four obvious stages (numpy re-import 310 ns, dtype guard 100 ns, getattr ndarray 70 ns, numpy.empty 220 ns) at 700 ns total, i.e. <=10% of the floor, so the remainder is argument handling and the delegation call shape. This is the delegation call shape.

SECOND LEVER, NOT IN SCOPE HERE, listed so it is not lost: __call__ is declared #[pyo3(signature = (x1, x2, /, out=None, *, where=None, casting="same_kind", order="K", dtype=None, subok=true, signature=None))] - nine parameters, six optional, all bound by PyO3 before any work. Switching to (*args, **kwargs) with lazy parsing would remove that binding cost, and it is SAFE for introspection because the type defines an explicit __signature__ property (it builds inspect.Parameter objects itself), so inspect.signature does not read PyO3's binding signature. Do that as a separate measured lever.

ACCEPTANCE: a row naming WORKER and HARNESS with the fnp-vs-numpy ratio for a DELEGATING op (add/subtract/multiply) at small n, before and after, measured on the same worker - banked either way. A loss or a wash is the success condition just as much as a win.
close_reason:
LANDED + BANKED. Row in 03e99c65; the lever and its control were swept into peer commits 1a50600d / an earlier one on the shared tree (content verified present in HEAD by grep).

MEASURED IN ISOLATION - one binary, one invocation, WORKER vmi1227854, HARNESS common::run_median_ci_contract (41 rounds, ABBAABBA, A/A null first). Both arms are NumPy's own multiply on identical operands with NO fnp code in either; they differ only in whether the three default-valued keywords are passed:
  with default kwargs 1227.0 ns
  bare call            500.0 ns
  ratio 2.442387 ci95 [2.420744,2.458586] DECIDABLE_WIN
  null  1.000000 ci95 [0.996022,1.004835]
  saved 727.0 ns per call
NumPy spends more time parsing three keywords it did not need than it spends multiplying 256 doubles. That is ~9-10% of the 6968-8375 ns wrapper floor on the delegating ops.

CLASS maintenance-self-speedup - base arm is our own former call shape. NOT a competitive claim; we are still behind NumPy on this surface.

WHY AN ISOLATED CONTROL RATHER THAN A BEFORE/AFTER: three independent confounds are live right now. (1) The rch fleet is heterogeneous with no pinning flag, so two builds land on different workers - my first after-run drew vmi1227854 while the existing before-numbers are from vmi1153651. (2) [profile.bench] inherits release (lto, codegen-units=1) and blows the 1800s SSH ceiling - three RCH-E104 timeouts before I moved to --profile bench-fast, which is the documented triage profile for exactly this. (3) A peer had an uncommitted route change in the same file, so any after-build carries their lever as well as mine. One binary with both arms and no fnp code defeats all three.

PARITY: conformance_ufunc_edge on WORKER hz2, 71 passed 0 failed. Omitting a keyword whose value equals its default cannot change behaviour, so this is a call-shape change, not a semantic one.

NEXT LEVER, named in the row's retry predicate: PyO3 argument binding. __call__ declares nine parameters, six optional with defaults, all bound before any work. Switching to (*args, **kwargs) with lazy parsing is SAFE for introspection because the type defines an explicit __signature__ property and inspect.signature reads that, not PyO3's binding signature. Measure it the same way - isolated control first, then the route.

title: [perf][fnp-python] 3,448 non-interned call_method sites vs SIX interned - PyO3 builds a fresh PyString for the method key on every call, and searchsorted's cold path pays it for asarray
description:
FOUND while doing the first read of ss_list_haystack, which RedLynx had flagged as never read
(deadlock-audit-v46rn). Filed separately because it is a crate-wide class, not a searchsorted fact.

THE STATIC FACT:
  call_method[01]("literal", ..)      NON-interned method key   3,448 sites
  call_method1(intern!(py, ".."), ..) interned                      6 sites

PyO3's call_method1 with a &str builds a fresh PyString for the method name on every call. That is
the same non-interned-key defect this campaign has already priced at ~795 insns/call for a hot
attribute read. Essentially the whole crate is unconverted: 6 sites out of 3,454.

For scale, the getattr("ndarray") class swept on 2026-08-18 was 487 sites. This is 7x larger.

*** SIZE IT WITH THE RIGHT NUMBER, AND DO NOT MULTIPLY ***
The applicable per-site figure is ~795 insns/call (interning a hot attribute key), NOT the 1,360.9
measured on the ndarray sweep. Those are different operations: the ndarray lever replaced the lookup
with a cached singleton and ELIMINATED it; interning only avoids building the key and the lookup still
happens. Confusing them would repeat the category error that made the 13.2 insns/ns rate fail its
cross-lever test the same day.

3,448 x 795 is the product-of-banked-numbers construct that was wrong repeatedly in this session. MOST
OF THESE 3,448 SITES ARE COLD. The prize is the reachable subset and it is unmeasured.

FIRST STEP, deliberately small: convert ONE hot site and price it. The obvious candidate is
`numpy.call_method1("asarray", ..)` on searchsorted's cold path, because ss_list_haystack at 2.19x is
a NAMED cell with no attributed mechanism, so a win there is attributable. Measure under the dual-null
contract that produced the family's other figures, not a counter probe.

DO NOT open with a 3,448-site pass. The ndarray sweep established that the reachable subset - not the
site count - is the prize, and that the sweep's remaining 220 sites turned out PROVABLY unreachable
from both measured cells. Same discipline applies here from the start.

BUILD FREEZE was in force when this was filed (/data 34G against a 42G brake); nothing is measured.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
PREMISE VERIFIED IN PyO3 SOURCE (SlateFinch 2026-08-18, ledger row 29c52c48). I filed this bead on a
remembered fact; it is now read out of pyo3-0.28.3 so nobody spends a build on an unchecked claim.

  types/any.rs  call_method1<N,A>  where N: IntoPyObject<'py, Target = PyString>
                 -> name.into_pyobject_or_pyerr(self.py())?
  conversions/std/string.rs  impl IntoPyObject for &str
                 -> Ok(PyString::new(py, self))

PyString::new PER CALL. No fast path, no cache, no short-string special case. All 3,448 sites allocate
a PyUnicode, copy the name bytes, and drop it again, once per call.

The interned form:
  macro_rules! intern! { static INTERNED: Interned = Interned::new($text); INTERNED.get($py) }
  Interned(&'static str, PyOnceLock<Py<PyString>>)
-> built once per process, every later call is a deref returning &Bound<'py, PyString>. Zero Python
work on the hot path.

MECHANISM NAMED BUT NOT CLAIMED: PyString::intern also calls PyUnicode_InternInPlace, which puts the
string in CPython's intern table, letting dict lookups shortcut to POINTER equality. So interning may
speed the attribute LOOKUP as well as removing the allocation. That is a source reading, not a
measurement; the banked ~795 insns/call already includes whatever share applies at a hot getattr site.

WHAT THIS CHANGES FOR THE BEAD: the first measurement now tests the SIZE of the effect rather than
having to establish that an effect exists. Everything else stands - convert ONE hot site (asarray on
searchsorted's cold path), price it under the dual-null contract, and do NOT open with a 3,448-site
pass.

title: [bug][fnp-python] fnp.save(path_string, arr) raises TypeError on numpy>=2.4 - the fallback always forwards fix_imports, which numpy removed
description:
LIVE BREAKAGE, not just a signature nit. fnp.save with a STRING PATH - the most
common way anyone calls it - raises TypeError on numpy >= 2.4.

MECHANISM, read off the source at crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs:
  fn save is declared (file, arr, allow_pickle=true, fix_imports=true) and its
  fallback closure does `kwargs.set_item("fix_imports", fix_imports)` -
  UNCONDITIONALLY, because the parameter is a plain bool with a default, not an
  Option. The native path only runs when `file` has a .write attribute, so a str
  path takes `return fallback()` on its first branch. numpy 2.4 REMOVED
  fix_imports from save, so that forwarded keyword is now fatal:
    np.save(p, arr, allow_pickle=True, fix_imports=True)
      -> TypeError: save() got an unexpected keyword argument 'fix_imports'
  Verified on the installed numpy 2.4.3; inspect.signature(np.save) reads
  (file, arr, allow_pickle=True).

np.load is NOT affected and must not be touched: its signature still carries
fix_imports on 2.4.3 (file, mmap_mode, allow_pickle, fix_imports, encoding, *,
max_header_size), and np.load(p, fix_imports=True) succeeds. fnp's load forwards
it correctly.

THREE SIBLINGS IN THIS AUDIT CLASS ARE ALREADY CORRECT - checked, not assumed,
and they are the model for the fix:
  corrcoef  - hands the WHOLE call to numpy the moment bias/ddof is supplied, so
              numpy's own TypeError surfaces (deadlock-audit-hp9u2)
  reshape   - forwards whichever of shape/newshape the caller bound
  nanpercentile / nanquantile - `interpolation.is_some()` forces the fallback,
              which forwards it, so numpy raises
Each takes Option<...> and forwards ONLY when the caller supplied it. save is
the one that made the keyword unconditional.

FIX: make fix_imports Option<bool> and forward it only when Some. On numpy <= 2.3
that preserves today's behaviour exactly; on 2.4+ an unsupplied fix_imports
disappears from the call (so save works again) and a supplied one reaches numpy
and raises numpy's own error. Fleet-safe on both halves, no invented semantic.

PROBE TO CLOSE: no-mock conformance that fnp.save(str_path, arr) round-trips
through np.load, that a file-object target still takes the native path, that
allow_pickle= still forwards, and that fix_imports= produces the SAME outcome as
numpy (TypeError on 2.4.x, accepted on 2.3.x) rather than a pinned verdict.
Green on a named worker with its numpy version cited.

Also surfaced by the same audit, NOT in this bead: asarray/asanyarray declare
device/copy/like as positional-or-keyword where numpy makes them KEYWORD-ONLY
(after the `*`), so fnp accepts np.asarray(a, dt, 'C', True) which numpy rejects
with "takes from 1 to 3 positional arguments but 4 were given". Widening, not
breakage - separate bead.
close_reason:
FIXED in ce236a11.

THE BREAKAGE WAS REAL AND ORDINARY: fnp.save(path_string, arr) raised TypeError on numpy >= 2.4. fix_imports was a plain defaulted bool, so the fallback closure sent it on EVERY call it handled, and a str has no .write so it always takes that fallback on its first branch. numpy 2.4 removed the parameter - inspect.signature(np.save) reads (file, arr, allow_pickle=True), verified on the installed 2.4.3 - so the forwarded keyword was fatal.

FIX: fix_imports is Option<bool>, forwarded only when the caller supplied it, and a supplied one forces the fallback so numpy decides whether it is still legal on this build. numpy <= 2.3 unchanged; 2.4+ works again for the normal call and raises numpy's own error for the removed spelling. No invented semantic, and fleet-safe across both numpy halves.

THREE SIBLINGS CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED - and all three were already correct, which is why this bead is one fix rather than four: corrcoef hands the whole call to numpy when bias/ddof appear (deadlock-audit-hp9u2), reshape forwards whichever of shape/newshape was bound, nanpercentile/nanquantile force the fallback on interpolation.is_some(). save was the only member of the removed-upstream class that made the keyword unconditional.

np.load DELIBERATELY UNTOUCHED: numpy did NOT remove fix_imports there (2.4.3 signature still carries it and np.load(p, fix_imports=True) succeeds), so a blanket 'strip fix_imports' would have broken load. The new test calls load with fix_imports= to hold that line.

WHY IT SURVIVED THIS LONG: every pre-existing save test in conformance_io.rs writes to a BytesIO, which HAS .write and therefore takes the native writer - the fallback was never on a tested path. That is the actual coverage gap, and the new test closes it.

TEST save_path_string_roundtrips_and_tracks_numpys_fix_imports_contract, 8 comparison cases plus a standalone regression assertion: path string, path string + allow_pickle, a name without the .npy suffix (numpy appends it and the fallback must keep doing so), a file object (native path), an int32 array through a path, fix_imports=True/False, and load(fix_imports=True). The fix_imports cases assert fnp's outcome EQUALS the installed numpy's rather than pinning TypeError, because the fleet runs 2.3.x and 2.4.x and the correct behaviour differs between them.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_io = 21 passed / 0 failed, exit 0. cargo clippy -p fnp-python --lib --tests -- -D warnings exit 0. cargo fmt --check -p fnp-python exit 0. All exit codes captured directly, not through a pipe.

HONEST LIMIT ON THE NON-VACUITY CLAIM: I did not run the new test against a pre-fix binary, so 'this test would have failed before' rests on the source read plus the numpy-side probe, not on a demonstrated red. Both are recorded above.

STILL OPEN from the audit: asarray/asanyarray declare device/copy/like as positional-or-keyword where numpy makes them KEYWORD-ONLY, so fnp accepts np.asarray(a, dt, 'C', True) which numpy rejects with 'takes from 1 to 3 positional arguments but 4 were given'. Widening rather than breakage - needs its own bead. Plus deadlock-audit-where-none-vs-absent-sentinel-bbk62.

title: [test][flaky] mr_sort_then_sum_equals_sum proptest tolerance too tight for ill-conditioned sums
description: metamorphic_proptest.rs:182 asserts sum(sort(x)) == sum(x) within rel_tol = sqrt(n)*1e-12*|sum|.max(1.0). Proptest discovered a failing case (persisted in crates/fnp-ufunc/tests/metamorphic_proptest.proptest-regressions) where reordering by sort changes the f64 accumulation enough to exceed this tolerance — classic catastrophic-cancellation: when sum_original.abs() << max|x_i|, the |sum|.max(1.0) factor floors rel_tol at ~sqrt(n)*1e-12 which is far smaller than the actual reordering error (~eps*sum|x_i|). PRE-EXISTING (reproduces on clean HEAD with the regressions file present; independent of the einsum Hadamard work). FIX: scale rel_tol by sum of magnitudes (sum|x_i|), not by |sum(x)| — e.g. rel_tol = n.sqrt()*1e-12*x.iter().map(|v|v.abs()).sum(). This is the correct conditioning bound for floating summation reordering.
close_reason: Fixed in 2a213e51: tolerance now scales by Sum|x_i| (summation conditioning) instead of |Sum(x)|.max(1). 22 proptests green, 6000 fresh cases pass.
