title: [test][fnp-python] all differential coverage is curated grids - no seeded RANDOMISED differential, so zero-size/NaN/extreme inputs are only tested where someone thought of them
description:
ELEVENTH PROBE, and the one my own y20e8 closure named as the remaining
METHODOLOGY gap rather than another coverage gap.

THE ARGUMENT: the ten probes so far are curated grids. A curated grid tests
exactly what its author enumerated - which means its blind spot is precisely the
author's blind spot, and mine is now well established (three of the ten probes
had artifacts in the PROBE, and the last five found nothing). Randomised inputs
do not share that blind spot: they reach zero-size shapes, single-element arrays,
all-NaN and mixed NaN/inf inputs, denormals, extreme magnitudes, high-rank
shapes and awkward axis values that no hand-written case list contains.

Zero-size input in particular has never been swept this session. numpy's
behaviour there is famously specific - sum of empty is 0.0, max of empty RAISES,
mean of empty warns and returns nan, argmin of empty raises - and every one of
those is a separate branch in fnp.

WHAT IT MUST NOT BE: flaky. A test whose inputs change per run is not a gate -
it fails for one agent and passes for the next, and the failure is unreproducible.
So the generator MUST be seeded with a FIXED seed, making the case list large,
arbitrary and CONSTANT. That is the difference between a differential regression
test and a fuzzer; a fuzzer belongs in the fuzz/ crates, which already exist
(docs/FUZZING.md, 7 crates / 27 targets).

PROBE TO CLOSE: a seeded randomised differential test that, for a few hundred
iterations, draws a dtype, a shape (including 0-size and 0-d), a value profile
(ordinary / with NaN / with inf / denormal / extreme), an operation and valid
parameters for it, then compares fnp against numpy on dtype, shape, NaN-safe
values, and exception class. On divergence it must print the ITERATION INDEX and
the full case description, so any failure is reproducible by re-running with the
same fixed seed. Assert as preconditions that the generated corpus actually
contains the interesting shapes - at least one zero-size case, one 0-d case and
one NaN-bearing case - so a generator that silently degenerates into "3-element
float64 vectors" reports rather than passes.

Any divergence is a real defect; fix it in the same bead.
close_reason:
FIXED. Landed in c881e5bf. THE RANDOMISED PROBE PAID OFF WHERE TEN CURATED GRIDS DID NOT, and the reason is the point of the bead: no hand-written case list contained 'trim_zeros of a 3-D array'.

THE DEFECT: fnp.trim_zeros returned the wrong SHAPE and a widened DTYPE for any input that is not 1-D. The zero-copy slice-view path is 1-D only, and the extract residual beneath it flattens to a Vec and canonicalises to f64/i64/u64. Measured against numpy 2.4.3:
  0-d float32     numpy float32 ()        fnp float64 (1,)
  (4,3) float32   numpy float32 (4, 3)    fnp float64 (12,)
  (3,0,4) float16 numpy float16 (0, 0, 0) fnp float64 (0,)
Values are all present, so it is silent on content - the array simply has the wrong rank and the wrong dtype. Same class as liz1c's take(complex64): a residual reached by input it cannot represent, by SHAPE here rather than by dtype. Non-1-D now delegates, one guard.

WHY THE EARLIER SWEEPS MISSED IT: succi swept LAYOUTS but only over ops I listed, and trim_zeros was not among them because I was thinking about contiguity. kue5j swept exotic DTYPES over 1-D samples. bikey swept keepdims over reductions. Every one of them was shaped by what I already suspected. The random generator drew shape=() and shape=(4,3) for trim_zeros because it does not know what I suspect.

THE TEST IS A REGRESSION TEST, NOT A FUZZER: the seed is FIXED (20260809), so the 400-case corpus is large, arbitrary and CONSTANT. A test whose inputs change per run is not a gate - it fails for one agent, passes for the next, and cannot be reproduced. Genuine fuzzing already exists in fuzz/ (docs/FUZZING.md, 7 crates / 27 targets). Divergences print the case index and full description so any failure replays under the same seed.

CORPUS SHAPE, from the green run: 400 cases, 108 zero-size, 94 zero-dim, 63 NaN-bearing. Preconditions require at least 5 of each, so a generator that silently degenerates into 3-element float64 vectors reports rather than passes - which is the specific way a randomised test rots.

A PROBE ARTIFACT CAUGHT FIRST, the fourth this session: the initial run reported 131 of 400 failures because make_array() drew from the shared rng INSIDE the per-module invocation, so fnp and numpy were compared on DIFFERENT random arrays. Reading the printed values (cumsum outputs that were not remotely close) rather than the failure count is what exposed it. The array is now built once per case and handed to both sides; 131 collapsed to 7, and all 7 were the single real trim_zeros defect. Four of eleven probes this session had a defect in the PROBE rather than the subject - which is the strongest argument I have for always printing both sides' values rather than a pass/fail count.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_return_types --test conformance_trim_zeros = 8 and 7 passed / 0 failed, exit 0, oracle numpy 2.4.3 - the sweep was red on exactly those 7 cases before the guard, so the red-to-green is demonstrated. cargo test -p fnp-python --lib = 557 passed / 0 failed. cargo clippy -p fnp-python --lib --tests -- -D warnings exit 0. cargo fmt --check -p fnp-python exit 0.

ATTRIBUTION: content landed in c881e5bf authored by Dicklesworthstone - a peer's tooling committed my working tree from the shared checkout for the third time this session (also f6c9c280 for succi, 1c4b42c8 for y20e8). Presence on origin/main verified by grepping the ndim guard, the test function and the shared-input fix out of origin/main directly.

TALLY, eleven probes: three live bugs (liz1c take(complex64), c7hqd/st00f concatenate .base, zgsrh trim_zeros non-1-D) and eight clean locks. Notably the ONE non-curated probe found a defect after five consecutive curated ones found nothing. If a successor continues this line, extend the generator rather than adding another grid: more operations in its table, binary ops with broadcasting pairs, and the fnp-ufunc/fnp-linalg surfaces no probe this session touched.

rewritten; only the warning predicate is exposed, which is precisely the kind of silent
divergence this crate's parity doctrine forbids.

UNORDERED FALLBACK TRANSPOSED: our own arm 1.023x -> 0.796x in ONE process; AND A FLEET-WIDE METHOD PROBLEM FOUND (BlackThrush, 2026-08-30). Do not close.

Committed 70488c72, pushed. Banked as maintenance-self-speedup, NOT a competitive claim - see the
second half, which is the part that matters beyond this cell.

THE LEVER. One bisection per key is a serial dependency chain: probe i+1's address is unknown until
probe i returns, so the search is latency-bound with exactly ONE outstanding miss per key.
Transposing the loops - all keys advance one LEVEL together - makes every key's probe at a given
level independent (m misses in flight, throughput-bound) and makes early levels nearly free (level
0 is a single shared pivot, level d has at most 2^d).

  new:    batched levels     bisect     7242133.5    5766896.6   0.796x   1.004    1.004

bench_elf_sha256=cb0df46b8dc25033f28bbee12b7c3a588a30ca81e48769d3ecbaac5925dd6456.

numpy/_core/src/npysort/binsearch.cpp, whose own comment gives the same two reasons ("cache
locality of pivots", "independent calculations for out-of-order execution"). Our loop was the naive
form of a search NumPy stopped doing. Transcription verified by simulating it against
numpy.searchsorted over 864 cells BEFORE writing any Rust: 0 divergences.

*** THE FLEET-WIDE FINDING: WORKERS RUN DIFFERENT NUMPY VERSIONS AND THE INCUMBENT'S ALGORITHM
DIFFERS BETWEEN THEM. ***

The INCUMBENT arm differs by 3.4x between workers on this cell (2.10 ms vs 7.24 ms) while the
out-of-family np.sum control says vmi1227854 is the FASTER machine. Hardware cannot explain

searchsorted explains both at once, and is consistent with the batched binsearch being present in
the vendored (newest) source. Recorded as an inference - I have NOT bisected it to a numpy commit.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE CAMPAIGN, not just this cell: against numpy 2.5.2 this cell is a 2.960x LOSS;
against numpy 2.3.5 it is a 0.796x win. Same code, clean nulls both times. Our worker-provenance
gate (new_measured_rows_name_their_worker) pins the HOST but says nothing about the INCUMBENT'S
VERSION, so two rows that both satisfy it can still be incomparable. Today's two searchsorted WIN
rows are unaffected - hz3 and hz4 both carry numpy 2.5.2, so they are mutually comparable and were
measured against the FASTER incumbent, i.e. conservatively. But the gate has a hole and I would
rather flag it than quietly benefit from it.

B-tree, software prefetch) before establishing which numpy the target worker runs and re-measuring

comments.text:
STALE-CONSTANT HYPOTHESIS RAISED AND REJECTED, WITH NUMBERS (BlackThrush, 2026-08-31). Commit 1d7cd64a, pushed main+master. Do not close.

Applied the stale-constant lens to this bead's own surface: is any threshold here tuned against a
path that no longer exists? One candidate was strong. It is now measured and wrong.

THE HYPOTHESIS: searchsorted_int_merge_typed is admitted by MERGE_MIN_HAYSTACK/MERGE_MIN_QUERIES,
both 1<<19. Those were fitted when the path sort+merge BEATS was a serial per-query bisection. THIS
SESSION DELETED THAT PATH - the fallback is now a batched (level-transposed) search with a parallel
arm above 1<<12. A threshold is only as good as the alternative it was measured against, and this
one's alternative got dramatically faster. That is the identical shape that made the three 1<<21
parallel gates worth 5-15x earlier today, so the prediction was that the router now prefers a route
that is no longer best at n,m >= 2^19.

IT DOES NOT REPRODUCE. `nosortmerge` forces the sort+merge route to decline, so both run in ONE
process against the same live numpy. worker=hz4 (64 cores, loadavg 31.87 - busy),
bench_elf_sha256=b2b290f8fe86ff9586cd0205d8ce2b7ecf30a63bdcae9162408e48ec1fa6a9d6,
invocation_id=hz4-911691-1788224124, numpy 2.5.2:

  cell                      impl           numpy_ns       fnp_ns    ratio  nullNP  nullFNP
  2^20 hay, 2^20 RANDOM q   sortmerge   109251420.5   30578965.2   0.280x   0.978   1.003  VOID
  2^20 hay, 2^20 RANDOM q   nosortmerge 111302113.2   29604949.5   0.266x   0.999   0.975  VOID
  2^20 hay, 2^20 sorted q   sortmerge    33025862.2   15464544.0   0.468x   1.016   0.983
  2^20 hay, 2^20 sorted q   nosortmerge  29928187.7   17195789.3   0.575x   0.995   0.997

SORTED NEEDLES: the SHIPPED sort+merge is 11% FASTER (15.46 ms vs 17.20 ms), both A/A nulls clean
on both arms. The decisive comparison is the ours-against-ours pair, NOT the ratio column - numpy's
own arm drifted 10% between the two impls (33.03 vs 29.93 ms) on a host at loadavg 31.87, and a
ratio built on a drifting denominator is not evidence.
RANDOM NEEDLES: 30.58 ms vs 29.60 ms, 3.2% apart, and BOTH cells VOID. Undecidable, so there is no
basis to move the gate in either direction.

VERDICT: the constant is NOT stale in the harmful direction. Nothing changed.

WHY THE PREDICTION FAILED, and this is worth more than the prediction would have been: the two
routes are not the alternatives I assumed. For an ORDERED batch the parallel arm DELIBERATELY
declines - the !ordered_batch guard I added earlier today exists precisely so that widening the
parallel gate cannot steal ordered needles from the merge win. So at m=2^20 a sorted batch never
meets a parallel search at all; it meets the SERIAL span-gated merge, and sort+merge beats that
because par_sort_unstable on already-sorted input is nearly free while its merge walk is the same
O(n+m). The guard I added to protect one win is exactly what makes this hypothesis wrong - and I
would not have learned that without forcing both sides rather than reasoning about them.

KEPT: the `nosortmerge` switch. It costs one relaxed atomic load on an already-admitted call and it
is the instrument any re-check needs.

reasoning is now measured and wrong, for the structural reason above. Re-open ONLY if the
ordered-batch guard is removed, or on a QUIET host for the random-needle cell, which is the one
this row leaves undecided at 3.2%. And note both routes are 2.1-3.6x FASTER than numpy here: this
was a choice between two wins, not a loss to recover.

title: [perf][fnp-python] SIMD horizontal min/max fold for int last-axis reductions (max/min/ptp)
description:
MEASURED un-dominated gap (BlackThrush 2026-06-22, py3.14/numpy2.4.3, 64-thread): int64 max/min/ptp along the last axis LOSE to numpy: 256x256 1.26x, 288x288 1.23x, 320x320 1.19x, decaying to 1024x1024 1.04x. ROOT CAUSE: minmax_int_typed lane_fold / ptp_axis_typed lane_ptp use a SCALAR data-dependent-branch min/max single pass that does not vectorize, vs numpy's vectorized fused reduction.

LEVER: portable_simd horizontal min/max fold over each contiguous lane (Simd<T,N> accumulator + simd_min/simd_max, reduce at lane end; scalar tail). BIT-EXACT for integers (min/max associative+commutative, no reassociation hazard) — unlike the cov/float cases this needs no golden-drift human decision. Sites: crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs minmax_int_typed (~L43260 lane_fold, inner==1 branch) and ptp_axis_typed (~L49170 lane_ptp).

RISK / why deferred not done inline: per memory [[mistuned-parallel-gates-systematic-lever]] argextreme evidence, Rust portable_simd reductions frequently DON'T beat numpy's fused C SIMD loops for memory-bound passes (the f64 SIMD argextreme path delegates large because copy+SIMD-scan loses). Here the lanes are already in-place (no copy) so SIMD min/max could reach parity or a small win, but payoff is uncertain and concentrated at small shapes (1.26x at 256x256 where absolute time is ~17us). Generic-over-int-T (i8/16/32/64,u*) SIMD needs careful trait bounds (SimdElement+SimdOrd). Worth a focused session with env-toggle A/B (scalar vs SIMD lane fold) BEFORE committing; REVERT if ~0-gain. title: [perf][fnp-python] f64 multiply/add/subtract have NO native route at any size - the small-n regime is ~708 ns of dispatch around ~20 ns of arithmetic
description:
SUCCESSOR to deadlock-audit-ei9jz, which closed with: "a micro-lever can only reach the ~473 insns/call of ours-only code; the other ~74% needs not making the second Python call at all."

THE GAP. The f64 native binop set in PyUFunc::__call__ is {Remainder, Power, Maximum, Minimum, Divide}. Multiply, Add and Subtract hit `_ => None` and therefore ALWAYS delegate to NumPy - there is no native route for them at any size. The recorded reason, in this file's own comments, is that f64 multiply is "SIMD-bound, no parallel win".

WHY THAT REASON DOES NOT SETTLE THE SMALL-n CASE. It is an argument about PARALLELISM: a rayon-parallel kernel cannot beat NumPy's own SIMD loop on the arithmetic. True, and irrelevant at small n, where almost nothing is arithmetic. At n=256 the 256 multiplies are ~64 AVX2 ops, order 20 ns. Everything else on the route is dispatch:

  measured this session, n=256 f64 multiply, delegating route:
    NumPy's own call            ~420 ns   (of which the arithmetic is ~20 ns)
    our excess over NumPy        1830.5 insns/call, ~288 ns by the 400k-call loop
    -> route total              ~708 ns to perform ~20 ns of arithmetic

A native serial route would still pay our wrapper and an output allocation (an earlier stage decomposition put output construction at 307.50 ns) but would pay NEITHER NumPy's ufunc dispatch NOR our probe chain, because it returns before the delegation tail.

CAVEAT THAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THE ABOVE, and it is this session's hardest-won lesson: those three figures come from THREE DIFFERENT INSTRUMENTS (a counted 400k-call loop, a min_ns stage replica, and a wall-clock partition whose absolute ns are suspect by ~1.6x and whose split was retired outright). Adding them is an ORDER-OF-MAGNITUDE argument for looking, NOT a prediction. Do not quote "708 ns" or any arithmetic derived from it as a measured quantity. Register a band from a single instrument before building anything.

WHAT MAKES THIS DIFFERENT FROM THE LEVERS ei9jz EXHAUSTED. Seven stage-levers each failed because the cost is diffuse across CPython and NumPy machinery - no single symbol clears twice the ~60 insns/call noise floor. A native route does not shave a stage; it removes the entire second Python call, which is where ~74% of the excess lives. That is a different class of change and the only one ei9jz's evidence supports.

THE SHAPE TO TEST FIRST, cheapest decisive experiment:
  Add a native f64 multiply gated to SMALL n only (the regime where dispatch dominates), taking the
  existing zero-copy machinery the other five binops already use. Measure the route at n=256 against
  NumPy. If it does not win at 256 it will not win anywhere, and the lane closes for one build.

GATES, all learned the hard way in ei9jz and rz8g0:
 - Parity first: bit-identical results including signed zeros, NaN payloads and non-contiguous
   inputs, or the route must decline. The five existing binops all DEFER to NumPy on their hard
   cases; match that discipline rather than inventing edge-case behaviour.
 - Pin OPENBLAS/OMP/MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 for any counted measurement; perf stat counts the OpenBLAS
   spinners at 15.5x inflation and the inflation is time-proportional, so it does not cancel.
 - Take instruction counts alongside wall clock (0.08% vs 4.8-6.1% spread).
 - Quote the WORST cell, not the best - and note the worst cell for a size-gated route is the size
   just above the gate, which is exactly what deadlock-audit-q00ev found for f64 divide.
 - Beware: a size gate that wins at 256 and loses at 2^16 is a REGRESSION for anyone above the gate
   unless the gate is set from measurement rather than guessed.

Filed by SlateFinch on the evidence from ei9jz; not started.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FEASIBILITY READ, no build. The experiment is far cheaper than this bead assumed - the machinery already exists and multiply is excluded by a one-line policy decision, not by a missing capability.

THREE PREREQUISITES, all already satisfied:

 1. THE KERNEL EXISTS. fnp-ufunc's BinaryOp enum already has Add, Sub and Mul alongside Div, Power,
    Remainder, Minimum, Maximum. Nothing needs writing.

 2. THERE IS NO SIZE FLOOR FOR NON-DIV OPS. f64_binary_route_is_worth_taking and
    f64_out_route_is_worth_taking both open with `if !matches!(op, BinaryOp::Div) { return true; }`.
    The entire F64_DIV_*_MIN_LEN gating machinery is divide-specific. A multiply routed natively
    would be accepted at ANY size, n=256 included, with no new gate.

 3. THE KERNEL IS SERIAL AT SMALL n. BINARY_PARALLEL_MIN_LEN is 1<<15 (32768), so at n=256 the
    kernel takes a plain serial loop - no rayon dispatch, which would otherwise be fatal in exactly
    the regime this bead targets.

SO THE EXPERIMENT IS: add `UFuncKind::Multiply => Some(BinaryOp::Mul)` to the binop match in
PyUFunc::__call__. One line, one build, one measurement. Not "new machinery".

PARITY IS TRIVIAL FOR THESE THREE OPS, WHICH IS THE IRONY. The ops excluded from the native set are
the ones EASIEST to make bit-exact. A real f64 multiply is a single rounded operation; so are add
and subtract. There is no FMA-contraction hazard, because contraction requires a multiply-add PAIR -
the concern that governs complex multiply (where numpy IS contracted and our kernel must fuse to
match) simply does not arise for a lone real multiply. Compare divide, which carries the FE-hazard
classifier and a whole gating apparatus, and power/remainder, which need careful edge-case deferral.

THE REAL DESIGN QUESTION, and it is the opposite of divide's: at LARGE n our serial kernel competes
with NumPy's own SIMD loop and will lose, so multiply likely needs an UPPER size bound - route
natively below some n, delegate above it. Divide's gate is a lower bound plus a decline BAND; this
one would be a ceiling. Anyone implementing must measure the crossover rather than guess it, and
must quote the WORST cell, which for a ceiling-gated route is the size just below the ceiling.

WHY IT WAS EXCLUDED, as recorded in the file's own comments: "f64 mul is SIMD-bound, no parallel
win". That is an argument about PARALLELISM and it is correct on its own terms. It does not address
the small-n regime, where almost nothing is arithmetic and the cost is dispatch on both sides.

STILL NOT MEASURED, and the order-of-magnitude case in this bead's description still rests on three
different instruments - do not treat it as a prediction. The one-line change plus a single counted
measurement at n=256 settles it either way, and that is now a cheap question to answer rather than a
project.

TEST BURDEN, and it is the part that would have produced FALSE CONFIDENCE. Read-only, no build.

The one-line change routes f64 multiply to the existing zero-copy ndarray kernel. The obvious question is whether current tests would catch a mistake in it. They would not.

  native array multiply was arbitrarily wrong.

That is this repo's recurring failure shape, already recorded twice in the ledger: a green conformance test on a route the change does not touch proves nothing, and green parity does not prove kernel ENGAGEMENT. Anyone landing the one-liner on the strength of "the multiply tests still pass" would be repeating it.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY NEEDED, in the order it should be written:

 1. AN ENGAGEMENT PROOF FIRST, before any parity test. Parity tests pass trivially while the route
    declines, so they cannot tell you the kernel ran. The existing pattern to copy is
    out_route_divide_matches_numpy_on_both_sides_of_the_size_gate (lib.rs:163459), which is

    when they should differ.

    discipline rather than invent behaviour.

    divide: divide's gate is a lower bound plus a decline band, multiply's would be an upper bound,
    so "just above the gate" and "just below" swap roles and the WORST cell is just BELOW the
    ceiling.

(single rounded op, no FMA-contraction hazard), but the TEST work is the real body of it - four test

comments.text:
REJECT, on the first measurement, and the rejection is mine to own - I filed this bead and argued for it.

  n=256, native f64 multiply on the plain binary route, isolated worktree off 63049f59:
    numpy_plain 3,193,711,032 (spread 0.064%)  wall 0.6803 s
    fnp_plain   7,318,017,189 (spread 0.262%)  wall 1.0518 s
    excess over NumPy 10,310.8 insns/call vs the delegating baseline's 1830.5  = 5.63x WORSE
    fnp/numpy wall clock 1.545x SLOWER

REGISTERED PREDICTIONS, scored: SIGN (native is faster) REFUTED. MAGNITUDE band 0.45-0.85 REFUTED at 1.545. ENGAGEMENT confirmed - fnp's instruction count moved 1.86x, so the arm took. PARITY passed on all 5 arms against the probe's built-in NumPy oracle, which would have panicked on a wrong answer. The route engages and computes NumPy's result; it is simply much slower.

WHY MY ARGUMENT FAILED. I reasoned that at n=256 the arithmetic is ~20 ns and the rest is dispatch, so removing NumPy's dispatch must win. The premise was right and the conclusion did not follow: taking the native route is not free. It swaps NumPy's dispatch for OUR zero-copy entry - buffer acquisition on both operands, dtype and contiguity validation, output construction, write-back - and that bundle costs ~10,300 insns/call more than the delegation it replaces, with only 256 elements of work to amortise it.

I also dismissed the historical exclusion ("f64 mul is SIMD-bound, no parallel win") as a parallelism argument that "does not address the small-n regime". It does not - and small n turns out to be WORSE, not better, for a reason that argument never mentioned. The exclusion was right; my critique of its reasoning was correct and irrelevant.

THE USEFUL RESIDUE, which is why this was worth one build: the measurement bounds any future native route for these ops. Entry cost must come under ~1830 insns/call before per-element work matters at all, because that is what delegation costs end to end. The five ops that ARE routed natively clear that bar only because their per-element work is expensive enough to amortise the same entry cost - a sharper statement of the size gate than "SIMD-bound".

DO NOT retry as a size-gated route with a lower gate. The cost measured here is per-CALL entry overhead, not per-element, so it does not shrink with n. A retry is justified only after the zero-copy entry cost itself is reduced, and that is wrapper work - which the corrected ei9jz split now identifies as the larger half (64%) of the delegating route's excess anyway.

comments.text:
INVESTIGATION by AzureHill 2026-08-06. Narrowed the mechanism and RULED OUT two hypotheses; root cause still needs a numpy-2.2.4 worker.

RULED OUT #1 - 'an early ? aborts the registration and the caller swallows it'. The enclosing function IS the #[pymodule] entry point itself (crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs:105644-105645, '#[pymodule] pub fn fnp_python(m) -> PyResult<()>'), so any ? propagates straight to Python and would make exec_module RAISE. The failing tests import fnp SUCCESSFULLY and only then find char absent. So the 'if let Ok(...)' guard is genuinely what skipped - numpy.getattr("char") really returned Err on those workers.

RULED OUT #2 - 'numpy deprecates np.char so the getattr warns/raises'. Read numpy's module __getattr__ directly (numpy 2.4.3): the char branch is a plain 'import numpy.char as char; return char' with no warning and no deprecation path. Same for strings.

ESTABLISHED. Both numpy.char and numpy.strings are LAZY - after 'import numpy' neither is in sys.modules (unlike numpy.linalg and numpy.matrixlib, which are eager). So these two guards depend entirely on numpy's module-level __getattr__ lazy loader firing correctly inside a C-extension module init. Note the ASYMMETRY with the neighbouring blocks in the same function: fft and linalg use py.import("numpy.fft") / py.import("numpy.linalg"), while strings and char use numpy.getattr(...). Only the getattr ones fail.

THAT ASYMMETRY IS THE LEAD. py.import("numpy.char") bypasses numpy's __getattr__ dispatch entirely and is what the working siblings already do. Switching to py.import with a getattr fallback is both a plausible real fix and strictly more robust, regardless of what 2.2.4 does differently.

DELIVERABLE SHAPE UNCHANGED (see description): resolve via py.import first, fall back to getattr, and on total failure record 'name -> ExcType: message' into a module attribute so the NEXT failing run names the cause instead of the consequence. rch exec refuses non-compilation commands, so shipping the instrument is the only way to learn what 2.2.4 actually does.

UNPACKBITS IS CONFIRMED SEPARATE - split out to its own bead, do not chase it here.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
ROOT CAUSE OBTAINED by AzureHill 2026-08-06, commit 3756a66f. The instrument worked, after I fixed the instrument.

FIRST, MY OWN BUG. The diagnostic I shipped could not report, because it was defeated by the exact condition it exists to explain: it built one dict literal whose values touched fnp.char.startswith directly, so on a host where char is missing the AttributeError fired during dict CONSTRUCTION and killed the script before __submodule_import_errors__ ever printed. Rewritten so the errors dict and numpy version print FIRST, unconditionally, with every probe behind a guard.

THE ANSWER, ovh-a, numpy 2.2.4:
  SUBMODULE_IMPORT_ERRORS {'char': "import numpy.char failed (AttributeError: module 'numpy.strings' has no attribute 'slice'); getattr fallback also failed (AttributeError: module 'numpy.strings' has no attribute 'slice')"}

numpy.strings.slice did not exist until NumPy 2.3. On 2.2.4 the numpy.char import chain itself raises, and BOTH of our routes hit the identical failure - the explicit import numpy.char, and the getattr fallback, which internally performs that same import. So fnp is not wrongly declining: NumPy's OWN char import fails in that environment, and declining is the correct response. This also kills my earlier working theory that the lazy __getattr__ dispatch was at fault; the dispatch is fine, the import behind it is not.

THE RESOLVER FIXED SOMETHING REAL, measured on the same worker class. conformance_strings_namespace now passes 9/0 on 2.2.4, where strings_namespace_attached_and_preserves_numpy_surface was one of the 18 reds at pristine HEAD. 'strings' resolves via py.import("numpy.strings") where plain attribute access had failed. Only 'char' remains. No regression: conformance_submodule_reexports is 9/0 on vmi1227854 (2.4.x) in the same sweep.

OPEN QUESTION worth one probe before anyone 'fixes' this: is that 2.2.4 install BROKEN, or does stock numpy 2.2.4 genuinely fail 'import numpy.char'? A stock 2.2.4 that cannot import its own char module would be remarkable, so suspect the install (or a shadowing numpy.strings on that worker) first. The error text is now printed by the test on every failing run, so the next person gets it for free.

WHAT CLOSES THIS BEAD, updated and narrower than before: either (a) the 2.2.4 workers get a numpy whose char imports, and the shard goes green with __submodule_import_errors__ == {}, or (b) the supported-oracle-floor decision in 1jqrw declares 2.2.4 out of scope. Note this is now the FOURTH independent symptom pointing at that same decision.

title: [perf][fnp-python] fnp.divide has never been measured against numpy.divide - the whole FE-hazard family is self-speedup only
description:

Nobody has ever run fnp.divide against numpy.divide, so we do not know whether the route we have been optimising is ahead of or behind the incumbent on a core surface.

title: [test][fnp-python] nothing asserts fnp's own submodule __all__ names resolve - fft copies numpy's __all__ but adds a hardcoded 18
description:
COVERAGE GAP, adjacent to a real past incident. conformance_module_metadata.rs
asserts that importing fnp does not corrupt NUMPY's __all__ and that
`from numpy import *` still works (deadlock-audit-335rd - the scipy breakage).
Nothing asserts the CONVERSE: that every name in fnp's OWN submodule __all__
actually resolves on fnp, i.e. that `from fnp_python.fft import *` works.

TWO MECHANISMS MAKE THAT FAIL SILENTLY, both visible in the module-init block:

1. __all__ is COPIED FROM NUMPY while the attributes are a HARDCODED LIST.
   numpy.fft's block sets
       fft_module.setattr("__all__", copied_all_names(&all_names)?)
   from numpy.fft.__all__, but only adds the 18 names in its own `fft_names`
   array, and its __getattr__ handles ONLY 'test' - everything else raises
   AttributeError. Measured today: numpy.fft.__all__ is exactly those 18, so
   there is no live gap. The moment numpy adds an fft name, fnp.fft.__all__
   advertises a name getattr refuses and star-import dies.

2. The registration loops SKIP SILENTLY:
       for (numpy_name, flat_name) in [...] {
           if let Ok(value) = m.getattr(flat_name) { linalg.add(numpy_name, value)?; }
       }
   If the fnp function behind a mapped name is ever renamed or removed, the name
   is quietly not added while __all__ still advertises it. linalg advertises
   numpy.linalg.__all__ (32 names, verified to match its public-name list
   exactly today), so any such skip is invisible until a user star-imports.

Neither is a defect I can demonstrate on today's numpy - this is a LOCK against
a class that has already bitten this project once from the other direction, and
it is cheap.

PROBE TO CLOSE: a no-mock conformance test that, for every fnp submodule that
declares __all__ (random, linalg, fft, ma, char, strings, polynomial, rec,
testing, lib, emath/scimath if present), asserts (a) every name in that __all__
resolves via getattr on the fnp submodule, listing any that do not, and (b)
`from fnp_python.<sub> import *` succeeds - the star-import being the assertion
that stays meaningful if __all__ is ever populated a different way, exactly the
doctrine conformance_module_metadata.rs already states for the numpy direction.
Green on a named worker with its numpy version cited.

Note for whoever runs it: fnp is loaded via importlib from a .so path in these
tests, so a submodule star-import must be spelled through the module object
(exec("from fnp_python.fft import *") only works if the parent is registered in
sys.modules) - use the module object's __all__ plus getattr, and additionally
register the loaded module in sys.modules so the real star-import spelling is
exercised too. If that registration turns out not to be possible in this
harness, say so rather than dropping the star-import half.
close_reason:
DELIVERED in 7597b3bf as a LOCK. No live defect is claimed - stated up front because the honest result here is 'the gap is latent, not open'.

WHAT WAS MISSING: conformance_module_metadata.rs guards the NUMPY direction (importing fnp must not corrupt numpy's __all__; from numpy import * must still work - the scipy breakage, deadlock-audit-335rd). Nothing guarded the converse, that every name fnp's OWN submodule __all__ advertises resolves on it.

TWO SILENT-FAILURE MECHANISMS, both read off the module-init block:
  1. numpy.fft's block sets __all__ from numpy.fft.__all__ (copied at runtime) but adds only the 18 names in its own hardcoded fft_names array, and its __getattr__ handles ONLY 'test'. I measured numpy.fft.__all__ against that list: exactly the same 18, so there is NO gap today. The day numpy adds an fft name, fnp.fft.__all__ advertises a name getattr refuses and star-import raises.
  2. The registration loops are 'if let Ok(value) = m.getattr(flat_name)' - a silent skip. Rename or drop the fnp function behind a mapped name and it is quietly not added while __all__ still advertises it. linalg advertises all 32 names of numpy.linalg.__all__ (verified: its hardcoded public-name list matches upstream exactly, 32/32), so such a skip would be invisible until a user star-imports.

TEST submodule_all_names_resolve_and_star_import_works walks every fnp submodule with a non-empty __all__, getattrs each advertised name, and registers the importlib-loaded module in sys.modules so the REAL spelling 'from fnp_python.<sub> import *' is exercised rather than getattr alone. The star-import half is load-bearing for the reason the neighbouring test's own docstring gives: it survives __all__ being populated a different way.

VACUITY GUARD, and this one is copied from that same docstring's scar tissue: a third assertion requires at least 3 submodules to have been checked. Without it, both empty-list assertions would pass if no submodule declared __all__ at all - which is precisely the 'structurally unable to fail' trap the neighbouring test records having shipped once (its leak baseline compared the corrupted list with itself and reported 0 leaked names in a run whose star-import was already broken). The guard is satisfied in the green run.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_module_metadata = 7 passed / 0 failed, exit 0, oracle numpy 2.4.3, with the >=3-submodule guard satisfied. cargo clippy -p fnp-python --test conformance_module_metadata -- -D warnings exit 0. cargo fmt --check -p fnp-python exit 0. All exit codes captured directly.

HOW THIS PROBE WAS FOUND: the signature-audit vein that produced 9w6uj / mkqw2 / khu6f / 2mikq / v0mxm / mi3k6 is exhausted (submodule line closed by 1jlkg), so this is a different probe class - comparing fnp's DECLARED public surface against what it can actually serve, rather than comparing signatures. Sibling probes in the same class not yet run: return-TYPE parity (numpy scalar vs 0-d array), exception-CLASS parity, and dtype-preservation per wrapper.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
MEASURED DIAGNOSIS by CreamGlen 2026-08-09 - and it CORRECTS the premise I filed this bead with. I wrote 'split or speed up the per-case subprocess', assuming 42 tests x python startup overhead. That is wrong.

THE CAUSE IS ONE TEST. Running the compiled shard binary directly named it: flat_multi_quantile_and_weighted_average_track_numpy (crates/fnp-python/tests/conformance_nan_funcs.rs:1104-1376, 274 lines) was still running after 60s while everything else had finished.

  timeout 120 cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_nan_funcs -- --skip flat_multi_quantile_and_weighted_average
    = 41 passed / 0 failed in 9.03s

So 41 tests cost 9s and the 42nd costs >110s. Subprocess overhead is not the problem and reducing oracle calls would not help.

WHY IT IS SLOW, and why it must not simply be shrunk: it builds two 8_000_000-element arrays plus a 2896x2896 matrix plus a 64x512x256 tensor, and runs multi-q quantile/percentile/nanpercentile/nanquantile byte-parity against numpy on BOTH sides across flat, last-axis, axis-0, 3-D strided, nan-compaction, keepdims and warning surfaces. THE SIZES ARE LOAD-BEARING: they are chosen to cross the native parallel dispatch gates (cf. the 1<<19 percentile gate), so shrinking the arrays would silently move the test onto the serial path and stop exercising what it exists to exercise. This is real conformance value, not a perf-only probe, despite the SURFACE_PROBE_AB rows it also prints.

TWO OPTIONS, both needing a human call - I deliberately did NOT pick one:
  (a) SPLIT the test into its own shard (e.g. conformance_nan_funcs_wide.rs, copying the file-local numpy_oracle/fnp_script helpers as every other shard does). Keeps default CI coverage intact and makes the remaining 41 verifiable in ~9s. Cost: a 274-line move.
  (b) Mark it #[ignore] with a run command, matching the existing fnp-ufunc convention for heavy probes. One line, but it REMOVES byte-parity-at-scale from default runs - that is a reduction in CI coverage, i.e. gate self-weakening, which is not mine to decide unilaterally.

I recommend (a). Leaving this bead OPEN rather than closing it on the diagnosis alone.

comments.text:
SCOPE BROADENED - this is a CLASS, not one shard. Measured by CreamGlen 2026-08-09 across the largest fnp-python conformance shards, each run with a 120s cap:

  conformance_nan_funcs      >120s  1 slow test  (flat_multi_quantile_and_weighted_average_track_numpy; 41 others = 9.03s)
  conformance_unravel_unique >120s  >=4 slow     (add_at_i64_large_target_parallel_matches_numpy, int_sort_class_stale_basis_probe_and_parity, setops_nd_flat_view_matches_numpy, unique_nd_flat_view_matches_numpy)
  conformance_setops         >120s  >=3 slow     (unique_and_sort_string_packed_latin1_large_matches_numpy, unique_full_string_packed_latin1_large_matches_numpy, unique_packed_wide_latin1_u9_u16_matches_numpy)
  conformance_ufunc_edge      58.88s  70 passed  - under the cap but within a factor of two of it
  conformance_einsum          40.10s  40 passed

So at least THREE shards cannot be verified inside a 120s budget, and a fourth is close. The common shape is the same one diagnosed on nan_funcs: a handful of large-array probes whose sizes are LOAD-BEARING because they cross native parallel dispatch gates (add_at large target, packed-latin1 wide-key unique, nd flat-view setops). Shrinking them would move the test onto the serial path and stop exercising what it exists to exercise, so 'make it faster' is not available without losing the point of the test.

CONSEQUENCE for anyone auditing this suite: a per-shard cap silently truncates. Twice this session a batched run reported verdicts for some shards while leaving another mid-execution - absence of evidence that reads exactly like a pass unless you check the Running/test-result line counts. Any sweep over these shards must either run them individually with a longer budget or check that every binary reported.

RECOMMENDATION unchanged in shape but now wider: split the heavy probes out of each shard into a companion 'wide' shard (conformance_<x>_wide.rs), so the fast conformance body stays verifiable in seconds and the heavy parity probes run on a longer budget. That is mechanical per shard, preserves all coverage, and changes no semantics. Still not doing it unilaterally at this size - it is now roughly 8+ tests across 3 files.

title: [perf][fnp-python] price PyUFunc::__call__'s 9-parameter signature - the largest never-measured stage of the unattributed 1444 ns
description:
THE LARGEST NEVER-PRICED STAGE ON THE PER-CALL FLOOR. deadlock-audit-ei9jz measured 1444 ns - 60.3% - of a 2394 ns fnp.multiply(f64, n=256) call as attributed to NO named stage, on worker=thinkstation1, elf ef5467cb2a43c00b. This turn (RedLynx) named a large part of it by READING the route: the delegating f64 route was paying up to THREE py.import("numpy") calls per invocation at 400 ns each (one in PyUFunc::__call__, one in the always-declining try_zerocopy_f16_binary_widen, one more in the per-family probe). Those are removed in e4cdd808, f8475a76, e42056a3, 5c7735da - all UNBUILT, all pending a gate.

WHAT IS LEFT ON THE LIST, and it is the biggest thing on it: PyO3 ARGUMENT HANDLING for PyUFunc::__call__'s nine-parameter signature.

  #[pyo3(signature = (x1, x2, /, out=None, *, where=None, casting="same_kind",
                      order="K", dtype=None, subok=true, signature=None))]

Every invocation parses two positionals and seven keyword-or-default parameters, and takes x1/x2 as OWNED Py<PyAny> rather than borrowed &Bound<'_, PyAny> - so each operand costs an incref on the way in and a decref on the way out, plus a .bind(py) at every use site. deadlock-audit-cydda bounded the four obvious stages at 700 ns combined and concluded the remainder is "argument handling and this call shape"; nobody has priced it.

TWO CANDIDATE LEVERS, to be measured before either is written:
  1. x1/x2 as &Bound<'_, PyAny> instead of Py<PyAny>. Removes two refcount round-trips per call and every .bind(py). Mechanical but touches many lines in __call__, so it needs a compiler and a real conformance gate, not a build-free edit.
  2. A #[pyo3(signature = (*args, **kwargs))] fast entry that hands the all-defaults shape straight to the route and only parses the full signature when kwargs are actually present. The all-defaults shape is the common case - deadlock-audit-s2fkk already found and removed a 727 ns cost on exactly that argument, by omitting kwargs whose values equalled numpy's defaults.

MEASURE IT THE WAY THE LAST SIX ROWS WERE MEASURED, and this is the part that decides whether the bead is worth anything: an isolated same-invocation control FIRST. Two #[pyfunction]s in the bench binary that do IDENTICAL trivial work and differ ONLY in their signature shape - one carrying the nine-parameter signature above, one taking (*args, **kwargs) - called with the same all-defaults operand pair, ONE binary, ONE invocation, ABBAABBA, A/A null first. That prices the signature itself rather than the route.

DECISION RULE, WRITTEN BEFORE THE MEASUREMENT: if the signature-shape control saves clearly more than ~150 ns, take lever 2 and re-price. If it is about zero, the nine-parameter signature is NOT the unattributed cost and this whole line closes - which is a result worth having, because it would leave the remainder in PyO3's call machinery itself and redirect the hunt there rather than at our own code. Either way, bank the row.

DO NOT DIVIDE INTO A FLOOR FROM ANOTHER WORKER. SlateHeron's correction on v8nx6 (0e16367b) records exactly that error costing a wrong conclusion: dividing 586 ns by a cross-worker "7-8 us" floor read as 7-8% and closed a line that, against the SAME-HOST 2394 ns floor, is ~24.5% of the call. Take the floor from the same ELF and host.

CONSTRAINT: df -h /data before building; below 52G do build-free work and retry.
close_reason: Priced: the 9-parameter signature costs ~10ns of a ~210ns floor (<5%). Varargs rewrite REJECTED as a large correctness risk for a twentieth of the floor. See NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE row 2026-08-16.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
LEDGER PREFLIGHT (orders 4) FROM THE AUTHOR OF ei9jz - NOT taking this bead, handing you the negative evidence before you spend a build on it.

YOUR HEADLINE HYPOTHESIS IS ALREADY REFUTED. deadlock-audit-7ocfa, docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md line 813: 'PyO3 nine-parameter argument binding costs NOTHING resolvable, so it is not the PyUFunc::__call__ wrapper floor'. TealOak measured it BEFORE touching the signature, with the right control: two #[pyfunction]s with IDENTICAL bodies differing ONLY in binding signature - probe_nine reproducing __call__'s exact nine-parameter shape against probe_varargs taking (*args, **kwargs) and parsing nothing. One binary, one invocation, ABBAABBA, A/A null. Result: nine_param_ns=60.0, varargs_ns=60.0, binding_cost_ns=0.0, ratio_median=1.000000.

That row states its own caveat honestly: at a 60 ns call the harness is at its resolution floor and the A/A null itself read 1.071429, so it does NOT claim exactly zero - it claims the cost is below a ~4 ns noise floor against a multi-microsecond wrapper floor, three orders of magnitude apart.

ITS RETRY PREDICATE, which this bead has not discharged: 'Reopen ONLY if a probe shows a per-call cost that scales with the NUMBER of declared parameters - e.g. the same two probes at 3, 9 and 20 parameters.' Run that scaling probe first. If cost is flat in parameter count, the parameter-count half of this bead is closed and no signature rewrite is justified.

WHAT IN YOUR BEAD 7ocfa DID **NOT** COVER, and is worth keeping: the OWNERSHIP half. You note x1/x2 are taken as owned Py<PyAny> rather than borrowed &Bound<'_, PyAny>, costing an incref per operand. 7ocfa's probes differed in SIGNATURE SHAPE, not in ownership, so incref/decref traffic was plausibly present in both arms and would have cancelled in the ratio. That mechanism is untested and is a legitimate separate lever - but it needs its own control (owned vs borrowed, same parameter count), not a nine-vs-varargs rerun.

ALSO: 7ocfa's row warns why the rewrite it would have justified is risky, not cosmetic - moving __call__ to (*args, **kwargs) means hand-parsing the keyword surface of every binary ufunc, the same class of change that previously drifted NumPy's keyword surface (where= was once exposed as where_arg, recorded in the reduce comment in lib.rs).

OVERLAP WITH MY IN-FLIGHT WORK, so we do not double-measure: bench_percall_floor_partition (landed a53b870f, UNRUN, blocked on the 52G disk brake) partitions the same delegating call into numpy_multiply_ns / probe_chain_ns / wrapper_residual_ns. Whatever this bead's stage costs, it sits INSIDE wrapper_residual_ns. Running my partition first bounds your stage from above for free - if wrapper_residual_ns comes back small, this bead is bounded small regardless of mechanism.

Finally, per the provenance row I banked in a53b870f: the 1444 ns / 2394 ns figures this bead cites are PRE-FIX, from an ELF built off an uncommitted tree before e4cdd808 and f8475a76 removed those per-call imports. Do not size this lever against them without re-measuring from a committed SHA.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
SCOPING DATA THAT CHANGES THIS BEAD'S PRIORITY - measured, not argued. From the multiply route sweep on thinkstation1 (existing ELF ef5467cb2a43c00b, numpy 2.4.3, dual-null contract, banked 74b1ca9e):

  n=2^8   ratio 0.166734  excess_ns 2044
  n=2^12  ratio 0.472202  excess_ns 2159
  n=2^16  ratio 0.839072  excess_ns 2991
  n=2^20  ratio 0.965590  excess_ns 9809
  n=2^24  ratio 0.998075  excess_ns 5425   UNDECIDED, at_parity=true

excess_ns is roughly CONSTANT across six orders of magnitude of n. That is the signature of a fixed per-call floor, not a per-element deficit - and it means THE ROUTE REACHES PARITY WITH NUMPY BY 2^24. The wrapper floor is a small-n phenomenon.

WHY THIS MATTERS TO t4lri: this bead is sized against '1444 ns of a 2394 ns call', i.e. against the n=256 regime, where we are 6x slower. That regime is real but it is the regime where the per-call floor is 100% of the work. Whatever fraction of the floor the nine-parameter signature turns out to own, its ABSOLUTE value is bounded by ~2-10 us per call and it buys nothing at all above ~2^20. Worth knowing before choosing between this and a lever that moves large-n throughput.

AND THE LARGE-n LOSS IS SOMEWHERE ELSE ENTIRELY. At n=2^20 multiply reads 0.9656 while divide reads 0.845461 on the SAME route - divide's excess over numpy is 9.52x multiply's. Normalising each side against its own multiply: numpy divide costs 1.2100x its multiply, ours 1.4032x ours, ratio-of-ratios 1.1597. So ~16% sits on the divide path that the route does not explain, which is deadlock-audit-0ppym, not this bead.

Combined with the 7ocfa preflight I left earlier (nine-parameter binding measured at 0.0 ns with an undischarged retry predicate), my read is: run 7ocfa's parameter-count scaling probe FIRST, cheaply. If cost is flat in parameter count, this bead closes without a signature rewrite - and that rewrite is the risky one, since hand-parsing the keyword surface is what previously drifted numpy's where= to where_arg.

comments.author: RedLynx
comments.text:
TRIAGE CONTROL LANDED, UNBUILT (d5bbafdb): bench_signature_keyword_binding_cost, registered in the group table.

I did NOT take the clean experiment, and the reason is a risk trade worth recording. Pricing a nine-parameter signature against (*args, **kwargs) needs two new #[pyclass]es with __call__. NO bench in this crate has ever declared a pyclass, so that is first-of-its-kind macro surface in a binary every other group shares, and it cannot be compiled while the build freeze holds (/data at the 42G floor). Landing an unverifiable macro expansion there risks a red bench for the whole fleet the moment builds resume.

WHAT LANDED INSTEAD, using the real route and no new types: both arms call the shipped ufunc and are semantically all-defaults, because the route's gate compares keyword VALUES not presence. Passing casting='same_kind', order='K', subok=True and out/where/dtype/signature=None leaves all seven gate conditions true, so the probe block still runs and the fast delegation tail is still chosen. The only difference is whether PyO3 binds seven keywords out of a dict or fills them from its own defaults. Parity is checksum-checked before either arm is timed.

THE DECISION RULE, written before the measurement: if binding seven PRESENT keywords is cheap, then filling seven defaults is cheaper still, PyO3's keyword machinery is not where ei9jz's 702 ns lives, and this whole bead can be closed WITHOUT writing the pyclass experiment - the better outcome. If it is expensive, the pyclass work is justified and should be done once builds are allowed.

WHAT IT CANNOT DECIDE, and the emitted row says so via prices_binding_present_keywords_NOT_eager_vs_lazy=true: this is not eager-versus-lazy binding on the hot path. The hot path passes NO keywords, and this control cannot isolate what PyO3 spends filling defaults there. It bounds the family; it does not price the lever. Do not close this bead on a cheap reading alone without stating that limit.

RUN IT WITH: <elf> --bench fnp-group=bench_signature_keyword_binding_cost. The elf must be rebuilt - the one at target/release/deps/criterion_python_elementwise-b3bfa783f49ff1ab predates this group. AGENT_NAME=RedLynx.

title: [perf][fnp-linalg] recursive (cache-oblivious) Cholesky to kill the scalar diagonal factor — residual 1.4-1.7x vs numpy after panel fix
close_reason: NO-SHIP (implemented + A/B-proven regression). Implemented in-place recursive (cache-oblivious) potrf: split sz->h+h, recurse L11, parallel TRSM (packed L11 + contiguous l21), then trailing SYRK via packed_gemm_sub_assign_strided. Tried both full-square SYRK (2x flops, lost badly) and lower-only tiled SYRK (half flops). Env-gated A/B (CHOL_REC=1 vs 0, same binary). Result: recursive REGRESSES or ties the existing cholesky_blocked at every size (n640 blocked 1.19x vs recursive 3.19x; n896 2.37 vs 2.57; n1024 2.10 vs 2.17; n1536 1.67 vs 1.63; n2048 1.71 vs 1.85). Parity was GOOD (allclose vs numpy, recon<1e-9). WHY: cholesky_blocked is already well-tuned — at panel=32 its trailing update is a hand-written PARALLEL lower-only rank-32 SYRK (cache-resident l21), not a skinny serial GEMM as I'd assumed; the recursion's per-level l21/l11/bblk allocations + transpose-pack + deeper call tree outweigh the larger-rank GEMM benefit. ROOT GAP IS FMA, NOT STRUCTURE: numpy=OpenBLAS 0.3.31 (Haswell AVX2+FMA); fnp packed_gemm at n=1024 = 76 GF/s vs OpenBLAS 97 GF/s = 1.28x, because .cargo/config disables +fma (for bit-exact parity; mul_add compiles to SOFTWARE fma w/o the feature). Cholesky's 1.4-1.7x residual is floor-limited by this same ~1.28x GEMM throughput gap. Closing it needs hardware FMA via #[target_feature]/std::arch (unsafe) OR loosening matmul/LU bit-exact conformance to allclose — both are the 8vdtg arch decision. Recursive potrf cannot beat the FMA floor and adds overhead, so it's not the lever. Reverted.

title: perf: the fresh-input surcharge scales with THREAD COUNT (0us at T=1, 706us at T=64, n=2^17) and pool WIDTH costs 1.35x independently of chunk count - the chunk gate contains both without explaining either
description:
RESIDUAL FROM deadlock-audit-iwt3o. The chunk-floor fix shipped and removed every standing loss
in the band, but it did NOT explain everything, and the leftovers point at a cost the kernel
cannot currently reach.

TWO COSTS, NOT ONE. Post-gate at n=2^18 the sqrt kernel runs 2 chunks in a 64-THREAD pool and
takes 128 us. Pre-gate, 2 chunks in a 2-THREAD pool took 95 us. Same n, same chunking, same
work - the only difference is how many rayon workers exist to be woken. So:

  (a) how many threads TOUCH a freshly-mapped input. LARGE. This is what the chunk gate fixes,
      and it is why the fresh-input ("np-written") cell improved 1.1-9.1x from 2^17 to 2^22.
  (b) how many workers WAKE on job injection. SMALLER but real, ~1.35x at 2^18, and a kernel
      choosing par_chunks size CANNOT influence it - chunk count is not pool width.

(b) is why the fix has a price on a SETTLED input, which has no fresh buffer and therefore only
pays (b): neutral at 2^17-2^19, better at 2^22, but 1.05-1.26x WORSE at 2^20-2^21 (0.169x ->
0.213x and 0.214x -> 0.243x, on cells still winning 4-5x). Fewer chunks leaves 56 already-woken
workers idle.

WHAT (a) ACTUALLY IS, STILL UNKNOWN. The parent bead pre-registered and REFUTED page-fault storm
(ru_minflt 0.0-0.4 per call for every arm) and glibc mmap churn (mallopt with M_MMAP_THRESHOLD
and M_TRIM_THRESHOLD at 512 MiB moved 1.399x to 1.388x). This bead adds the decisive shape those
two never had: THE PENALTY SCALES WITH THREAD COUNT. At n=2^17 the settled kernel costs 92 us at
T=1 and 91 us at T=64, while the composed one costs 129 us at T=1 and 834 us at T=64 - so the
fresh-input surcharge is ~0 us at T=1, ~133 us at T=4 and ~706 us at T=64, against an np.abs that
costs only 37 us. A per-thread first-touch or cross-core ownership cost fits; nothing that is
purely per-call does.

WHY IT IS WORTH CHASING: (a) is the difference between a 0.59x win and a 5.3x loss at 2^17. The
gate contains it by using fewer threads, but if the mechanism were addressed directly the kernel
could keep BOTH the wide fan-out and the win, and (b)'s price would disappear with it.

WHAT WOULD DECIDE IT, in rough order of cost:
  - perf c2c / HITM counters on the composed vs settled cell at fixed n and T (the parent bead
    named this and it was never run)
  - NUMA: is the fresh buffer's first touch landing all pages on the writing thread's node? Try
    numactl --interleave and see whether the T-scaling of the surcharge flattens
  - madvise/THP: a fresh 1-16 MiB mapping may be served by huge pages differently than a settled
    one; compare /proc/self/smaps AnonHugePages for the two inputs
  - whether the surcharge survives when the fresh buffer is written by the SAME 64 threads that
    read it (the "fnp-written" cell of h2h_sqrt_threads, which round 1 measured at 0.51x-0.68x
    against 1.12x for np-written at the same n and T - suggestive, never isolated)

TOOL: crates/fnp-python/examples/h2h_sqrt_threads.rs already installs explicit rayon pools, so n
and T move independently in one process against one numpy, and carries the three cells.

ACCEPTANCE: a named mechanism with a measurement that distinguishes it from the alternatives, or
a recorded null saying which candidates are dead. A null is a success here - the parent bead
killed two hypotheses and that is why this one is well posed.

title: [perf][fnp-python] instrument PyBuffer acquisition and output construction - the only unexplored stages left in the wrapper floor
description:
TARGET: the ~7-8 us PyUFunc::__call__ wrapper floor (6968-8375 ns of excess on the three delegating ops, 7.97x slower than numpy at n=256). This is the campaign's worst measured gap and it is charged to EVERY fnp binary ufunc.

THE SEARCH IS NOW NARROW. Everything else named has been measured and eliminated:
  deadlock-audit-cydda: numpy re-import 310 ns, dtype guard 100 ns, getattr ndarray 70 ns, numpy.empty 220 ns = 700 ns total, <=10% of the floor.
  deadlock-audit-s2fkk: the delegation default-kwargs dict, 727 ns/call, REMOVED (2.442387x isolated control, null 1.000000).
  deadlock-audit-7ocfa: PyO3 nine-parameter argument binding, 0.0 ns - indistinguishable from (*args, **kwargs) at a 60 ns call, REFUTED.
That leaves two stages nobody has instrumented: PyBuffer::<f64>::get acquisition for both operands, and the output construction path (numpy.empty + reshape + the Bound/Py round trip back into Python).

WHY THE REMAINDER MUST BE THERE: the delegating ops (add/subtract/multiply) map to None in the f64 binop match and never take the native route at all, yet they carry the same floor. So the cost is in what __call__ does around the delegation, not in a kernel. With binding and the kwargs dict gone, buffer acquisition and result construction are what is left on that path.

METHOD - use the shape that has now worked three times, and NOT a two-build before/after. A before/after is unsound here for three live reasons: the rch fleet is heterogeneous with no pinning flag so two builds land on different workers; [profile.bench] inherits release (lto, codegen-units=1) and blows the 1800s SSH ceiling, so use --profile bench-fast; and the shared tree carries peers' uncommitted changes so an 'after' build can contain someone else's lever. Build an ISOLATED same-invocation control that holds each stage up on its own, exactly like bench_delegation_kwargs_shape and bench_pyo3_signature_binding_cost.

WATCH THE RESOLUTION FLOOR. deadlock-audit-7ocfa's probe bottomed out: at a 60 ns call two IDENTICAL arms read 7% apart from timer quantisation, so a stage cheaper than ~10 ns cannot be resolved by a single-call arm. If a stage looks like zero, either batch N calls inside one timed observation or state the floor explicitly - do not report an unresolvable stage as 'free'.

ACCEPTANCE: a row naming WORKER and HARNESS that attributes or bounds both stages, banked either way. If both are also small, that is a real result - it would mean the floor is in PyO3/CPython call dispatch itself rather than in anything fnp does, which would close this line of attack and redirect the campaign to ops where the per-call floor is amortised (large n) rather than to shaving it.
close_reason:
MEASURED, search CLOSED. Landed 070c3782.

WORKER vmi1152480, numpy 2.4.3, n=256, HARNESS batched_min_of_401_minus_empty_loop:
  PyBuffer::get both operands          302.95 ns
  output: numpy.empty + reshape       1310.34 ns
  numpy's ENTIRE add call (same run)   718.84 ns
  two stages combined                 1613.29 ns
Output construction alone is 1.8x NumPy's whole add call; the two stages together are 2.2x it - on a route whose purpose is to beat that call.

THE RESHAPE IS THE EXPENSIVE HALF, NOT THE ALLOCATION: cydda measured numpy.empty alone at 220 ns, and empty+reshape is 1310 ns here, so the reshape plus its attribute lookup is ~1.1 us. That is the single largest identified stage in the entire floor.

THE WRAPPER-FLOOR SEARCH IS NOW COMPLETE across four beads: cydda bounded four stages at 700 ns, s2fkk removed the default-kwargs dict at 727 ns, 7ocfa refuted PyO3 argument binding at 0.0 ns, and this attributes the remainder to output construction (1310 ns) and buffer acquisition (303 ns).

BATCHING WAS REQUIRED: 7ocfa's probe bottomed out at the timer floor (two IDENTICAL arms 7% apart at a 60 ns call). Each observation here runs 256 reps inside one timer minus a measured empty loop of 0.59 ns/iter, so a 10 ns stage is resolvable. This bead's own description warned about that floor and the design followed it.

LIMITS: standalone replicas are LOWER BOUNDS per stage - safe for 'this stage is expensive', unsafe for the reverse. Absolute ns are not comparable to floor figures from other workers/profiles; the sound comparison is against numpy_add_whole_call_ns measured beside them in the same invocation.

NEXT LEVER, filed as the row's retry predicate: allocate the output at its FINAL shape (numpy.empty(shape)) instead of numpy.empty(n).reshape(shape), in zerocopy_f64_binary_flat and the try_zerocopy_f64_binary wrapper that reshapes after it. Expected to recover most of the ~1.1 us. Measure with an isolated same-invocation control first, as the three preceding rows did. Do NOT attack PyBuffer acquisition first - at 302.95 ns it is a quarter of the output path.

title: perf: 95 kernels chunk by n/current_num_threads() while gating on a per-CALL floor - sqrt lost 2-5x to numpy in the band above its own floor and the same shape is repo-wide
description:
AMENDMENT 1, BlackThrush, 2026-09-01. THREE CORRECTIONS TO THIS BEAD AS FILED. Read these
before acting on the candidate list above - one of them is prior art that already solves the
problem for one family, and one demotes the family I ranked first.

(1) THE LAW IS ALREADY KNOWN HERE, AND MEASURED. `transcendental_map_f64` (lib.rs ~8677) was
fixed under `deadlock-audit-w9po3` and carries the evidence in a comment:

        threads   n=2^14    n=2^16    n=2^18
              1    0.76x     0.95x     0.98x
              8    0.80x     0.28x <-  0.33x
             32    0.76x     0.38x     0.23x <-
             64    0.73x     0.65x     0.33x
    "BOTH OPTIMA ARE ~8192 ELEMENTS PER TASK - n=2^16 peaks at 8 tasks, n=2^18 at 32, and
     65536/8 = 262144/32 = 8192. That is a size-independent rule rather than a fitted constant."

    const TRANSCENDENTAL_MIN_CHUNK: usize = 8192;
    let chunk = n.div_ceil(rayon::current_num_threads()).max(TRANSCENDENTAL_MIN_CHUNK);

So TRANSCENDENTAL_PARALLEL_MIN = 1 << 15 must be STRUCK from the worst-first list - its 512
elements/thread at the floor is exactly what the .max() already prevents. That prior work also
found a 0.65x-at-64-threads dip at n=2^16, the same shape sqrt showed, independently.

(2) THE CENSUS NEEDED THE `.max()` DISTINCTION, and now has it. Of the 95 lib.rs sites:
        10 apply `.max(..)` to the chunk - but NINE of those are `.max(1)`, a divide-by-zero
           guard and NOT a floor, so they are still candidates
         1 applies a real floor (TRANSCENDENTAL_MIN_CHUNK)
        85 are bare `n.div_ceil(rayon::current_num_threads())`
    => 94 candidates, not 95, and `.max(1)` must not be mistaken for protection when triaging.

(3) THE CONSTANT IS FAMILY-SPECIFIC. DO NOT CARRY ONE NUMBER ACROSS FAMILIES.
    transcendental (scalar-libm, compute-bound): optimum 8192 elements = 64 KiB
    sqrt (compute-bound but far cheaper per element): loss persisted up to 256 KiB chunks;
        shipped floor is SQRT_PARALLEL_MIN = 131072 elements = 1 MiB, 16x larger
    unary_map_f64 (pure memory): its floor is 1 << 21, so reusing it as the chunk floor would
        force SERIAL at n=2^21 and only reach full width at 2^27. That would be a large
        regression, and it is what the "measure, do not assume" clause exists to prevent.
    The rule that transfers is "floor the work per task"; the number does not.

(4) UNARY IS DEMOTED, on a first measurement. `negative` over n = 2^21/2^22/2^23 x
    T = 64/16/8/4/2/1, hz4: fnp WINS at every T >= 2 (0.33x-0.81x) and is at PARITY at T=1
    (0.975x-1.010x). NO CONFIGURATION LOSES, so there is no standing loss to recover here -
    at most an optimum shift, and T=16 vs T=64 at 2^23 (0.436/0.493 vs 0.414/0.448) is a wash.
    HONEST LIMIT ON THAT ROW: the run was at loadavg 20-62, most cells VOID with spreads to
    68%, so only the coarse SIGN survives it (every T>=2 row below 1.0 in both passes at all
    three sizes). The finer question - whether an optimum is worth capturing, and whether
    UNARY_PARALLEL_MIN = 1 << 21 is itself too high because it was fitted ON TOP of the
    tiny-chunk defect - is NOT decided and needs a quiet host.

REVISED WORST-FIRST LIST (chunk at the family's own floor, on a 64-thread host):
    FLOAT_POWER_PARALLEL_MIN_LEN = 16_384  -> 256 elem/task    <-- now the worst candidate
    NAN_TO_NUM_PARALLEL_MIN      = 1 << 17 -> 2048 elem/task
    INT_GCD/LCM/POW/FLOORDIV/REM/DIVMOD, TD_ADDSUB/FLOORDIV/REM, CUM_AXIS = 1 << 18 -> 4096
    PUTMASK_PARALLEL_MIN         = 1 << 19 -> 8192 elem/task (at w9po3's measured optimum)
    ISCLOSE_PARALLEL_MIN         = 1 << 20 -> 16384
    UNARY/CLIP/WHERE/TAKE_AXIS/ACCUMULATE/CUMSUM/TILE/DIFF = 1 << 21 -> 32768  [unary demoted]
  struck: TRANSCENDENTAL (already floored), SQRT (fixed, b64b5f78)

TOOL: crates/fnp-python/examples/h2h_chunk_floor.rs (renamed from h2h_sqrt_threads and now takes
the op as argv[2], since this vein needs the same grid per family).

--- as filed ---

GENERALISED FROM deadlock-audit-iwt3o, WHICH MEASURED ONE INSTANCE AND FIXED IT.

THE DEFECT SHAPE. A kernel gates parallelism on its own floor and then chunks by thread count:

    const FAMILY_PARALLEL_MIN: usize = 1 << K;
    if n >= FAMILY_PARALLEL_MIN && rayon::current_num_threads() >= 2 {
        let chunk = n.div_ceil(rayon::current_num_threads());

Those two lines disagree. The floor says "a fan-out is worth it once there are 2^K elements to
do". The chunk says "give each of 64 threads 2^K/64 elements" - which at n just above the floor
is a fan-out the SAME function has already judged not worth doing, only spelled per-thread. The
floor is checked per CALL and never per THREAD, so on a wide host every family loses its floor
by a factor of the core count.

THE ONE MEASURED INSTANCE, and it was not small. sqrt (floor 1 << 17) on hz4, 64 cores, numpy
2.5.2 live in the same invocation, thread count set by an INSTALLED rayon pool, interleaved
AB/BA with dual A/A nulls, both sweep directions, loadavg 8-12:

    n      chunk@64    fnp.sqrt(np.abs(a)) vs numpy      after chunk >= floor
    2^17    16 KiB     3.821x / 5.344x   LOSS            0.591x / 0.588x
    2^18    32 KiB     5.220x / 2.670x   LOSS            0.869x / 0.569x
    2^19    64 KiB     2.111x / 2.086x   LOSS            1.001x / 0.825x
    2^20   128 KiB     1.260x / 1.311x   LOSS            0.925x / 0.696x
    2^21   256 KiB     0.945x                            0.758x / 0.748x
Four standing LOSSES to numpy, up to 5.3x, in the band directly above the family's own floor -
and nothing marked any of them, because every benchmark that looked at sqrt looked at ONE size.

THE CENSUS, and read it as a candidate list, NOT a defect count:
    95 sites in crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs match `n.div_ceil(rayon::current_num_threads())`
    (104 across crates/, the rest in benches/examples).
Not every site is wrong. A site is a candidate exactly when its floor divided by the host's
thread count lands below roughly 1 MiB of payload, which is where the sqrt loss began. Sorting
the floors that way, WORST FIRST:

    FLOAT_POWER_PARALLEL_MIN_LEN = 16_384   -> 256 elem/thread at the floor
    TRANSCENDENTAL_PARALLEL_MIN  = 1 << 15  -> 512 elem/thread
    SQRT_PARALLEL_MIN            = 1 << 17  -> MEASURED, 3.8-5.3x, FIXED
    NAN_TO_NUM_PARALLEL_MIN      = 1 << 17  -> 2048 elem/thread
    INT_GCD/LCM/POW/FLOORDIV/REM/DIVMOD, TD_ADDSUB/FLOORDIV/REM, CUM_AXIS = 1 << 18
    PUTMASK_PARALLEL_MIN         = 1 << 19
    ISCLOSE_PARALLEL_MIN         = 1 << 20 (two sites; two more at 1 << 21)
    UNARY/CLIP/WHERE/TAKE_AXIS/ACCUMULATE/CUMSUM/TILE/DIFF = 1 << 21 -> 32768 elem/thread
The 1 << 23 / 1 << 24 byte-denominated floors are probably safe and should be checked last.

UNARY_PARALLEL_MIN IS THE FIRST ONE TO MEASURE. It is 1 << 21, which is 32768 f64 per thread =
256 KiB at 64 threads - the same width where sqrt still read 0.945x, i.e. right at the edge -
and it covers abs/negative/square/rint/floor/ceil/trunc/sign/reciprocal/degrees/radians, so one
fix would carry the whole unary family.

THE FIX, WHERE ONE IS WARRANTED, IS ONE LINE AND NEEDS NO NEW CONSTANT:
    let threads = rayon::current_num_threads().min(n / FAMILY_PARALLEL_MIN);
    if n >= FAMILY_PARALLEL_MIN && threads >= 2 {
        let chunk = n.div_ceil(threads);
It is the identity once n >= threads * floor, so large buffers are untouched BY CONSTRUCTION -
which also gives every measurement a free null control at the top of its range. Reusing the
family's own floor keeps the per-call and per-thread decisions consistent instead of
introducing a second number that has to be kept in sync.

MEASURE, DO NOT ASSUME. The sqrt fix was NOT free: on a SETTLED (not freshly written) input it
was neutral at 2^17-2^19, better at 2^22, and 1.05-1.26x WORSE at 2^20-2^21, because reducing
chunk count does not reduce how many rayon workers WAKE - only how many touch a fresh buffer.
A family whose inputs are usually resident may show the cost without the benefit. Use
crates/fnp-python/examples/h2h_sqrt_threads.rs: it installs explicit rayon ThreadPools so n and
T move independently in ONE process against ONE numpy, which is what makes the chunk-size story
separable from host oversubscription (a dual A/A null CANNOT see that confound - it compares
fnp to fnp, so a bias hitting the wide arm and sparing the narrow one passes it perfectly).

ACCEPTANCE: the worst-first list above is walked, each family either fixed with a measured
before/after (including its identity-region null control) or recorded as a null with the rows
that show the floor is already wide enough. Nulls are successes here.

title: [perf][fnp-ufunc] SIMD-vectorize last-axis (inner==1) f64 ptp lane scan
description: gap_sweep2 (2026-06-13): np.ptp(M[1000,1000],axis=1) np=247us fnp=1783us = 7.2x (verified-ok). UFuncArray::ptp (lib.rs ~23357) last-axis branch uses a SCALAR single-pass lane_ptp (if mn<v{mn}else{v} per element) over each contiguous row; numpy uses SIMD vmaxpd/vminpd. The sibling inner>1 (non-last-axis, e.g. axis0) branch ALREADY has a register-blocked portable-SIMD reduction (LANES=8, simd_lt/simd_gt select + nan accumulator) — apply the SAME pattern to the last-axis case but as a HORIZONTAL reduction WITHIN each contiguous row (accumulate mn/mx/nan SIMD vectors over LANES-chunks of the row, then reduce_min/reduce_max + scalar tail). PARITY PROOF (already worked out — signed-zero is SAFE for ptp specifically): ptp value = mx - mn; the only signed-zero divergence would be a -0.0 vs +0.0 result, which requires mx=-0.0 AND mn=+0.0 simultaneously — impossible since reduce_max>=reduce_min (max prefers +0.0, min prefers -0.0). For all-equal/all-zero rows scalar keep-2nd makes mn==mx==last-element so ptp=+0.0; SIMD reduce gives mx-mn=+0.0 too. When mn/mx is zero but the other operand nonzero, x-(±0)=x and (±0)-x=-x so sign-of-zero never affects the result. => bit-identical to the scalar two-reduction reference for ALL inputs. Proof obligations: keep ptp_axis_single_pass_golden_sha256 + ptp_axis_single_pass_matches_two_reduction_reference + ptp_axis_parallel_matches_serial_reference_bits green; add a signed-zero/NaN/inf row differential. CAVEAT: measured under load 7-10 — the 7.2x is PARTLY rayon-starvation (parallel fnp vs single-threaded numpy SIMD), like einsum_outer; re-measure at low load to confirm the SIMD compute win is real (target the per-row scalar->SIMD ratio ~4x, NOT the raw 7.2x). Do NOT just delegate to numpy (NO-GAPS: build our own kernel). int ptp + full-reduction f64 (already delegated) out of scope.
close_reason: NO-SHIP (Score~1.0-1.2x, memory-bound). Implemented the SIMD horizontal-reduction last-axis lane_ptp (bit-identical: golden ptp_axis_single_pass_golden_sha256 + both differential refs stayed GREEN, confirming the signed-zero invariance proof). But A/B at low load (same rayon pool, both parallel): [1000,1000] par_scalar=0.327ms par_simd=0.273ms ser_simd=0.243ms; [15625,256] par_scalar=1.083 par_simd=0.898 ser_simd=1.928. SIMD is ~1.0-1.2x and NOISY — the per-row scan is MEMORY-BANDWIDTH-bound, not compute-bound, so vectorizing the inner loop barely moves it. ROOT CAUSE OF THE ORIGINAL 7.2x: it was a HIGH-LOAD (7-10) ARTIFACT — fnp's parallel scan gets starved while numpy's single-threaded SIMD streaming is unaffected. At normal load fnp KERNEL is at PARITY with numpy (Rust 327us vs numpy 329us @1000x1000); the python-boundary residual (3.13x@1000² shrinking to 1.25x@2000²) is PyO3 MARSHALLING overhead (array extract+construct ~700us), NOT the kernel — a cross-cutting concern, not ptp-specific. Reverted the SIMD change (no regression but fails Score>=2.0 + adds complexity). DON'T re-attempt last-axis ptp SIMD or de-parallelization (serial is worse: ser_scalar 0.95ms). Real residual = PyO3 small-array overhead, uniform across ops.

title: [bench][fnp-python] bench_percall_floor_partition is structurally invalid - its probe-skipping arm pays a 727ns kwargs tail the probed arm does not, so probe_chain_ns is biased negative
description:
MEASURED DEFECT, banked in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md 2026-08-16 (RedLynx). `bench_percall_floor_partition` now PANICS on its own validity guard:

  thread 'main' panicked at crates/fnp-python/benches/criterion_python_elementwise.rs:2650:
  probe chain measured NEGATIVE (-40.0 ns): the casting=unsafe arm was not cheaper than
  the probed arm, so this partition is invalid

THE GUARD IS RIGHT AND MUST NOT BE RELAXED. The cause is structural, not noise.

MECHANISM. The method computes probe_chain_ns = whole_ns - skipped_ns, where `skipped_ns` is a `casting="unsafe"` call, chosen because that kwarg makes the shipped guard in `PyUFunc::__call__` skip the native probe block. But the two arms no longer differ ONLY by the probe chain. `deadlock-audit-s2fkk` added a fast path: an ALL-DEFAULTS call returns `np_ufunc.call1((x1, x2))` and sends NO keywords, while any non-default kwarg - `casting="unsafe"` included - falls to the slow tail that allocates a PyDict, sets casting/order/subok, and makes NumPy parse three keywords. s2fkk priced that shape at 727 ns.

So the subtraction is really `probe_chain - kwargs_construction_and_parse`. Once the probe chain got cheap (the per-call imports were removed from it in f8475a76 and 5c7735da), the kwargs term dominates and the difference goes negative. The bench's own comment anticipated the failure mode - "on a cheap probe chain, driving it negative" - without noticing that the shipped fast path GUARANTEES it.

DO NOT INVERT THE READING. -40 ns is NOT evidence the probe chain is free; it is evidence this instrument cannot measure it.

THE FIX: make the two arms differ ONLY by the probe chain. Options, in preference order:
  1. Give the probe-skipping arm the same call SHAPE as the probed arm - i.e. find a way to skip the probes that does not push the call onto the kwargs tail. A bench-only cfg or an env-gated early return in the route would do it, but must not special-case bench INPUTS (bench-path hardcoding is banned).
  2. Failing that, give BOTH arms the same non-default kwarg, so the kwargs cost cancels in the subtraction and only the probe chain remains. This is the cheapest correct change: pass `casting="unsafe"` to the probed arm too and instead vary something that toggles the probes without touching the call shape.

comments.author: RedLynx
comments.text:
SELF-CORRECTION ON MY OWN SPEC, before anyone implements it. Options 1 and 2 as I wrote them in this bead's description DO NOT WORK, and option 2 is flatly impossible. Read this before touching the bench.

WHY OPTION 2 IS IMPOSSIBLE ("give BOTH arms the same non-default kwarg so the kwargs cost cancels"). The probe block in PyUFunc::__call__ is gated on ALL SEVEN conditions holding at once:

    out.is_none() && r#where.is_none() && dtype.is_none() && signature.is_none()
      && casting == "same_kind" && order == "K" && subok

So ANY non-default keyword disables the probes. "Probes engaged" and "no kwargs tail" are not two independent knobs - they are the SAME knob, because s2fkk's fast path keys off exactly the same predicate. There is no public spelling of "probes on, kwargs tail on", so no pair of arms differing only in the probe chain can be built from the call surface. That is the real content of this bug, and my option 2 assumed the opposite.

OPTION 1 ("skip the probes without changing the call shape") still stands but needs a route change - a cfg(bench) or env-gated early return - and must not special-case bench INPUTS or shapes, which is banned.

THE OPTION I NOW PREFER, which neither of the original three named: CANCEL the kwargs term rather than eliminate it. Keep both arms as they are and measure the term that biases the subtraction, then correct for it:

    probe_chain_ns = whole_ns - (skipped_ns - kwargs_overhead_ns)

where kwargs_overhead_ns has two measurable parts:
  (a) numpy's own parse of the three keywords our slow tail always sets. Measure as
      theirs.call(args, {casting:"unsafe", order:"K", subok:True}) minus theirs.call1(args)
      - the SAME three keys our tail sets, on numpy's own ufunc, so no probe chain is involved.
  (b) our PyDict construction: PyDict::new + three set_item, as a standalone replica.

This keeps the partition's structure, is honest about being part-replica (the existing header already declares stage numbers to be LOWER BOUNDS), and removes the term that is currently driving the result negative. It also predicts the sign: (a)+(b) should come out near the 727 ns s2fkk measured for that call shape, which is a built-in sanity check - if it does not, the correction itself is wrong and the row must not publish.

WHAT MUST NOT HAPPEN: relaxing or deleting the `probe_chain_ns >= 0.0` assertion to make the group run. The guard is correct; it is the only reason this defect was visible at all. -40 ns is NOT evidence the probe chain is free.

STILL UNBUILT AND UNVERIFIED: /data has been at 43-49G all session, below every build threshold, so none of this is compiled. AGENT_NAME=RedLynx.
