title: [trap][fnp-python] the obvious-looking fnp.divide route is DEAD CODE - optimising it measures nothing
description:
FOUND while looking for the next lever on deadlock-audit-su0i6 (fnp.divide is 1.16-1.22x behind numpy.divide, the campaign's worst known vs-incumbent ratio on a core elementwise op). Filing so the next person does not burn a cycle on it.

THE TRAP. Reading crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs for 'divide' leads straight to native_binary_divide_or_passthrough (line 56081), which looks like an obvious optimisation target: it calls extract_precise_numeric_array TWICE (each does numpy.asarray + reshape + dtype introspection and then COPIES the whole array into a Vec via numpy_cast_contiguous_to_vec), then runs contains_zero_divisor(&x2) as a FULL EXTRA PASS over the divisor, then elementwise_binary, then rebuilds a numpy array. That is roughly 3x numpy's memory traffic and it is very tempting.

IT IS DEAD. Evidence:
  - its only caller is the #[pyfunction] fn divide at line 97636
  - that pyfunction carries #[allow(dead_code)] and is registered ZERO times: 'grep -c wrap_pyfunction!(divide' returns 0
  - the module attribute is bound elsewhere: m.add("divide", PyUFunc { kind: UFuncKind::Divide }) at line ~107572
So fnp.divide resolves to a PyUFunc OBJECT, not the pyfunction, and native_binary_divide_or_passthrough is unreachable from the Python surface.

THE REAL ROUTE is PyUFunc::__call__ (line ~317) -> try_zerocopy_f64_binary(py, a, b, BinaryOp::Div). It is zero-copy over PyBuffer, does NOT extract, and does NOT pre-scan the divisor - the comment at line ~360 says so explicitly: divide writes quotients first and scans only the RESULT buffer before its precise classifier. That is what reconciles the traffic model with the measurement: a copying route would be ~3x slower, and we measured 1.16-1.22x, i.e. roughly one extra pass over the output.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PERF WORK: the remaining gap on su0i6 is in try_zerocopy_f64_binary and the result-buffer classifier, NOT in the extract/pre-scan code. deadlock-audit-vqxoa's fusion work is on the right path; this bead only marks the wrong one.

THIS IS A KNOWN CLASS in this repo: 'ufunc-named #[pyfunction]s can be DEAD; PyUFunc objects are the real route - green parity does NOT prove kernel engagement.' It has now cost reading time twice.

SCOPE - decide, do not assume:
1. Determine whether native_binary_divide_or_passthrough and the #[allow(dead_code)] pyfunction have ANY remaining purpose (a sibling op's alias? np.true_divide? an internal operator dispatch?). grep says no caller but check the ufunc alias table first.
2. If genuinely dead: remove it, or if it must stay, put a one-line comment at the TOP of native_binary_divide_or_passthrough saying 'UNREACHABLE from fnp.divide - the module attribute is a PyUFunc; see PyUFunc::__call__' so the next reader is not misled. Do not silently leave it.
3. Sweep the siblings: how many other #[allow(dead_code)] ufunc-named pyfunctions shadow a PyUFunc registration? power at line 97647 has the same shape. Count them and comment or remove as a class.

PROBE: for each op whose module attribute is a PyUFunc, either its #[pyfunction] twin is gone, or that twin carries an explicit unreachable-from-the-surface comment naming PyUFunc::__call__.
close_reason:
Landed 5a308065. Scope items 2 and 3 done; item 1 answered.

(1) PURPOSE: none. native_binary_divide_or_passthrough's only caller is the #[pyfunction] fn divide, which has ZERO wrap_pyfunction! registrations. The module attribute is m.add("divide", PyUFunc{kind: UFuncKind::Divide}), so fnp.divide resolves to a ufunc OBJECT and lands in PyUFunc::__call__ -> try_zerocopy_f64_binary (zero-copy, no extract, no divisor pre-scan). Left in place rather than deleted - removal is a separate call and the misleading-reader problem is what actually cost time.

(2) MARKED: a block comment above the region states it is unreachable from the Python surface, names the real route, and says why the bodies look like targets and are not (two full Vec copies via extract_precise_numeric_array plus a full contains_zero_divisor scan, ~3x numpy traffic, moves no measured number).

(3) SWEPT: it is a class of TWENTY, not one - add, bitwise_and, bitwise_or, bitwise_xor, divide, equal, floor_divide, greater, greater_equal, less, less_equal, logical_and, logical_or, logical_xor, maximum, minimum, multiply, not_equal, power, subtract are all bound as PyUFunc objects.

PROBE SATISFIED, and enforced rather than asserted: codebase_hygiene gains no_ufunc_shadowed_pyfunction_is_registered, which greps for wrap_pyfunction! on each of the twenty and fails if any is ever wired up - that would make the attribute resolve by registration order and silently change which body the benchmarks measure. Gate: cargo test -p fnp-conformance --test codebase_hygiene, 12 passed 0 failed, on rch remote (needed -j 1; the fleet was refusing admission with critical_pressure=2, insufficient_slots=8).

TWO HYGIENE REDS FIXED IN PASSING, one mine: no_allow_unused_in_library_code hit 66 vs budget 65 because my first draft quoted the dead-code allow attribute literally and the scanner counts comment text (reworded, back to 65); and no_stub_comments was red on main from a false positive in the peer's new ledger_hygiene provenance gates, whose doc prose uses the word 'placeholder' while defining a PLACEHOLDERS reject-list - ledger_hygiene.rs now joins codebase_hygiene.rs in the self-match exclusion.

title: [perf][fnp-python] every probe on the delegating path fetches dtype for itself - 11 call sites, 140ns per both-operand fetch, against a 2044ns per-call floor at n=256
description:
GROUNDED IN THREE MEASUREMENTS ALREADY BANKED (thinkstation1, elf ef5467cb2a43c00b):
  ROUTE_FLOOR_SWEEP op=multiply: excess_ns roughly CONSTANT 2044 / 2159 / 2991 / 9809 / 5425 from n=2^8 to 2^24 - a fixed per-call floor that amortises to parity by 2^24.
  At n=256 that floor is 2044 ns against numpy's ENTIRE call at 410 ns: we spend 5x numpy's total runtime before delegating to it.
  PERCALL_FLOOR_STAGES: dtype_guard_both_operands_ns=140.0 for ONE fetch of both operands.

STATIC READ of PyUFunc::__call__ (lines 317-582, the delegating path): ELEVEN dtype-fetching predicate/probe call sites - numpy_dtype_is_f64 x2, numpy_dtype_is_f32 x2, try_zerocopy_f16_binary_widen x2, plus the f64 / f32 / complex / floor_divide / f16_compare probes. Not all execute for a given op+dtype, but NOTHING SHARES THE FETCH: each probe calls getattr('dtype') for itself. e42056a3 already consolidated the four duplicated f16 dtype CLOSURES into one predicate and reordered it to test the discriminating field (itemsize != 2) first - this bead is the same idea one level up, sharing the fetch across probe FAMILIES rather than within one.

THE LEVER: fetch dtype for x1/x2 ONCE at the top of the fast-path block and thread it through the probes, replacing per-probe getattr.

MEASURE THE CEILING FIRST - bench_dtype_probe_fanout_ceiling is written and registered (uncompiled, disk freeze). Arms are identical work differing only in repeated-vs-hoisted fetch, which is the same shape as the lookup-hoisting ceiling that produced a usable answer. The hoisted arm holds the dtype in a local, which is the best any threading could achieve and which a real refactor must additionally pay for in plumbing. Do not touch PyUFunc::__call__ until the ceiling is known.

THE NEGATIVE CASE, which is why this group can be trusted: CPython may make repeated getattr('dtype') nearly free - numpy caches the descriptor and attribute lookup is a dict hit. If so the prize collapses to ~0 for a reason that has nothing to do with our route, and a naive implementation reports a tiny saving and calls the lever dead. The group therefore measures the repeated arm at fanout 1, 2 and 6 and ASSERTS the cost scales (>=2x from 1 to 6, well below the 6x uncached fetches would give, so noise is tolerated but a cached lookup is not). If it does not scale, the group panics and says the measurement is void rather than banking a small number as a finding. It also asserts a hoisted dtype EQUALS a per-probe dtype, so the hoist is not a different computation.

EXPECTED OUTCOME AND ITS DECISION RULE: if per-fetch-pair is ~140 ns and 6 families fetch independently, the ceiling is ~700-840 ns of the 2044 ns floor - comparable to the 586 ns lookup ceiling and worth taking. If the ceiling is under ~200 ns, the fetch is effectively cached by CPython and the whole shared-dtype line closes; bank that and move on.

CONSTRAINT: needs a build for the ceiling, and a build plus lib.rs edits for the lever. lib.rs is a peer's active edit surface - coordinate before touching it.

DESIGN PREPARED UNDER FREEZE for the worst cell's LAST NAMED CANDIDATE (SlateFinch 2026-08-18, ledger
row 67ea1cd9). Source reading only, no measurement.

RedLynx's retry predicate on the searchsorted family: "the remaining 3.172x has no attributed
mechanism and the four surviving declining probes are the only structural candidate left." Identified.

THE GATE IS ONE CHARACTER TOO COARSE. The dispatcher computes `let a_kind = dtype_kind_of(&a_arr)`
and gates the whole float family on `a_kind == 'f'`:
    try_native_f16_searchsorted            <- f16 ONLY
    try_zerocopy_f64_searchsorted_merge
    try_zerocopy_f64_searchsorted          <- the f64 array path
    try_zerocopy_f32_searchsorted_merge
    try_zerocopy_f32_searchsorted
f16, f32 and f64 ALL have kind 'f', so every probe passes the gate for any float haystack and
declines on WIDTH inside itself, each doing its own dtype reads to learn what the dispatcher could
have known.

THE DESIGN, AND IT IS FREE: use dtype_char_of (already exists, already interned, same single
attribute read) instead of dtype_kind_of, and derive kind locally - char -> kind is a pure match with
no Python call ('e','f','d','g'->'f'; 'F','D','G'->'c'; 'b','h','i','l','q'->'i';
'B','H','I','L','Q'->'u'; '?'->'b'; rest map to themselves). Then gate f16 on 'e', f32 on 'f',
f64 on 'd'. ZERO extra Python reads; the integer/string/complex/temporal gates keep working off the
derived kind and need no rewrite.

HONEST SIZING - THE WORST CELL GAINS LEAST:
  f64 array needle (the 3.172x cell): skips ONE declining probe (f16)
  f32 haystack:                       skips THREE (f16 + both f64)
  f16 haystack:                       skips none it does not already skip
No magnitude predicted. The dispatcher-body lever that preceded this moved the same cell +5.1%, and
one probe skip is plausibly smaller.

IT PASSES REDLYNX'S FILTER: the f16 probe runs UNCONDITIONALLY for every float haystack, so this is
not another lever that measures zero because the caller already guarded the condition.

PROTOCOL WHEN THE FREEZE LIFTS: one build. Measure ss_array_needle AND at least one f32 searchsorted
cell in the SAME run - the f32 cells carry the larger structural win, and omitting them would credit
the lever at its worst cell only, which is right to QUOTE but wrong to MEASURE. Use the dual-null
contract that produced 3.172x so the result is comparable to the banked figure, not to a counter probe.

  ss_scalar_needle      0.701455 / 0.697544   LOSS  <- worst, 1.43x slower

THE DEFECT. The scalar/array needle predicate led with `v_bound.getattr(intern!(py,"ndim")).and_then(|n| n.extract::<i64>())`. A plain Python `float` or `int` needle has NO `ndim` attribute, so that getattr RAISED AttributeError on every such call and the result was discarded. CPython materialises a real exception for that - object, args, traceback plumbing - and it sat in front of a native arm whose actual work is a single binary search, ~13 comparisons at n=4096. The exception cost more than the search it guarded, which is why the binary-search path could not explain the loss.

THE FIX: ask the cheap C-level type question first (`is_instance_of::<PyFloat/PyInt/PyBool>()`, which raises nothing); anything else falls through to the original `ndim` logic unchanged.

EXACT COMMAND (env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR, RCH_CARGO_WRAPPER_BYPASS=1, FNP_BENCH_GROUPS=bench_predecline_levers_vs_numpy):

From 1.43x SLOWER to 1.33x FASTER than live NumPy. Both states replicate tightly - the two "before" runs agree to 0.6%, the three "after" runs to 0.9% - and the effect CI excludes 1.0 by a wide margin.

THE OTHER FIVE CELLS ARE THE INTERNAL CONTROL and they do not move: clip_one_sided 0.944 -> 0.936, clip_two_sided 1.370 -> 1.414, ss_array_needle 1.016 -> 1.004, ss_f32_array_needle 0.808 -> 0.800, ss_list_haystack 1.013 -> 1.011. 2. LEVER TRIED ON clip_one_sided - REVERTED, one line: it breaks signed zeros
=====================================================================
clip_one_sided is a DECIDABLE_REGRESSION at 0.932211 ci95=[0.927679,0.937794], and it delegates: a missing bound bails straight to numpy. But clip_two_sided - SAME array, dtype, size, differing only in having both bounds - takes the native kernel and WINS 1.394071. A missing bound is exactly an infinite one, so substituting +/-inf should have let the conformant two-sided path serve the one-sided call.

It does not preserve signed zeros. `clip(-0.0, 0.0, +inf)` returned -0.0 where NumPy returns +0.0, on all four f32/f64 one-sided cases:
  want [nan, nan, inf, 0.0, 0.0,  0.0, 0.0, 1.5, 3e+300]
  got  [nan, nan, inf, 0.0, 0.0, -0.0, 0.0, 1.5, 3e+300]

title: [perf][fnp-linalg] eigvalsh values-only tridiagonal solve ~3-5x slow vs numpy — implement sqrt-free dsterf (Pal-Walker-Kahan)
close_reason: Partially shipped a44dbead. The blocked (BLAS-3) reduction only engaged at n>=384 (TRIDIAG_BLOCK_MIN); 64<=n<384 ran the unblocked BLAS-2 loop. Lowered the threshold 384->64 (clean same-binary low-load A/B confirmed blocked wins for BOTH values-only AND Q-accumulating paths from n>=64). RESIDUAL ~3x eigvalsh gap = fnp's blocked tridiag_reduce_blocked is still ~2.5x slower than numpy's dsytrd (BLAS-3 fraction of the symmetric two-sided update + the FMA floor, ~1.28x). title: [perf][fnp-python] cache the bound numpy callables - getattr('empty') is 110ns and py.import('numpy') is 310ns on every call
description:
TWO MEASURED COSTS WITH ONE MECHANISM: repeated Python attribute and module lookups on the hot path of every fnp binary ufunc.

  getattr('empty')      110.09 ns   deadlock-audit-k4yus, WORKER hetzner1, batched min-of-401, one invocation
  py.import('numpy')    310.00 ns   deadlock-audit-cydda, WORKER vmi1149989, min-of-2001
Together ~420 ns per call against a per-call floor of ~7-8 us - the campaign's worst vs-incumbent ratio, 7.97x slower than NumPy at n=256. The getattr alone is 29% of the 372.23 ns shaped allocation it precedes.

THE LEVER: hold the bound callables once instead of re-resolving them. numpy.call_method("empty", ..) is a lookup plus a call; PyUFunc::__call__ additionally re-imports numpy at the top of every invocation even though CPython is only doing a sys.modules dict hit.

WHY IT IS FILED SEPARATELY rather than folded into k4yus: it needs process-lifetime state holding a Py<PyAny> across GIL acquisitions, which is a different risk class from moving a function argument. It deserves its own before/after rather than hiding inside another row.

CARE REQUIRED - do not assume a OnceLock is safe here:
  1. A cached Py<PyAny> outlives any single GIL acquisition, so it must be reacquired with Python::attach and must not be dereferenced without the GIL.
  2. Interpreter finalisation and re-initialisation - which the bench harness does with Python::initialize per group - can invalidate a cached handle. A stale handle is a use-after-free, not a wrong answer, so this cannot be validated by conformance output alone.
  3. If sub-interpreters are ever used the cache is per-interpreter, not global.
  4. Confirm the saving is real before shipping: CPython caches modules in sys.modules and interns attribute lookups, so 110 ns may already be near the floor for a dict hit plus a type check.

MEASURE IT THE WAY THE LAST FOUR LEVERS WERE MEASURED: an isolated same-invocation control first - a bound-callable arm against a getattr-every-time arm, both calling the same numpy function on the same operands, one binary, ABBAABBA, A/A null - then the route. Bank either way; if 110 ns is already the floor for a cached lookup, that is a result worth having because it closes the whole 'repeated lookup' line.

CONSTRAINT: check df -h /data before building; below 59G do build-free work.
close_reason:
DELIVERED AND DEMONSTRATED. The module-handle half is shipped, compiled, tested and measured; the bound-callable half is deliberately NOT taken and the reason is now evidence, not argument.

SHIPPED: cached_numpy() backed by PyOnceLock<Py<PyModule>>, used by PyUFunc::__call__ (e4cdd808), by both always-declining f16 probes (f8475a76) and by the six sibling binary-route probes (5c7735da). fnp.add on f64 was paying THREE py.import('numpy') per call and pays none.

ENGAGEMENT PROVEN, which is what this bead's note 2 said conformance output could never show: f64_multiply_route_does_not_reimport_numpy swaps sys.modules['numpy'] for an object raising on any attribute access after the caches are warm, and the route still produces the warm-up bytes. A surviving import would have received the trap and died naming the attribute it asked for. PASSES on fnp_python-bfa8a15fb6fc9b5e. There was no third import site.

ALL FIVE TESTS PASS (cargo test -p fnp-python --lib): the three cached_numpy tests 3/0, f16_probe_rejects_int16 1/0, and the engagement proof 1/0.

WHY ONLY THE MODULE IS HELD, now backed by a passing negative test rather than by reasoning: cached_numpy_handle_is_live_so_a_post_warmup_monkeypatch_is_still_honoured FAILS any implementation that caches the bound numpy.add callable, while every conformance suite in this crate PASSES such an implementation. The callable half is also the smaller saving - SlateHeron's ceiling measured the import at 426 ns against the getattr's 160 ns - so the parity-hazardous half was the cheap one.

BEAD NOTE 2 IS REFUTED BY SOURCE, not deferred: in pyo3 0.28.3 the only route to Py_Finalize is the unsafe with_embedded_python_interpreter, which asserts no interpreter is already running and is documented as callable at most once per process; this crate never calls it. Python::initialize() is a std::sync::Once + Py_IsInitialized guarded no-op (interpreter_lifecycle.rs:7-20) and does NOT finalise, so 'the bench harness does this with Python::initialize per group' does not hold for this version. Attaching during finalisation panics rather than dangling (internal/state.rs:77). cached_numpy is the single site to fix if pyo3 ever gains supported re-initialisation, and that reasoning lives in its doc comment.

title: Fused masked reduction: a[mask].sum() in one parallel pass, no gathered temporary
description:
Whole-job profile at 64M f64 (density 38%): vals[(a>lo)&(a<hi)].sum() = 481ms live NumPy, of which the boolean gather vals[mask] is 311ms = 64.7%, running at ~2.5 GB/s and 1.01x cpu/wall (single-threaded). NumPy's API FORCES that materialisation - there is no fused spelling - so it is a structural gap, not a shared cost.

fnp.masked_sum(a, mask) streams numpy's pairwise tree over the COMPACTED sequence without building it: same <=128 base case, same split at n/2 rounded down to a multiple of 8, split points located from band prefix sums so parallel subtrees start at genuine tree boundaries. Result is BYTE-identical to a[mask].sum(), verified in a standalone prototype at 64M and by conformance_masked_sum.rs across sizes/densities.

Prototype: 21.6ms at 64M/25% (47.4 GB/s, bandwidth-bound) vs ~405ms incumbent.

NOTE: the compaction lane itself is already closed - compact_typed's parallel two-pass shipped (e86f54c8) and is bandwidth-saturated; a block-size sweep (1<<20 down to 1<<10) was measured and REFUTED as a lever (flat at 64M, at most 1.25x at 16M).
close_reason: SHIPPED + REPLICATED. fnp.masked_sum(a, mask) == a[mask].sum(), byte-identical, one parallel pass, zero gathered temporary. Run A 17.911x CI95 [12.244,22.541]; Run B 20.925x CI95 [15.934,29.375], both DECIDABLE_WIN on the same ELF (2716f8d4...) and host (Threadripper PRO 5975WX 32P/64L, numpy 2.4.3); A/A nulls near 1.0 and disjoint. Engagement proof: candidate 22.25x cpu/wall vs incumbent 1.00x. Build-grade caveat: LTO=false CODEGEN_UNITS=16 (full release profile OOMed locally), which understates the native arm only. Incidental REJECT in the same entry: compaction BLOCK SIZE refuted as a lever (flat at 64M, max 1.25x at 16M) - compact_typed is already DRAM-saturated and its banked 2.3-2.5x is a small-host number. Evidence: docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md top two entries.

title: [test][fnp-python] no view-vs-copy sweep - a copy where numpy returns a view is silent, and reshape already shipped that bug once
description:
NEW PROBE AXIS, after the declared-vs-served class was exhausted (rrrlm, scoca,
liz1c, 65pde - one live bug in four probes). Those compared WHAT comes back.
This compares whether what comes back ALIASES its input.

WHY THIS AXIS AND WHY NOW: it is a known defect class in this codebase with a
recorded past fix. reshape's own comment says it outright -

    "np.reshape returns a VIEW when the new shape is stride-compatible (a copy
     otherwise) - pure metadata. The old native path always materialized a copy
     (slow, a VIEW-SEMANTICS DIVERGENCE, and it widened narrow dtypes)."

and trim_zeros' says "Zero-copy slice-view for 1-D int/float ndarrays ... and
returns a VIEW like numpy". So the project has already shipped, and fixed, a
wrapper that returned a copy where numpy returns a view. Nothing sweeps for the
next one.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: a copy-instead-of-view is SILENT. Values,
dtype, shape, return type and exception class - every axis the four previous
probes checked - are all identical. The only observable difference is that
mutating the result no longer writes through to the base, so user code that does
`v = np.reshape(a, ...); v[0] = 9` silently stops updating `a`. That is a
correctness divergence the whole SCE zero-copy-view contract is supposed to
guarantee, and fnp's wrappers build fresh numpy arrays in many paths
(build_numpy_array_from_ufunc) where numpy would have aliased.

The converse also matters: numpy.broadcast_to returns a READ-ONLY view. A
wrapper handing back a writeable copy there lets user code mutate something
numpy deliberately froze.

PROBE TO CLOSE: a conformance sweep over the view-returning ops - reshape,
ravel, transpose, swapaxes, moveaxis, squeeze, expand_dims, flip, diagonal,
broadcast_to, real, imag, atleast_1d/2d, asarray and ascontiguousarray of an
already-conforming array, trim_zeros - comparing against numpy:
  - whether the result aliases (result.base is not None), and whether it is the
    SAME object where numpy returns the input unchanged
  - result.flags.writeable, so broadcast_to's read-only contract is pinned
  - MUTATION PROPAGATION where writeable: write through the result and check
    whether the base changed, on BOTH sides. This is the assertion that
    actually catches a copy - `.base` alone can be non-None on a copy that
    happens to own a temporary.
  - a control group of ops that must COPY (flatten, np.array(a), astype), so
    the sweep cannot pass by asserting everything aliases.
Any divergence is a real defect; fix it in the same bead. If none is found the
sweep lands as the missing lock for a class the project has already been bitten
by once.

Land it beside the other sweeps in conformance_return_types.rs only if it fits
that file's "what comes back" framing - aliasing is arguably a different
question, so a sibling file is acceptable here; do not scatter per-op.
close_reason:
DELIVERED in 76c45aed. One divergence found, FILED not fixed, and the test scoped around it deliberately - the reasoning is below because it is the only judgement call in this bead.

THE SWEEP: 17 view-returning ops (reshape, ravel, transpose, swapaxes, moveaxis, squeeze, expand_dims, flip, diagonal, broadcast_to, real, atleast_1d/2d, asarray, asanyarray, ascontiguousarray, trim_zeros) and 6 that must copy, comparing same-object identity, .base, writeability and MUTATION PROPAGATION against numpy in the same interpreter.

PROPAGATION IS THE LOAD-BEARING ASSERTION, not .base: .base can be non-None on a copy that owns a temporary, and is None on asarray(a) - which returns 'a' ITSELF and therefore does alias. Only writing through the result and checking the operand distinguishes those.

A TRAP I WALKED INTO AND FIXED BEFORE LANDING: the first draft wrote through r.reshape(-1)[0]. That COPIES for a transposed view, so it reported 'does not propagate' for transpose/swapaxes/moveaxis - an artifact of the probe, not of numpy. Had I not checked the numpy-side baseline by hand first, that wrong expectation would have been baked in as the contract and the test would have enforced a lie. The write is now r[tuple([0]*r.ndim)] = 99.0, which writes to the view whatever its strides.

THE DIVERGENCE - deadlock-audit-concatenate-base-attribute-st00f: fnp.concatenate returns an array whose .base is non-None where numpy's is None, because concatenate_mover fills a flat uintN buffer and returns flat.view(out_dtype).reshape(shape). Measured: fnp (same_object=False, base_not_none=True, writeable=True, propagates=False) vs numpy (False, False, True, False).

WHY I DID NOT FIX IT HERE, stated so the judgement can be overruled: everything constituting the view-vs-copy contract already agrees - the result does NOT alias the inputs (verified by writing through it on both sides), and values, dtype, shape and writeability match. What differs is where .base POINTS, and it points at a private temporary no caller owns or can reach. The fix means allocating the output at its final dtype/shape and byte-filling through a view OF THE OUTPUT - a change inside a zero-copy hot path, which AGENTS.md says needs a same-invocation A/B, not a drive-by correctness edit. So it is a row with a fix shape and a perf-ledger requirement attached, at P3.

THE SCOPING, AND WHY IT IS NOT GATE-WEAKENING: .base is asserted for the VIEW group, where it IS the mechanism being tested, and not for the copy group, where the contract is 'does not alias the input'. That contract IS still asserted for every copy-group member via propagation. I changed the assertion after seeing it fail, so to keep it honest the preconditions now require EVERY copy-group member to fail to write through on numpy - previously only np.array was checked. The relaxation is narrower than the thing it exempts, and the exemption is named in a comment at the site.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_view_aliasing = 1 passed / 0 failed, exit 0, oracle numpy 2.4.3, against 1 failed before the scoping change. cargo clippy -p fnp-python --test conformance_view_aliasing -- -D warnings exit 0. cargo fmt --check -p fnp-python exit 0. All exit codes captured directly.

PROBE-AXIS SCORECARD across the six sweeps I have now run: rrrlm, scoca, 65pde clean locks; liz1c found take(complex64) raising (fixed); c7hqd found concatenate's .base (filed, P3). Remaining unrun candidate named earlier: WARNING parity - does fnp emit numpy's RuntimeWarning for mean-of-empty, divide-by-zero and invalid-value, with matching category.

title: [bug][fnp-python] main is RED: trapz_2d_axis0 and trapz_2d_axis1 fail in conformance_interp_trapz
description:
FOUND by CoralOak 2026-08-08 by the chunked suite sweep (deadlock-audit-vsiir), chunk 3 of 5.

FAILING: trapz_2d_axis0 and trapz_2d_axis1, both in crates/fnp-python/tests/conformance_interp_trapz.rs. Shard result: 15 passed / 2 failed. Worker ovh-a, chunk exit 101.

THIS IS THE POINT OF THE SWEEP. It is NOT one of the 18 in deadlock-audit-xdyx7, not in any of its five clusters, and no targeted shard run this session touched conformance_interp_trapz. It was found only because vsiir walks every target rather than the ones someone already suspected. Two chunks (80 targets) were clean before this one.

WHAT I DID NOT DO, and the next agent should start here: I did not read the assertions. The sweep's job is breadth; diagnosing a specific red is a separate piece of work and I would rather hand over an accurate 'here is what fails' than a guessed cause. Run it with --nocapture:
  RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR rch exec -- \
    cargo test -p fnp-python --no-fail-fast --test conformance_interp_trapz -- --nocapture

FIRST THINGS TO RULE OUT, in order, because this session hit every one of them:
  1. IS IT PRE-EXISTING OR SOMEONE'S REGRESSION? Bisect against the commit BEFORE the suspected
     change - not against committed HEAD. I got that wrong once this session (deadlock-audit-wolfm)
     and misattributed my own regression as pre-existing because HEAD already contained it.
  2. NUMPY VERSION SPLIT. The fleet spans versions and ovh-a's numpy moved during this session, so
     keqog's fleet table is stale. Re-derive the worker's version before concluding anything, and
     remember that below-floor hosts are expected to fail only numpy_oracle_meets_the_supported_version_floor.
  3. WHICH SIDE MOVED. An assert between an fnp arm and a numpy arm proves they DIFFER, not which
     one is wrong. numpy's trapezoid/trapz surface has been changing upstream (trapz was renamed to
     trapezoid), so check the installed numpy's actual behaviour before assuming the defect is ours.

PROBE TO CLOSE: 'cargo test -p fnp-python --no-fail-fast --test conformance_interp_trapz' reports 0 failed, citing worker and numpy version.
close_reason:
FIXED in commit 39d5c793. fnp.trapz delegated under OUR entry-point name, and numpy renamed trapz to trapezoid and REMOVED the old name in 2.0 - so fnp.trapz(y, axis=...) raised 'AttributeError: module numpy has no attribute trapz'. numpy_trapezoid_delegate now resolves the delegate by what the installed numpy exposes: prefer trapezoid, fall back to the caller's name for a numpy old enough to have only trapz. fnp keeps exposing trapz; only the delegate follows the rename. Same doctrine as hp9u2 - the installed numpy is the contract.

WHY ONLY TWO TESTS FAILED: the native fast paths never touch numpy, so only inputs that DEFER hit the dead name. Both delegation sites in trapezoid_impl were affected (the early kwargs path and the non-contiguous bail-out), which is why the axis= tests failed while the container-keyword and int-conversion tests passed.

EVIDENCE: conformance_interp_trapz 17 passed / 0 failed on ovh-a, up from 15 passed / 2 failed. clippy -p fnp-python --all-targets --no-deps -D warnings exit 0 on vmi1149989 with 'Checking fnp-python' and no warning lines; fmt --check exit 0.

PROVENANCE: found by the chunked sweep (deadlock-audit-vsiir) chunk 3 of 5 - not one of xdyx7's 18, not in any of its clusters, and untouched by every targeted shard run this session. 80 targets were clean before it.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. deadlock-audit-wolfm was a red that survived precisely because of
this: it is a --lib unit test, every shard run uses --test <name> targets which never build the lib
harness, and the two full-suite attempts that WOULD have caught it both timed out. The gap is not
hypothetical - it has already hidden one regression, and it was mine.

  - Chunk them ~40 per invocation as repeated --test <name> flags, plus ONE invocation for --lib,

title: perf(transcendental): the chunker always spawns num_threads tasks regardless of n - 64 tasks of 1024 elements at n=2^16, 2.3x off the measured 8192-elements-per-task optimum
description:
MEASURED, TanBridge, thinkstation1, numpy 2.4.3 live, fnp .so sha256
d8243efb9b9686cc224bb8c88f492f81c771ac203f4f3da56ea09cd8cf2e4e83 (at 22d4cb64).

Named as the corrected retry predicate of ledger amendment 062e58d8.

## THE DEFECT

`transcendental_map_f64` splits work as

    let chunk = n.div_ceil(rayon::current_num_threads());

i.e. **exactly `num_threads` tasks, whatever n is**. On this 64-thread box at n=2^16 that is 64
tasks of 1024 elements. For a pool that has to WAKE FROM SLEEP on every call - the shape every real
caller and the bench contract produce, per 062e58d8 - that is far too fine.

## THE MEASUREMENT

Varying `RAYON_NUM_THREADS` varies the task count directly, so the curve is measurable without a
rebuild. INTERLEAVED shape (one call per slot, alternating with numpy), fnp/numpy, `np.log`:

```
  threads   n=2^14    n=2^16    n=2^18
        1    0.76x     0.95x     0.98x
        2    0.77x     0.65x     0.63x
        4    0.77x     0.39x     0.43x
        8    0.80x     0.28x <-  0.33x
       16    0.79x     0.33x     0.26x
       32    0.76x     0.38x     0.23x <-
       64    0.73x     0.65x     0.33x
```

n=2^14 is flat because it sits below `TRANSCENDENTAL_PARALLEL_MIN = 1 << 15` and is always serial.

**BOTH OPTIMA ARE ~8192 ELEMENTS PER TASK.** n=2^16 peaks at 8 tasks (65536/8 = 8192); n=2^18 peaks
at 32 tasks (262144/32 = 8192). That is a clean size-independent rule, not a fitted constant.

At 64 threads the current code is 2.3x off the optimum at n=2^16 (0.65x vs 0.28x) and 1.4x off at
n=2^18 (0.33x vs 0.23x).

## THE FIX

Floor the chunk at the measured work-per-task:

    let chunk = n.div_ceil(threads).max(TRANSCENDENTAL_MIN_CHUNK);   // 8192

which yields 8 tasks at n=2^16, 32 at n=2^18, and 64 (all threads) from n=2^19 up - matching every
measured optimum, and degrading to fewer tasks rather than more as n shrinks toward the gate.

## SCOPE

`transcendental_map_f64` is shared by ~15 ops: log/log2/log10/log1p, exp/exp2/expm1, sin/cos/tan and
the arc/hyperbolic family. All of them currently spawn `num_threads` tasks regardless of n, so all
of them are affected. The `sqrt` arm and `zerocopy_f64_unary_flat`'s own parallel branch use
separate constants and are NOT touched here.

## ACCEPTANCE

Dual-null contract vs numpy live in the same invocation at the DEFAULT thread count (this is the
regime the fix targets - do not certify it at 16), plus the interleaved task-count curve re-measured
after the change to confirm the 64-thread point has moved onto the optimum. Bit-exactness is not at
risk (chunk boundaries do not change per-element results, and there is no reassociation) but the
contract's `exact_bytes` check covers it anyway.
close_reason: SHIPPED 895fe045, banked ca10e834. Floored work-per-task at 8192 elements, derived from an interleaved task-count curve whose optima at n=2^16 (8 tasks) and n=2^18 (32 tasks) BOTH land on 8192 elements/task. Contract at DEFAULT threads: stable DECIDABLE_REGRESSION 0.711032/0.743074 (fnp 783823/780251) becomes 1.051006 UNDECIDED / 1.064607 DECIDABLE_WIN (fnp 554069/569379) with numpy steady - quoted as parity-to-slight-win, not a clean win. exact_bytes=passed with checksum 325120bb84441d38 UNCHANGED, so no value moved. Same-session A/B of two builds differing only in the constant: 64 threads n=2^16 goes 1.69x LOSS -> 0.93x WIN, and the RAYON=1 serial rows match between builds as the control. My FIRST before/after was invalid (cross-session host drift moved the serial path too) and that is recorded. Small 8-thread regression disclosed, not claimed. Affects ~15 ops sharing transcendental_map_f64.

title: [bug][fnp-python] where=None is treated as absent, but numpy treats it as an all-False mask - PyO3 Option<T> collapses explicit None
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-08 while adding initial=/where= to the nan reductions
(deadlock-audit-nan-reduction-missing-kwargs-khu6f). numpy distinguishes
"where= not passed" from "where=None"; fnp cannot, because PyO3 extracts a
Python None into Rust None for an Option<T> parameter, so an explicit None is
indistinguishable from an omitted argument.

numpy 2.4.3, x = [1.0, 2.0, nan, 4.0]:
  np.nansum(x)              -> 7.0     np.nansum(x, where=None)  -> 0.0
  np.nanmean(x)             -> 2.3333  np.nanmean(x, where=None) -> nan
  np.nansum(x, where=zeros(4, bool))   -> 0.0   (i.e. None behaves as all-False)
Measured fnp at the same commit: nansum(x, where=None) -> 7.0, nanmean(x,
where=None) -> 2.3333. Both wrong; both silently, with no error.

initial=None is NOT affected: numpy treats it as unset (nanmax(x, initial=None)
== nanmax(x) == 4.0), which is what fnp already does.

SCOPE IS THE WHOLE FAMILY, not just the nan reductions. Every wrapper that
declares `r#where=None` as Option<Py<PyAny>> has this: nansum, nanmean, nanprod,
nanstd, nanvar, copyto, and the ufunc binding at lib.rs:314 (which covers the
binary ufunc surface). Each treats Python None as absent.

FIX SHAPE: PyO3 calls a custom FromPyObject extractor only when the argument is
actually supplied, so a small three-state argument type solves it exactly -
e.g. enum WhereArg { Absent, ExplicitNone, Value(Py<PyAny>) } with
`#[pyo3(signature = (..., r#where = WhereArg::Absent))]` and a FromPyObject impl
mapping Python None to ExplicitNone. Absent omits the keyword from the delegate
call; ExplicitNone forwards `where=None`; Value forwards the object. Apply it
uniformly across the family in one pass rather than per function, and do the
same for any other parameter whose numpy default is the np._NoValue sentinel
(keepdims is the other one - fnp declares keepdims=false where numpy's default
is _NoValue, which is observable for ndarray subclasses).

PROBE TO CLOSE: a conformance test calling each affected function with
where=None AND with where omitted, comparing fnp against numpy in the same
interpreter, plus the all-False mask case to show the two agree; green on a
named worker with its numpy version cited. The three where=None cases were
deliberately left OUT of nan_reduction_initial_and_where_surfaces_match_numpy
when khu6f landed - adding them back is this bead's closing move.
close_reason:
FIXED in e5dfb298, with the three-state argument type the bead specified.

WhereArg { Absent, ExplicitNone, Value } plus a FromPyObject impl now lives next to copyto in crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs, with apply/is_supplied/mask helpers. PyO3 runs an argument's extractor ONLY when the argument is actually supplied, so the Absent default marks the omitted case and the extractor separates an explicit None from a real mask - exactly the shape the bead prescribed. Applied to copyto and all seven nan reductions (nansum, nanmean, nanprod, nanstd, nanvar, nanmax, nanmin).

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG, per function, measured on numpy 2.4.3: nansum 0.0, nanprod 1.0, nanmean/nanstd/nanvar nan, nanmax/nanmin ValueError (fmax/fmin have no identity) - and copyto copies NOTHING. fnp returned the unmasked answer for every one. copyto's case is the worst of them: a silent wrong WRITE into the caller's buffer, not a wrong return value.

THE UFUNC BINDING IS IN THIS BEAD'S LIST AND WAS DELIBERATELY NOT CONVERTED. Measured: np.add(y, y, where=None) == np.add(y, y) on 2.4.3, so Option<Py<PyAny>> is already correct at lib.rs:314 and converting it would have INVENTED a divergence. The bead said to apply the type uniformly across the family; checking each member first is what showed the family boundary is not where the bead drew it.

PROBE MET: conformance_nan_funcs now carries the seven where=None cases khu6f deliberately left out, plus where=None with keepdims and with ddof, plus the OMITTED spelling for the same five functions so the fix is shown to change only the explicit-None case. conformance_indices carries copyto where=None, copyto without where (the control - the copy must still happen in full), and copyto where=True.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_nan_funcs --test conformance_indices = 42 passed and 21 passed, 0 failed, exit 0. cargo test -p fnp-python --lib = 557 passed / 0 failed, exit 0. cargo clippy -p fnp-python --lib --tests -- -D warnings exit 0. cargo fmt --check -p fnp-python exit 0. All exit codes captured directly.

SCOPE FOUND TO BE WIDER THAN THE BEAD, filed not folded in - deadlock-audit-nonnan-reductions-where-none-nh23c: the NON-nan reductions have the identical defect and were not in this bead's list. Measured omitted vs where=None: sum 10.0 -> 0.0, prod 24.0 -> 1.0, mean/std/var -> TypeError, max/min -> ValueError, any True -> False.  is the one that genuinely does not differ. WhereArg is now in the tree so that pass is three mechanical edits per site, and the new bead spells them out along with the two traps (do not touch the ufunc binding; assert  is UNCHANGED rather than raising).

title: [bug][fnp-ufunc] window kernels are 1-ULP off numpy and NOT symmetric - i-indexed formula instead of numpy's symmetric arange(1-M,M,2)
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-08 on worker vmi1227854 (numpy 2.4.3) while byte-comparing the
window functions for deadlock-audit-kwname-case-divergence-9w6uj. fnp's window
kernels are allclose to numpy but NOT bit-identical, and unlike numpy's they are
not exactly symmetric.

hanning(7): fnp[1] = 0x3fcffffffffffffe (0.24999999999999994)
            numpy[1] = 0x3fd0000000000002 (0.25000000000000006)
            fnp[1] != fnp[5] (0x...fe vs 0x...02) - numpy's are equal.
Same shape of divergence on hamming(7)/hamming(12), blackman(7)/blackman(12),
hanning(12). bartlett and kaiser matched byte-for-byte in that run at the sizes
probed; confirm rather than assume when fixing.

ROOT CAUSE is the evaluation form, not the maths. crates/fnp-ufunc/src/lib.rs:
  hamming  (22559): 0.54 - 0.46 * cos(2*PI*i/(M-1))
  hanning  (22594): 0.5  - 0.5  * cos(2*PI*i/(M-1))
  blackman (22625): same 2*PI*i/(M-1) shape
numpy evaluates over a SYMMETRIC index n = arange(1-M, M, 2) (so n = 2i-(M-1)):
  hamming  0.54 + 0.46*cos(pi*n/(M-1))
  hanning  0.5  + 0.5 *cos(pi*n/(M-1))
  blackman 0.42 + 0.5 *cos(pi*n/(M-1)) + 0.08*cos(2.0*pi*n/(M-1))
  bartlett where(n <= 0, 1 + n/(M-1), 1 - n/(M-1))
  kaiser   i0(beta*sqrt(1-((n-alpha)/alpha)**2.0))/i0(float(beta)),
           n = arange(0, M), alpha = (M-1)/2.0
Because cos is even and n comes in +/- pairs, numpy's window is symmetric by
construction. fnp's i-indexed form rounds the two halves differently, so it is
both off by an ULP and asymmetric - a real property loss for anyone who relies
on window symmetry (overlap-add / COLA reconstruction).

FIX: port numpy's exact expression, preserving its association order
(pi*n first, then / (M-1); 0.54 + 0.46*cos, not 0.54 - 0.46*cos), in the five
UFuncArray window constructors. The i-indexed loop is otherwise fine and the
parallel gate above HAMMING_PARALLEL_MIN can stay as is - the per-point formula
is what changes.

PROBE TO CLOSE: in crates/fnp-python/tests/conformance_window_funcs.rs, tighten
window_length_keyword_is_capital_m_like_numpy's fnp-vs-numpy comparison from
np.allclose back to result.tobytes() equality (the byte form is in that test's
git history at the commit that filed this bead), add an explicit
window == window[::-1] symmetry assertion, and run
cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_window_funcs green on a named worker
with its numpy version cited. Also re-run cargo test -p fnp-ufunc, whose inline
window tests may pin the current values.
close_reason:
FIXED in d8c8dd55.

hamming/hanning/blackman now evaluate numpy's expression over the symmetric index n = arange(1-M, M, 2) instead of the i-indexed form, including numpy's association order (pi*n first, THEN divided by M-1; blackman's second harmonic formed as a fresh cos(2.0*pi*n/(M-1)), not cos(2*x) of the first argument). Recipe validated byte-exact in Python against numpy at M = 2,3,4,5,7,8,12,17,33,64,101,255,1024 BEFORE any Rust was written - the bead's own comment records it.

SCOPE CORRECTED BY MEASUREMENT, not assumed: the bead said to change five kernels and to confirm bartlett/kaiser rather than assume. Measured, bartlett is ALREADY byte-identical and symmetric (its triangle is exact in f64 wherever (i-half)/half is), and kaiser already matched byte-for-byte including its own bessel_i0 against numpy's i0 across 4 betas x 13 sizes. Both were LEFT ALONE and bartlett now carries a comment saying why, so the next reader does not 'fix' it into the n-form for no reason. Three kernels changed, not five.

PROBE MET AS WRITTEN: conformance_window_funcs.rs's keyword test is tightened from atol=1e-15 back to raw tobytes() equality, gained the explicit window == window[::-1] symmetry assertion the bead asked for, and a wider sweep (12 sizes, kaiser across betas 0.0/2.5/8.6/14.0). cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_window_funcs = 14 passed / 0 failed on worker vmi1149989 with those assertions live. cargo test -p fnp-ufunc = 2264 passed / 0 failed, including window_and_special_functions_match_numpy_golden, whose stored goldens were symmetric all along while the implementation was not - the tolerance hid it.

ISA CHECK before landing a byte-strict assertion, per the standing rule that hz1/hz2 are the fleet's only avx512f hosts and numpy's SIMD transcendental kernels part from libm there: on hz2 (numpy 2.4.3) numpy's vectorized cos agrees with scalar libm cos on all four windows at all 13 sizes. So the byte comparison is safe on AVX-512, not merely on the AVX2 worker that happened to run it.

cargo clippy -p fnp-ufunc --lib -- -D warnings clean on hz2; cargo fmt --check clean.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
RECIPE VALIDATED before any Rust is written (python3, numpy 2.4.3, this box): the per-index SCALAR form

  value[i] = 0.5 + 0.5 * cos(pi * (1 - M + 2*i) / (M - 1))     # hanning

reproduces np.hanning byte-for-byte at M = 7, 12, 33, 101, and is exactly symmetric at every one. So the fix does NOT need numpy's vectorised arange - keeping fnp's existing per-index map and changing only the per-point expression is enough, which means the parallel gate and the rest of each constructor stay untouched. Note the association order that made it match: pi * n computed FIRST, then divided by (M-1), and the cosine term ADDED (0.5 + 0.5*cos), not subtracted.

title: perf(vander): one rayon task PER ROW - 256 tasks of 256 elements at the sweep's size, 32x finer than the measured wake-from-sleep floor
description:
MEASURED, TanBridge, thinkstation1, numpy 2.4.3 live, fnp .so sha256
4c9142598161b658d916685b307387ce4f83640988deaf9abdb2bf60ff51c522 (at 895fe045).

## THE CELL

`vander[f64@tiny]` is the last sweep cell above 150 us: 175363 ns delta, 1.86x (numpy 205038, fnp
380401). The `@tiny` suffix means the sweep feeds it a 256-element operand, because vander's output
is quadratic in its input - so the cell is a 256x256 output, 65536 elements.

**In a plain process fnp WINS this handily**, and the loss only appears at high thread counts:

```
  threads   N=64            N=256           N=1024
        1   0.19x           0.21x           0.22x
        8   0.18x           0.21x           0.06x
       64   0.18x           0.39x  <-       0.07x
  sweep (bench, 64 threads)  1.86x  <-
```

N=256 is the size that degrades with threads (0.21x -> 0.39x from 8 to 64), and it is exactly the
size the sweep measures.

## MECHANISM - SAME CLASS AS deadlock-audit-w9po3, DIFFERENT SHAPE

`try_zerocopy_f64_vander` parallelises as

    o.par_chunks_mut(cols).zip(data.par_iter()).for_each(|(row, &xv)| fill_row(xv, row));

**one task per ROW**, i.e. `rows` tasks regardless of the pool size. At N=256 that is 256 tasks of
256 elements each on a 64-thread pool. `deadlock-audit-w9po3` measured that a wake-from-sleep rayon
pool wants ~8192 elements per task for the transcendental family; 256 is 32x finer than that.

Note the difference from w9po3: there the task count was `num_threads` (too coarse a rule, too many
tasks at small n); here it is `rows` (independent of the pool entirely). Both produce far too many
tasks at the sizes that matter.

## WHY THE FLOOR CANNOT SIMPLY BE COPIED FROM w9po3

8192 elements/task was measured for a per-element cost of one libm call. vander's per-element cost
is one multiply and one store - far cheaper - so the same fixed overhead needs MORE elements to
amortise. The floor must be measured for this kernel, not inherited.

## THE FIX

Block whole rows per task so each task carries at least a measured floor of elements:

    let rows_per_task = FLOOR.div_ceil(cols.max(1)).max(1);
    o.par_chunks_mut(cols * rows_per_task)
        .zip(data.par_chunks(rows_per_task))
        .for_each(|(block, xs)| block.chunks_mut(cols).zip(xs).for_each(..));

`VANDER_PARALLEL_MIN = 1 << 16` (the serial/parallel gate) is a separate constant and is NOT the
defect here - at N=256 total is exactly 65536, so the cell sits right at the gate and does go
parallel.

## ACCEPTANCE

Same-session A/B of builds differing ONLY in the floor constant (the method that corrected my
invalid cross-session comparison in ca10e834), across thread counts AND sizes, plus a dual-null
contract at the DEFAULT thread count. Bit-exactness is not at risk - blocking changes which task
writes a row, not what is written, and each row's cumulative product is computed independently -
but the contract's `exact_bytes` covers it.
close_reason: SHIPPED abdf2d33, banked e4cdbf51. Blocked rows into 65536-element tasks (was one task PER ROW = 256 tasks of 256 elements at the sweep's size). Contract at DEFAULT threads, twice: DECIDABLE_WIN 4.605964 [4.594179,4.613354] and 4.648663 [4.643210,4.654736], numpy ~202000 / fnp 44279 and 43222, both nulls straddling, exact_bytes=passed checksum c64592cbd230eb91. Was 1.86x LOSS (fnp 380401) - an 8.8x improvement in fnp's own time. Floor MEASURED for this kernel not inherited: w9po3 needed 8192 for a libm call, this needs 65536 for multiply-and-store. Same-session A/B, interleaved: 64 threads N=256 goes 4.20x LOSS -> 0.21x WIN; neutral at 8 threads. A TIGHT LOOP reads the old code at 0.39x instead of 4.20x - third cell this session where that would have hidden the defect. Systematic 95-site vein filed separately.

title: [bug][fnp-python] main is RED: lib unit test ma_core_classes_constants_helpers_match_numpy_oracles fails at HEAD on three workers
description:
FOUND by CoralOak 2026-08-08 while running the correctness gate for deadlock-audit-ae85t. NOT one of the xdyx7 18 and not in any of its five clusters - a fresh red on main.

FAILING: tests::ma_core_classes_constants_helpers_match_numpy_oracles, a #[cfg(test)] unit test inside crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs (panic site moves with edits above it; it was lib.rs:108497 at commit 2ff37d87 and lib.rs:108633 with a later working tree).

PRE-EXISTING, VERIFIED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. It fails at COMMITTED HEAD 2ff37d87 with --base 2ff37d87 --clean-overlay --no-overlay, i.e. the committed tree with no working-tree changes at all, so it is not attributable to any in-flight work. Reproduced on THREE workers: ovh-a, vmi1152480 and vmi1149989. Filtered run at HEAD: 0 passed / 1 failed / 557 filtered out.

WHY IT WAS NOT SEEN EARLIER: it is a --lib unit test. The xdyx7 sweep and every shard run this session used --test <name> targets, which never build or run the lib test harness. 'cargo test -p fnp-python' does include --lib, but the two full-suite attempts this session both died at rch's SSH timeout partway through the integration shards. So this whole class has effectively been unexercised.

WHAT I DID NOT DO: read the assertion. I only established WHICH test fails and that it is not mine - my bead needed that distinction and nothing more. Start by running it with --nocapture to see the actual mismatch; the name says it compares numpy.ma core classes, constants and helpers against live numpy oracles, so the numpy-version split is the first thing to rule out (ovh-a and vmi1149989 have moved versions during this session, and vmi1152480 is 2.4.x).

PROBE TO CLOSE: 'cargo test -p fnp-python --lib --no-fail-fast' reports 0 failed, citing worker and numpy version. Run --lib explicitly: no --test target will ever exercise it.
close_reason:
FIXED in commit 17a86a50 - and it was MY regression, not pre-existing as this bead claimed.

CAUSE: 57ab8d1f (deadlock-audit-335rd) made every submodule bind a COPY of numpy's __all__ rather than numpy's own list. For fnp.ma the bind sat BEFORE a loop that still calls ma.add(...), and PyO3's add appends the added name to __all__, so fnp.ma.__all__ carried names numpy.ma does not export. The assertion had only ever passed because the two were the SAME object and it was comparing an object with itself - the third tautological comparison this __all__ work has un-masked.

FIX: bind after the last add, the same ordering already applied at the top level. ma was the only submodule affected; random, polynomial, linalg and fft have no add after their bind (checked, not assumed).

ATTRIBUTION CORRECTED BY BISECTION: the test PASSES at cb0f84c4 (before 57ab8d1f) and FAILS at 2ff37d87. My original diagnosis compared against committed HEAD, which already contained my own commit - so 'pre-existing' was measured against the wrong baseline. The lesson is one line: pre-existing means before MY COMMIT, not before my uncommitted working tree, and the check is a bisect against the commit that precedes my change.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fnp-python --lib --no-fail-fast 558 passed / 0 failed on ovh-a, up from 557 passed / 1 failed. clippy --all-targets --no-deps -D warnings exit 0 on hz1 with 'Checking fnp-python'; fmt --check exit 0.

STILL TRUE AND WORTH KEEPING from the original filing: --lib unit tests are effectively unexercised by this fleet's habits. Every shard run uses --test <name> targets, which never build the lib harness, and both full-suite attempts this session died at rch's SSH timeout partway through the integration shards. That is how a lib-only red survived. Run --lib explicitly.

title: [perf][fnp-python] isolate the delegating-path probe chain with an in-situ casting control
description:
TARGET: the ~5.6-5.8 us of pure overhead a DELEGATING fnp binary ufunc adds. At n=256 fnp.divide is 6.8x slower than numpy while delegating (deadlock-audit-qapyb), and add/subtract/multiply carry 6968-8375 ns of excess while sharing no kernel (deadlock-audit-cydda). Stages attributed so far total only ~1.4 us: numpy re-import 310, dtype guard 100, getattr ndarray 70, numpy.empty 220 (cydda) plus the default-kwargs dict 727 (s2fkk, shipped). Roughly 4-6 us is unattributed.

I have guessed twice and been wrong twice - the numpy.empty dtype string (~110 ns) and the delegation kwargs, which I refuted at 28 ns from a local timeit loop before a peer measured it properly at 727 ns on-worker. So this is an in-situ control, not another guess.

THE CONTROL, which already exists in the code: the entire probe chain in PyUFunc::__call__ sits behind a guard requiring out/where/dtype/signature to be None, casting == same_kind, order == K, and subok true. Passing any other casting value SKIPS EVERY PROBE and falls straight to the delegation tail.

  arm A: fnp.multiply(a, b)                    full probe chain, then delegate
  arm B: fnp.multiply(a, b, casting=unsafe)    no probes, delegate directly

Both enter through the same PyO3 __call__ with the same nine parameters and leave through the same delegation tail, so the difference is the probe chain and nothing else. The comparison is CONSERVATIVE: arm B additionally pays for a non-empty kwargs dict on the delegation, which a peer measured at 727 ns, so it is biased AGAINST finding probe cost.

Results are identical - casting only governs type coercion and both operands are already float64 - so the contract's cross-arm checksum assertion holds and a divergence would fail the measurement rather than win it.

Acceptance: both arms under the dual-null contract in ONE invocation, naming WORKER and HARNESS, replicated across two runs, worst bound quoted. If the probe chain is small, that is the result and the remaining microseconds are in PyO3 entry or the pyclass call machinery, which is worth knowing and narrows what is left. Bank it either way.
close_reason: MEASURED AND REPLICATED ON TWO WORKERS, banked in 3bc2077a. The declined probe chain is ~40% of a delegating binary-ufunc call. In-situ control using a guard already in the shipped code: the probe block sits behind casting == same_kind, so arm B (casting=unsafe) skips EVERY probe and delegates directly while entering the same PyO3 __call__ with the same nine parameters and leaving through the same delegation tail. harness=common::run_dual_null_median_ci_contract, n=256 f64, numpy 2.4.3, release profile, both A/A nulls on unity in both runs: worker=vmi1152480 elf 29c2d0402a7b3539 ratio 1.396597 ci95=[1.389674,1.400306] probed 6347 ns skipped 4569 ns chain 1778 ns DECIDABLE_WIN; worker=vmi1227854 elf 1c0707d511640b45 ratio 1.403108 ci95=[1.389629,1.414874] probed 3004 ns skipped 2128 ns chain 876 ns DECIDABLE_WIN. QUOTED AT THE WORST BOUND 1.389629x. The RATIO replicates with overlapping CIs across two workers - the cleanest replication in this ledger - while the ABSOLUTE cost does not (1778 vs 876 ns), so the fraction is durable and the nanoseconds are worker-scoped. The control is biased AGAINST its own conclusion: arm B additionally pays a non-empty kwargs dict on its delegation (727 ns measured elsewhere) and still comes out ~40% faster, so the true chain cost is LARGER than reported. What it leaves: skipping the probes still leaves 2128-4569 ns in a call that does nothing but hand two arrays to NumPy, so the delegating floor splits into a ~40% probe chain plus a larger remainder in PyO3 entry and the delegation tail. Retry predicate names the lever this enables: an early-out for ops with no possible native route at the operand dtype (f64 multiply is the clean case - Mul is absent from the f64 binop set and the complex probe requires kind=='c'), measured at 2^8-2^12 where the floor dominates.

title: [bug][test][fnp-python] remaining_top_level_attrs identity list still demands unpackbits be numpy's, but it is deliberately a native pyfunction
description:
Split out of deadlock-audit-xdyx7 / smr32, where it was flagged as 'MAY BE A SEPARATE CAUSE'. It is separate, and unlike the char/strings cluster it is VERSION-INDEPENDENT and fully diagnosed.

SYMPTOM. remaining_top_level_attrs_identity_equal_to_numpy fails with [('unpackbits', 'not-identity-equal')]. Reproduced at pristine HEAD b86ce6ef.

THE CONTRADICTION, both halves in the tree today:
  - crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs:106480 registers a NATIVE parallel unpackbits:
      m.add_function(wrap_pyfunction!(unpackbits, m)?)?;   (fn at :97014)
  - crates/fnp-python/src/lib.rs:107179 DELIBERATELY omits it from the verbatim
    re-export list, with the comment: '"unpackbits" is registered as a native
    parallel pyfunction (above) - must NOT be re-exported here or the numpy
    version would override it (m.add overwrites).'
  - but crates/fnp-python/tests/conformance_remaining_top_level_attrs.rs:78 still
    lists 'unpackbits' among names asserted 'getattr(fnp,n) is getattr(np,n)'.
So the test demands object identity with numpy for a name the implementation
deliberately owns. Someone landed the native perf lever and updated the
registration list but not the test's list. 'packbits' IS still a re-export and is
correctly identity-equal - only unpackbits diverges.

FIX SHAPE, and the distinction matters. Do NOT just delete the name from the list -
that is deleting coverage to get green. Identity is simply the WRONG contract for a
name we implement natively, so replace it with the assertion that is actually true
and actually protective: assert fnp.unpackbits is NOT numpy's AND that it still
matches numpy behaviourally. The behavioural half already exists and must keep
passing - packbits_unpackbits_round_trip_matches_numpy (same file, :128) and
unpackbits_large_contiguous_uint8_matches_numpy (lib.rs :129843).

NEGATIVE CASE REQUIRED: the new assertion must FAIL if someone re-adds unpackbits to
the verbatim re-export list (which would silently kill the native parallel path by
overwrite, exactly what the :107179 comment warns about). That is the regression this
bead exists to prevent; a test that only checks 'not identity' without checking the
native path still works would be tautological.

PROBE TO CLOSE: 'cargo test -p fnp-python --test conformance_remaining_top_level_attrs'
green, with the unpackbits round-trip test still passing in the same run.
close_reason:
FIXED in commit ff67019a. The test was stale, not the code.

DIAGNOSIS. lib.rs registers a NATIVE parallel unpackbits (wrap_pyfunction!, fn at :97014, registered :106480) and DELIBERATELY omits it from the verbatim re-export list at :107179, with a comment stating it must not be re-exported because m.add overwrites. The identity list in conformance_remaining_top_level_attrs.rs:78 still demanded getattr(fnp,'unpackbits') is getattr(np,'unpackbits'). A perf lever landed with the registration list updated and the test list not. packbits IS still a genuine re-export and remains in the identity list, which is why only unpackbits diverged.

FIX. Object identity is the wrong contract for a name we implement ourselves. I did NOT simply delete the name - that would be removing coverage to get green. It is replaced by unpackbits_is_native_not_a_numpy_reexport, which asserts fnp.unpackbits is NOT numpy's, and because 'not identity' would also be satisfied by the attribute being missing or broken, additionally requires presence, callability, agreement with numpy, and a round-trip in the same script. packbits is asserted IS-equal alongside as the contrast case, so the deliberate asymmetry is what gets pinned.

NEGATIVE CASE VERIFIED, as this bead required. I re-added 'unpackbits' to the re-export list and re-ran: unpackbits_is_native_not_a_numpy_reexport FAILED with exactly ['unpackbits is native, not numpy'] - only that check tripped. In the SAME run packbits_unpackbits_round_trip_matches_numpy still PASSED, which is the whole justification for the new test: the behavioural test cannot catch this regression because numpy's answer is what it compares against, so an m.add overwrite that silently kills the native parallel path is invisible to it. Reverted; lib.rs now differs only by two comment lines naming the guard test.

EVIDENCE on numpy-2.2.4 worker vmi1149989: remaining_top_level_attrs_identity_equal_to_numpy ok (was FAILED), unpackbits_is_native_not_a_numpy_reexport ok, packbits_unpackbits_round_trip_matches_numpy ok, 12 passed / 1 failed.

PROBE AMENDMENT, stated openly rather than quietly. This bead's written probe was 'the shard is green'. It is NOT: fnp_python_covers_full_numpy_all still fails on ['char'] when the run lands on a 2.2.4 worker. That is deadlock-audit-smr32, a different root cause in the same shard, which this change neither fixes nor worsens. I am closing on test-granularity evidence for the two tests this bead owns; the shard-green criterion transfers to smr32 and is already its probe.

title: [perf][fnp-linalg][no-gaps] mid-size cholesky (128<=n<896) runs trailing SYRK serially — panel=32 < parallel-GEMM gate
description:
np.linalg.cholesky is consistently SLOWER than numpy's dpotrf on SPD f64 (numpy NOT thrashing here, legit gap): cholesky 512 fnp 9.64ms vs numpy 3.14ms = 3.07x; cholesky 1024 fnp 26.45ms vs numpy 12.89ms = 2.05x (perf_linalg sweep 2026-06-14, box load ~6). cholesky_512 win would be larger relative gap than 1024.

ROOT (read of cholesky_blocked, fnp-linalg/src/lib.rs:1369): the size dispatch (cholesky_nxn:1531) uses CHOL_PANEL_NB=128 only for n>=CHOL_BLOCK_MIN=896; for CHOL_MID_MIN=128<=n<896 it uses CHOL_MID_PANEL=32. The trailing rank-bw SYRK update (step 3, the O(n^2*bw) BULK of cholesky flops) only takes the PARALLEL packed_gemm_sub_assign_strided path when 'bw >= MATMUL_PARALLEL_MIN_DIM(=128) && trail >= SYRK_COL_BLOCK(=256)' (line 1467). With mid-panel bw=32 < 128 that test is FALSE, so the dominant trailing update for ALL 128<=n<896 falls into the ELSE small-panel branch (line 1493): a single serial packed_gemm(&l21,&l21t,trail,bw,trail) + serial subtract. So mid-size cholesky does its bulk flops single-threaded => the 3x gap at n=512 (16 panels of 32, each with a serial 480x480-ish trailing GEMM). At n=1024 panel=128 hits the parallel SYRK => only 2.05x. The recent 'shrink mid cholesky panel' commit (1382622d) tuned diagonal/TRSM but left the mid-size trailing SYRK serial.

LEVER (no-ceiling, attack the bulk): make the mid-size trailing SYRK parallel. Options: (a) parallelize the else-branch small-panel SYRK over trailing output row-bands (rayon par_chunks_mut over work rows, each band subtracts its l21·l21t block — the lower-triangle-only tiling already in the bw>=128 path generalizes; just drop/lower the bw>=128 gate and instead gate on TOTAL trailing work trail*trail*bw), OR (b) raise CHOL_MID_PANEL so bw>=128 (but that enlarges the serial diagonal-block factor + may hurt the 128..256 range — measure). Prefer (a): gate the parallel SYRK on trail*trail*bw work, not on bw alone, so a thin (bw=32) but wide (trail~480) trailing update still parallelizes.

OBLIGATIONS: cholesky is allclose-contract in numpy but fnp likely has an EXACT-repr golden (check cholesky_matches_numpy_* + any golden sha256). Parallelizing the SYRK must keep each cell's subtraction order identical (each (i,j) cell still subtracts the same bw-term dot in the same order) => BIT-IDENTICAL, no parity relaxation (same discipline as the cov register-tile fallback on deadlock-audit-mtjkm). Prove with golden sha256 of L across SPD fixtures (incl n=129,255,512,895 to cover mid-range + boundaries) baseline-vs-new + the cholesky conformance tests. Clean rch criterion or pinned-thread A/B; target >=2x at n=512, no regression at n=1024/n<128/n>=896. NOTE perf_linalg also flagged eigvalsh 1024 4.2x and det512 2.95x as separate (numpy-thrash-confounded) candidates.

Found via cc perf_linalg sweep 2026-06-14 while deadlock-audit-mtjkm (cov) was peer-owned; cholesky is the cleanest uncontended consistent vs-numpy gap (2-3x both sizes, numpy not thrashing).
close_reason: Shipped ff302aa3: thin-panel cholesky trailing SYRK parallelized over the trailing-row dimension. BYTE-IDENTICAL (golden fbe05ee0 matches baseline across n=129..1024; all cholesky tests green; allclose vs numpy). Self-speedup n=895 2.3x, n=768 1.6-1.8x; n=512 flips from 3.07x-slower-than-numpy to 0.92x (beats numpy). No regression on n<416 / n>=896 (unchanged paths).

title: perf(reductions): nanmin/nanmax on BOOL is up to 388x slower - numpy short-circuits on the first False and fnp scans the whole array
description:
MEASURED, TanBridge, thinkstation1, numpy 2.4.3 live, build f10d576025f2.

  nanmin bool n=4096     fnp 0.018ms numpy 0.0058ms   3.10x
  nanmin bool n=65536    fnp 0.101ms numpy 0.0046ms  22.15x
  nanmin bool n=1048576  fnp 1.438ms numpy 0.0037ms 387.81x
  nanmax bool n=1048576  fnp 0.993ms numpy 0.0037ms 268.65x
  nansum bool n=1048576  fnp 3.035ms numpy 0.3156ms  9.62x
  nanmean bool n=1048576 fnp 3.152ms numpy 0.3557ms  8.86x
  nanmedian bool n=2^20  fnp 24.4ms  numpy 4.88ms     5.00x
All values EQUAL; this is pure perf.

DIAGNOSIS TO CONFIRM BEFORE CODING: numpy's time is FLAT IN N (5.8us, 4.6us, 3.7us as n goes 4096 -> 1048576), which is the signature of an EARLY EXIT, not of a faster loop. min() of a bool array can stop at the first False, and with random data that is immediate. fnp appears to scan the whole array.

So the honest comparison is adversarial on random data and the ratio would collapse on an ALL-TRUE array. VERIFY FIRST: time both on np.ones(n,bool) as well as random. If numpy is also O(n) there, the real defect is a constant factor, not the early exit, and the 388x headline is an artifact of the input.

If the early exit IS the mechanism, the fix is a short-circuiting bool min/max, and the win is real for the common case.

ACCEPTANCE: dual-null A/B on BOTH random and all-True bool inputs at 2^12/2^16/2^20, plus parity on empty/all-True/all-False/one-False.

title: [bug][fnp-ufunc] chebroots returned WRONG roots at degree >= 5 - hand-rolled companion matrix, not numpy's chebcompanion
close_reason:
FOUND AND FIXED in the same round (CreamGlen, 2026-08-09), by polynomial_fromroots_roots_randomised_differential_matches_numpy - the last untested corner of the polynomial family surface.

THE DEFECT WAS WRONG ANSWERS, not accuracy. Building a Chebyshev series from six known roots and asking chebroots to recover them:
  got   -2.0823697396464427
  want  -1.335143916125675   (an actual input root, which numpy recovers)
Our fromroots coefficients matched numpy to 2.75e-15 in the same case, so the series was right and the root-finder was wrong.

MECHANISM: chebroots hand-rolled a companion matrix - unscaled 0.5 sub/super-diagonals with the coefficients subtracted into the LAST ROW. numpy's chebcompanion is a SYMMETRISED matrix scaled by sqrt(1/2), with the coefficient term subtracted from the LAST COLUMN: top[0]=sqrt(.5), top[1:]=.5, bot=top, then mat[:, -1] -= (c[:-1]/c[-1])*(scl/scl[-1])*.5 where scl = [1, sqrt(.5), ...]. Those are different matrices and they do not share eigenvalues beyond low degree.

WHY IT SURVIVED: degrees up to four agree between the two constructions, and every existing chebroots test used a low degree - chebroots_constant, chebroots_linear, chebroots_quadratic and the fromroots round-trip goldens. The defect starts at five or six roots. A golden suite built from small hand-picked cases cannot find this; the randomised differential hit it on its first run at six roots.

FIXED by implementing numpy's chebcompanion. After: fromroots worst relative 2.75e-15, roots worst absolute 8.49e-13, across all five families and 2/3/4/6 roots.

SCOPE: only chebroots was wrong. legroots/hermroots/hermeroots/lagroots convert to the power basis and use the standard polynomial companion, which is valid; they passed the same differential unchanged.

VERIFIED: timeout cargo test -p fnp-ufunc --lib = 2285 passed / 0 failed; cargo test -p fnp-conformance --lib = 215 passed / 0 failed; cargo clippy -p fnp-ufunc --all-targets -- -D warnings = clean; cargo fmt --check exit 0 run UNPIPED.

title: [parity][fnp-ufunc] poly2X basis conversions are ~1e-13 accurate where numpy is ~1e-16 - the gap is ours, not conditioning
close_reason:
FIXED. poly2leg, poly2herm, poly2herme and poly2lag now use numpy's Horner-in-basis form - res = Xadd(Xmulx(res), pol[i]) - instead of building an n x n basis-conversion matrix and calling solve_linear_system. That was the whole mechanism: a dense solve carries its own conditioning, which is why we sat ~6.1e-13 from numpy at degree 15 while numpy's own conversion is within 4e-16 of a longdouble reference. It was also O(n^3) where the recurrence is O(n^2), and it reuses the *mulx primitives added for *mul under 50prg, so the fix was short.

MEASURED, by the differential that found this, printing its worst observed deviation each run:
  before                          6.077e-13  (poly2lag, degree 15)
  after poly2lag alone            5.160e-14  (poly2herm, degree 15)
  after leg/herm/herme/lag        4.674e-15  (lag2poly, degree 15)
about 130x, and the worst is now the OTHER direction (X2poly) sitting near machine precision rather than any poly2X.

ACCEPTANCE TEST MET: the differential's bound is tightened from 1e-11 to 1e-13, keeping ~20x headroom over the new worst rather than sitting just above the data.

NET -43 LINES: four matrix builders and their solve calls are gone, replaced by three-line recurrences.

REMAINING, deliberately not done and NOT an accuracy problem: poly2cheb still builds a conversion matrix. It is no longer the worst offender - it sits below the 4.67e-15 lag2poly figure - so converting it is simplicity and O(n^2)-vs-O(n^3), not parity. It would need a chebmulx helper, which does not exist yet (numpy's: prd[0]=c[0]*0, prd[1]=c[0], then prd[2:] = c[1:]/2 and prd[0:-2] += c[1:]/2).

VERIFIED: timeout cargo test -p fnp-ufunc --lib = 2284 passed / 0 failed; cargo test -p fnp-conformance --lib = 215 passed / 0 failed (these conversions are reached through the differential dispatch and by *div internally, so the cross-crate run matters here); cargo clippy -p fnp-ufunc --all-targets -- -D warnings = clean; cargo fmt --check exit 0 run UNPIPED.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FOUND by polynomial_basis_conversion_randomised_differential_matches_numpy (CreamGlen, 2026-08-09), added while pinning the conversions that 50prg implicated.

OBSERVATION: worst deviation from numpy across cheb/leg/herm/herme/lag, both directions, degrees 2..15, is 6.077e-13 - at poly2lag, degree 15. Everything else sits far below it.

WHY THAT IS OURS RATHER THAN THE PROBLEM'S: my first reading was that poly2X is simply ill-conditioned at high degree, which is exactly what 50prg established for *mul's round trip. That reading is WRONG for the conversion itself. Checking numpy's own float64 poly2lag against a numpy longdouble reference:
    n=10  rel err 2.17e-16
    n=13  rel err 9.43e-17
    n=16  rel err 3.87e-16
numpy's conversion is stable to machine precision at these degrees. Since numpy is ~2e-16 from truth and we are ~6e-13 from numpy, we are ~6e-13 from truth - roughly three thousand times less accurate than numpy at degree 15, and the gap is in our algorithm, not in the conditioning of the task.

SEVERITY: low, hence P3. Nothing user-facing routes through it today - fnp-python delegates the polynomial surface to numpy - and 6e-13 relative is far below any tolerance in the suite. It matters for two reasons: *div still uses these conversions internally (X2poly -> poly_div -> poly2X), so their accuracy is div's accuracy floor; and if the polynomial surface is ever wired natively the way hermeder/hermeint were under mlz0s, this becomes the user-visible number.

NEXT STEP for whoever takes it: compare our poly2X against numpy's algorithm directly - numpy builds the result with a Horner-style in-basis accumulation (repeated Xmulx/Xadd), and we may be doing something more direct that accumulates error. The *mulx helpers landed under 50prg are exactly the primitive numpy's conversion uses, so the fix may now be a short one.

The differential prints its worst observed deviation under --nocapture and is bounded at 1e-11, chosen for headroom over the observed 6.08e-13 rather than sitting 1.6x above it where an unlucky draw would flake. Tightening that bound toward 1e-15 is this bead's acceptance test.

title: perf(take): a SCALAR index makes fnp.take copy the WHOLE source - O(n) to read one element, 191.87x slower than numpy at n=2^20
description:
MEASURED, TanBridge, thinkstation1, numpy 2.4.3 live, pinned `taskset -c 40`, fnp .so sha256
3e2d03f8b7bc3e025e76c8d71124a005633f3a048c5eec525eb1e679963a7c95 (at 2838f77e/f70ed871).

## THE CELL

`bench_vs_numpy_loss_sweep` ranked `take[f64_scalar]` WORST at 21.1050x (numpy 1372 ns, fnp
28956 ns) after the as*array ship. The sweep uses n=2^16 only. The real cell is far worse: the
cost is LINEAR IN THE SOURCE LENGTH while numpy's is flat.

```
      N   numpy_ns      fnp_ns    slower
     64      972.1      8039.7     8.27x
    256      966.1      8117.6     8.40x
   1024      962.7      8301.1     8.62x
   4096      971.5      8876.4     9.14x
  16384      957.6     11363.2    11.87x
  65536      949.9     20662.1    21.75x
 262144      955.6     50888.2    53.25x
1048576      939.3    180230.3   191.87x     <- WORST CELL
```

Not a corner of the float-scalar oddity the ladder happened to pick. Pinned dual-null survey at
n=2^16, all nulls PASS:

```
  scalar_float  take(a,2.0)          23.609x
  scalar_int    take(a,2)            23.496x   <- the ordinary call
  scalar_np_int take(a,np.int64(2))  23.222x
  list10        take(a,[0..9])       19.079x
  idx1k         take(a,i64[1024])     2.060x
  idx64k        take(a,i64[65536])    2.370x
  2d_flat       take(m2,i64[1024])    2.021x
```

## MECHANISM

`try_zerocopy_f64_take` / `try_zerocopy_int_take` gate on the INDEX operand:

    if !a.is_exact_instance(&ndarray_type) || !indices.is_exact_instance(&ndarray_type) {
        return Ok(None);
    }
    // ... and then indices dtype must be kind 'i' with itemsize 8

A Python `int`, a `float`, a numpy scalar, or a list is not an exact int64 ndarray, so every fast
path declines. Control then reaches the residual, which calls
`extract_numeric_array(py, a, "take(a)")` - a FULL COPY OF THE SOURCE ARRAY - to gather one
element. 8 MB materialised to read 8 bytes.

The fast paths decline on the TINY operand and the fallback then copies the HUGE one. That is the
whole bug.

## THE LEVER

O(1) scalar path. `np.take(x, i)` with `axis=None` is by definition a gather from the C-order
flattening, so for an integer scalar index it IS `x[i]` (1-D) or `x.reshape(-1)[i]` (C-contiguous
n-D). Priced against the installed interpreter at N=2^20:

```
  np.take(a,2)      937.0 ns   <- incumbent
  a[2]               56.9 ns   <- 16.5x FASTER than numpy's own take
  a.reshape(-1)[2]  185.8 ns
```

Verified equivalent: `np.take(a,5) == a[5]`, `np.take(a,-3) == a[-3]`,
`np.take(m,5) == m.reshape(-1)[5]`, and both return a numpy SCALAR (`float64`), not a 0-d array.

## TRAPS THE GATE MUST HANDLE (all verified against numpy 2.4.3)

1. `np.take(a, True)` -> a float64 scalar (bool indexes as 1). `a[True]` -> an ARRAY (adds an
   axis). Python `bool` subclasses `int`, so the gate MUST use an exact-int test, not `is_instance`.
2. `np.take(a, 2.0)` and `np.take(a, 2.7)` both succeed (truncating). `a[2.0]` raises IndexError.
   So FLOAT scalars must NOT route to `__getitem__`.
3. Out-of-range must fall through to numpy: `take` says "index 5 is out of bounds for size 4",
   `a[5]` says "...for axis 0 with size 4". Different message; this repo pins exception text.
4. `mode='clip'/'wrap'` are not `__getitem__` semantics -> gate to `mode="raise"`.
5. n-D `reshape(-1)` is a free view only when C-contiguous; on a transposed source it COPIES,
   which would reintroduce the very O(n) this bead removes.
6. `a.item(i)` is cheaper (48.2 ns) but returns a PYTHON float, not `np.float64`. Not equivalent.

## SECOND, SMALLER LEVER (separate, do not bundle without its own parity argument)

`list10` at 19.079x and any non-int64 index ARRAY have the same shape of defect. Fix by
normalising the INDICES to int64 (O(len(indices))) and re-entering the existing zero-copy gather,
rather than falling to the residual that copies the source. Shape contract differs from the scalar
case: an ndim>=1 index returns an ARRAY, so it can reuse the helpers directly.

## ACCEPTANCE

Dual-null median-CI contract vs numpy live in the same invocation, plus a dtype/edge parity probe
covering at minimum: bool index, float index, negative index, out-of-range both signs, 0-d index
array, numpy integer scalars of every width, n-D C-contiguous and transposed sources, mode=
clip/wrap, and non-numeric dtypes (str/datetime/object/void/complex128). Quote the lever at its
WORST cell (n=2^20), not at the sweep's n=2^16.
close_reason: SHIPPED a8585812 + 9acbe632, banked 1660c2c2. Scalar take at n=2^20: 191.87x slower becomes 7.2x FASTER (931.5 ns numpy vs 125.1 ns fnp, ratio 0.140x, 12/12 A/A nulls PASS). Flat in n now (128.7 ns at 2^6, 125.1 at 2^20) where it was 8040 to 180230. Parity 2300 cases: 18 fixed (every bool spelling), 0 introduced. Container-index half split out to deadlock-audit-g0dfm with the normalise-and-retry design already priced and rejected.
